=== PDF page 13 / printed label xiii ===
[p0013-l0001] [30.0pt] foreword
[p0013-l0002] [10.0pt] It is truly an honor to receive a request to write a foreword for a book like this, in
[p0013-l0003] [10.0pt] this particular space, at this specific time in history, and by an author who I believe
[p0013-l0004] [10.0pt] will make significant contributions to this industry during his tenure. That book is
[p0013-l0005] [10.0pt] Domain-Specific Small Language Models, the space is generative AI, the time in history is
[p0013-l0006] [10.0pt] the tremendous evolutionary acceleration of AI, and the author is Guglielmo Iozzia.
[p0013-l0007] [10.0pt] In an era when AI discourse is dominated by ever-larger frontier models and
[p0013-l0008] [10.0pt] eye‑catching demos, this book takes a refreshingly pragmatic stance: it is about making
[p0013-l0009] [10.0pt] language models actually work for your domain, your data, and your hardware con­
[p0013-l0010] [10.0pt] straints. It is written with the practitioner’s learning curve squarely in mind, moving
[p0013-l0011] [10.0pt] from foundational concepts to hands‑on experience so that by the time you turn the
[p0013-l0012] [10.0pt] last page, you will not only understand why small, domain‑specific language models
[p0013-l0013] [10.0pt] matter, you will have run them, tuned them, optimized them, and deployed them on
[p0013-l0014] [10.0pt] real‑world infrastructure.
[p0013-l0015] [10.0pt] What distinguishes this work is its relentless focus on the realities of distributed and
[p0013-l0016] [10.0pt] edge AI. Rather than treating GPUs in the cloud as an infinite resource, the author
[p0013-l0017] [10.0pt] leans into the constraints most organizations actually face: tight budgets, on-prem clus­
[p0013-l0018] [10.0pt] ters, laptops, and even mobile or embedded devices. From the opening chapters on
[p0013-l0019] [10.0pt] the definition and role of small language models (SLMs), it becomes clear that the
[p0013-l0020] [10.0pt] goal is not to worship scale, but to show how carefully chosen, well‑tuned models in the
[p0013-l0021] [10.0pt] 100M to 10B parameter range can deliver outsized business value when pushed as close
[p0013-l0022] [10.0pt] as possible to where data is generated and decisions are made. The walkthroughs of
[p0013-l0023] [10.0pt] ONNX, quantization techniques, and hardware‑aware optimizations anchor the discus­
[p0013-l0024] [10.0pt] sion in concrete practices that materially reduce latency and cost at the edge while pre­
[p0013-l0025] [10.0pt] serving useful accuracy.
[p0013-l0026] [9.0pt] xii

=== PDF page 14 / printed label xiv ===
[p0014-l0001] [9.0pt] xiii
[p0014-l0002] [7.2pt] foreword
[p0014-l0003] [9.0pt] xiii
[p0014-l0004] [10.0pt] This is also an excellent grounding text for anyone trying to navigate the LLM-­
[p0014-l0005] [10.0pt] versus-SLM decision space with intellectual honesty. The early chapters provide a clear,
[p0014-l0006] [10.0pt] hype‑free tour of the Transformer architecture, training paradigms, open source eco­
[p0014-l0007] [10.0pt] systems, and the tradeoffs between generalist closed LLMs and domain‑specific models.
[p0014-l0008] [10.0pt] From there, the book steadily builds into a toolkit: data preparation, classic fine‑tuning,
[p0014-l0009] [10.0pt] PEFT methods such as LoRA, and retrieval‑augmented generation are all presented
[p0014-l0010] [10.0pt] with enough depth and runnable code that you can reproduce, adapt, and extend the
[p0014-l0011] [10.0pt] examples for your own environment. The result is a rare combination of conceptual
[p0014-l0012] [10.0pt] clarity and practical guidance that serves both as an introduction for those new to the
[p0014-l0013] [10.0pt] field and as a structured reference for experienced practitioners formalizing their
[p0014-l0014] [10.0pt] approach.
[p0014-l0015] [10.0pt] Perhaps most compelling is the way the book repeatedly returns to domain reality.
[p0014-l0016] [10.0pt] Coding assistants are explored not as abstractions but via end‑to‑end fine‑tuning of
[p0014-l0017] [10.0pt] GPT‑2 on Manim code, complete with hyperparameter search and evaluation workflows
[p0014-l0018] [10.0pt] that mirror production‑grade ML engineering. Chemistry and life sciences are treated
[p0014-l0019] [10.0pt] with equal seriousness, from protein and antibody sequence generation to discussion of
[p0014-l0020] [10.0pt] validation workflows and specialized tooling, illustrating how SLMs unlock high‑value
[p0014-l0021] [10.0pt] use cases in regulated, data‑sensitive industries. Later chapters connect these capabili­
[p0014-l0022] [10.0pt] ties to modern application patterns—RAG pipelines, agentic systems, deployment and
[p0014-l0023] [10.0pt] serving patterns, and running on commodity hardware—so that readers finish with a
[p0014-l0024] [10.0pt] mental model that spans from theory to architecture to code.
[p0014-l0025] [10.0pt] If you are serious about applying generative AI beyond glossy prototypes—especially
[p0014-l0026] [10.0pt] in domains where data is sensitive, regulation is strict, or infrastructure is constrained—
[p0014-l0027] [10.0pt] this book is worthy of your time. It will not just tell you that small language models are
[p0014-l0028] [10.0pt] important; it will show you, step by step, how to build, adapt, and ship them responsibly
[p0014-l0029] [10.0pt] in the environments where they matter most.
[p0014-l0030] [10.0pt] —Matthew R. Versaggi,
[p0014-l0031] [10.0pt] White House Presidential Innovation Fellow in AI, Special cohort of ’24,
[p0014-l0032] [10.0pt] former senior director of artificial intelligence and
[p0014-l0033] [10.0pt] cognitive technology at Optum Technology/United Healthcare

[p0015-l0001] [30.0pt] preface
[p0015-l0002] [10.0pt] In early 2022, after finally having the time to complete reading the “Attention is all
[p0015-l0003] [10.0pt] you need” paper, I started getting curious about the Transformer architecture and the
[p0015-l0004] [10.0pt] potential great use cases in diverse industries (and in life sciences in particular, because
[p0015-l0005] [10.0pt] that is the field where I work) for this new kind of neural network. One concern I had
[p0015-l0006] [10.0pt] at that time was the concrete risk that such technology could quickly become a prerog­
[p0015-l0007] [10.0pt] ative of the large tech organizations that could afford the vast computational resources
[p0015-l0008] [10.0pt] necessary to train and execute these models.
[p0015-l0009] [10.0pt] Then, inspired by the “run Doom on anything” challenge (a popular trend for soft­
[p0015-l0010] [10.0pt] ware engineers to find ways to optimize the source code of that 1993 videogame to run
[p0015-l0011] [10.0pt] on any sort of device), I started thinking about ways to optimize small Transformer mod­
[p0015-l0012] [10.0pt] els, trained on domain-specific tasks and data, so they could be deployed and executed
[p0015-l0013] [10.0pt] in hardware-constrained environments. In June of the same year, I did an ­in-person
[p0015-l0014] [10.0pt] ­hands-on workshop on this subject at the ODSC Europe conference in London, which
[p0015-l0015] [10.0pt] got a lot of interest from ML engineers at the event.
[p0015-l0016] [10.0pt] When Manning Publications contacted me a few months later, asking me to write a
[p0015-l0017] [10.0pt] book on this topic, I didn’t think twice about accepting. A few weeks after I started writ­
[p0015-l0018] [10.0pt] ing the book, OpenAI released the ChatGPT service to the public, powered at that time
[p0015-l0019] [10.0pt] by their GPT-3.5 model, and other large tech organizations, such as Google, Anthropic,
[p0015-l0020] [10.0pt] and X.AI, soon joined the race to build larger, closed source generalist models to try to
[p0015-l0021] [10.0pt] win the consumer market for generative AI.
[p0015-l0022] [10.0pt] But the open source community didn’t just watch this happen: lots of initiatives
[p0015-l0023] [10.0pt] involving open architectures and weights, and techniques for optimize the training and
[p0015-l0024] [10.0pt] execution of language models, started being proposed. It was the right time to write a
[p0015-l0025] [10.0pt] book on this topic and provide ML practitioners with a centralized source of informa­
[p0015-l0026] [10.0pt] tion about what capabilities are available beyond the commercial offerings, for specific
[p0015-l0027] [10.0pt] tasks, and in heavily regulated industries.

[p0017-l0001] [30.0pt] about this book
[p0017-l0002] [10.0pt] The focus of this book is on understanding techniques for improving inference per­
[p0017-l0003] [10.0pt] formance and costs on pretrained and customized small language models (SLMs)
[p0017-l0004] [10.0pt] through optimization and quantization, serving them through diverse API ecosys­
[p0017-l0005] [10.0pt] tems, deploying them on diverse hardware (including your own laptop), and integrat­
[p0017-l0006] [10.0pt] ing them with other paradigms such as RAG and Agentic AI. All these concepts are
[p0017-l0007] [10.0pt] explained in depth and come with complete source code examples. You’ll learn to
[p0017-l0008] [10.0pt] minimize the computational horsepower their models require while retaining high–
[p0017-l0009] [10.0pt] quality performance times and output.
[p0017-l0010] [10.0pt] While a few examples presented in this book describe how to preprocess the data
[p0017-l0011] [10.0pt] for training/test, and PEFT (parameter-efficient fine tuning) techniques are also intro­
[p0017-l0012] [10.0pt] duced, this book doesn’t focus on training and data-preparation techniques.
[p0017-l0013] [12.5pt] Who should read this book
[p0017-l0014] [10.0pt] This book is first for ML engineers and data scientists interested in learning how to
[p0017-l0015] [10.0pt] manage LLMs in the typical hardware-constrained environment that their company
[p0017-l0016] [10.0pt] budget allows for. But it is also for tech leaders motivated to understand how applying
[p0017-l0017] [10.0pt] custom language models on corporate data could generate extra business value.
[p0017-l0018] [10.0pt] The minimally qualified reader should have the following skills and knowledge:
[p0017-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ General understanding of deep learning concepts
[p0017-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Knowledge of the Transformer model’s architecture and internals and the basics
[p0017-l0021] [10.0pt] of their training process
[p0017-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Intermediate Python language skills
[p0017-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Hands-on experience with a deep learning framework (PyTorch preferable)

[p0018-l0027] [10.0pt] Part 3 focuses on real-world examples of the concepts introduced in parts 1 and 2:

[p0024-l0001] [30.0pt] Small language models
[p0024-l0002] [225.0pt] 1
[p0024-l0003] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0024-l0004] [9.8pt] ¡ Defining small language models
[p0024-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ Limits and risks of using closed source general­
[p0024-l0006] [9.8pt] ist LLMs
[p0024-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Open source alternatives to closed source LLMs
[p0024-l0008] [9.8pt] ¡ Comparing LLMs and domain-specific language
[p0024-l0009] [9.8pt] models
[p0024-l0010] [10.0pt] Whenever a new, potentially disruptive technology emerges, or an existing one
[p0024-l0011] [10.0pt] undergoes a radical change, there’s inevitable hype about it. If expectations aren’t
[p0024-l0012] [10.0pt] met, interest can drop quickly; if they are, investments and projects can surge before
[p0024-l0013] [10.0pt] the real business potential and risks are understood. Either way, the “next big thing”
[p0024-l0014] [10.0pt] rarely ends well. You can see the same thing happening today with large language
[p0024-l0015] [10.0pt] models (LLMs): there’s so much hype that it’s difficult to understand what they
[p0024-l0016] [10.0pt] really can (and can’t) do and whether they would be a good fit for your own busi­
[p0024-l0017] [10.0pt] ness needs. This chapter aims to clarify the LLM world by highlighting the pros,
[p0024-l0018] [10.0pt] risks, and challenges of both generalist and domain-specific models. Hype is the
[p0024-l0019] [10.0pt] one thing you won’t find in this book.
[p0024-l0020] [9.0pt] 3

=== PDF page 25 / printed label 4 ===
[p0025-l0001] [9.0pt] 4
[p0025-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 1  Small language models
[p0025-l0003] [12.5pt] 1.1
[p0025-l0004] [12.5pt] What are small language models?
[p0025-l0005] [10.0pt] Today, regardless of their technical background, most people are familiar with popular
[p0025-l0006] [10.0pt] commercial LLMs such as GPT, Claude, and Gemini, which power chatbots and ser­
[p0025-l0007] [10.0pt] vices from providers such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and Microsoft. But there’s
[p0025-l0008] [10.0pt] still limited awareness of a related category: small language models (SLMs). Like
[p0025-l0009] [10.0pt] LLMs, SLMs are designed for natural language processing tasks, but they use fewer
[p0025-l0010] [10.0pt] parameters, have a smaller memory footprint, and require less computational power.
[p0025-l0011] [10.0pt] That makes them suitable for applications that run on mobile or edge devices or on-­
[p0025-l0012] [10.0pt] premises servers or small clusters. SLMs typically range from a few hundred million
[p0025-l0013] [10.0pt] to a few billion parameters; there’s no official cutoff, but most stay under 10 billion
[p0025-l0014] [10.0pt] parameters. That’s much smaller than LLMs, which often have hundreds of billions of
[p0025-l0015] [10.0pt] parameters or more. Because of their small size, SLMs can be optimized for speed and
[p0025-l0016] [10.0pt] energy efficiency, which are especially important for on-device or commodity hard­
[p0025-l0017] [10.0pt] ware deployments. They can run well on CPUs (when no GPU is available) or on con­
[p0025-l0018] [10.0pt] sumer GPUs. Since they run locally, the data can stay local, which is important for tasks
[p0025-l0019] [10.0pt] involving sensitive or personal information. Their deployment flexibility also expands
[p0025-l0020] [10.0pt] the range of use cases, making them ideal for offline, embedded, and near–real time
[p0025-l0021] [10.0pt] applications in areas such as robotics and smart devices (such as mobile phones, lab
[p0025-l0022] [10.0pt] equipment, appliances, and manufacturing machinery).
[p0025-l0023] [10.0pt] Although SLMs are smaller than LLMs, they aren’t a new type of model. Both are
[p0025-l0024] [10.0pt] built on the same core technology—the Transformer architecture and later improve­
[p0025-l0025] [10.0pt] ments. The difference is mostly in scale, not the underlying mathematical and architec­
[p0025-l0026] [10.0pt] tural principles. As a result, they can address the same kinds of tasks, with SLMs being
[p0025-l0027] [10.0pt] optimized more for efficiency than raw power.
[p0025-l0028] [10.0pt] NOTE  The Transformer architecture was introduced in the “Attention
[p0025-l0029] [10.0pt] is All You Need” paper by Ashish Vaswani and others (https://arxiv.org/
[p0025-l0030] [10.0pt] abs/1706.03762).
[p0025-l0031] [10.0pt] An important benefit of SLMs is that you can specialize them for specific domains and
[p0025-l0032] [10.0pt] tasks at relatively low cost, using domain-specific and private data plus domain knowl­
[p0025-l0033] [10.0pt] edge, and apply techniques that don’t require full fine-tuning. Domain-specific tasks
[p0025-l0034] [10.0pt] for language models are common in heavily regulated industries where privacy isn’t
[p0025-l0035] [10.0pt] optional—healthcare, pharma/biotech, manufacturing, chemistry, finance, and oth­
[p0025-l0036] [10.0pt] ers. You’ll see real-world examples in later chapters.
[p0025-l0037] [10.0pt] Beyond the well-understood reasons to choose SLMs over LLMs in specific use cases,
[p0025-l0038] [10.0pt] another emerged with the rise of agentic AI and was highlighted in a mid-2025 NVIDIA
[p0025-l0039] [10.0pt] research paper: “Small Language Models are the Future of Agentic AI” (https://arxiv
[p0025-l0040] [10.0pt] .org/abs/2506.02153). The authors argue that SLMs are powerful enough, better
[p0025-l0041] [10.0pt] suited, and more economical for many uses in agentic systems, making them central to
[p0025-l0042] [10.0pt] the future of agentic AI. They also suggest that, even when general-purpose conversa­
[p0025-l0043] [10.0pt] tion is required, heterogeneous agentic systems—agents that invoke multiple models,

=== PDF page 26 / printed label 5 ===
[p0026-l0001] [9.0pt] 5
[p0026-l0002] [9.0pt] The Transformer architecture
[p0026-l0003] [10.0pt] LLMs and SLMs—are the natural choice. The final chapters of this book explore the
[p0026-l0004] [10.0pt] relationship between SLMs and agentic AI.
[p0026-l0005] [12.5pt] 1.2
[p0026-l0006] [12.5pt] The Transformer architecture
[p0026-l0007] [10.0pt] Before transformers, most tasks on unstructured text were performed using recurrent
[p0026-l0008] [10.0pt] neural network (RNN) models. Trained on labeled data, these architectures use their
[p0026-l0009] [10.0pt] internal state to process variable-length sequences of text. Later evolutions, such as
[p0026-l0010] [10.0pt] LSTM (long short-term memory) or GRU (gated recurrent unit) architectures, intro­
[p0026-l0011] [10.0pt] duced the capability to remember and forget important information, but they didn’t
[p0026-l0012] [10.0pt] solve one of the major challenges of RNNs: slow training. The data must be processed
[p0026-l0013] [10.0pt] sequentially, which limits parallelism across processor cores. The attention mechanism
[p0026-l0014] [10.0pt] addressed some RNN limitations by emphasizing relevant parts of the input and down­
[p0026-l0015] [10.0pt] playing others, effectively expanding the amount of information the model could
[p0026-l0016] [10.0pt] carry forward. Still, it didn’t solve the scalability issues. That required the Transformer
[p0026-l0017] [10.0pt] model, which introduced two major changes compared to RNNs:
[p0026-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ It uses the self-attention mechanism (a specialization of the attention mechanism
[p0026-l0019] [10.0pt] that relates different positions in a sequence to compute a representation of the
[p0026-l0020] [10.0pt] sequence itself) so that it can process the entire input all at once.
[p0026-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ It has no recurrent structure, so a transformer allows more parallelism than an
[p0026-l0022] [10.0pt] RNN, significantly reducing training time.
[p0026-l0023] [10.0pt] Transformers didn’t only succeed because of their architecture. Another key com­
[p0026-l0024] [10.0pt] ponent is word embeddings—high-dimensional vector representations of words that
[p0026-l0025] [10.0pt] capture their semantic and syntactic properties. Embeddings let a Transformer model
[p0026-l0026] [10.0pt] manipulate words in a numerical space, where related words end up near one another.
[p0026-l0027] [10.0pt] This helps the model treat words as connected, not isolated, entities and understand
[p0026-l0028] [10.0pt] how they interact in context.
[p0026-l0029] [10.0pt] Transformer architectures have also been proposed for tasks involving other data
[p0026-l0030] [10.0pt] types, but multimodal use cases are out of scope for this book, which focuses on genera­
[p0026-l0031] [10.0pt] tive models for unstructured text.
[p0026-l0032] [10.0pt] The Transformer architecture initially proposed by Google Brain was just the start. As
[p0026-l0033] [10.0pt] soon as researchers and professionals started to use it, they quickly found ways to improve
[p0026-l0034] [10.0pt] and tailor it for text tasks. The original architecture was encoder–decoder based: the
[p0026-l0035] [10.0pt] encoder part converts the input text into a numerical representation, while the decoder
[p0026-l0036] [10.0pt] part takes that representation and converts it back to text. Both use an attention mecha­
[p0026-l0037] [10.0pt] nism. Over time, it has become clear that some tasks need only the encoder, while others
[p0026-l0038] [10.0pt] can rely only on the decoder. This led to two different families of transformers:
[p0026-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ BERT (bidirectional encoder representation from transformers) uses only the
[p0026-l0040] [10.0pt] encoder part. This kind of architecture performs better on text classification or
[p0026-l0041] [10.0pt] prediction tasks.
[p0026-l0042] [10.0pt] ¡ GPT (generative pretrained transformer) uses only the decoder and generally
[p0026-l0043] [10.0pt] performs better on text generation tasks.

=== PDF page 27 / printed label 6 ===
[p0027-l0001] [9.0pt] 6
[p0027-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 1  Small language models
[p0027-l0003] [10.0pt] Ultimately, your architecture choice will depend on the tasks you want to accomplish.
[p0027-l0004] [10.0pt] The examples in this book cover both families.
[p0027-l0005] [10.0pt] Another important concept in the Transformer model’s evolution is reinforcement
[p0027-l0006] [10.0pt] learning from human feedback (RLHF), a technique used behind the scenes for
[p0027-l0007] [10.0pt] OpenAI’s LLMs. As the name suggests, it applies reinforcement learning so an LLM can
[p0027-l0008] [10.0pt] learn a policy that maximizes a reward. The models behind ChatGPT are an evolution
[p0027-l0009] [10.0pt] of the GPT architecture (the first two versions were open source; later versions moved
[p0027-l0010] [10.0pt] to closed source), with RLHF applied for fine-tuning and improved performance.
[p0027-l0011] [12.5pt] 1.3
[p0027-l0012] [12.5pt] Areas of application
[p0027-l0013] [10.0pt] The term “LLM” can be misleading. “Large” is clear enough: models range from a few
[p0027-l0014] [10.0pt] billion to more than 100 billion parameters, or from tens to hundreds of gigabytes. But
[p0027-l0015] [10.0pt] “language” can make people think that these models generate only natural-language
[p0027-l0016] [10.0pt] text. Early natural-language processing (NLP) applications did focus on translation
[p0027-l0017] [10.0pt] tasks, but newer architectures and capabilities let LLMs handle many tasks beyond
[p0027-l0018] [10.0pt] translation:
[p0027-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ Language understanding
[p0027-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Text classification
[p0027-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Test generation
[p0027-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Question answering
[p0027-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Document summarization
[p0027-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Semantic parsing
[p0027-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Pattern recognition
[p0027-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ Basic math solving
[p0027-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Code generation
[p0027-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Dialogue
[p0027-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ General knowledge
[p0027-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Logical inference chains
[p0027-l0031] [10.0pt] This makes it possible for an LLM to handle text beyond natural language—anything
[p0027-l0032] [10.0pt] that symbolically represents something—as shown in figure 1.1.
[p0027-l0033] [10.0pt] LLMs will unlock many real-world use cases across industries.
[p0027-l0034] [12.5pt] 1.4
[p0027-l0035] [12.5pt] The open source revolution
[p0027-l0036] [10.0pt] The Transformer architecture didn’t only ignite interest among companies such
[p0027-l0037] [10.0pt] as OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google; the open source community also began releas­
[p0027-l0038] [10.0pt] ing LLMs under varying licenses for models, code, and training data. Figure 1.2,
[p0027-l0039] [10.0pt] taken from a paper titled “A Survey of Large Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/
[p0027-l0040] [10.0pt] abs/2303.18223), shows a timeline of the major commercial and open source LLMs
[p0027-l0041] [10.0pt] from 2019 to mid-2023 (the paper’s latest update; more models have appeared
[p0027-l0042] [10.0pt] since).

[p0031-l0003] [12.5pt] 1.5
[p0031-l0004] [12.5pt] Risks and challenges with generalist LLMs
[p0031-l0005] [10.0pt] Commercial, generalist, closed source LLMs from third-party vendors are powerful and
[p0031-l0006] [10.0pt] can handle diverse tasks. They can also provide a good experience for non-­technical
[p0031-l0007] [10.0pt] users, and you pay only for usage (since you don’t have to manage deployment and
[p0031-l0008] [10.0pt] maintenance). But they also come with risks that can outweigh these benefits:
[p0031-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ Deployment outside your organization’s network—Any information you include in a
[p0031-l0010] [10.0pt] prompt may leave your company and, depending on the usage terms, be used
[p0031-l0011] [10.0pt] to fine-tune the model and be exposed to other customers. You’ve likely read
[p0031-l0012] [10.0pt] of cases in which employees at large corporations sent sensitive or proprietary
[p0031-l0013] [10.0pt] data to external model-hosting services (for example, at Samsung, as discussed in
[p0031-l0014] [10.0pt] “Samsung Bans Staff’s AI Use After Spotting ChatGPT Data Leak” [Bloomberg,
[p0031-l0015] [10.0pt] May 2, 2023, https://mng.bz/AGEE], and others).
[p0031-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Data leakage risks—Because the model is hosted on infrastructure you don’t con­
[p0031-l0017] [10.0pt] trol, a weak cybersecurity posture (unknown to you and hard to mitigate) can
[p0031-l0018] [10.0pt] allow malicious actors to access private data. There is evidence that something like
[p0031-l0019] [10.0pt] this happened once with ChatGPT (“OpenAI Confirms ChatGPT Data Breach,”
[p0031-l0020] [10.0pt] Trend Micro’s blog, May 13, 2023, https://news.trendmicro.com/2023/05/13/
[p0031-l0021] [10.0pt] openai-chatgpt-data-breach/).
[p0031-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Model or version drift—A provider can update a model without notice, potentially
[p0031-l0023] [10.0pt] changing the behavior and accuracy of applications built on top of it.
[p0031-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Cost unpredictability—Token-based billing can spike, as a provider can decide at
[p0031-l0025] [10.0pt] any time to change their subscription prices.
[p0031-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ Closeness—You don’t have details about how an LLM was implemented and
[p0031-l0027] [10.0pt] trained, so there’s no chance of reproducibility or interpretability, which is often
[p0031-l0028] [10.0pt] a requirement in heavily regulated sectors. You also may not see infrastructure or
[p0031-l0029] [10.0pt] model-version changes.
[p0031-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Transparency—Data used to train closed source models isn’t publicly disclosed,
[p0031-l0031] [10.0pt] so there’s no way to verify whether it’s biased or contains copyrighted data used
[p0031-l0032] [10.0pt] without the owner’s permission.
[p0031-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ Hallucinations—Generated information may conflict with the source (intrin­
[p0031-l0034] [10.0pt] sic hallucination) or be unverifiable from the available source (extrinsic hallu­
[p0031-l0035] [10.0pt] cination). Intrinsic hallucinations can occur even in an organization’s models
[p0031-l0036] [10.0pt] trained on proprietary data—a challenge with LLMs in general. But extrinsic
[p0031-l0037] [10.0pt] hallucinations can’t be mitigated when you don’t have access to, or knowledge
[p0031-l0038] [10.0pt] of, the training data.
[p0031-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Compliance—Commercial and closed source LLMs, because of their generalist
[p0031-l0040] [10.0pt] nature, don’t follow any sectoral rules.
[p0031-l0041] [10.0pt] ¡ Harmful content generation—Models can not only reflect societal biases and stereo­
[p0031-l0042] [10.0pt] typing but can also produce unsafe content. In the rare cases where a provider

=== PDF page 32 / printed label 11 ===
[p0032-l0001] [9.0pt] 11
[p0032-l0002] [9.0pt] Domain-specific vs. generalist LLMs for business value
[p0032-l0003] [10.0pt] has set safety filters on generalist models, this can unnecessarily block legitimate
[p0032-l0004] [10.0pt] content as a side effect.
[p0032-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ Code generation—This emergent LLM ability makes it possible for a broader audi­
[p0032-l0006] [10.0pt] ence, including people with limited coding skills, to inadvertently generate code
[p0032-l0007] [10.0pt] with malicious elements or even produce malware. Many third-party LLMs lack
[p0032-l0008] [10.0pt] robust guardrails, and those that exist can be bypassed with carefully crafted
[p0032-l0009] [10.0pt] prompts. Organizations can build their own guardrails (which isn’t a trivial task)
[p0032-l0010] [10.0pt] or shift the responsibility to internal users to properly validate outputs.
[p0032-l0011] [10.0pt] All these risks, plus the fact that large models are trained on many tasks using broad but
[p0032-l0012] [10.0pt] generalist data sets, mean they aren’t always suitable for important business uses.
[p0032-l0013] [12.5pt] 1.6
[p0032-l0014] [12.5pt] Domain-specific vs. generalist LLMs for business value
[p0032-l0015] [10.0pt] Should you move to a custom domain-specific LLM? Several factors can help you make
[p0032-l0016] [10.0pt] the right choice.
[p0032-l0017] [10.0pt] Generalist pretrained LLMs (both commercial and open source) are largely trained
[p0032-l0018] [10.0pt] on content scraped (with or without consent) from the web, drawn from public scien­
[p0032-l0019] [10.0pt] tific or code repositories, or taken from human conversations on generic topics. For
[p0032-l0020] [10.0pt] tasks that don’t require domain specialization, these models are often powerful enough
[p0032-l0021] [10.0pt] to generate useful content that can be reused with little or no refinement. But for spe­
[p0032-l0022] [10.0pt] cialized domains and tasks, you’ll need a strategy to tune the pretrained model on
[p0032-l0023] [10.0pt] domain-specific data (whether public or private). This process is commonly referred
[p0032-l0024] [10.0pt] to as transfer learning. In brief, transfer learning involves taking a model trained on one
[p0032-l0025] [10.0pt] task or domain and applying it to a related task or domain.
[p0032-l0026] [10.0pt] In heavily regulated domains, there are stricter requirements for staying compliant.
[p0032-l0027] [10.0pt] Decisions based on model outcomes cannot cause any sort of harm. In this context, the
[p0032-l0028] [10.0pt] availability and quality of domain-specific training data (which you may already have in
[p0032-l0029] [10.0pt] house) plays a key role.
[p0032-l0030] [10.0pt] Transfer learning does not necessarily involve the full training of a language model.
[p0032-l0031] [10.0pt] That’s a possibility, but there are options, as listed in table 1.1.

[p0033-l0053] [7.0pt] and a hydroxy

[p0033-l0055] [8.0pt] Figure 1.5  An LLM trained for tasks on molecule structures (generation and captioning)

[p0034-l0002] [9.0pt] Domain-specific vs. generalist LLMs for business value
[p0034-l0003] [10.0pt] descriptions and structures represented in the SMILES format, this LLM can generate
[p0034-l0004] [10.0pt] molecular structures from description, or vice versa. This use case is discussed in chap­
[p0034-l0005] [10.0pt] ter 8.
[p0034-l0006] [10.0pt] Any situation where you must prevent private data leakage is a good reason to switch
[p0034-l0007] [10.0pt] to a private, offline, domain-specific LLM that runs inside your corporate network
[p0034-l0008] [10.0pt] boundaries. In these cases, people often worry whether their existing on-premises or
[p0034-l0009] [10.0pt] private-cloud infrastructure has enough computational power, especially when budgets
[p0034-l0010] [10.0pt] are limited. We’ll look at optimization techniques to reduce the memory footprint and
[p0034-l0011] [10.0pt] computational requirements of custom LLMs, with working examples in each chapter.
[p0034-l0012] [10.0pt] Table 1.2 summarizes the pros and cons of generalist and domain-specific LLMs.

[p0034-l0047] [8.0pt] resources
[p0034-l0048] [10.0pt] Another advantage of choosing an open source baseline model is that it will likely
[p0034-l0049] [10.0pt] have only a few billion parameters. After tuning it for domain-specific tasks with pri­
[p0034-l0050] [10.0pt] vate data, the model will likely remain below 10 billion parameters. From a sustainabil­
[p0034-l0051] [10.0pt] ity standpoint, these smaller models generate less CO2 and have less environmental
[p0034-l0052] [10.0pt] impact than larger models during training and doing inference.
[p0034-l0053] [10.0pt] Finally, let’s look at LLM alignment with users, which you’ve probably heard about.
[p0034-l0054] [10.0pt] A common definition of “alignment” in this context is adhering to principles of help­
[p0034-l0055] [10.0pt] fulness (following user instructions, completing a task, and providing results), truthful­
[p0034-l0056] [10.0pt] ness (providing factual information and acknowledging limitations), and harmlessness
[p0034-l0057] [10.0pt] (avoiding biased or toxic responses and refusing to assist with harmful tasks). Commer­
[p0034-l0058] [10.0pt] cial closed-source LLM vendors often pursue this by defining what is right and wrong
[p0034-l0059] [10.0pt] from their own perspective and then shaping the models accordingly.

=== PDF page 35 / printed label 14 ===
[p0035-l0001] [9.0pt] 14
[p0035-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 1  Small language models
[p0035-l0003] [10.0pt] In my opinion, alignment should focus less on imposing the provider’s definition of
[p0035-l0004] [10.0pt] “right” and more on matching the user’s intent. This is similar to working with a human
[p0035-l0005] [10.0pt] collaborator: motives and knowledge/ability are different. Improving knowledge and
[p0035-l0006] [10.0pt] ability may lower the mistake rate, but it doesn’t mean the intent is aligned with the per­
[p0035-l0007] [10.0pt] son making the request. When you specialize your own models—especially by narrow­
[p0035-l0008] [10.0pt] ing the scope to a specific domain—you may have more room to improve this, because
[p0035-l0009] [10.0pt] “intent” can take on a domain-specific meaning.
[p0035-l0010] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0035-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Transformers use self-attention mechanisms to process entire text sequences at
[p0035-l0012] [10.0pt] once instead of word by word.
[p0035-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ Self-supervised learning creates training labels automatically from text data with­
[p0035-l0014] [10.0pt] out human annotation.
[p0035-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ BERT models use only the encoder part of transformers for classification and
[p0035-l0016] [10.0pt] prediction tasks.
[p0035-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ GPT models use only the decoder part of transformers for text-generation tasks.
[p0035-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Word embeddings convert words into numerical vectors that capture semantic
[p0035-l0019] [10.0pt] relationships.
[p0035-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ RLHF uses reinforcement learning to improve large language model (LLM)
[p0035-l0021] [10.0pt] responses based on human feedback.
[p0035-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ LLMs can generate any symbolic content including code, math expressions, and
[p0035-l0023] [10.0pt] structured data.
[p0035-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Open source LLMs reduce development costs by providing pretrained models as
[p0035-l0025] [10.0pt] starting points.
[p0035-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ Transfer learning adapts pretrained models to specific domains using
[p0035-l0027] [10.0pt] domain-specific data.
[p0035-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Generalist LLMs risk data leakage when they’re deployed outside organizational
[p0035-l0029] [10.0pt] networks.
[p0035-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Closed source models lack transparency about training data and model
[p0035-l0031] [10.0pt] architecture.
[p0035-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Domain-specific LLMs provide better accuracy for specialized tasks than gener­
[p0035-l0033] [10.0pt] alist models.
[p0035-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Smaller specialized models require less computational power than large gener­
[p0035-l0035] [10.0pt] alist models.
[p0035-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ Fine-tuning costs significantly less than training models from scratch.
[p0035-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ Regulatory compliance often requires domain-specific models with known train­
[p0035-l0038] [10.0pt] ing data.

[p0038-l0013] [12.5pt] 2.1
[p0038-l0014] [12.5pt] Data preparation
[p0038-l0015] [10.0pt] Fine-tuning a Transformer model for a given task starts with formatting your dataset
[p0038-l0016] [10.0pt] for training. In this section, we’ll look at two PyTorch examples using Hugging Face
[p0038-l0017] [10.0pt] Transformers (https://github.com/huggingface/transformers): an encoder-only
[p0038-l0018] [10.0pt] model (BERT) and a decoder-only model (GPT-2). You’ll see that the workflow is
[p0038-l0019] [10.0pt] largely the same, with only minor changes based on the model architecture and
[p0038-l0020] [9.0pt] 17

=== PDF page 39 / printed label 18 ===
[p0039-l0001] [9.0pt] 18
[p0039-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 2  Tuning for a specific domain
[p0039-l0003] [10.0pt] task. Finally, you’ll see how to prepare data for cases where retrieval-augmented gener­
[p0039-l0004] [10.0pt] ation (RAG) is a better choice than fine-tuning.
[p0039-l0005] [10.5pt] 2.1.1
[p0039-l0006] [10.5pt] Data preparation for BERT fine-tuning
[p0039-l0007] [10.0pt] Let’s consider a classification task using the pretrained bert-base-uncased model
[p0039-l0008] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/bert-base-uncased). We first need to gather our data, making
[p0039-l0009] [10.0pt] sure each text sample has a class label. Format it as a list of tuples like this:
[p0039-l0010] [8.0pt] dataset = [("This movie is a masterpiece!", "Positive"),
[p0039-l0011] [8.0pt]     ("Not worth watching!", "Negative"),
[p0039-l0012] [8.0pt]     ("Terrific!", "Positive") go here
[p0039-l0013] [8.0pt] ]
[p0039-l0014] [10.0pt] Next, we need to tokenize the training texts, because BERT models work with tokens
[p0039-l0015] [10.0pt] rather than raw text.
[p0039-l0016] [10.5pt] Notes on tokens
[p0039-l0017] [9.5pt] For LLMs, a token is a unit of text the model processes during training and infer­
[p0039-l0018] [9.5pt] ence. Tokens can represent words, subwords, characters, punctuation, and special
[p0039-l0019] [9.5pt] characters.
[p0039-l0020] [9.5pt] How text is tokenized directly affects model performance and language understand­
[p0039-l0021] [9.5pt] ing by shaping how well it manages vocabulary, handles out-of-vocabulary words, and
[p0039-l0022] [9.5pt] generates coherent responses.
[p0039-l0023] [9.5pt] Tokenization is vital in NLP: the token count determines input size and affects pro­
[p0039-l0024] [9.5pt] cessing time and memory use. LLMs have a maximum number of tokens they can
[p0039-l0025] [9.5pt] accept in a single prompt.
[p0039-l0026] [10.0pt] Most pretrained models on the Hugging Face Hub include a custom tokenizer, since
[p0039-l0027] [10.0pt] each architecture expects a specific token format. For this example, we’ll use the bert
[p0039-l0028] [10.0pt] -base-­uncased tokenizer:
[p0039-l0029] [8.0pt] from transformers import BertTokenizer
[p0039-l0030] [8.0pt] tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased')
[p0039-l0031] [10.0pt] For this kind of transformer, special tokens are used to mark the start and end of each
[p0039-l0032] [10.0pt] input sequence, and a separator token is used between segments:
[p0039-l0033] [8.0pt] max_length = 128
[p0039-l0034] [8.0pt] formatted_data = [(f"[CLS] {text} [SEP]", label) for text, label in dataset]
[p0039-l0035] [8.0pt] tokenized_data = tokenizer(formatted_data,
[p0039-l0036] [10.0pt]                ➥padding=True,
[p0039-l0037] [10.0pt]                ➥truncation=True,
[p0039-l0038] [10.0pt]                ➥max_length=max_length,
[p0039-l0039] [10.0pt]                ➥return_tensors='pt')

=== PDF page 40 / printed label 19 ===
[p0040-l0001] [9.0pt] 19
[p0040-l0002] [9.0pt] Data preparation
[p0040-l0003] [10.0pt] Here, [CLS] marks the beginning, and [SEP] separates segments. A best practice is to
[p0040-l0004] [10.0pt] keep input sequences a consistent length by padding shorter ones or truncating longer
[p0040-l0005] [10.0pt] ones, as in previous tokenizer parameters.
[p0040-l0006] [10.0pt] We now need to convert the tokenized, formatted text into numerical representa­
[p0040-l0007] [10.0pt] tions. We’ll assign each token a unique ID (or index) and then represent sequences—
[p0040-l0008] [10.0pt] and labels—as sequences of these IDs:
[p0040-l0009] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0040-l0010] [8.0pt] from sklearn.preprocessing import LabelEncoder
[p0040-l0011] [8.0pt] input_ids = tokenized_data['input_ids']
[p0040-l0012] [8.0pt] attention_mask = tokenized_data['attention_mask']
[p0040-l0013] [8.0pt] labels = torch.tensor(LabelEncoder()
[p0040-l0014] [10.0pt] ➥.fit_transform([label for _, label in dataset]))
[p0040-l0015] [10.0pt] We can now split the initial dataset into training and validation sets:
[p0040-l0016] [8.0pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0040-l0017] [8.0pt] train_inputs, val_inputs, train_labels, val_labels,
[p0040-l0018] [10.0pt] ➥ train_mask, val_mask = train_test_split(
[p0040-l0019] [10.0pt] ➥input_ids, labels, attention_mask,
[p0040-l0020] [10.0pt] ➥random_state=42, test_size=0.1
[p0040-l0021] [8.0pt] )
[p0040-l0022] [10.0pt] The split is performed with the scikit-learn package (https://scikit-learn.org/
[p0040-l0023] [10.0pt] stable/), as is standard in many machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) use
[p0040-l0024] [10.0pt] cases.
[p0040-l0025] [10.0pt] Before feeding data to the model, we need training and validation data loaders for
[p0040-l0026] [10.0pt] our custom data. First, let’s define a custom dataset class:
[p0040-l0027] [8.0pt] from torch.utils.data import Dataset
[p0040-l0028] [8.0pt] class CustomDataset(Dataset):
[p0040-l0029] [8.0pt]     def __init__(self, input_ids, attention_mask,
[p0040-l0030] [10.0pt]         ➥ labels):
[p0040-l0031] [8.0pt]         self.input_ids = input_ids
[p0040-l0032] [8.0pt]         self.attention_mask = attention_mask
[p0040-l0033] [8.0pt]         self.labels = labels
[p0040-l0034] [8.0pt]     def __len__(self):
[p0040-l0035] [8.0pt]         return len(self.input_ids)
[p0040-l0036] [8.0pt]     def __getitem__(self, idx):
[p0040-l0037] [8.0pt]         return {'input_ids': self.input_ids[idx],
[p0040-l0038] [8.0pt]                 'attention_mask':
[p0040-l0039] [8.0pt]                  self.attention_mask[idx],
[p0040-l0040] [8.0pt]                 'labels': self.labels[idx]}

=== PDF page 41 / printed label 20 ===
[p0041-l0001] [9.0pt] 20
[p0041-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 2  Tuning for a specific domain
[p0041-l0003] [10.0pt] We’ll use this class to create the data loaders:
[p0041-l0004] [8.0pt] from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
[p0041-l0005] [8.0pt] batch_size = 4
[p0041-l0006] [8.0pt] train_dataset = CustomDataset(train_inputs,
[p0041-l0007] [10.0pt]                 ➥train_mask, train_labels)
[p0041-l0008] [8.0pt] train_dataloader = DataLoader(train_dataset,
[p0041-l0009] [10.0pt]                 ➥batch_size=batch_size,
[p0041-l0010] [10.0pt]                 ➥shuffle=True)
[p0041-l0011] [8.0pt] val_dataset = CustomDataset(val_inputs,
[p0041-l0012] [10.0pt]               ➥val_mask, val_labels)
[p0041-l0013] [8.0pt] val_dataloader = DataLoader(val_dataset,
[p0041-l0014] [10.0pt]               ➥batch_size=batch_size,
[p0041-l0015] [10.0pt]               ➥ shuffle=False)
[p0041-l0016] [10.0pt] We can now load the model from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0041-l0017] [8.0pt] from transformers import BertForSequenceClassification
[p0041-l0018] [8.0pt] model = BertForSequenceClassification
[p0041-l0019] [10.0pt]         ➥.from_pretrained('bert-base-uncased',
[p0041-l0020] [8.0pt]     num_labels=len(set(labels)))
[p0041-l0021] [10.0pt] Now we can start the fine-tuning, which will be discussed in sections 2.3 and 2.4.
[p0041-l0022] [10.5pt] 2.1.2
[p0041-l0023] [10.5pt] Data preparation for GPT fine-tuning
[p0041-l0024] [10.0pt] For this example, we’ll consider a text completion task using the pretrained GPT-2 base
[p0041-l0025] [10.0pt] model (the smallest version, with 124M parameters, available at https://huggingface
[p0041-l0026] [10.0pt] .co/gpt2). Gather your own private data, and ensure that each sample is a piece of text
[p0041-l0027] [10.0pt] with a clear context (or prompt) and an associated target (or completion):
[p0041-l0028] [8.0pt] dataset = [("Once upon a time in a faraway swamp,",
[p0041-l0029] [8.0pt]             "there lived an ugly ork."),
[p0041-l0030] [8.0pt]           # More samples
[p0041-l0031] [8.0pt] ]
[p0041-l0032] [10.0pt] We need to pair each context (input) with its target (output) so the model learns to
[p0041-l0033] [10.0pt] generate the target from the context. Then, as with the BERT model, we tokenize the
[p0041-l0034] [10.0pt] inputs using the GPT-2 tokenizer:
[p0041-l0035] [8.0pt] from transformers import GPT2Tokenizer
[p0041-l0036] [8.0pt] tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained('gpt2')
[p0041-l0037] [8.0pt] formatted_data = [(f"[CLS] {context} [SEP]
[p0041-l0038] [10.0pt]                  ➥{target} [SEP]",) for context,
[p0041-l0039] [10.0pt]                  ➥ target in dataset]
[p0041-l0040] [8.0pt] numerical_data = [tokenizer.encode(example[0],
[p0041-l0041] [10.0pt]                 ➥ add_special_tokens=True)
[p0041-l0042] [10.0pt]                 ➥for example in formatted_data]

=== PDF page 42 / printed label 21 ===
[p0042-l0001] [9.0pt] 21
[p0042-l0002] [9.0pt] Data preparation
[p0042-l0003] [10.0pt] In this case, we again need special tokens to mark the beginning and end of each input
[p0042-l0004] [10.0pt] sequence, plus a separator token. We must ensure that all sequences have a consistent
[p0042-l0005] [10.0pt] length by padding shorter ones or truncating longer ones to match our desired length.
[p0042-l0006] [10.0pt] We then convert the tokenized, formatted text into numbers by assigning each token a
[p0042-l0007] [10.0pt] unique ID and representing sequences as lists of these IDs:
[p0042-l0008] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0042-l0009] [8.0pt] max_length = max(len(seq) for seq in numerical_data)
[p0042-l0010] [8.0pt] padded_data = [seq + [tokenizer.pad_token_id]
[p0042-l0011] [10.0pt]              ➥* (max_length - len(seq))
[p0042-l0012] [10.0pt]              ➥for seq in numerical_data]
[p0042-l0013] [8.0pt] input_ids = torch.tensor(padded_data)
[p0042-l0014] [10.0pt] Before feeding data to the model, we need to create a training data loader for our cus­
[p0042-l0015] [10.0pt] tom dataset. Let’s first define a custom dataset class:
[p0042-l0016] [8.0pt] from torch.utils.data import Dataset
[p0042-l0017] [8.0pt] class CustomDataset(Dataset):
[p0042-l0018] [8.0pt]   def __init__(self, input_ids):
[p0042-l0019] [8.0pt]     self.input_ids = input_ids
[p0042-l0020] [8.0pt]   def __len__(self):
[p0042-l0021] [8.0pt]     return len(self.input_ids)
[p0042-l0022] [8.0pt]   def __getitem__(self, idx):
[p0042-l0023] [8.0pt]     return {'input_ids': self.input_ids[idx]}
[p0042-l0024] [10.0pt] The implementation is similar to the BERT use case; what differs is the definition of
[p0042-l0025] [10.0pt] the __init__ and __getitem__ functions, which reflect the model architecture’s input
[p0042-l0026] [10.0pt] configuration. We’ll use this class to create the training data loader:
[p0042-l0027] [8.0pt] from torch.utils.data import DataLoader
[p0042-l0028] [8.0pt] batch_size = 4
[p0042-l0029] [8.0pt] custom_dataset = CustomDataset(input_ids)
[p0042-l0030] [8.0pt] dataloader = DataLoader(custom_dataset,
[p0042-l0031] [10.0pt]             ➥batch_size=batch_size,
[p0042-l0032] [10.0pt]             ➥shuffle=True)
[p0042-l0033] [10.0pt] Finally, we can load the model from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0042-l0034] [8.0pt] from transformers import GPT2LMHeadModel
[p0042-l0035] [8.0pt] model = GPT2LMHeadModel.from_pretrained('gpt2')
[p0042-l0036] [10.0pt] We can now start the fine tuning, as discussed in sections 2.3 and 2.4.

[p0043-l0001] [9.0pt] 22
[p0043-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 2  Tuning for a specific domain
[p0043-l0003] [10.0pt] As you’ve seen, thanks to the Transformers library’s friendly API, switching between
[p0043-l0004] [10.0pt] pretrained models keeps the code largely the same.
[p0043-l0005] [10.5pt] 2.1.3
[p0043-l0006] [10.5pt] Data preparation for RAG
[p0043-l0007] [10.0pt] For cases where RAG (discussed in section 2.2) is the best way to specialize a pretrained
[p0043-l0008] [10.0pt] language model, you must convert your knowledge base to embeddings and store
[p0043-l0009] [10.0pt] them in a vector database. This makes it easy to retrieve information on demand with­
[p0043-l0010] [10.0pt] out sacrificing performance or scalability. Many open source and commercial options
[p0043-l0011] [10.0pt] are available for this purpose.
[p0043-l0012] [10.0pt] In this chapter, we’ll use Facebook AI Similarity Search (FAISS, https://github.com/
[p0043-l0013] [10.0pt] facebookresearch/faiss), released as open source under an MIT license and maintained
[p0043-l0014] [10.0pt] by Meta Research. FAISS is a library for efficient similarity search and clustering of dense
[p0043-l0015] [10.0pt] vectors. It’s implemented in C++ and provides a Python API, so developers don’t need
[p0043-l0016] [10.0pt] to worry about implementation details. Used internally at Meta, it supports searches
[p0043-l0017] [10.0pt] that are inefficient or impractical with other approaches. It includes nearest-neighbor
[p0043-l0018] [10.0pt] implementations for million-to-billion-scale datasets, optimizing the memory/speed/
[p0043-l0019] [10.0pt] accuracy tradeoff, and it supports GPUs via the Compute Unified Device Architecture
[p0043-l0020] [10.0pt] (CUDA). FAISS offers several similarity-search methods and assumes that instances
[p0043-l0021] [10.0pt] are represented as vectors (each identified by an integer) that can be compared using
[p0043-l0022] [10.0pt] Euclidean (L2) distance. The most similar vectors to a query vector are those with the
[p0043-l0023] [10.0pt] smallest L2 distance.
[p0043-l0024] [10.0pt] To get familiar with FAISS, I’ve provided a companion Colab notebook. We’ll walk
[p0043-l0025] [10.0pt] through its code in this section. You’ll classify a new input text by calculating its similar­
[p0043-l0026] [10.0pt] ity to other text samples in a given category.
[p0043-l0027] [10.0pt] In addition to FAISS, we’ll use the sentence-transformers package (https://www
[p0043-l0028] [10.0pt] .sbert.net), a framework for sentence, text, and image embeddings.
[p0043-l0029] [10.0pt] We’ll first set up the sample data, which is a few sentences about Marvel superheroes,
[p0043-l0030] [10.0pt] categorized into three labels: spiderman, ironman, and captainamerica:
[p0043-l0031] [8.0pt] data = [['His secret identity is Peter Parker', 'spiderman'],
[p0043-l0032] [8.0pt]         ['A businessman and engineer who ' +
[p0043-l0033] [8.0pt]          'runs the company Stark Industries',
[p0043-l0034] [8.0pt]          'ironman'],
[p0043-l0035] [8.0pt]         ['Superhuman spider-powers and abilities ' +
[p0043-l0036] [8.0pt]          'after being bitten by a radioactive spider',
[p0043-l0037] [8.0pt]          'spiderman'],
[p0043-l0038] [8.0pt]         ['A frail man enhanced to the peak of human ' +
[p0043-l0039] [8.0pt]          'physical perfection by an experimental
[p0043-l0040] [10.0pt]           ➥super-soldier serum', 'captainamerica']
[p0043-l0041] [8.0pt]         ]

[p0044-l0001] [9.0pt] 23
[p0044-l0002] [9.0pt] Data preparation
[p0044-l0003] [10.0pt] We’ll use the sentence_transformers API to generate embeddings for each text row in
[p0044-l0004] [10.0pt] the DataFrame:
[p0044-l0005] [8.0pt] from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer

[p0044-l0007] [8.0pt] encoder = SentenceTransformer("paraphrase-mpnet-base-v2")
[p0044-l0008] [8.0pt] vectors = encoder.encode(text)
[p0044-l0009] [10.0pt] Now that we have the word embeddings, we can create a FAISS index and add them to it:
[p0044-l0010] [8.0pt] import faiss
[p0044-l0011] [8.0pt] vector_dimension = vectors.shape[1]
[p0044-l0012] [8.0pt] l2_index = faiss.IndexFlatL2(vector_dimension)
[p0044-l0013] [8.0pt] faiss.normalize_L2(vectors)
[p0044-l0014] [8.0pt] l2_index.add(vectors)
[p0044-l0015] [10.0pt] An index object makes similarity search efficient in FAISS. If you’re familiar with
[p0044-l0016] [10.0pt] relational databases, you’re familiar with a table index: a pointer to data in a table
[p0044-l0017] [10.0pt] used to speed up retrieval. Think of FAISS indexes the same way. Here, they speed
[p0044-l0018] [10.0pt] up retrieval within a data cluster, so FAISS doesn’t rely on brute-force search. Note
[p0044-l0019] [10.0pt] that embeddings are normalized before being added to the index so they share a
[p0044-l0020] [10.0pt] common scale.
[p0044-l0021] [10.0pt] The Euclidean distance is the length of a line segment between two points. FAISS
[p0044-l0022] [10.0pt] calculates it using the standard formula, where qi and pi are the Cartesian coordinates of
[p0044-l0023] [10.0pt] two points p and q:
[p0044-l0024] [10.0pt] Let’s look at a search example. Set a search text related to Spider-Man:
[p0044-l0025] [8.0pt] search_text = 'He throws webs'
[p0044-l0026] [10.0pt] As a result of the search, we expect smaller distances between the search string and
[p0044-l0027] [10.0pt] the two spiderman samples in the original text corpus. Before searching, we need a few
[p0044-l0028] [10.0pt] transformations to generate embeddings for the search text—in the same way as we
[p0044-l0029] [10.0pt] previously did for all the embeddings in scope for this example before adding them to
[p0044-l0030] [10.0pt] the FAISS index—convert them to a NumPy array, and normalize them:
[p0044-l0031] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0044-l0032] [8.0pt] search_vector = encoder.encode(search_text)
[p0044-l0033] [8.0pt] search_vector_as_array = np.array([search_vector])
[p0044-l0034] [8.0pt] faiss.normalize_L2(search_vector_as_array)

[p0045-l0027] [12.5pt] 2.2
[p0045-l0028] [12.5pt] Retrieval-augmented generation
[p0045-l0029] [10.0pt] Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) integrates data retrieval into LLM content
[p0045-l0030] [10.0pt] generation. As shown in figure 2.1, it retrieves relevant data from a larger corpus and
[p0045-l0031] [10.0pt] feeds it to a pretrained LLM as an external knowledge base, helping the model pro­
[p0045-l0032] [10.0pt] duce more accurate, up-to-date answers.
[p0045-l0033] [10.0pt] This is a way to select external information to improve a model’s response. We can
[p0045-l0034] [10.0pt] identify two phases:
[p0045-l0035] [10.0pt] 1	 Retrieval phase—The algorithm searches for and retrieves information based on
[p0045-l0036] [10.0pt] the user’s prompt, from private or public data sources, or both.
[p0045-l0037] [10.0pt] 2	 Content generation phase—After retrieving the relevant embeddings, an LLM uses
[p0045-l0038] [10.0pt] the context to generate a natural-language response. The pipeline can also check
[p0045-l0039] [10.0pt] the output against the sources to improve transparency and accuracy.
[p0045-l0040] [10.0pt] For domain-specific data and tasks, or unstructured text that isn’t natural language,
[p0045-l0041] [10.0pt] prompt engineering (few-shot, chain-of-thought, and so on) often won’t produce

[p0047-l0003] [10.0pt] Fine-tuning is similar to pretraining, but it uses a smaller, task-specific, labeled dataset.
[p0047-l0004] [10.0pt] To explain the fine-tuning steps, I have provided a companion Colab notebook. This
[p0047-l0005] [10.0pt] section walks through the code in that notebook. Note that this section covers the full
[p0047-l0006] [10.0pt] fine-tuning of a pretrained LLM (that is, updating all the parameters). In contrast, sec­
[p0047-l0007] [10.0pt] tion 2.4 introduces one of the most effective PEFT (parameter-efficient fine-tuning)
[p0047-l0008] [10.0pt] techniques, an alternative for adapting a pretrained model to a domain by training only
[p0047-l0009] [10.0pt] a small number of parameters; that section also surveys other PEFT methods.
[p0047-l0010] [10.0pt] The pretrained LLM in this example is DistilBERT-base, available on the Hugging
[p0047-l0011] [10.0pt] Face Hub. It’s a Transformer model that’s smaller and faster than BERT, pretrained
[p0047-l0012] [10.0pt] on the same corpus via self-supervised learning, with BERT-base as the teacher. It was
[p0047-l0013] [10.0pt] trained on raw text, using an automatic process to generate inputs and labels (no
[p0047-l0014] [10.0pt] human labeling), again based on BERT-base. DistilBERT is uncased, meaning it doesn’t
[p0047-l0015] [10.0pt] distinguish between uppercase and lowercase letters. In this example, we’ll fine-tune
[p0047-l0016] [10.0pt] the model for question answering.
[p0047-l0017] [10.0pt] The training dataset must have these three important fields:
[p0047-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ question—The question the model should answer
[p0047-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ context—The background information from which the model needs to extract
[p0047-l0020] [10.0pt] the answer
[p0047-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ answers—The starting location of the answer token and the answer text
[p0047-l0022] [10.0pt] Several question-answering datasets are available on the Hugging Face Hub. Choose
[p0047-l0023] [10.0pt] one for this exercise using the Hugging Face Datasets library (https://github.com/
[p0047-l0024] [10.0pt] huggingface/datasets):

[p0050-l0024] [8.0pt]     outputs = model(**inputs)
[p0050-l0025] [10.0pt] Select the highest-probability start and end positions from the model’s output:
[p0050-l0026] [8.0pt] answer_start_index = outputs.start_logits.argmax()
[p0050-l0027] [8.0pt] answer_end_index = outputs.end_logits.argmax()
[p0050-l0028] [10.0pt] Finally, decode the predicted tokens to get the answer:
[p0050-l0029] [8.0pt] predict_answer_tokens = inputs.input_ids[0,
[p0050-l0030] [10.0pt] ➥ answer_start_index : answer_end_index + 1]
[p0050-l0031] [8.0pt] tokenizer.decode(predict_answer_tokens)
[p0050-l0032] [10.0pt] It should return 36 (as of this writing).
[p0050-l0033] [12.5pt] 2.4
[p0050-l0034] [12.5pt] LoRA
[p0050-l0035] [10.0pt] Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) is a set of techniques for adapting a pre­
[p0050-l0036] [10.0pt] trained model by updating only a small fraction of its parameters. An LLM pretrained
[p0050-l0037] [10.0pt] on a large dataset already captures many language patterns and facts, so it’s often

=== PDF page 51 / printed label 30 ===
[p0051-l0001] [9.0pt] 30
[p0051-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 2  Tuning for a specific domain
[p0051-l0003] [10.0pt] unnecessary—and inefficient—to tune the entire model for a new task. PEFT fine-
[p0051-l0004] [10.0pt] tunes only a small subset of parameters, reducing computational costs compared with
[p0051-l0005] [10.0pt] full fine-tuning while maintaining comparable accuracy and robustness.
[p0051-l0006] [10.0pt] These are some major PEFT methods:
[p0051-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ LoRA (Low-rank Adaptation)—The main topic of this section
[p0051-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Prefix tuning—Keeps the LLM parameters frozen and optimizes a sequence of
[p0051-l0009] [10.0pt] continuous, task-specific vectors called the prefix
[p0051-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ LoftQ—A framework that quantizes an LLM and provides a low-rank initializa­
[p0051-l0011] [10.0pt] tion for LoRA fine-tuning
[p0051-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ AdaLoRA—A LoRA variant that adaptively allocates the parameter budget across
[p0051-l0013] [10.0pt] weight matrices based on importance scores
[p0051-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ P-tuning—Uses trainable continuous prompt embeddings concatenated with dis­
[p0051-l0015] [10.0pt] crete prompts
[p0051-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Prompt tuning—A simpler form of prefix tuning that scales better to larger
[p0051-l0017] [10.0pt] models
[p0051-l0018] [8.0pt] Pretrained
[p0051-l0019] [8.0pt] weights
[p0051-l0020] [10.0pt] One of the most widely used and efficient
[p0051-l0021] [10.0pt] approaches is LoRA (low-rank adaptation),
[p0051-l0022] [10.0pt] introduced in 2021 for LLMs and later
[p0051-l0023] [10.0pt] adapted to vision transformers. Figure 2.3,
[p0051-l0024] [10.0pt] from the “LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of
[p0051-l0025] [10.0pt] Large Language Models” paper (https://
[p0051-l0026] [10.0pt] arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685), summarizes the
[p0051-l0027] [10.0pt] LoRA process: the pretrained weights are
[p0051-l0028] [10.0pt] kept frozen, and only a subset of parameters
[p0051-l0029] [10.0pt] is fine-tuned.
[p0051-l0030] [8.0pt] Figure 2.3  The LoRA fine-tuning process
[p0051-l0031] [10.0pt] A companion Colab notebook has been
[p0051-l0032] [10.0pt] provided to show how LoRA works; this sec­
[p0051-l0033] [10.0pt] tion walks through its code. We’ll start with
[p0051-l0034] [10.0pt] a pretrained model called FLAN-T5 (80M
[p0051-l0035] [10.0pt] parameters, https://huggingface.co/google/flan-t5-small). FLAN-T5 combines FLAN
[p0051-l0036] [10.0pt] (Finetuned Language Net) with T5, a language model Google released in 2020. It uses
[p0051-l0037] [10.0pt] an encoder–decoder architecture and extends the original T5 model to improve zero-
[p0051-l0038] [10.0pt] shot performance. It’s open source under the Apache License 2.0. Although we’ll use
[p0051-l0039] [10.0pt] the smallest FLAN-T5 model, the same code and considerations apply to larger versions
[p0051-l0040] [10.0pt] (250M to 11B parameters).
[p0051-l0041] [10.0pt] The dataset used in this example is samsum (https://huggingface.co/datasets/
[p0051-l0042] [10.0pt] knkarthick/samsum):

[p0055-l0027] [12.5pt] 2.5
[p0055-l0028] [12.5pt] RAG or fine-tuning?
[p0055-l0029] [10.0pt] Which of these two strategies for specializing LLMs should we prefer—RAG or fine-­
[p0055-l0030] [10.0pt] tuning? As is often the case, it depends on the specific situation.
[p0055-l0031] [10.0pt] RAG is useful when you need up-to-date information (recent data or new data
[p0055-l0032] [10.0pt] sources) that wasn’t part of an LLM’s initial training set. It can reduce hallucinations
[p0055-l0033] [10.0pt] and improve interpretability because you can trace each answer back to its sources.
[p0055-l0034] [10.0pt] RAG is usually less costly than fine-tuning because it requires less labeling and no model
[p0055-l0035] [10.0pt] training. But RAG has downsides. In some cases, extra context isn’t enough: if an LLM
[p0055-l0036] [10.0pt] struggles with the task it was trained for, additional context won’t help. And at large
[p0055-l0037] [10.0pt] data volumes, you also need to account for the infrastructure costs of a vector database
[p0055-l0038] [10.0pt] and the implementation and maintenance of data pipelines.
[p0055-l0039] [10.0pt] Fine-tuning often outperforms RAG on tasks that require learning complex pat­
[p0055-l0040] [10.0pt] terns and relationships, such as drug discovery or code generation. By training on
[p0055-l0041] [10.0pt] a task-­specific dataset, an LLM can learn domain nuances, including specialized

=== PDF page 56 / printed label 35 ===
[p0056-l0001] [9.0pt] 35
[p0056-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0056-l0003] [10.0pt] jargon, concepts, and structures. As a result, when it encounters new examples from
[p0056-l0004] [10.0pt] that domain, a fine-tuned model is more likely to produce accurate, relevant outputs.
[p0056-l0005] [10.0pt] Fine-tuning typically costs more than RAG, but as you learned in section 2.4, PEFT
[p0056-l0006] [10.0pt] techniques can make it less computationally hungry (and cheaper) than full fine-­
[p0056-l0007] [10.0pt] tuning—sometimes comparable to, or even lower than, the infrastructure costs of a
[p0056-l0008] [10.0pt] RAG solution. Fine-tuning also requires more ML engineering expertise than RAG to
[p0056-l0009] [10.0pt] optimize training and control costs.
[p0056-l0010] [10.0pt] RAG is usually more interpretable, while fine-tuning requires more careful
[p0056-l0011] [10.0pt] training-data curation to mitigate hallucinations. Fine-tuning or PEFT can reduce
[p0056-l0012] [10.0pt] domain-specific hallucinations, whereas more generic domain hallucinations can be
[p0056-l0013] [10.0pt] better mitigated with RAG.
[p0056-l0014] [10.0pt] Take time to choose the right path for each use case; no single strategy fits all
[p0056-l0015] [10.0pt] situations.
[p0056-l0016] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0056-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ BERT tokenization adds special tokens [CLS] and [SEP] to mark sequence bound­
[p0056-l0018] [10.0pt] aries for classification tasks.
[p0056-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ GPT models use context-target pairs, learning to generate target text from the
[p0056-l0020] [10.0pt] input context.
[p0056-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Tokenizers convert text to numerical representations that models can process
[p0056-l0022] [10.0pt] during training and inference.
[p0056-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ FAISS builds vector indexes for efficient similarity search over large text embed­
[p0056-l0024] [10.0pt] ding datasets.
[p0056-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ RAG combines retrieval and text generation to give models access to external
[p0056-l0026] [10.0pt] knowledge.
[p0056-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ RAG retrieves relevant information from vector databases before generating
[p0056-l0028] [10.0pt] responses, improving accuracy.
[p0056-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ Fine-tuning adjusts all parameters of a pretrained model using task-specific
[p0056-l0030] [10.0pt] labeled datasets.
[p0056-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ LoRA fine-tunes only a small subset of a model’s parameters, retaining the origi­
[p0056-l0032] [10.0pt] nal weights.
[p0056-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ PEFT techniques like LoRA cut computational costs compared with full fine-­
[p0056-l0034] [10.0pt] tuning while maintaining performance.
[p0056-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ RAG works better for up-to-date information and reduces hallucinations through
[p0056-l0036] [10.0pt] source traceability.
[p0056-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ Fine-tuning produces better results for complex, domain-specific tasks that
[p0056-l0038] [10.0pt] require specialized knowledge.
[p0056-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Vector databases store embeddings and support fast similarity search for RAG
[p0056-l0040] [10.0pt] implementations.

[p0057-l0017] [10.0pt] prompts. Manim (https://github.com/ManimCommunity/manim) is an open
[p0057-l0018] [10.0pt] source Python animation engine for explanatory math videos—it creates precise
[p0057-l0019] [10.0pt] animations programmatically. Figure 3.1 shows an example of Manim code and its

[p0057-l0021] [9.0pt] 36

[p0058-l0001] [9.0pt] 37
[p0058-l0002] [9.0pt] Data preparation
[p0058-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 3.1  An example of Manim code (bottom) and the corresponding rendering (top)
[p0058-l0004] [10.0pt] I chose GPT-2 small as a baseline not only because it can’t produce Manim code, but
[p0058-l0005] [10.0pt] also to show that you can start with a small model and a high-quality, domain-specific
[p0058-l0006] [10.0pt] dataset—even a relatively small one—and still specialize it for a task and achieve good
[p0058-l0007] [10.0pt] performance. A companion Colab notebook contains the full source code from this
[p0058-l0008] [10.0pt] chapter. Hardware acceleration (GPU, free tier) is required.

[p0059-l0030] [12.5pt] 3.2
[p0059-l0031] [12.5pt] Fine-tuning
[p0059-l0032] [10.0pt] To fine-tune the model, we’ll use Hugging Face’s Transformers library, introduced
[p0059-l0033] [10.0pt] in chapter 2, along with Optuna (https://optuna.org/) for hyperparameter search.
[p0059-l0034] [10.0pt] This process involves systematically exploring the most suitable set of hyperparameters
[p0059-l0035] [10.0pt] that can elevate the performance of a model. Hyperparameters, distinct from model
[p0059-l0036] [10.0pt] parameters, aren’t inherently learned during the training phase. Instead, they’re pre­
[p0059-l0037] [10.0pt] determined. Their precise configuration can profoundly influence a model’s perfor­
[p0059-l0038] [10.0pt] mance, bridging the gap between an average model and one that excels. Optuna is
[p0059-l0039] [10.0pt] an ML framework-agnostic, open source Python library for automatic hyperparameter

[p0060-l0005] [10.0pt] ies, we’ll use it as the search backend without working directly with its API.

[p0061-l0021] [10.0pt] We’ll define the search space for hyperparameter tuning as follows:
[p0061-l0022] [8.0pt] def hp_space(trial):
[p0061-l0023] [8.0pt]     return {
[p0061-l0024] [8.0pt]         "learning_rate": trial.suggest_float("learning_rate",
[p0061-l0025] [10.0pt]         ➥1e-5, 5e-4, log=True),
[p0061-l0026] [8.0pt]         "per_device_train_batch_size":
[p0061-l0027] [10.0pt]         ➥ trial.suggest_categorical("per_device_train_batch_size",
[p0061-l0028] [10.0pt]         ➥ [2, 4, 8]),
[p0061-l0029] [8.0pt]         "weight_decay": trial.suggest_float("weight_decay", 0.0, 0.3),
[p0061-l0030] [8.0pt]         "num_train_epochs": trial.suggest_int("num_train_epochs", 3, 6),
[p0061-l0031] [8.0pt]         "warmup_steps": trial.suggest_int("warmup_steps", 0, 500),
[p0061-l0032] [8.0pt]         "gradient_accumulation_steps":
[p0061-l0033] [10.0pt]         ➥ trial.suggest_categorical("gradient_accumulation_steps",
[p0061-l0034] [10.0pt]         ➥ [1, 2, 4]),
[p0061-l0035] [8.0pt]     }
[p0061-l0036] [10.0pt] We’ve defined a function that takes a trial object as input, which Optuna will use to
[p0061-l0037] [10.0pt] sample hyperparameter values. In the body of the hp_space function, we specify value
[p0061-l0038] [10.0pt] ranges to define the search space. The hyperparameters are the learning rate, batch
[p0061-l0039] [10.0pt] size per device, weight decay, number of training epochs, warmup steps, and gradient
[p0061-l0040] [10.0pt] accumulation steps. Some ranges were chosen to fit the computational power available
[p0061-l0041] [10.0pt] in the free-tier Colab VM (a single NVIDIA Tesla T4). In other hardware settings, some
[p0061-l0042] [10.0pt] hyperparameters (such as batch size or gradient accumulation steps) may need differ­
[p0061-l0043] [10.0pt] ent values or ranges.
[p0061-l0044] [10.0pt] NOTE  Gradient accumulation steps are the number of mini-batches over
[p0061-l0045] [10.0pt] which gradients are accumulated before the model’s weights are updated. This
[p0061-l0046] [10.0pt] enables a larger effective batch size without exceeding GPU memory limits,
[p0061-l0047] [10.0pt] which is especially useful when GPU memory is scarce.

[p0065-l0020] [12.5pt] 3.4
[p0065-l0021] [12.5pt] Domain-specific evaluation
[p0065-l0022] [10.0pt] Many statistical metrics can evaluate a language model’s performance at test time. These
[p0065-l0023] [10.0pt] metrics provide useful insights for general-domain tasks, especially those based only on
[p0065-l0024] [10.0pt] unstructured natural language. But when benchmarking on a specific domain—whether
[p0065-l0025] [10.0pt] the model is large, small, or fine-tuned—and the outputs diverge from human language,
[p0065-l0026] [10.0pt] you’ll still need a qualitative review by subject matter experts (SMEs) and sometimes also
[p0065-l0027] [10.0pt] external strategies and tools. Building on the fine-tuned model for the Manim dataset
[p0065-l0028] [10.0pt] we’ve discussed in this chapter, we’ll look at downstream strategies to automate the evalu­
[p0065-l0029] [10.0pt] ation of the generated code and reduce the burden on SMEs.
[p0065-l0030] [10.0pt] In this case, a complete evaluation pipeline could include the following automated
[p0065-l0031] [10.0pt] steps:
[p0065-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Syntax checking—The generated content is Python code, so we must ensure it’s
[p0065-l0033] [10.0pt] syntactically valid.
[p0065-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Static analysis for Manim API usage—Parse the generated code to check for
[p0065-l0035] [10.0pt] expected Manim classes, methods, or function calls.
[p0065-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ After checking that the generated Manim code is syntactically valid, we need to
[p0065-l0037] [10.0pt] verify that its execution completes as expected.
[p0065-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ Optional—Verify the rendering’s correctness (because Manim output is always an
[p0065-l0039] [10.0pt] image or an animation).
[p0065-l0040] [10.0pt] You can implement syntax checking with a custom function using Python’s built-in ast
[p0065-l0041] [10.0pt] package :

[p0066-l0003] [8.0pt] import ast
[p0066-l0004] [8.0pt] def is_syntax_valid(code_str):
[p0066-l0005] [8.0pt]     try:
[p0066-l0006] [8.0pt]         ast.parse(code_str)
[p0066-l0007] [8.0pt]         return True, ""
[p0066-l0008] [8.0pt]     except SyntaxError as e:

[p0066-l0010] [10.0pt] NOTE  Python’s ast package (Abstract Syntax Trees, https://docs.python
[p0066-l0011] [10.0pt] .org/3/library/ast.html) lets you work with Python’s abstract syntax trees.
[p0066-l0012] [10.0pt] We’ll cover it in chapter 7 in the context of Python code generation with
[p0066-l0013] [10.0pt] SLMs.
[p0066-l0014] [10.0pt] The is_syntax_valid function calls ast.parse and returns True if the generated code
[p0066-l0015] [10.0pt] is valid Python syntax, and False otherwise. It checks only syntax, not whether the code
[p0066-l0016] [10.0pt] uses a specific API, but it’s a useful first step to catch invalid model responses before
[p0066-l0017] [10.0pt] running more complex checks.
[p0066-l0018] [10.0pt] The next step is static analysis for the Manim API. It will still use ast, but it will be
[p0066-l0019] [10.0pt] tailored to the package being tested. To do that, we can create a dedicated class that
[p0066-l0020] [10.0pt] extends the ast module’s NodeVisitor:
[p0066-l0021] [8.0pt] from ast import NodeVisitor
[p0066-l0022] [8.0pt] class ManimCodeAnalyzer(ast.NodeVisitor):
[p0066-l0023] [8.0pt]     def __init__(self):
[p0066-l0024] [8.0pt]         self.imports_manim = False
[p0066-l0025] [8.0pt]         self.scene_subclass_names = []
[p0066-l0026] [8.0pt]         self.play_calls = 0
[p0066-l0027] [8.0pt]         self.create_calls = 0
[p0066-l0028] [8.0pt]         self.errors = []
[p0066-l0029] [10.0pt] This class includes several utility functions that override the parent class’s visit method
[p0066-l0030] [10.0pt] and must be named with the visit_ prefix. The first verifies whether the Manim pack­
[p0066-l0031] [10.0pt] age is imported directly in the generated code:
[p0066-l0032] [8.0pt] def visit_Import(self, node):
[p0066-l0033] [8.0pt]     for alias in node.names:
[p0066-l0034] [8.0pt]         if alias.name == "manim":
[p0066-l0035] [8.0pt]             self.imports_manim = True
[p0066-l0036] [8.0pt]     self.generic_visit(node)
[p0066-l0037] [10.0pt] Another function will check whether Manim elements are imported via from ... import:
[p0066-l0038] [8.0pt] def visit_ImportFrom(self, node):
[p0066-l0039] [8.0pt]     if node.module and node.module.startswith("manim"):
[p0066-l0040] [8.0pt]         self.imports_manim = True
[p0066-l0041] [8.0pt]     self.generic_visit(node)

[p0067-l0003] [10.0pt] Manim programs are usually defined as a Scene class (or subclass). It’s useful to add a
[p0067-l0004] [10.0pt] function that checks whether a generated class is a Scene or a subclass of Scene:
[p0067-l0005] [8.0pt] def visit_ClassDef(self, node):
[p0067-l0006] [8.0pt]     for base in node.bases:
[p0067-l0007] [8.0pt]         if isinstance(base, ast.Name) and base.id == "Scene":
[p0067-l0008] [8.0pt]             self.scene_subclass_names.append(node.name)
[p0067-l0009] [8.0pt]         elif isinstance(base, ast.Attribute):
[p0067-l0010] [8.0pt]             if base.attr == "Scene":
[p0067-l0011] [8.0pt]                 self.scene_subclass_names.append(node.name)
[p0067-l0012] [8.0pt]     self.generic_visit(node)
[p0067-l0013] [10.0pt] Finally, we need a function that counts calls to the play method in our Scene subclass
[p0067-l0014] [10.0pt] and Manim Create initializations:
[p0067-l0015] [8.0pt] def visit_Call(self, node):
[p0067-l0016] [8.0pt]     if isinstance(node.func, ast.Attribute):
[p0067-l0017] [8.0pt]         if (isinstance(node.func.value, ast.Name) and
[p0067-l0018] [10.0pt]         ➥node.func.value.id == "self"
[p0067-l0019] [8.0pt]             and node.func.attr == "play"):
[p0067-l0020] [8.0pt]             self.play_calls += 1
[p0067-l0021] [8.0pt]     if isinstance(node.func, ast.Name) and node.func.id == "Create":
[p0067-l0022] [8.0pt]         self.create_calls += 1
[p0067-l0023] [8.0pt]     self.generic_visit(node)
[p0067-l0024] [10.0pt] Now we can define a function that uses the ManimCodeAnalyzer class:
[p0067-l0025] [8.0pt] def analyze_manim_code(code_str):
[p0067-l0026] [8.0pt]     analyzer = ManimCodeAnalyzer()
[p0067-l0027] [10.0pt] analyze_manim_code first checks the input code’s Python syntax:
[p0067-l0028] [8.0pt] try:

[p0067-l0030] [8.0pt] except SyntaxError as e:
[p0067-l0031] [8.0pt]     return {
[p0067-l0032] [8.0pt]         "syntax_valid": False,

[p0067-l0034] [8.0pt]         "imports_manim": False,
[p0067-l0035] [8.0pt]         "scene_subclass_names": [],

[p0067-l0037] [8.0pt]         "create_calls": 0,
[p0067-l0038] [8.0pt]     }
[p0067-l0039] [10.0pt] If the Python code isn’t valid, execution stops, and the function returns insights about

[p0070-l0016] [10.0pt] Running evaluate_manim_code also saves the generated scene or animation as a local
[p0070-l0017] [10.0pt] MP4 file. If your test dataset includes reference videos or images, you can extract
[p0070-l0018] [10.0pt] frames or thumbnails, compute similarity metrics such as SSIM or LPIPS between the
[p0070-l0019] [10.0pt] generated and reference images, and compare them against quality thresholds. This
[p0070-l0020] [10.0pt] validation is out of scope for this chapter, but you can implement it by checking these
[p0070-l0021] [10.0pt] metrics against your chosen thresholds.
[p0070-l0022] [10.0pt] NOTE  The structural similarity index measure (SSIM) predicts the perceived
[p0070-l0023] [10.0pt] quality of digital TV, cinematic images, and other digital images and videos.
[p0070-l0024] [10.0pt] It also measures similarity between two images. The scikit-image Python
[p0070-l0025] [10.0pt] image-processing package (https://scikit-image.org/) provides a ready-to-use
[p0070-l0026] [10.0pt] implementation. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS) is a per­
[p0070-l0027] [10.0pt] ceptual similarity metric that uses deep-network activations to measure the dis­
[p0070-l0028] [10.0pt] tance between image patches. It can also serve as a perceptual loss for image
[p0070-l0029] [10.0pt] optimization.
[p0070-l0030] [10.0pt] Here are some final recommendations for validating execution and rendering correct­
[p0070-l0031] [10.0pt] ness in tasks like these:
[p0070-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Sandboxing—Running arbitrary generated code is risky. Use sandboxing tools (for
[p0070-l0033] [10.0pt] example, Docker containers or restricted environments) to isolate execution.
[p0070-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Timeouts—Set timeouts to prevent hangs or infinite loops.
[p0070-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Resource limits—Limit CPU, GPU, and memory usage during rendering to save
[p0070-l0036] [10.0pt] time and money.
[p0070-l0037] [10.0pt] That completes our introduction to tuning SLMs for specific domains and tasks. In the
[p0070-l0038] [10.0pt] next chapter, we’ll shift our focus to the book’s core topics: SLM optimization, com­
[p0070-l0039] [10.0pt] pression, and deployment in hardware-constrained environments.
