[p0071-l0003] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0071-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ GPT-2 small models can be fine-tuned for domain-specific tasks with datasets of a
[p0071-l0005] [10.0pt] few hundred samples.
[p0071-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Manim is a Python animation engine for creating mathematical visualizations
[p0071-l0007] [10.0pt] with code.
[p0071-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Before tokenizing for language model training, concatenate the instruction and
[p0071-l0009] [10.0pt] output fields during preprocessing.
[p0071-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Optuna automates hyperparameter searches and integrates with the Hugging
[p0071-l0011] [10.0pt] Face Transformers library.
[p0071-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Model initialization functions create a fresh model instance for each hyperpa­
[p0071-l0013] [10.0pt] rameter trial during search.
[p0071-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ Training arguments set evaluation strategies, logging intervals, checkpoint sav­
[p0071-l0015] [10.0pt] ing, and mixed-precision training.
[p0071-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Early stopping callbacks prevent overfitting by stopping training when the valida­
[p0071-l0017] [10.0pt] tion loss stops improving.
[p0071-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Hyperparameter search spaces define ranges for the learning rate, batch size,
[p0071-l0019] [10.0pt] weight decay, number of epochs, and other parameters.
[p0071-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ You can use Python’s ast module to validate generated code syntax.
[p0071-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Static analysis verifies domain-specific API usage patterns in generated code.
[p0071-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Custom NodeVisitor classes extend ast functionality to analyze framework-­
[p0071-l0023] [10.0pt] specific code structures.
[p0071-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Execution testing runs generated code via command-line tools to verify func­
[p0071-l0025] [10.0pt] tional correctness.
[p0071-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ Rendering validation compares generated outputs to reference images via simi­
[p0071-l0027] [10.0pt] larity metrics.
[p0071-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Sandboxing and timeouts improve safety when running generated code
[p0071-l0029] [10.0pt] automatically.
[p0071-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Small language models perform well on specialized tasks with curated,
[p0071-l0031] [10.0pt] domain-specific datasets.
[p0071-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Automated evaluation pipelines reduce the burden on subject matter experts for
[p0071-l0033] [10.0pt] assessing code quality.

[p0073-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 4  Running inference
[p0073-l0003] [10.0pt] Our reference open source model is GPT-Neo large (2.7 billion trainable parame­
[p0073-l0004] [10.0pt] ters, https://huggingface.co/EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B) from the EleutherAI research
[p0073-l0005] [10.0pt] group (https://www.eleuther.ai/). Although GPT-Neo is no longer actively developed
[p0073-l0006] [10.0pt] and has been replaced by newer models, it remains a useful example for explaining
[p0073-l0007] [10.0pt] the topics in this chapter because it is a Transformer model that replicates the GPT-3
[p0073-l0008] [10.0pt] architecture. The topics in this chapter are not limited to GPT-Neo; they apply to any
[p0073-l0009] [10.0pt] LLM available through the Hugging Face Transformers and Accelerate (https://
[p0073-l0010] [10.0pt] github.com/huggingface/accelerate) libraries (both used in this example) and to
[p0073-l0011] [10.0pt] domain-specific models trained on your own data. The code examples in this chapter
[p0073-l0012] [10.0pt] are also provided in the two companion Colab notebooks.
[p0073-l0013] [10.5pt] 4.1.1
[p0073-l0014] [10.5pt] Text completion
[p0073-l0015] [10.0pt] You can load the GPT-Neo model and its tokenizer the usual way:
[p0073-l0016] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0073-l0017] [8.0pt] from transformers import GPTNeoForCausalLM, GPT2Tokenizer
[p0073-l0018] [8.0pt] device = torch.device("cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu")
[p0073-l0019] [8.0pt] model_id = "EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B"
[p0073-l0020] [8.0pt] tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0073-l0021] [8.0pt] model = GPTNeoForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, device_map="auto")
[p0073-l0022] [8.0pt] model.to(device)
[p0073-l0023] [10.0pt] The pretrained model (available on the Hugging Face Hub) is loaded onto a GPU to
[p0073-l0024] [10.0pt] speed up inference. GPTNeoForCausalLM, a specialized PreTrainedModel class for GPT-
[p0073-l0025] [10.0pt] Neo, is available in the Transformers library, and the tokenizer can be downloaded via
[p0073-l0026] [10.0pt] the GPT2Tokenizer class. We set device_map to auto so the Accelerate library can run
[p0073-l0027] [10.0pt] inference even when the model doesn’t fully fit on the GPU. Accelerate places as many
[p0073-l0028] [10.0pt] layers as possible on the fastest devices (here, a single GPU) and offloads the rest to
[p0073-l0029] [10.0pt] the CPU—or even disk if RAM is limited. This split is transparent to developers, so the
[p0073-l0030] [10.0pt] inference code stays the same. In this example, the model is loaded in float32 type
[p0073-l0031] [10.0pt] (the default) because the free-tier Colab GPU can fit it in that format. In other envi­
[p0073-l0032] [10.0pt] ronments, you’ll likely need lower precision.
[p0073-l0033] [10.0pt] To estimate the memory needed to load a model, Accelerate also provides a
[p0073-l0034] [10.0pt] command-­line tool. For GPT-Neo 2.7B, it looks like this:
[p0073-l0035] [8.0pt] accelerate estimate-memory EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B
[p0073-l0036] [10.0pt] Pass the model ID from the Hugging Face Hub to the command (that’s the only
[p0073-l0037] [10.0pt] required argument). The command returns the download size for each available pre­
[p0073-l0038] [10.0pt] cision type:
[p0073-l0039] [8.0pt] Loading pretrained config for `EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B` from `transformers`...

[p0077-l0024] [10.5pt] 4.1.3
[p0077-l0025] [10.5pt] Code generation
[p0077-l0026] [10.0pt] The generated output isn’t limited to natural language. Trained on the Pile dataset,
[p0077-l0027] [10.0pt] which includes many samples from GitHub repositories, the model can generate code
[p0077-l0028] [10.0pt] too. The prompt must follow this format:
[p0077-l0029] [8.0pt] Instruction: <Your instructions to generate the desired code> Answer:
[p0077-l0030] [10.0pt] Let’s ask the model to write a function to reverse a list of integers (even though Python
[p0077-l0031] [10.0pt] lists already support reversing):
[p0077-l0032] [8.0pt] prompt = """Instruction: Generate a Python function that lets you reverse a
[p0077-l0033] [8.0pt] list of integers.
[p0077-l0034] [8.0pt] Answer: """
[p0077-l0035] [8.0pt] input_ids = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").input_ids.to(device)

=== PDF page 78 / printed label 57 ===
[p0078-l0001] [9.0pt] 57
[p0078-l0002] [9.0pt] How to generate content
[p0078-l0003] [10.0pt] Code generation can be performed just like the other use cases:
[p0078-l0004] [8.0pt] generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids,
[p0078-l0005] [8.0pt]                                do_sample=True,
[p0078-l0006] [8.0pt]                                temperature=0.9,
[p0078-l0007] [8.0pt]                                max_length=200,
[p0078-l0008] [8.0pt]                                pad_token_id=50256
[p0078-l0009] [8.0pt]                                )
[p0078-l0010] [8.0pt] generated_text = tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0])
[p0078-l0011] [10.0pt] The generated content will look like the following; it includes the input and is trun­
[p0078-l0012] [10.0pt] cated to the first 200 tokens because the generation request sets max_length:
[p0078-l0013] [8.0pt] Instruction: Generate a Python function that lets you reverse a list of integers.
[p0078-l0014] [8.0pt] Answer:
[p0078-l0015] [8.0pt] def reverse(x):
[p0078-l0016] [8.0pt]         return x[::-1]
[p0078-l0017] [8.0pt] A:
[p0078-l0018] [8.0pt] The way I would do it differently is to create a wrapper function that looks
[p0078-l0019] [8.0pt] similar to this for one list of integers:
[p0078-l0020] [8.0pt] def reverse(aList):
[p0078-l0021] [8.0pt]     new_aList = [int(i) for i in aList]
[p0078-l0022] [8.0pt]     new_aList = new_aList[::-1]
[p0078-l0023] [8.0pt]     return new_aList
[p0078-l0024] [8.0pt] And then iterate over the list to reverse it.
[p0078-l0025] [8.0pt] Def reverse_list(aList):
[p0078-l0026] [8.0pt]     tmp = None
[p0078-l0027] [8.0pt]     for x in aList:
[p0078-l0028] [8.0pt]         if tmp is None:
[p0078-l0029] [8.0pt]             tmp = x
[p0078-l0030] [10.0pt] Code generated by this model always needs developer review. You may need to lint or
[p0078-l0031] [10.0pt] refine it, and other models are better at producing working code (as will be discussed in
[p0078-l0032] [10.0pt] later chapters). This example simply illustrates the possibilities of using a single LLM.
[p0078-l0033] [10.0pt] Note that GPT-Neo and other open source pretrained models aren’t meant to be
[p0078-l0034] [10.0pt] used as is; they typically require fine-tuning or techniques like LoRA or RAG. If you
[p0078-l0035] [10.0pt] try to replicate this chapter’s examples without that, expect hallucinations or lower-­
[p0078-l0036] [10.0pt] quality results. For now, we’ll pretend we’re working with a model we’ve already custom­
[p0078-l0037] [10.0pt] ized. My goal here is to show you what happens behind the high-level Python inference
[p0078-l0038] [10.0pt] API—these are details you’ll need to keep in mind when deciding on an optimization
[p0078-l0039] [10.0pt] or quantization strategy.
[p0078-l0040] [10.5pt] 4.1.4
[p0078-l0041] [10.5pt] Evaluating the generated content
[p0078-l0042] [10.0pt] Before deploying an LLM to production, it’s good practice to evaluate it to measure
[p0078-l0043] [10.0pt] output quality and decide what to do next (mitigate or deploy). LLM evaluation is

=== PDF page 79 / printed label 58 ===
[p0079-l0001] [9.0pt] 58
[p0079-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 4  Running inference
[p0079-l0003] [10.0pt] tedious and complex, with challenges that vary by model architecture and the task the
[p0079-l0004] [10.0pt] model was trained for.
[p0079-l0005] [10.0pt] The Evaluation Harness library (https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation
[p0079-l0006] [10.0pt] -­harness) from EleutherAI, also known as LM-Eval, offers a unified way to test LLMs
[p0079-l0007] [10.0pt] across many evaluation tasks. It’s implemented in Python and is open source (MIT
[p0079-l0008] [10.0pt] license). It includes more than 200 built-in tasks and lets you create custom tasks on
[p0079-l0009] [10.0pt] third-party or private data. In addition to its task coverage, it supports several Trans­
[p0079-l0010] [10.0pt] former model sources: open source models from the Hugging Face Hub (via the Trans­
[p0079-l0011] [10.0pt] formers library), commercial models via the OpenAI API (requires an OpenAI key) and
[p0079-l0012] [10.0pt] other providers, models in Neural Magic’s SparseZoo repository (via the DeepSparse
[p0079-l0013] [10.0pt] OSS library), and GPTQ-, GGUF-, or GGML-quantized models (covered in chapters 6
[p0079-l0014] [10.0pt] and 9).
[p0079-l0015] [10.0pt] Depending on the task, different evaluation metrics are supported. Because the
[p0079-l0016] [10.0pt] framework is open source and flexible, you can easily extend it and tailor existing tasks.
[p0079-l0017] [10.0pt] Task versioning is another key feature, ensuring reproducibility even after tasks are
[p0079-l0018] [10.0pt] updated.
[p0079-l0019] [10.0pt] LM-Eval isn’t currently available through a Python package installer, so you must
[p0079-l0020] [10.0pt] install it from source. Clone the official GitHub repository, and install it with pip
[p0079-l0021] [10.0pt] (Python 3.8+ required):
[p0079-l0022] [8.0pt] git clone https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness
[p0079-l0023] [8.0pt] cd lm-evaluation-harness
[p0079-l0024] [8.0pt] pip install -e .
[p0079-l0025] [10.0pt] You’re now ready to run evaluation tests. To evaluate a model hosted on the Hugging
[p0079-l0026] [10.0pt] Face Hub for a given task, use the provided main.py script:
[p0079-l0027] [8.0pt] python main.py \
[p0079-l0028] [8.0pt]     --model hf-causal \
[p0079-l0029] [8.0pt]     --model_args pretrained=EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B,dtype="float16" \
[p0079-l0030] [8.0pt]     --tasks wikitext \
[p0079-l0031] [8.0pt]     --device cuda:0
[p0079-l0032] [10.0pt] The following options can be set in the script:
[p0079-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ model—The model type.
[p0079-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ model_args—A list of arguments that specify which model to download from the
[p0079-l0035] [10.0pt] Hub and evaluate. Only pretrained is required, and its value must match the
[p0079-l0036] [10.0pt] exact Hugging Face Hub model ID. We’ll use GPT-Neo 2.7B throughout this
[p0079-l0037] [10.0pt] chapter. You can also pass any other arguments supported by the Transformers
[p0079-l0038] [10.0pt] PreTrainedModel class’s from_pretrained method.
[p0079-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ tasks—A list of evaluation tasks to run.
[p0079-l0040] [10.0pt] ¡ device—The device or devices to use (GPU or CPU). Use hardware acceleration
[p0079-l0041] [10.0pt] for evaluation tests.

[p0080-l0002] [9.0pt] Calculating inference cost
[p0080-l0003] [10.0pt] In the preceding example, the evaluation task is wikitext, one of LM-Eval’s built-in
[p0080-l0004] [10.0pt] tests. It uses 62 samples from a dataset of verified good and featured Wikipedia articles
[p0080-l0005] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/datasets/Salesforce/wikitext) to compute three metrics for
[p0080-l0006] [10.0pt] the model under test: word_perplexity (predictive power), byte_perplexity (how well
[p0080-l0007] [10.0pt] the model predicts the next byte given prior bytes), and bits_per_byte (average bits
[p0080-l0008] [10.0pt] needed to predict the next symbol). LM-Eval can compute additional metrics depend­
[p0080-l0009] [10.0pt] ing on the task; see the official GitHub repository for the current list of tasks and met­
[p0080-l0010] [10.0pt] rics. For the GPT-Neo model on wikitext, the results are as follows:
[p0080-l0011] [8.0pt] hf-causal (pretrained=EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B,dtype=float16), limit: None,
[p0080-l0012] [8.0pt] provide_description: False, num_fewshot: 0, batch_size: None
[p0080-l0013] [8.0pt] |  Task  |Version|    Metric     | Value |   |Stderr|
[p0080-l0014] [8.0pt] |--------|------:|---------------|------:|---|------|
[p0080-l0015] [8.0pt] |wikitext|      1|word_perplexity|13.9382|   |      |
[p0080-l0016] [8.0pt] |        |       |byte_perplexity| 1.6367|   |      |
[p0080-l0017] [8.0pt] |        |       |bits_per_byte  | 0.7108|   |      |
[p0080-l0018] [10.0pt] We’ll reference LM-Eval and other libraries when evaluating models.
[p0080-l0019] [12.5pt] 4.2
[p0080-l0020] [12.5pt] Calculating inference cost
[p0080-l0021] [10.0pt] Deploying an LLM to production to handle multiple inference requests costs money.
[p0080-l0022] [10.0pt] In the previous section, you learned that larger models cost more because their weights
[p0080-l0023] [10.0pt] require more GPU memory, and you often need extra headroom to maintain perfor­
[p0080-l0024] [10.0pt] mance. You also saw a CLI tool in the Accelerate library that estimates the required
[p0080-l0025] [10.0pt] memory. It’s worth understanding how it makes that calculation so you can estimate
[p0080-l0026] [10.0pt] memory needs when serving LLMs outside the Transformers library and make other
[p0080-l0027] [10.0pt] sizing decisions. Model documentation for available pretrained open source models
[p0080-l0028] [10.0pt] usually lists the number of trainable parameters, but for deployment, you need the
[p0080-l0029] [10.0pt] model’s in-memory size so you can decide which GPU (or combination of GPUs) you’ll
[p0080-l0030] [10.0pt] need. The formula for estimating inference memory (in GB) is
[p0080-l0031] [10.0pt] where
[p0080-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ 4 is the number of bytes for each trainable parameter.
[p0080-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ P is the model’s total number of trainable parameters (in billions).
[p0080-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ F is the number of bits for the chosen precision (32 for FP32, 16 for FP16, 8 for
[p0080-l0035] [10.0pt] INT8).
[p0080-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ 1.2 is a factor that includes an average 20% overhead due to several factors
[p0080-l0037] [10.0pt] (detailed later in this chapter).
[p0080-l0038] [10.0pt] Returning to our GPT-Neo example from section 4.1, the model has 2.7 billion param­
[p0080-l0039] [10.0pt] eters. We loaded it in FP32, so applying the preceding formula gives us 12.96 GB.

=== PDF page 81 / printed label 60 ===
[p0081-l0001] [9.0pt] 60
[p0081-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 4  Running inference
[p0081-l0003] [10.0pt] Loading the same model in FP16 reduces this to 5.4 GB. If we run the same calculation
[p0081-l0004] [10.0pt] for a different model, such as Mistral 7B (https://huggingface.co/mistralai/­Mistral
[p0081-l0005] [10.0pt] -7B-v0.3), it requires about 33.6 GB of GPU memory in FP32, or about 16.2 GB in
[p0081-l0006] [10.0pt] FP16. Most open source Transformers models are trained in mixed precision (FP16
[p0081-l0007] [10.0pt] + FP32 or BF16 + FP32), which reduces the memory needed for training and, as the
[p0081-l0008] [10.0pt] formula shows, for inference too, without a major performance loss when casting an
[p0081-l0009] [10.0pt] LLM from FP32 to FP16 (and to INT8, as you’ll see in subsequent chapters). So if you
[p0081-l0010] [10.0pt] need to fit within your hardware constraints, it’s fine to load a pretrained model in
[p0081-l0011] [10.0pt] FP16.
[p0081-l0012] [10.0pt] An LLM’s size is one factor to consider when deciding whether to deploy it to pro­
[p0081-l0013] [10.0pt] duction, but it’s not the only one. There are several other important factors:
[p0081-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ Full GPU power utilization—Even if GPUs are available in your environment (we’ll
[p0081-l0015] [10.0pt] also cover CPU-only setups later), deploying a model and running inference
[p0081-l0016] [10.0pt] doesn’t automatically use all GPU resources—or use them efficiently. Techniques
[p0081-l0017] [10.0pt] can help you better use the available hardware acceleration.
[p0081-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Time to first token (TTFT)—How quickly does a user see the model’s first output
[p0081-l0019] [10.0pt] token after entering a prompt?
[p0081-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Time per output token (TPOT)—How long does it take to generate an output token
[p0081-l0021] [10.0pt] for each active user?
[p0081-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Latency—How long does it take to generate a complete response for a user? This
[p0081-l0023] [10.0pt] depends on TTFT and TPOT.
[p0081-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Throughput—How many output tokens can the serving system generate per sec­
[p0081-l0025] [10.0pt] ond for all users and requests?
[p0081-l0026] [10.0pt] Optimization and quantization techniques (the core topic of this book) can reduce
[p0081-l0027] [10.0pt] the hardware requirements for LLM serving and help meet latency and throughput
[p0081-l0028] [10.0pt] targets. But there are also other challenges, validations, and factors to consider before
[p0081-l0029] [10.0pt] and after optimization and quantization. We’ll look at those next.
[p0081-l0030] [12.5pt] 4.3
[p0081-l0031] [12.5pt] Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
[p0081-l0032] [10.0pt] The metrics in the previous section give you a clear picture of how well your LLM’s
[p0081-l0033] [10.0pt] inference serving performs, helping you spot areas for improvement that can reduce
[p0081-l0034] [10.0pt] costs (use only the computational power you need, get the most from it, and keep users
[p0081-l0035] [10.0pt] engaged). Next, we’ll look at what you can do up front to address common inference-­
[p0081-l0036] [10.0pt] serving challenges. Although this section uses GPT-Neo as an example, the same con­
[p0081-l0037] [10.0pt] siderations apply to other LLM architectures.
[p0081-l0038] [10.5pt] 4.3.1
[p0081-l0039] [10.5pt] Getting the most from your GPU
[p0081-l0040] [10.0pt] The companion code for this chapter is a Colab notebook that uses hardware accelera­
[p0081-l0041] [10.0pt] tion (an NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU, https://www.nvidia.com/en-us/data-center/tesla-t4/,
[p0081-l0042] [10.0pt] also available in Colab’s free tier).

=== PDF page 82 / printed label 61 ===
[p0082-l0001] [9.0pt] 61
[p0082-l0002] [9.0pt] Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
[p0082-l0003] [10.0pt] When choosing a GPU, we focus on three characteristics: compute throughput,
[p0082-l0004] [10.0pt] memory, and memory bandwidth. According to the T4’s datasheet, it provides 65
[p0082-l0005] [10.0pt] TFLOPS (tera floating-point operations per second) in full (FP32) or half precision
[p0082-l0006] [10.0pt] (FP16), 16 GB of memory, and 300 GB/sec of memory bandwidth (that is, up to 300 GB
[p0082-l0007] [10.0pt] of data can move from GPU memory to on-chip shared [SRAM] memory per second).
[p0082-l0008] [10.0pt] For GPT-Neo, memory isn’t a concern: in half precision it requires 12.96 GB, leaving
[p0082-l0009] [10.0pt] room for other inference-time operations.
[p0082-l0010] [10.0pt] Using the remaining specs, we can compute the device’s ops/byte ratio, which is the
[p0082-l0011] [10.0pt] number of floating-point operations (FLOPS) per second per byte of memory accessed.
[p0082-l0012] [10.0pt] We calculate it as follows:
[p0082-l0013] [10.0pt] For the T4 GPU, this value is 216.6 ops/byte. To fully use its computational power,
[p0082-l0014] [10.0pt] we must perform 216.6 floating-point operations for every byte read from memory.
[p0082-l0015] [10.0pt] At runtime, if we observe fewer than 216.6 operations per byte, our system is memory
[p0082-l0016] [10.0pt] bound: performance is limited by the data-transfer rate. Conversely, if we need to per­
[p0082-l0017] [10.0pt] form more than 216.6 operations per byte but can’t, our system is compute bound:
[p0082-l0018] [10.0pt] performance is limited by available compute units, not memory. Our goal is to deter­
[p0082-l0019] [10.0pt] mine which case applies on our hardware and optimize accordingly. To do that, we
[p0082-l0020] [10.0pt] need to compute the model’s arithmetic intensity: the number of compute operations
[p0082-l0021] [10.0pt] divided by the number of bytes accessed. This metric is hardware-agnostic. Next, we
[p0082-l0022] [10.0pt] need to identify which model layers demand the most computational power. In Trans­
[p0082-l0023] [10.0pt] former architectures, the attention layers are prime candidates because weighting
[p0082-l0024] [10.0pt] each next-token prediction based on the relevance of previous tokens is computation­
[p0082-l0025] [10.0pt] ally intensive.
[p0082-l0026] [10.0pt] Generative Transformer inference sampling has two phases: prefill and autoregres­
[p0082-l0027] [10.0pt] sive sampling. In the prefill phase, the model ingests the prompt tokens in parallel
[p0082-l0028] [10.0pt] and populates the key–value (KV) cache. This cache stores the model’s state inside the
[p0082-l0029] [10.0pt] attention operation. No token generation happens in this phase. In the autoregressive
[p0082-l0030] [10.0pt] sampling phase, the model uses the state in the KV cache to sample and decode the
[p0082-l0031] [10.0pt] next token. The cache costs storage (GPU VRAM, or CPU RAM when no GPU is avail­
[p0082-l0032] [10.0pt] able), but it avoids recomputing attention on all prior tokens at each step. Without the
[p0082-l0033] [10.0pt] KV cache, each successive token would take longer to sample because all previously
[p0082-l0034] [10.0pt] seen tokens would need to pass through the model again. The generate function in the
[p0082-l0035] [10.0pt] Transformers library’s PreTrainedModel classes (encoder-decoder and decoder-only)
[p0082-l0036] [10.0pt] exposes a use_cache parameter to enable KV caching; it defaults to True. Still, when
[p0082-l0037] [10.0pt] you import third-party code, verify that KV caching is actually enabled—frameworks
[p0082-l0038] [10.0pt] other than Transformers may not turn it on by default. Figure 4.1 summarizes how KV
[p0082-l0039] [10.0pt] caching works.

[p0084-l0012] [10.0pt] Now let’s calculate the arithmetic intensity for our use case. The formula for multi-
[p0084-l0013] [10.0pt] head attention is as follows:
[p0084-l0014] [10.0pt] where
[p0084-l0015] [10.0pt] In this equation, Q, K, and V are matrices used to compute attention: Q represents the
[p0084-l0016] [10.0pt] query tokens, and K and V represent the keys and values (as discussed earlier in the
[p0084-l0017] [10.0pt] context of the KV cache). We can express the preceding formula with the following
[p0084-l0018] [10.0pt] pseudocode algorithm, which repeats the same basic steps—load values from memory,
[p0084-l0019] [10.0pt] compute, and store the results back in memory:
[p0084-l0020] [8.0pt] Require: Matrices Q, K, V ∈ RNxd in memory.
[p0084-l0021] [8.0pt] Step 1: Load Q, K from memory, then compute S = QKT and write it to memory.
[p0084-l0022] [8.0pt] Step 2: Read S from memory, then compute P = softmax(S) and write it to memory.
[p0084-l0023] [8.0pt] Step 3: Load P and V from memory, then compute O = P x V and write it to memory.
[p0084-l0024] [10.0pt] The sqrt(dk) term in the previous equation can be ignored because it’s minor compared
[p0084-l0025] [10.0pt] with the others. For completeness, N is the model’s context window (2048 for GPT-
[p0084-l0026] [10.0pt] Neo), and dk is the dimension of a single attention head (128 for GPT-Neo). The Q, K,
[p0084-l0027] [10.0pt] and V matrices are 2048 × 128; S and P are 2048 × 2048; and O is 2048 × 128. Arithmetic
[p0084-l0028] [10.0pt] intensity depends on total memory movement and total computation. For the three
[p0084-l0029] [10.0pt] operations in each step of the algorithm, the formulas to compute these values are as
[p0084-l0030] [10.0pt] follows (the first is in bytes; the second is in FLOPS):
[p0084-l0031] [8.0pt] total_memory_movement
[p0084-l0032] [8.0pt]     = (2 * 4 * (N * d)) + (4 * (N * N)) + (4 * ((N*N) + (N * d))) + (4 * (N *
[p0084-l0033] [8.0pt] N)) + (4 * (N * N)) + (4 * (N * d))

[p0085-l0001] [9.0pt] 64
[p0085-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 4  Running inference
[p0085-l0003] [10.0pt] and
[p0085-l0004] [8.0pt] total_compute
[p0085-l0005] [8.0pt]     = ((2 * d) * (N * N)) + (3 * (N * N)) + ((2 * N) * (N * d))
[p0085-l0006] [10.0pt] The arithmetic intensity can then be calculated this way:
[p0085-l0007] [8.0pt]  arithmetic_intensity
[p0085-l0008] [8.0pt]     = total compute / total memory movement
[p0085-l0009] [10.0pt] For GPT-Neo, these metrics are
[p0085-l0010] [8.0pt] total_memory_movement = 71303168
[p0085-l0011] [8.0pt] total_compute = 2160066560
[p0085-l0012] [8.0pt] arithmetic_intensity = 30.29 ops/byte
[p0085-l0013] [10.0pt] Given the ops/byte ratio we calculated for this device (216.6 ops/byte on a T4 GPU),
[p0085-l0014] [10.0pt] our system appears memory-bound: in the time it takes to move one byte from memory
[p0085-l0015] [10.0pt] to compute, the GPU could have done many more calculations. In other words, we’re
[p0085-l0016] [10.0pt] not fully using the available GPU compute. Can we fix this? The next section answers
[p0085-l0017] [10.0pt] that question.
[p0085-l0018] [10.5pt] 4.3.2
[p0085-l0019] [10.5pt] Batching
[p0085-l0020] [10.0pt] You can also pass an LLM a batch of prompts and generate responses for all of them
[p0085-l0021] [10.0pt] at once. We can use static batching (multiple prompts from the same request), or, to
[p0085-l0022] [10.0pt] reduce memory-boundedness, we can use dynamic batching: instead of starting genera­
[p0085-l0023] [10.0pt] tion immediately for each incoming request, queue requests, and run them together in
[p0085-l0024] [10.0pt] a single pass. This reuses model state already loaded in GPU memory across the batch,
[p0085-l0025] [10.0pt] increasing arithmetic intensity (more compute per memory access) and making the
[p0085-l0026] [10.0pt] workload less memory-bound. The next question is how large the batch can be, which
[p0085-l0027] [10.0pt] depends on available GPU memory. In our GPT-Neo example, FP32 precision requires
[p0085-l0028] [10.0pt] 12.96 GB; on a T4 GPU with 16 GB of VRAM, that leaves 3.04 GB theoretically avail­
[p0085-l0029] [10.0pt] able. Let’s calculate how many sequences can fit in that spare memory. We also need to
[p0085-l0030] [10.0pt] account for the KV cache. During the prefill phase, the cache is populated with the input
[p0085-l0031] [10.0pt] sequence and stores the K and V matrices used in the attention computation. First, we
[p0085-l0032] [10.0pt] need the KV-cache size for our case, which we can compute with the following formula:
[p0085-l0033] [8.0pt] kv_cache_size = (2 * num_bytes * n_layers * model_dim)
[p0085-l0034] [10.0pt] This is measured in bytes/token. In our example, we use 4 bytes (full precision), 24
[p0085-l0035] [10.0pt] attention layers, and a model dimension of 2,048. That gives a KV cache size of 393,216
[p0085-l0036] [10.0pt] bytes/token (about 0.00039 GB/token), which translates to the following:
[p0085-l0037] [8.0pt] kv_cache_tokens
[p0085-l0038] [8.0pt]     = 3.04 GB / 0.00039 GB/token
[p0085-l0039] [8.0pt]     = 7795 tokens

=== PDF page 86 / printed label 65 ===
[p0086-l0001] [9.0pt] 65
[p0086-l0002] [9.0pt] Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
[p0086-l0003] [10.0pt] With GPT-Neo’s standard sequence length of 2,048 tokens, our example has enough
[p0086-l0004] [10.0pt] capacity to handle a batch of three sequences at once. During inference, batching
[p0086-l0005] [10.0pt] three requests to fill the KV cache will increase throughput.
[p0086-l0006] [10.0pt] Batching helps in some cases but hurts in others. It’s a good strategy when you’re using
[p0086-l0007] [10.0pt] LLMs to process a large document queue asynchronously, because throughput is much
[p0086-l0008] [10.0pt] higher than when processing items one by one. You can also schedule inference calls to fill
[p0086-l0009] [10.0pt] batches quickly and keep added latency low. But for chatbot-style systems, where latency
[p0086-l0010] [10.0pt] must be minimal, batching is usually a poor fit because queuing increases the response
[p0086-l0011] [10.0pt] time users feel. In those cases, your main options are to use a GPU with more memory or
[p0086-l0012] [10.0pt] better performance, or to use model quantization (covered starting in chapter 5).
[p0086-l0013] [10.5pt] 4.3.3
[p0086-l0014] [10.5pt] Estimating the generation time
[p0086-l0015] [10.0pt] Given an LLM and one or more GPUs, it can be useful to estimate up front how long
[p0086-l0016] [10.0pt] content generation will take. To do this, we first need to estimate the time to generate
[p0086-l0017] [10.0pt] a single token. We can approximate it by dividing the total number of bytes moved by
[p0086-l0018] [10.0pt] the GPU’s memory bandwidth:
[p0086-l0019] [8.0pt]   time/token = total number of bytes moved/GPU memory bandwidth
[p0086-l0020] [10.0pt] You can estimate the number of bytes moved by multiplying the model’s trainable
[p0086-l0021] [10.0pt] parameters by the bytes per parameter (based on your chosen precision). For our
[p0086-l0022] [10.0pt] GPT-Neo example, the model has 2.7 billion parameters, it’s loaded in full precision
[p0086-l0023] [10.0pt] (4 bytes each), and the T4 GPU has 300 GB/s memory bandwidth, so generating a sin­
[p0086-l0024] [10.0pt] gle token takes roughly 36 ms.
[p0086-l0025] [10.0pt] This isn’t exact: it assumes no on-chip communication during inference, perfect par­
[p0086-l0026] [10.0pt] allelism, and no overhead for a forward pass. A more accurate estimate would include
[p0086-l0027] [10.0pt] the prefill phase. If we batch all prompt tokens into a single forward pass, a formula for
[p0086-l0028] [10.0pt] that metric is shown here:
[p0086-l0029] [8.0pt] prefill time = number of tokens * (total number of bytes moved/ GPU compute
[p0086-l0030] [8.0pt] bandwidth)
[p0086-l0031] [10.0pt] In our GPT-Neo example, assuming 300 tokens and a T4 compute bandwidth of 65
[p0086-l0032] [10.0pt] TFLOPS, the prefill time is about 50 ms. Taking this into account, the total generation
[p0086-l0033] [10.0pt] time is
[p0086-l0034] [8.0pt] total generation time = prefill time + (number of tokens * time/token)
[p0086-l0035] [10.0pt] For our example (300 tokens), that’s 50 + (300 × 36) = 10.85 seconds. We can verify if
[p0086-l0036] [10.0pt] this estimate is accurate or not:
[p0086-l0037] [8.0pt] import time
[p0086-l0038] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0086-l0039] [8.0pt] prompt = "The story so far: in the beginning, the universe was created."

[p0087-l0020] [10.0pt] These observed times also include overhead from other operations beyond the GPU
[p0087-l0021] [10.0pt] computation.
[p0087-l0022] [10.0pt] LLM inference can benefit from techniques such as the following:
[p0087-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Operator fusion—This combines adjacent operators, often improving latency.
[p0087-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Quantization—This compresses an LLM’s weights or activations to use fewer bits.
[p0087-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Compression strategies, such as sparsity (making parts of a model inactive or
[p0087-l0026] [10.0pt] zero-valued to reduce computation) or distillation (training a smaller model
[p0087-l0027] [10.0pt] using a larger one as a “teacher,” to compress knowledge).
[p0087-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Parallelization—Use tensor parallelism across devices or pipeline parallelism for
[p0087-l0029] [10.0pt] larger models.
[p0087-l0030] [10.0pt] The rest of the book covers multiple techniques related to quantization, but it also
[p0087-l0031] [10.0pt] touches on the other areas listed here.
[p0087-l0032] [10.5pt] 4.3.4
[p0087-l0033] [10.5pt] Optimizing GPU use with DeepSpeed
[p0087-l0034] [10.0pt] To reduce compute and memory use—and fit larger models on a single GPU or GPU
[p0087-l0035] [10.0pt] cluster—you can use DeepSpeed (https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed). Deep­
[p0087-l0036] [10.0pt] Speed is an open source library from Microsoft (Apache 2.0 license) for deep learning
[p0087-l0037] [10.0pt] optimization. It makes distributed training and inference easier and more efficient, it
[p0087-l0038] [10.0pt] supports PyTorch, and it integrates with Hugging Face’s Transformers and Accelerate
[p0087-l0039] [10.0pt] libraries. Key features include ZeRO (Zero Redundancy Optimizer, https://arxiv.org/
[p0087-l0040] [10.0pt] abs/1910.02054), mixed-precision training, custom model parallelism, and optimiza­
[p0087-l0041] [10.0pt] tions for low-latency, high-throughput inference. Model parallelism doesn’t just help
[p0087-l0042] [10.0pt] models fit in GPU memory; it can also reduce inference latency for smaller language
[p0087-l0043] [10.0pt] models. DeepSpeed also provides inference-specific kernels to further reduce latency

[p0088-l0002] [9.0pt] Areas for improvement (cost savings and performance)
[p0088-l0003] [10.0pt] and cost. For compatible Transformer-based models trained with DeepSpeed, Hug­
[p0088-l0004] [10.0pt] ging Face, or Megatron, DeepSpeed’s inference mode works without exporting the
[p0088-l0005] [10.0pt] model or creating new checkpoints. It automatically partitions the model as needed,
[p0088-l0006] [10.0pt] injects high-performance kernels, and manages inter-GPU communication in multi-
[p0088-l0007] [10.0pt] GPU environments. This section focuses on inference with DeepSpeed.
[p0088-l0008] [10.0pt] Let’s see how DeepSpeed works. For our first example, we’ll again use the GPT-Neo
[p0088-l0009] [10.0pt] model, running on a Colab VM with hardware acceleration (a T4 GPU). You can run
[p0088-l0010] [10.0pt] Python scripts that use the DeepSpeed API via the deepspeed CLI or programmatically,
[p0088-l0011] [10.0pt] which is what we’ll do in this section.
[p0088-l0012] [10.0pt] Note that to run inference in Colab or Jupyter notebooks, we’ll need some ini­
[p0088-l0013] [10.0pt] tialization code because, at the time of writing, no DeepSpeed launcher is available.
[p0088-l0014] [10.0pt] We’ll mock DeepSpeed’s native launcher by setting a few environment variables, as
[p0088-l0015] [10.0pt] follows:
[p0088-l0016] [8.0pt] import os
[p0088-l0017] [8.0pt] os.environ['MASTER_ADDR'] = 'localhost'
[p0088-l0018] [8.0pt] os.environ['MASTER_PORT'] = '9999'
[p0088-l0019] [8.0pt] os.environ['RANK'] = "0"
[p0088-l0020] [8.0pt] os.environ['LOCAL_RANK'] = "0"
[p0088-l0021] [8.0pt] os.environ['WORLD_SIZE'] = "1"
[p0088-l0022] [10.0pt] The master port can be any available port, and the world size is the number of GPUs.
[p0088-l0023] [10.0pt] Rank and world size define the DeepSpeed state; here, we’ll set rank to 0 because we
[p0088-l0024] [10.0pt] aren’t using a distributed PyTorch backend.
[p0088-l0025] [10.0pt] Now we’ll initialize the DeepSpeed engine and set the default device to CUDA, since
[p0088-l0026] [10.0pt] we’ll run inference on an NVIDIA GPU:
[p0088-l0027] [8.0pt] import deepspeed
[p0088-l0028] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0088-l0029] [8.0pt] device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
[p0088-l0030] [8.0pt] deepspeed.init_distributed()
[p0088-l0031] [8.0pt] ds_device = torch.device(device, int(os.getenv('LOCAL_RANK')))
[p0088-l0032] [10.0pt] If you’re not running in a notebook, you can skip the code so far. The rest doesn’t
[p0088-l0033] [10.0pt] depend on the execution environment.
[p0088-l0034] [10.0pt] Now that the DeepSpeed engine is initialized, we can load the GPT-Neo model the
[p0088-l0035] [10.0pt] usual way. For this example, we’ll use half precision to fit both the base model and the
[p0088-l0036] [10.0pt] DeepSpeed-optimized version in GPU memory:
[p0088-l0037] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0088-l0038] [8.0pt] from transformers import GPTNeoForCausalLM, GPT2Tokenizer
[p0088-l0039] [8.0pt] model_id = "EleutherAI/gpt-neo-2.7B"
[p0088-l0040] [8.0pt] tokenizer = GPT2Tokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)

[p0091-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 4  Running inference
[p0091-l0003] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0091-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ The GPT-Neo 2.7B model, using the Transformers library, can complete text,
[p0091-l0005] [10.0pt] learn from few-shot prompts, and generate code.
[p0091-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Memory requirements are calculated using this formula: memory (GB) = (4 × P)
[p0091-l0007] [10.0pt] / (32 ÷ F) × 1.2, where P is the number of parameters (in billions) and F is the
[p0091-l0008] [10.0pt] precision (in bits).
[p0091-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ GPT-Neo 2.7B needs 12.96 GB (FP32) or 5.4 GB (FP16); Mistral 7B needs 33.6
[p0091-l0010] [10.0pt] GB (FP32) or 16.2 GB (FP16).
[p0091-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Key inference metrics are time to first token (TTFT), time per output token
[p0091-l0012] [10.0pt] (TPOT), latency, and throughput.
[p0091-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ The KV cache stores attention-layer states to avoid recalculating them for each
[p0091-l0014] [10.0pt] token, yielding a 5× speedup in tests.
[p0091-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ The operations/byte ratio determines whether a system is memory-bound or
[p0091-l0016] [10.0pt] compute-bound; the T4 GPU’s ratio is 216.6 ops/byte.
[p0091-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ Arithmetic intensity is operations per byte accessed; GPT-Neo’s 30.29 ops/byte
[p0091-l0018] [10.0pt] suggests memory-bound performance.
[p0091-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ Dynamic batching processes multiple requests at once, improving throughput by
[p0091-l0020] [10.0pt] reusing model weights already in GPU memory.
[p0091-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Batch size is limited by available GPU memory after accounting for model weights
[p0091-l0022] [10.0pt] and the KV cache.
[p0091-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Token generation time is estimated by dividing bytes moved by GPU memory
[p0091-l0024] [10.0pt] bandwidth; on a T4 GPU, GPT-Neo generates about one token every 36 ms.
[p0091-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ The LM-Eval framework standardizes evaluation with 200+ built-in tasks and met­
[p0091-l0026] [10.0pt] rics, such as word perplexity, byte perplexity, and bits per byte.
[p0091-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ The DeepSpeed library optimizes inference through model parallelism, kernel
[p0091-l0028] [10.0pt] injection, and the ZeRO optimizer.
[p0091-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ DeepSpeed reduced GPT-Neo inference latency by 18% compared to a baseline
[p0091-l0030] [10.0pt] implementation.
[p0091-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ The Accelerate library includes the estimate-memory command for calculating
[p0091-l0032] [10.0pt] memory requirements across precision levels.

[p0092-l0001] [30.0pt] Exploring ONNX
[p0092-l0002] [225.0pt] 5
[p0092-l0003] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0092-l0004] [9.8pt] ¡ The ONNX standard format
[p0092-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ The ONNX runtime
[p0092-l0006] [9.8pt] ¡ How ONNX can be useful for LLMs, with or
[p0092-l0007] [9.8pt] without hardware acceleration
[p0092-l0008] [10.0pt] This chapter introduces the ONNX framework, which plays an important role in
[p0092-l0009] [10.0pt] model optimization, quantization, and portability across frameworks and hard­
[p0092-l0010] [10.0pt] ware vendors. If you’re new to ONNX, take the time to absorb the concepts in this
[p0092-l0011] [10.0pt] chapter—­they’re used heavily in later chapters.
[p0092-l0012] [12.5pt] 5.1
[p0092-l0013] [12.5pt] The ONNX format
[p0092-l0014] [10.0pt] ONNX (Open Neural Network Exchange, https://onnx.ai/) is an open standard
[p0092-l0015] [10.0pt] for ML interoperability. First released in 2017, it is now a graduate project of the
[p0092-l0016] [10.0pt] Linux Foundation for Artificial Intelligence (LFAI, https://lfaidata.foundation/).
[p0092-l0017] [10.0pt] ONNX aims to improve interoperability across machine learning (ML) and deep
[p0092-l0018] [10.0pt] learning (DL) frameworks (including Keras, TensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn,
[p0092-l0019] [9.0pt] 71

=== PDF page 93 / printed label 72 ===
[p0093-l0001] [9.0pt] 72
[p0093-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0093-l0003] [10.0pt] XGBoost, and others) and to maximize performance across hardware accelerators
[p0093-l0004] [10.0pt] (not just NVIDIA, but also Intel OpenVINO, Habana, Qualcomm, Apache TVM, Hug­
[p0093-l0005] [10.0pt] ging Face Optimum, and more). Figure 5.1 gives a high-level view of the ONNX ecosys­
[p0093-l0006] [10.0pt] tem, including the framework- and platform-agnostic model format and the optional
[p0093-l0007] [10.0pt] ONNX Runtime.
[p0093-l0008] [7.02pt] ML/DL frameworks
[p0093-l0009] [7.02pt] ONNX model
[p0093-l0010] [7.02pt] ONNX runtime
[p0093-l0011] [7.02pt] Hardware
[p0093-l0012] [7.61pt] GPU
[p0093-l0013] [7.61pt] TPU
[p0093-l0014] [7.61pt] CPU
[p0093-l0015] [7.61pt] FPGA
[p0093-l0016] [7.02pt] Devices
[p0093-l0017] [8.0pt] Figure 5.1  ONNX overview
[p0093-l0018] [10.0pt] As ML and DL frameworks evolve, portability becomes critical—what we use today may
[p0093-l0019] [10.0pt] not be what we’ll use tomorrow. ONNX is a robust open standard that reduces lock-in
[p0093-l0020] [10.0pt] to specific frameworks and hardware accelerators, helping ensure an organization’s
[p0093-l0021] [10.0pt] models remain usable over time.
[p0093-l0022] [10.0pt] ONNX is a community project with open governance, so anyone can contribute. It
[p0093-l0023] [10.0pt] was created at Facebook and was soon backed by other companies such as Microsoft,
[p0093-l0024] [10.0pt] IBM, Huawei, Intel, AMD, Arm, and Qualcomm. Since then, it has grown into a widely
[p0093-l0025] [10.0pt] adopted standard for ML/DL inference. Figure 5.2 lists the companies that currently
[p0093-l0026] [10.0pt] support ONNX.
[p0093-l0027] [10.0pt] ONNX consists of two projects: the ONNX format and the ONNX runtime. This
[p0093-l0028] [10.0pt] section and section 5.2 cover the ONNX format, while sections 5.3 and 5.4 cover the
[p0093-l0029] [10.0pt] ONNX runtime.

=== PDF page 94 / printed label 73 ===
[p0094-l0001] [9.0pt] 73
[p0094-l0002] [9.0pt] The ONNX format
[p0094-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 5.2  The list of organizations supporting the ONNX initiative
[p0094-l0004] [10.0pt] Besides being cross-framework, ONNX provides APIs for multiple programming lan­
[p0094-l0005] [10.0pt] guages. In this book, we’ll use Python (and a little C/C++). Figure 5.3 summarizes all
[p0094-l0006] [10.0pt] the possible options with ONNX.
[p0094-l0007] [10.0pt] Once you’ve trained a model in a DL framework (or received one from someone
[p0094-l0008] [10.0pt] else), you can convert it to ONNX (and optimize it) and then choose from the follow­
[p0094-l0009] [10.0pt] ing options:
[p0094-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Executing it directly in the ONNX Runtime (or any other runtime supported by
[p0094-l0011] [10.0pt] the framework)
[p0094-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Converting it to another DL framework
[p0094-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ Optimizing it further through quantization
[p0094-l0014] [10.0pt] At the end of the process described in either of the last two options, you can run the
[p0094-l0015] [10.0pt] final model with any supported runtime. In figure 5.3, the block where the model is
[p0094-l0016] [10.0pt] run in another framework is highlighted in a different color because it’s out of scope
[p0094-l0017] [10.0pt] for this book. From here on, we’ll discuss converting models to ONNX format and
[p0094-l0018] [10.0pt] optimizing and quantizing them, and we’ll reference other Python libraries that sup­
[p0094-l0019] [10.0pt] port this standard.
[p0094-l0020] [10.0pt] ONNX defines a common set of operators and a standard file format for storing
[p0094-l0021] [10.0pt] trained ML/DL models and pipelines, with enough detail to move them between plat­
[p0094-l0022] [10.0pt] forms. ONNX can also compile stored operations to lower-level languages for embed­
[p0094-l0023] [10.0pt] ding on a range of devices, including edge devices. Conceptually, an ONNX file defines
[p0094-l0024] [10.0pt] a directed graph: each edge represents a typed tensor moving from one node to the
[p0094-l0025] [10.0pt] next. The nodes are called operators: they consume inputs and pass their results to their

[p0095-l0025] [8.0pt] Figure 5.3  The possible operations on ML/DL models in ONNX
[p0095-l0026] [10.0pt] children. ONNX’s standard operations are broad enough to express most ML/AI
[p0095-l0027] [10.0pt] workloads, and you can extend them with custom operators when needed.
[p0095-l0028] [10.0pt] ONNX provides a common language that any ML/DL framework can use to describe
[p0095-l0029] [10.0pt] its models, making production deployment easier. It also lets you build a unique deploy­
[p0095-l0030] [10.0pt] ment pipeline independent of the framework used to create the model. This frame­
[p0095-l0031] [10.0pt] work includes a Python runtime for evaluating ONNX models and operators, but use
[p0095-l0032] [10.0pt] it with care: it’s intended to clarify ONNX semantics and help with debugging, not for
[p0095-l0033] [10.0pt] production—especially when you need high performance.
[p0095-l0034] [10.0pt] Regardless of the ML/DL model or framework, building an ONNX graph involves
[p0095-l0035] [10.0pt] defining a combination of operators, as described in the next section.
[p0095-l0036] [12.5pt] 5.2
[p0095-l0037] [12.5pt] ONNX operators and types
[p0095-l0038] [10.0pt] Operators are the basic building blocks for defining ONNX models; almost any ML/DL
[p0095-l0039] [10.0pt] model from various frameworks can be described using them. ONNX operators include
[p0095-l0040] [10.0pt] standard matrix operations, reductions, image transformations, deep neural network
[p0095-l0041] [10.0pt] layers, and activation functions. Table 5.1 provides a nonexhaustive list of operators rel­
[p0095-l0042] [10.0pt] evant to LLMs (see the official ONNX documentation for the complete list).
[p0095-l0043] [8.0pt] Table 5.1  The most relevant ONNX operators for LLMs
[p0095-l0044] [8.0pt] Operator
[p0095-l0045] [8.0pt] Description
[p0095-l0046] [7.5pt] Add
[p0095-l0047] [8.0pt] Performs element-wise binary addition. It supports multidirectional broad­
[p0095-l0048] [8.0pt] casting (like NumPy).
[p0095-l0049] [7.5pt] And
[p0095-l0050] [8.0pt] Returns the tensor resulted from performing the and logical operation ele­
[p0095-l0051] [8.0pt] mentwise on the input tensors

[p0096-l0004] [8.0pt] Operator
[p0096-l0005] [8.0pt] Description
[p0096-l0006] [7.5pt] ArgMax
[p0096-l0007] [8.0pt] Computes the indices of the max elements of the input tensor’s element
[p0096-l0008] [8.0pt] along the provided axis
[p0096-l0009] [7.5pt] ArgMin
[p0096-l0010] [8.0pt] Computes the indices of the min elements of the input tensor’s element
[p0096-l0011] [8.0pt] along the provided axis
[p0096-l0012] [7.5pt] Atan
[p0096-l0013] [8.0pt] Calculates the arctangent (inverse of tangent) of the given input tensor,

[p0096-l0015] [7.5pt] AveragePool
[p0096-l0016] [8.0pt] Consumes an input tensor and applies average pooling across the tensor

[p0096-l0020] [8.0pt] tensor for further processing.
[p0096-l0021] [7.5pt] BatchNormalization

[p0096-l0025] [7.5pt] DFT

[p0096-l0027] [7.5pt] Det
[p0096-l0028] [8.0pt] Calculates the determinant of a square matrix (or a batch of square
[p0096-l0029] [8.0pt] matrices)
[p0096-l0030] [7.5pt] Div
[p0096-l0031] [8.0pt] Performs element-wise binary division of the input
[p0096-l0032] [7.5pt] Equal
[p0096-l0033] [8.0pt] Returns the tensor resulted from performing the equal logical operation

[p0096-l0035] [7.5pt] Exp

[p0096-l0037] [7.5pt] Floor

[p0097-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0097-l0003] [8.0pt] Table 5.1  The most relevant ONNX operators for LLMs (continued)
[p0097-l0004] [8.0pt] Operator
[p0097-l0005] [8.0pt] Description
[p0097-l0006] [7.5pt] Pad
[p0097-l0007] [8.0pt] Given a tensor containing the data to be padded, a tensor containing the
[p0097-l0008] [8.0pt] number of start and end pad values for axis, and, optionally, a mode and a
[p0097-l0009] [8.0pt] constant value, a padded tensor is generated as output.
[p0097-l0010] [7.5pt] QuantizeLinear
[p0097-l0011] [8.0pt] The linear quantization operator. It consumes a high-precision tensor, a
[p0097-l0012] [8.0pt] scale, and a zero point to compute the low-precision/quantized tensor.
[p0097-l0013] [7.5pt] Reciprocal
[p0097-l0014] [8.0pt] Takes one input tensor and produces one output tensor where the recipro­
[p0097-l0015] [8.0pt] cal, y = 1/x, is applied to the tensor element-wise
[p0097-l0016] [7.5pt] RegexFullMatch
[p0097-l0017] [8.0pt] Performs a full regex match on each element of the input tensor. If an
[p0097-l0018] [8.0pt] element fully matches the regex pattern specified as an attribute, the corre­
[p0097-l0019] [8.0pt] sponding element in the output is true, and it is false otherwise.
[p0097-l0020] [7.5pt] Reshape
[p0097-l0021] [8.0pt] Reshapes the input tensor. First input is the data tensor; second input is
[p0097-l0022] [8.0pt] a shape tensor which specifies the output shape. It outputs the reshaped
[p0097-l0023] [8.0pt] tensor.
[p0097-l0024] [7.5pt] Softmax
[p0097-l0025] [8.0pt] Computes the normalized exponential values for the given input:
[p0097-l0026] [7.5pt] Softmax(input, axis) = Exp(input) / ReduceSum(Exp(input),
[p0097-l0027] [8.0pt] axis=axis, keepdims=1)  The axis attribute indicates the dimension
[p0097-l0028] [8.0pt] along which Softmax will be performed. The output tensor has the same
[p0097-l0029] [8.0pt] shape and contains the Softmax values of the corresponding input.
[p0097-l0030] [7.5pt] Transpose
[p0097-l0031] [8.0pt] Transposes the input tensor
[p0097-l0032] [7.5pt] Unique
[p0097-l0033] [8.0pt] Finds the unique elements of a tensor. When an optional attribute axis is
[p0097-l0034] [8.0pt] provided, unique subtensors sliced along the axis are returned. Otherwise,
[p0097-l0035] [8.0pt] the input tensor is flattened, and unique values of the flattened tensor are
[p0097-l0036] [8.0pt] returned.
[p0097-l0037] [10.0pt] ONNX is optimized for numerical computation with tensors (multidimensional arrays)
[p0097-l0038] [10.0pt] defined by an element type, a shape, and a contiguous array of values. Although ONNX
[p0097-l0039] [10.0pt] initially supported only 32-bit floating-point values, later versions added all common
[p0097-l0040] [10.0pt] types. You can programmatically list all the supported ONNX types:
[p0097-l0041] [8.0pt] import re
[p0097-l0042] [8.0pt] from onnx import TensorProto
[p0097-l0043] [8.0pt] reg = re.compile('^[0-9A-Z_]+$')
[p0097-l0044] [8.0pt] values = {}
[p0097-l0045] [8.0pt] for att in sorted(dir(TensorProto)):
[p0097-l0046] [8.0pt]     if att in {'DESCRIPTOR'}:
[p0097-l0047] [8.0pt]         continue
[p0097-l0048] [8.0pt]     if reg.match(att):
[p0097-l0049] [8.0pt]         values[getattr(TensorProto, att)] = att
[p0097-l0050] [8.0pt] for i, att in sorted(values.items()):
[p0097-l0051] [8.0pt]     si = str(i)
[p0097-l0052] [8.0pt]     if len(si) == 1:
[p0097-l0053] [8.0pt]         si = " " + si
[p0097-l0054] [8.0pt]     print("%s: onnx.TensorProto.%s" % (si, att))

[p0098-l0025] [10.0pt] As a concrete example of using the ONNX API, let’s consider a linear regression
[p0098-l0026] [10.0pt] model, represented by the following expression:
[p0098-l0027] [10.0pt] All the variables are matrices. In ONNX, we must represent this with two operators,
[p0098-l0028] [10.0pt] 𝑌 = 𝑋𝐴 + 𝐵
[p0098-l0029] [10.0pt] MatMul and Add (see the operator list in table 5.1):
[p0098-l0030] [8.0pt] y = Add(MatMul(X, A), B)
[p0098-l0031] [10.0pt] To build the graph, we’ll use four functions from the ONNX API:
[p0098-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ make_tensor_value_info—Declares an input or output variable with a given
[p0098-l0033] [10.0pt] shape and type
[p0098-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ make_node—Creates a node from an operation and its inputs and outputs
[p0098-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ make_graph—Creates an ONNX graph from the objects created by the previous
[p0098-l0036] [10.0pt] two functions
[p0098-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ make_model—Merges the graph with additional metadata
[p0098-l0038] [10.0pt] ONNX is strongly typed, so you must define the shape and type of each function’s
[p0098-l0039] [10.0pt] inputs and outputs. ONNX is built on protobuf (https://github.com/protocolbuffers/
[p0098-l0040] [10.0pt] protobuf), a language- and platform-neutral format for serializing structured data.
[p0098-l0041] [10.0pt] protobuf provides the definitions needed to describe an ML/DL model; ONNX is
[p0098-l0042] [10.0pt] used to serialize and deserialize it. protobuf is responsible for keeping the saved graph
[p0098-l0043] [10.0pt] compact.

[p0099-l0037] [10.0pt] We can define a linear regression model by first declaring the matrices involved:
[p0099-l0038] [8.0pt] X = make_tensor_value_info('X', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])

[p0099-l0043] [8.0pt] node1 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A'], ['XA'])
[p0099-l0044] [8.0pt] node2 = make_node('Add', ['XA', 'B'], ['Y'])

[p0102-l0001] [9.0pt] 81
[p0102-l0002] [9.0pt] The ONNX runtime
[p0102-l0003] [12.5pt] 5.3
[p0102-l0004] [12.5pt] The ONNX runtime
[p0102-l0005] [10.0pt] The ONNX format defines the ML/DL models converted to this
[p0102-l0006] [10.0pt] framework. Another key part of the ecosystem is the ONNX Run­
[p0102-l0007] [10.0pt] time (ORT, https://onnxruntime.ai/), which executes ONNX mod­
[p0102-l0008] [10.0pt] els efficiently across a wide range of hardware and software platforms
[p0102-l0009] [10.0pt] (illustrated earlier in figure 5.1). ORT supports the deployment of
[p0102-l0010] [10.0pt] ONNX models on local or cloud servers, as well as on mobile phones
[p0102-l0011] [10.0pt] and edge devices, for consistent performance across environments.
[p0102-l0012] [10.0pt] When available, ORT uses hardware acceleration for faster inference.
[p0102-l0013] [10.0pt] It also includes optimizations such as kernel fusion, quantization,
[p0102-l0014] [10.0pt] and layout transformations to speed execution while maintaining
[p0102-l0015] [10.0pt] good accuracy. Although ORT supports both training and inference,
[p0102-l0016] [10.0pt] it’s most often used for inference, with training left to the original
[p0102-l0017] [10.0pt] ML/DL framework. Training with ORT is out of scope for this book.
[p0102-l0018] [10.0pt] NOTE  ORT provides bindings for multiple programming lan­
[p0102-l0019] [10.0pt] guages; in this book, we’ll use Python.
[p0102-l0020] [10.0pt] The inference process follows a fixed set of steps. Once we’ve
[p0102-l0021] [10.0pt] trained a model and converted it to ONNX, or implemented one
[p0102-l0022] [10.0pt] directly with the ONNX API (such as the linear regression model
[p0102-l0023] [10.0pt] in section 5.2), we load it and create an inference session (using
[p0102-l0024] [10.0pt] ORT’s InferenceSession class):
[p0102-l0025] [8.0pt] Figure 5.4
[p0102-l0026] [8.0pt] Visualizing a linear
[p0102-l0027] [8.0pt] regression model
[p0102-l0028] [8.0pt] in ONNX with
[p0102-l0029] [8.0pt] Netron
[p0102-l0030] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0102-l0031] [8.0pt] onnx_model_path = "path_to_the_onnx_model"
[p0102-l0032] [8.0pt] session = rt.InferenceSession(onnx_model_path)
[p0102-l0033] [10.0pt] Next, we prepare the model input (in this example, it will be a NumPy array):
[p0102-l0034] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0102-l0035] [8.0pt] input_data = np.array([[2.0, 4.0, 6.0, 8.0]], dtype=np.float32)
[p0102-l0036] [10.0pt] We can now run inference:
[p0102-l0037] [8.0pt] input_name = session.get_inputs()[0].name
[p0102-l0038] [8.0pt] output_name = session.get_outputs()[0].name
[p0102-l0039] [8.0pt] result = session.run([output_name], {input_name: input_data})
[p0102-l0040] [10.0pt] Finally, we can print the result:
[p0102-l0041] [8.0pt] print(f"Output: {result[0]}")
[p0102-l0042] [10.0pt] When passing input values to the model, make sure you use the correct input name.
[p0102-l0043] [10.0pt] You can retrieve it from the inference session object with get_inputs, which returns

=== PDF page 103 / printed label 82 ===
[p0103-l0001] [9.0pt] 82
[p0103-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0103-l0003] [10.0pt] the list of names for a model’s inputs. Similarly, get_outputs returns the model’s out­
[p0103-l0004] [10.0pt] put names. The command sequence for ORT inference is always the same; what varies
[p0103-l0005] [10.0pt] by architecture is input preprocessing, output postprocessing, and how you handle
[p0103-l0006] [10.0pt] multiple inputs and outputs.
[p0103-l0007] [10.0pt] A JavaScript library for running ONNX models in web browsers or on Node.js is also
[p0103-l0008] [10.0pt] available. It’s called ONNX Runtime Web (https://microsoft.github.io/onnxruntime
[p0103-l0009] [10.0pt] -web-demo), and it’s built on WebAssembly and WebGL. It supports CPU and GPU exe­
[p0103-l0010] [10.0pt] cution and enables interactive, install-free, device-independent ML, with lower server–
[p0103-l0011] [10.0pt] client latency and improved privacy and security. After you specialize your model,
[p0103-l0012] [10.0pt] convert it to ONNX, and optimize it, you can use this as another serving option.
[p0103-l0013] [12.5pt] 5.4
[p0103-l0014] [12.5pt] ONNX runtime providers
[p0103-l0015] [10.0pt] To get the most from the underlying hardware on which an ONNX model runs, ORT
[p0103-l0016] [10.0pt] uses runtime (execution) providers. These interfaces let you deploy ONNX mod­
[p0103-l0017] [10.0pt] els across environments and optimize execution by using each platform’s compute
[p0103-l0018] [10.0pt] capabilities. Through a dedicated execution provider, ORT assigns specific nodes or
[p0103-l0019] [10.0pt] subgraphs to run on the available hardware, drivers, and related libraries in the deploy­
[p0103-l0020] [10.0pt] ment environment. Figure 5.5, from the official ORT documentation, shows how ORT
[p0103-l0021] [10.0pt] improves a model’s execution for a given hardware specification.

[p0104-l0001] [9.0pt] 83
[p0104-l0002] [9.0pt] ONNX runtime providers
[p0104-l0003] [10.0pt] At the time of writing, ORT offers many execution providers. Some are production-­
[p0104-l0004] [10.0pt] ready; others are preview releases for evaluation. Providers marked as in review are
[p0104-l0005] [10.0pt] generally stable and may be suitable for production, but test carefully before deploying
[p0104-l0006] [10.0pt] an ONNX model with any provider still labeled as in preview.
[p0104-l0007] [10.0pt] Here are ORT’s currently stable execution providers:
[p0104-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Default CPU—Vendor-agnostic CPU.
[p0104-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ Intel OpenVINO—Uses the OpenVINO toolkit (https://mng.bz/Jw5p) on CPUs
[p0104-l0010] [10.0pt] and GPUs, including edge and mobile devices.
[p0104-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Intel oneDNN—Uses optimized primitives from the Intel Math Kernel Library for
[p0104-l0012] [10.0pt] Deep Neural Networks (Intel DNNL). CPU-only.
[p0104-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ XNNPACK—Uses XNNPACK (https://github.com/google/XNNPACK), an
[p0104-l0014] [10.0pt] optimized floating-point NN inference library for ARM (Android/iOS), Web­
[p0104-l0015] [10.0pt] Assembly, and x86.
[p0104-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ NVIDIA CUDA—Enables hardware-accelerated computation on CUDA-enabled
[p0104-l0017] [10.0pt] NVIDIA GPUs.
[p0104-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ NVIDIA TensorRT—Uses NVIDIA’s TensorRT engine (https://developer.nvidia
[p0104-l0019] [10.0pt] .com/tensorrt) on supported NVIDIA GPUs.
[p0104-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ DirectML—Uses DirectML’s low-level API for ML (https://mng.bz/wZw7); Win­
[p0104-l0021] [10.0pt] dows GPUs only.
[p0104-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ AMD MIGraphX—AMD’s MiGraphX optimization engine for AMD GPUs
[p0104-l0023] [10.0pt] (https://github.com/ROCm/AMDMIGraphX).
[p0104-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ AMD ROCm—For AMD GPUs with ROCm (https://mng.bz/qRwK).
[p0104-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Android Neural Networks API—A unified interface to CPUs, GPUs, and neural net­
[p0104-l0026] [10.0pt] work accelerators on Android devices (https://mng.bz/7QOx).
[p0104-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Qualcomm QNN—Uses the Qualcomm AI Engine Direct SDK (https://mng.bz/
[p0104-l0028] [10.0pt] mZwn) on Qualcomm chipsets.
[p0104-l0029] [10.0pt] This is the current list of ORT execution providers still in preview:
[p0104-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ TVM—Uses Apache TVM (https://tvm.apache.org/) to optimize models for
[p0104-l0031] [10.0pt] CPUs, GPUs, and edge and mobile devices. Currently tested on Linux and Win­
[p0104-l0032] [10.0pt] dows, but not on macOS.
[p0104-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ ARM Compute Library—Runs inference on Armv8 cores using the Arm Compute
[p0104-l0034] [10.0pt] Library engine (https://github.com/ARM-software/ComputeLibrary).
[p0104-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ ARM-NN—ArmNN inference engine (https://github.com/ARM-software/
[p0104-l0036] [10.0pt] armnn) for Armv8 cores.
[p0104-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ CoreML—Uses the Core ML framework (https://developer.apple.com/
[p0104-l0038] [10.0pt] machine-learning/core-ml/) to run on Apple’s CPUs, GPUs, and Neural Engine.
[p0104-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Rockchip-NPU—Uses the RKNPU DDK.
[p0104-l0040] [10.0pt] ¡ Xilinx Vitis-AI—Uses AMD’s development stack for hardware-accelerated AI
[p0104-l0041] [10.0pt] inference on AMD platforms.

=== PDF page 105 / printed label 84 ===
[p0105-l0001] [9.0pt] 84
[p0105-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0105-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Huawei CANN—Uses the CANN Execution Provider with Huawei Ascend
[p0105-l0004] [10.0pt] hardware.
[p0105-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ AZURE—Invokes a remote Azure endpoint for inference.
[p0105-l0006] [10.0pt] You can programmatically check the available providers in the destination
[p0105-l0007] [10.0pt] environment:
[p0105-l0008] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0105-l0009] [8.0pt] rt.get_available_providers()
[p0105-l0010] [10.0pt] This returns a Python list. For example, on a system with a CPU and an NVIDIA GPU
[p0105-l0011] [10.0pt] (with CUDA drivers installed), the preceding method returns the following:
[p0105-l0012] [8.0pt] ['CPUExecutionProvider', 'CUDAExecutionProvider']
[p0105-l0013] [10.0pt] If multiple providers are available, you can tell ORT the order in which to try them.
[p0105-l0014] [10.0pt] Here’s an example:
[p0105-l0015] [8.0pt] providers_list = ['CUDAExecutionProvider', 'CPUExecutionProvider']
[p0105-l0016] [8.0pt] sess = rt.InferenceSession("model.onnx", providers=providers_list)
[p0105-l0017] [10.0pt] Here, we tell ORT to prefer the CUDA provider (when available) over others in the
[p0105-l0018] [10.0pt] execution environment.

[p0107-l0040] [10.0pt] and ort_outputs. The allclose function returns True when the arrays are element-wise
[p0107-l0041] [10.0pt] equal within a tolerance defined by rtol (relative tolerance) and atol (absolute

[p0108-l0004] [10.0pt] tolerance), which are typically very small values. allclose evaluates the following

[p0110-l0018] [10.0pt] tion 5.5 or this section’s companion notebook. Inference with the ONNX-converted
[p0110-l0019] [10.0pt] model is also similar, but you must configure the ONNX inference session to use the
[p0110-l0020] [10.0pt] CUDA execution provider as follows:
[p0110-l0021] [8.0pt] session = onnxruntime.InferenceSession(export_model_path, sess_options,
[p0110-l0022] [10.0pt] ➥providers=['CUDAExecutionProvider'])
[p0110-l0023] [10.0pt] That’s all you need to run an ONNX-converted model on a GPU runtime in a standard
[p0110-l0024] [10.0pt] way. There are other considerations, but before we explore them, let’s look at another
[p0110-l0025] [10.0pt] example.
[p0110-l0026] [10.5pt] 5.6.1

[p0111-l0043] [10.0pt] applies the best possible optimizations. This is often true, but sometimes extra steps are

=== PDF page 112 / printed label 91 ===
[p0112-l0001] [9.0pt] 91
[p0112-l0002] [9.0pt] ONNX for LLMs on GPU
[p0112-l0003] [10.0pt] needed. You can usually do this programmatically; manually inspecting the generated
[p0112-l0004] [10.0pt] ONNX graph should be a last resort. One way to do this (not the only one—we’ll cover
[p0112-l0005] [10.0pt] more later) is to use the ONNX Runtime library’s built-in Transformer optimizer. Con­
[p0112-l0006] [10.0pt] tinuing the GPT-2 example, here’s how we can apply it to an already converted model:
[p0112-l0007] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime.transformers import optimizer
[p0112-l0008] [8.0pt] optimized_model_path = os.path.join(output_dir, 'gpt-2-onnx_opt_gpu.onnx')
[p0112-l0009] [8.0pt] optimized_model = optimizer.optimize_model(export_model_path,
[p0112-l0010] [8.0pt]                                            model_type='gpt2',
[p0112-l0011] [8.0pt]                                            use_gpu=True,
[p0112-l0012] [8.0pt]                                            num_heads=12,
[p0112-l0013] [8.0pt]                                            hidden_size=768)
[p0112-l0014] [8.0pt] optimized_model.save_model_to_file(optimized_model_path)
[p0112-l0015] [10.0pt] We use the optimizer’s optimize_model method, as in the earlier bert-base-uncased
[p0112-l0016] [10.0pt] example. We pass the full path to the converted model, the LLM family type, and the
[p0112-l0017] [10.0pt] number of heads and hidden size, and we specify GPU optimization. You can also set
[p0112-l0018] [10.0pt] the graph optimization level: 0 (none; the default), 1 (basic), 2 (extended), or 99 (all,
[p0112-l0019] [10.0pt] including layout). The same code applies to LLMs with architectures other than GPT-2.
[p0112-l0020] [10.0pt] Basic optimization performs constant folding (statically computing parts of the graph
[p0112-l0021] [10.0pt] that rely only on constant initializers), removes redundant nodes (such as identity,
[p0112-l0022] [10.0pt] slice, unsqueeze, and dropout), and applies semantics-preserving fusions. Extended
[p0112-l0023] [10.0pt] optimization applies more complex fusions after graph partitioning, and only to nodes
[p0112-l0024] [10.0pt] assigned to the CPU, CUDA, or ROCm (AMD Radeon Open Compute Ecosystem)
[p0112-l0025] [10.0pt] execution provider. Layout optimization changes the data layout for applicable nodes
[p0112-l0026] [10.0pt] for higher performance; it runs after graph partitioning and only for nodes assigned to
[p0112-l0027] [10.0pt] the CPU execution provider.
[p0112-l0028] [10.0pt] ONNX optimizations can be done offline or online. The previous code snippet is an
[p0112-l0029] [10.0pt] example of offline optimization. Alternatively, you can enable the same optimizations
[p0112-l0030] [10.0pt] at inference time by setting the ONNX Runtime session mode, as follows:
[p0112-l0031] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0112-l0032] [8.0pt] sess_options = rt.SessionOptions()
[p0112-l0033] [8.0pt] sess_options.graph_optimization_level =
[p0112-l0034] [10.0pt] ➥rt.GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_EXTENDED
[p0112-l0035] [8.0pt] sess_options.optimized_model_filepath = "<model_path\optimized_model.onnx>"
[p0112-l0036] [8.0pt] session = rt.InferenceSession(None, sess_options)
[p0112-l0037] [10.0pt] The optimization levels are defined by the GraphOptimizationLevel class:
[p0112-l0038] [8.0pt] GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_DISABLE_
[p0112-l0039] [8.0pt] GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_BASIC
[p0112-l0040] [8.0pt] GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_EXTENDED
[p0112-l0041] [8.0pt] GraphOptimizationLevel.ORT_ENABLE_ALL

=== PDF page 113 / printed label 92 ===
[p0113-l0001] [9.0pt] 92
[p0113-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0113-l0003] [10.0pt] In online mode, ONNX Runtime applies all enabled graph optimizations when the
[p0113-l0004] [10.0pt] session is initialized, before inference runs. This can increase model startup time
[p0113-l0005] [10.0pt] (especially for complex models), which can make it unsuitable for production. In
[p0113-l0006] [10.0pt] offline mode, ONNX Runtime applies the optimizations and then serializes the opti­
[p0113-l0007] [10.0pt] mized model to disk. Subsequent startups are faster because the model is already
[p0113-l0008] [10.0pt] optimized.
[p0113-l0009] [10.5pt] 5.6.2
[p0113-l0010] [10.5pt] I/O binding
[p0113-l0011] [10.0pt] Before we move on, consider input and output data when running ONNX models with
[p0113-l0012] [10.0pt] execution providers (CPU and GPU). So far, you’ve learned that ONNX models con­
[p0113-l0013] [10.0pt] sist of a computation graph implemented as optimized operator kernels for different
[p0113-l0014] [10.0pt] hardware, and that ONNX Runtime (ORT) orchestrates execution through execution
[p0113-l0015] [10.0pt] providers for a specific target (CPU, GPU, and so on). But what about the data con­
[p0113-l0016] [10.0pt] sumed and produced?
[p0113-l0017] [10.0pt] By default, ORT places data—regardless of structure (NumPy arrays, dictionaries, or
[p0113-l0018] [10.0pt] lists of NumPy arrays)—on the CPU. That’s fine when there’s no hardware acceleration,
[p0113-l0019] [10.0pt] but it’s not ideal when a GPU is available and the inference session is configured to run
[p0113-l0020] [10.0pt] on the GPU first. In that case, data is copied between CPU and GPU, adding unneces­
[p0113-l0021] [10.0pt] sary overhead. ORT provides a custom data structure that supports ONNX data formats
[p0113-l0022] [10.0pt] and lets you place data on a device, such as a CUDA-capable GPU. It’s called IOBinding.
[p0113-l0023] [10.0pt] With it, input and output data (or just one of them, depending on your configuration)
[p0113-l0024] [10.0pt] can be placed on the same device where the ONNX graph runs.
[p0113-l0025] [10.0pt] You can configure IOBinding programmatically, as you’ll see next. To keep the
[p0113-l0026] [10.0pt] concept simple, we’ll use a small PyTorch model that sums two tensors, but the
[p0113-l0027] [10.0pt] same approach applies to more complex models, including LLMs. Let’s define the
[p0113-l0028] [10.0pt] model:
[p0113-l0029] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0113-l0030] [8.0pt] def model():
[p0113-l0031] [8.0pt]     class Model(torch.nn.Module):
[p0113-l0032] [8.0pt]         def __init__(self):
[p0113-l0033] [8.0pt]             super(Model, self).__init__()
[p0113-l0034] [8.0pt]         def forward(self, x, y):
[p0113-l0035] [8.0pt]             return x.add(y)
[p0113-l0036] [8.0pt]     return Model()
[p0113-l0037] [10.0pt] Now let’s convert it to ONNX programmatically:
[p0113-l0038] [8.0pt] MODEL_FILE = '.model.onnx'
[p0113-l0039] [8.0pt] type = torch.float32
[p0113-l0040] [8.0pt] sample_x = torch.ones(3, dtype=type)
[p0113-l0041] [8.0pt] sample_y = torch.zeros(3, dtype=type)

=== PDF page 114 / printed label 93 ===
[p0114-l0001] [9.0pt] 93
[p0114-l0002] [9.0pt] ONNX for LLMs on GPU
[p0114-l0003] [8.0pt] torch.onnx.export(model(), (sample_x, sample_y),
[p0114-l0004] [10.0pt] ➥MODEL_FILE, input_names=["x", "y"], output_names=["z"],
[p0114-l0005] [10.0pt]                     ➥dynamic_axes={"x": {0 : "array_length_x"}, "y":
[p0114-l0006] [10.0pt]                     ➥{0: "array_length_y"}})
[p0114-l0007] [10.0pt] We’ll create an inference session as usual (assuming the target environment has a GPU
[p0114-l0008] [10.0pt] and CUDA):
[p0114-l0009] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0114-l0010] [8.0pt] providers = ['CUDAExecutionProvider', 'CPUExecutionProvider']
[p0114-l0011] [8.0pt] session = rt.InferenceSession(MODEL_FILE, providers=providers)
[p0114-l0012] [10.0pt] The new part starts after we’ve created the session. Instead of running inference with
[p0114-l0013] [10.0pt] run, we’ll use run_with_iobinding. First, we’ll prepare the data for IOBinding. Create
[p0114-l0014] [10.0pt] an IOBinding instance from the inference session:
[p0114-l0015] [8.0pt] binding = session.io_binding()
[p0114-l0016] [10.0pt] Create two tensors containing random values, and move them to the GPU:
[p0114-l0017] [8.0pt] DEVICE = 'cuda'
[p0114-l0018] [8.0pt] x = torch.rand(5).to(DEVICE)
[p0114-l0019] [8.0pt] y = torch.rand(5).to(DEVICE)
[p0114-l0020] [8.0pt] x_tensor = x.contiguous()
[p0114-l0021] [8.0pt] y_tensor = y.contiguous()
[p0114-l0022] [10.0pt] Then tell ONNX Runtime to load the model inputs onto the CUDA device:
[p0114-l0023] [8.0pt] DEVICE_INDEX = 0
[p0114-l0024] [8.0pt] np_type = np.float32
[p0114-l0025] [8.0pt] binding.bind_input(
[p0114-l0026] [8.0pt]     name='x',
[p0114-l0027] [8.0pt]     device_type=DEVICE,
[p0114-l0028] [8.0pt]     device_id=DEVICE_INDEX,
[p0114-l0029] [8.0pt]     element_type=np_type,
[p0114-l0030] [8.0pt]     shape=tuple(x_tensor.shape),
[p0114-l0031] [8.0pt]     buffer_ptr=x_tensor.data_ptr(),
[p0114-l0032] [8.0pt]     )
[p0114-l0033] [8.0pt] binding.bind_input(
[p0114-l0034] [8.0pt]     name='y',
[p0114-l0035] [8.0pt]     device_type=DEVICE,
[p0114-l0036] [8.0pt]     device_id=DEVICE_INDEX,
[p0114-l0037] [8.0pt]     element_type=np_type,
[p0114-l0038] [8.0pt]     shape=tuple(y_tensor.shape),
[p0114-l0039] [8.0pt]     buffer_ptr=y_tensor.data_ptr(),
[p0114-l0040] [8.0pt]     )

=== PDF page 115 / printed label 94 ===
[p0115-l0001] [9.0pt] 94
[p0115-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 5  Exploring ONNX
[p0115-l0003] [10.0pt] You can run inference with IOBInding as follows:
[p0115-l0004] [8.0pt] session.run_with_iobinding(binding)

[p0115-l0019] [10.0pt] Other examples with more complex data will be presented in chapters 7 and 8.
[p0115-l0020] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0115-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX is an open standard format for interoperable machine learning models
[p0115-l0022] [10.0pt] across frameworks and hardware platforms.
[p0115-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX Runtime (ORT) efficiently runs ONNX models on CPUs, GPUs, and
[p0115-l0024] [10.0pt] edge devices.
[p0115-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX operators are the building blocks that can describe machine learning
[p0115-l0026] [10.0pt] models from most frameworks.
[p0115-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX supports multiple data types, including float32, int8, int16, int32,
[p0115-l0028] [10.0pt] int64, and specialized formats like bfloat16.
[p0115-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX Runtime execution providers optimize performance by using hardware
[p0115-l0030] [10.0pt] accelerators such as NVIDIA CUDA.
[p0115-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ You can optimize ONNX models offline during conversion or online when ini­
[p0115-l0032] [10.0pt] tializing an inference session.
[p0115-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX graph optimizations range from constant folding to node fusion and lay­
[p0115-l0034] [10.0pt] out transformations.
[p0115-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ IOBinding in ONNX Runtime eliminates CPU–GPU copies by keeping data on
[p0115-l0036] [10.0pt] the target execution device.
[p0115-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX-converted models typically achieve faster inference times than their orig­
[p0115-l0038] [10.0pt] inal framework implementations.

[p0116-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Validation of ONNX models means verifying schema consistency and ensuring

[p0116-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX Runtime supports multiple language bindings, but Python offers the
