[p0117-l0001] [30.0pt] Quantizing for
[p0117-l0002] [30.0pt] your production
[p0117-l0003] [30.0pt] environment
[p0117-l0004] [225.0pt] 6
[p0117-l0005] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0117-l0006] [9.8pt] ¡ Precision formats for training and running LLMs
[p0117-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Quantizing LLMs to smaller-precision formats
[p0117-l0008] [9.8pt] ¡ Quantizing LLMs with multiple techniques and
[p0117-l0009] [9.8pt] libraries
[p0117-l0010] [10.0pt] In chapter 5, you learned the core ONNX concepts and capabilities. I only briefly
[p0117-l0011] [10.0pt] mentioned model quantization, but it’s crucial for LLM inference performance, so
[p0117-l0012] [10.0pt] it deserves its own chapter. That’s our focus here.
[p0117-l0013] [12.5pt] 6.1
[p0117-l0014] [12.5pt] Transformers precision formats
[p0117-l0015] [10.0pt] Previous chapters have mentioned several numeric precision formats used for LLM
[p0117-l0016] [10.0pt] training and inference. It’s time to look at them more closely and to introduce addi­
[p0117-l0017] [10.0pt] tional formats used for model quantization.
[p0117-l0018] [10.0pt] In traditional scientific computing, 64-bit floating point (double precision) was
[p0117-l0019] [10.0pt] the default because it represents a wide range of values accurately. But deep neural
[p0117-l0020] [10.0pt] networks on GPUs typically use 32-bit floating point (single precision) because 64-bit
[p0117-l0021] [9.0pt] 96

=== PDF page 118 / printed label 97 ===
[p0118-l0001] [9.0pt] 97
[p0118-l0002] [9.0pt] Transformers precision formats
[p0118-l0003] [10.0pt] operations are unnecessary, slower, and often not well supported by GPU hardware. As
[p0118-l0004] [10.0pt] a result, FP32 became the standard for deep-learning training.
[p0118-l0005] [10.0pt] In floating-point numbers, bits are the binary digits used to store a value in a com­
[p0118-l0006] [10.0pt] puter’s memory. More bits mean higher precision and a wider representable range. A
[p0118-l0007] [10.0pt] floating-point value has three parts: the sign, the exponent, and the mantissa. In 32-bit
[p0118-l0008] [10.0pt] floating point, 1 bit is for the sign, 8 bits are for the exponent, and 23 bits are for the
[p0118-l0009] [10.0pt] mantissa (see figure 6.1).
[p0118-l0010] [8.0pt] Figure 6.1  Representation of 32-bit floating point numbers
[p0118-l0011] [10.0pt] A 32-bit floating-point number’s value is given by the following formula:
[p0118-l0012] [10.0pt] In this formula
[p0118-l0013] [10.0pt] are the mantissa bits, and
[p0118-l0014] [10.0pt] There are two main reasons why 32-bit floating-point operations are preferred to 64-bit
[p0118-l0015] [10.0pt] operations for training deep neural networks on GPUs:
[p0118-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Reduced memory footprint—They use half the memory of 64-bit floats, letting
[p0118-l0017] [10.0pt] you train larger models and use larger batch sizes.
[p0118-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Increased compute and speed—32-bit floating point operations use less mem­
[p0118-l0019] [10.0pt] ory, so GPUs can run them more quickly and reduce training time.
[p0118-l0020] [10.0pt] Can we go even further? Mixed-precision training has become a common approach,
[p0118-l0021] [10.0pt] in which 16-bit (“half”) precision is temporarily used for floating-point computations
[p0118-l0022] [10.0pt] (see figure 6.2).

=== PDF page 119 / printed label 98 ===
[p0119-l0001] [9.0pt] 98
[p0119-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0119-l0003] [10.0pt] FP16 uses 1 bit for the sign, 5 bits for the
[p0119-l0004] [10.0pt] exponent, and 10 bits for the mantissa. An
[p0119-l0005] [10.0pt] FP16 value uses the same formula as the
[p0119-l0006] [10.0pt] 32-bit format, but with fewer exponent and
[p0119-l0007] [10.0pt] mantissa bits.
[p0119-l0008] [8.0pt] Figure 6.2  Representation of 16-bit floating
[p0119-l0009] [8.0pt] point numbers
[p0119-l0010] [10.0pt] DL models are generally robust to lower­
[p0119-l0011] [10.0pt] precision arithmetic. In most cases, the
[p0119-l0012] [10.0pt] small loss of precision from using 32-bit
[p0119-l0013] [10.0pt] floats instead of 64-bit floats doesn’t notice­
[p0119-l0014] [10.0pt] ably affect predictive performance, so the
[p0119-l0015] [10.0pt] tradeoff is worth it. But moving to 16-bit
[p0119-l0016] [10.0pt] precision can be trickier. That’s why mixed-precision training is used instead of pure
[p0119-l0017] [10.0pt] 16-bit training. With mixed precision, only some parameters and operations use 16-bit
[p0119-l0018] [10.0pt] floats, switching between 16-bit and 32-bit during training. The typical workflow is to
[p0119-l0019] [10.0pt] convert weights to lower precision for faster computation, compute gradients in lower
[p0119-l0020] [10.0pt] precision, convert gradients back to higher precision for numerical stability, and then
[p0119-l0021] [10.0pt] update the original weights using scaled gradients.
[p0119-l0022] [10.0pt] So far, we’ve focused on training. What about inference? If you train the same LLM
[p0119-l0023] [10.0pt] in FP32 and FP16, memory use is roughly half for the latter (as expected), but perfor­
[p0119-l0024] [10.0pt] mance can degrade significantly. With mixed precision (FP16 + FP32), memory use is
[p0119-l0025] [10.0pt] higher than with pure FP16 but still lower than pure FP32, while performance is compa­
[p0119-l0026] [10.0pt] rable, and often slightly better. This may sound odd, but lower precision can introduce
[p0119-l0027] [10.0pt] noise during training that improves generalization and reduces overfitting, potentially
[p0119-l0028] [10.0pt] increasing accuracy.
[p0119-l0029] [10.0pt] Another floating-point format has been
[p0119-l0030] [10.0pt] introduced recently and is increasingly
[p0119-l0031] [10.0pt] used: brain floating point (BF16), devel­
[p0119-l0032] [10.0pt] oped by Google for ML/DL on tensor pro­
[p0119-l0033] [10.0pt] cessing units (TPUs). Compared to F16 (see
[p0119-l0034] [10.0pt] figure 6.3), it extends dynamic range at the
[p0119-l0035] [10.0pt] cost of lower precision.
[p0119-l0036] [8.0pt] Figure 6.3  Representation of BF16 numbers
[p0119-l0037] [10.0pt] BF16 uses 1 bit for the sign, 8 for the
[p0119-l0038] [10.0pt] exponent, and 7 for the mantissa. This
[p0119-l0039] [10.0pt] lower precision may affect the accuracy of
[p0119-l0040] [10.0pt] some calculations, but in most deep learn­
[p0119-l0041] [10.0pt] ing applications, it has minimal effect on model performance. Models trained in BF16
[p0119-l0042] [10.0pt] typically deliver comparable inference performance and memory use to those trained
[p0119-l0043] [10.0pt] with FP16 mixed precision. BF16 is supported not only by TPUs but also by NVIDIA
[p0119-l0044] [10.0pt] Ampere GPUs. To check whether your NVIDIA GPU supports this format in PyTorch,
[p0119-l0045] [10.0pt] run the following commands:
[p0119-l0046] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0119-l0047] [8.0pt] torch.cuda.is_bf16_supported()

=== PDF page 120 / printed label 99 ===
[p0120-l0001] [9.0pt] 99
[p0120-l0002] [9.0pt] 8-bit quantization
[p0120-l0003] [10.0pt] This method returns True if BF16 is supported, and False otherwise.
[p0120-l0004] [10.0pt] To further improve inference performance, we can go beyond reduced floating-­
[p0120-l0005] [10.0pt] point precision and use quantization—converting an LLM’s weights from floats to low-
[p0120-l0006] [10.0pt] bit integers (typically 8-bit or 4-bit). The rest of this chapter explains LLM quantization
[p0120-l0007] [10.0pt] and provides complete code examples using Hugging Face Transformers and other
[p0120-l0008] [10.0pt] open source libraries.
[p0120-l0009] [12.5pt] 6.2
[p0120-l0010] [12.5pt] 8-bit quantization
[p0120-l0011] [10.0pt] In scenarios with tight computational power constraints, or when deploying to small
[p0120-l0012] [10.0pt] devices, LLMs can be too large and too slow for inference. Using reduced precision
[p0120-l0013] [10.0pt] (FP16) alone may not make a model fit the target hardware. Two common solutions
[p0120-l0014] [10.0pt] are knowledge distillation and quantization, both of which reduce model size with lim­
[p0120-l0015] [10.0pt] ited performance loss. Knowledge distillation trains a smaller model to mimic a larger
[p0120-l0016] [10.0pt] one—this can happen by transferring knowledge from the larger to the smaller model.
[p0120-l0017] [10.0pt] For hardware-specific deployment, quantization is often the better choice, and recent
[p0120-l0018] [10.0pt] advances in stable quantization have made it preferable to distillation in many cases.
[p0120-l0019] [10.0pt] This book focuses on quantization to simplify LLM deployment and improve perfor­
[p0120-l0020] [10.0pt] mance across a wide range of hardware.
[p0120-l0021] [10.0pt] Quantization reduces numeric precision: lowering the bit width of an LLM’s weights
[p0120-l0022] [10.0pt] and activations shrinks the model and can speed up inference. By using lower-precision
[p0120-l0023] [10.0pt] types, such as 8-bit integers, you reduce the memory footprint at the cost of quantiza­
[p0120-l0024] [10.0pt] tion error. For example, 8-bit values can pack about four times as many numbers as
[p0120-l0025] [10.0pt] 32-bit floats in the same amount of memory. The goal is to balance precision against
[p0120-l0026] [10.0pt] memory use (and speed).
[p0120-l0027] [10.0pt] There are two types of quantization: post-training quantization (PTQ), applied after
[p0120-l0028] [10.0pt] training, and quantization-aware training (QAT), done during training. This book
[p0120-l0029] [10.0pt] focuses mostly on PTQ, because starting from a pretrained LLM baseline typically
[p0120-l0030] [10.0pt] doesn’t require full training—only fine-tuning, PEFT, or RAG to adapt it to a specific
[p0120-l0031] [10.0pt] domain.
[p0120-l0032] [10.0pt] How does 8-bit quantization work in practice? Let’s walk through a numerical
[p0120-l0033] [10.0pt] example. There are several quantization schemes; the most common are zero-point and
[p0120-l0034] [10.0pt] absmax. Suppose we want to convert an FP32 tensor to INT8. With zero-point quantiza­
[p0120-l0035] [10.0pt] tion, we assume an asymmetric input distribution, so we scale by the INT8 value range
[p0120-l0036] [10.0pt] (255) divided by the difference between the input’s maximum and minimum values
[p0120-l0037] [10.0pt] (X in the following formula):
[p0120-l0038] [10.0pt] The scaled distribution is then mapped to the [-127, 128] range:

=== PDF page 121 / printed label 100 ===
[p0121-l0001] [9.0pt] 100
[p0121-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0121-l0003] [10.0pt] Finally, we use the calculated scale and zeropoint values to quantize or dequantize a
[p0121-l0004] [10.0pt] model’s weights:
[p0121-l0005] [10.0pt] Let’s look at an example (8-bit quantization): suppose the minimum value is -4.0 and
[p0121-l0006] [10.0pt] the maximum value is 4.1. The scale is 255/(4.1 + 4.0) = 31.48, and the zero-point is
[p0121-l0007] [10.0pt] -round(31.48 × -4.0) – 128 = -3. If the weight is 0.2, then, using the preceding quantiza­
[p0121-l0008] [10.0pt] tion formula, its quantized value is 3. Dequantizing gives 0.19—not exactly the original
[p0121-l0009] [10.0pt] weight (quantization isn’t lossless), but close.
[p0121-l0010] [10.0pt] With absmax quantization, each input value is divided by its tensor’s absolute maxi­
[p0121-l0011] [10.0pt] mum and multiplied by a scale factor (127) to map values to the [-127, 127] range:
[p0121-l0012] [10.0pt] To dequantize, we use this equation:
[p0121-l0013] [10.0pt] For example, using the same maximum value as in the previous zero-point example
[p0121-l0014] [10.0pt] (4.1), absmax quantization maps a weight of 0.2 to round(127 × 0.2 / 4.1) = 6. With
[p0121-l0015] [10.0pt] zero-point quantization, you would get a different value. Dequantizing introduces an
[p0121-l0016] [10.0pt] error: 6 × 4.1 / 127 = 0.19.
[p0121-l0017] [10.0pt] To recap, LLM quantization offers major benefits:
[p0121-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Reduced model size
[p0121-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ Speed and hardware compatibility (low-precision arithmetic can run faster on
[p0121-l0020] [10.0pt] some hardware accelerators)
[p0121-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Memory efficiency
[p0121-l0022] [10.0pt] It also has a few cons:
[p0121-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Accuracy tradeoffs (lower precision can affect model performance)
[p0121-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Implementation challenges
[p0121-l0025] [10.0pt] As for the downsides, don’t worry—this book will help you overcome them.
[p0121-l0026] [10.5pt] 6.2.1
[p0121-l0027] [10.5pt] Hands-on 8-bit quantization
[p0121-l0028] [10.0pt] Let’s walk through a practical example of 8-bit post-training quantization (PTQ) for an
[p0121-l0029] [10.0pt] LLM using PyTorch and the Hugging Face Transformers library (we’ll set ONNX aside

=== PDF page 122 / printed label 101 ===
[p0122-l0001] [9.0pt] 101
[p0122-l0002] [9.0pt] 8-bit quantization
[p0122-l0003] [10.0pt] for now). We’ll use GPT-2 small, but the same considerations apply to other GPT-2
[p0122-l0004] [10.0pt] variants and GPT-based LLMs. We’ll load the pretrained model in 32-bit floating point
[p0122-l0005] [10.0pt] and quantize it to 8-bit integers. A companion Colab notebook includes the full source
[p0122-l0006] [10.0pt] code. No hardware acceleration is required at this stage.
[p0122-l0007] [10.0pt] We’ll load the FP32 model from the Hugging Face Hub as usual:
[p0122-l0008] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
[p0122-l0009] [8.0pt] device = 'cpu'
[p0122-l0010] [8.0pt] model_id = 'openai-community/gpt2'
[p0122-l0011] [8.0pt] model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id).to(device)
[p0122-l0012] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0122-l0013] [10.0pt] In FP32, the model is about 548 MB.
[p0122-l0014] [10.0pt] We can convert all model layers to INT8 format and then quantize the full model
[p0122-l0015] [10.0pt] weights. Let’s define a custom function to do this using the absmax technique:
[p0122-l0016] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0122-l0017] [8.0pt] def absmax_quantize(X):
[p0122-l0018] [8.0pt]     scale = 127 / torch.max(torch.abs(X))
[p0122-l0019] [8.0pt]     X_quant = (scale * X).round()
[p0122-l0020] [8.0pt]     X_dequant = X_quant / scale
[p0122-l0021] [8.0pt]     return X_quant.to(torch.int8), X_dequant
[p0122-l0022] [10.0pt] As described earlier in section 6.2, it runs three steps: calculate the scale, quantize to
[p0122-l0023] [10.0pt] INT8, and dequantize back to FP32. For a given input, it returns both the quantized
[p0122-l0024] [10.0pt] and dequantized values. Let’s use it to quantize all the GPT-2 model weights:
[p0122-l0025] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0122-l0026] [8.0pt] from copy import deepcopy
[p0122-l0027] [8.0pt] weights = [param.data.clone() for param in model.parameters()]
[p0122-l0028] [8.0pt] model_abs = deepcopy(model)
[p0122-l0029] [8.0pt] weights_abs = []
[p0122-l0030] [8.0pt] for param in model_abs.parameters():
[p0122-l0031] [8.0pt]     _, dequantized = absmax_quantize(param.data)
[p0122-l0032] [8.0pt]     param.data = dequantized
[p0122-l0033] [8.0pt]     weights_abs.append(dequantized)
[p0122-l0034] [10.0pt] We have created a copy of the source model and applied our absmax_quantize function
[p0122-l0035] [10.0pt] to all its weights to quantize them.
[p0122-l0036] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll verify the resulting performance of this process. One useful check is to
[p0122-l0037] [10.0pt] plot the distribution of the model’s weights before and after quantization to see how

[p0123-l0004] [10.0pt] (https://matplotlib.org/) to build a histogram (see the notebook for the full code). In
[p0123-l0005] [10.0pt] figure 6.4, you can see a spike around 0, which suggests that quantization is quite lossy
[p0123-l0006] [10.0pt] in this case, since reversing the process doesn’t reproduce the exact original values.

[p0124-l0034] [10.0pt] Rather than trying to decide empirically which of these two outputs makes more sense,
[p0124-l0035] [10.0pt] you can compute a quantitative score by calculating the perplexity of each one. Perplex­
[p0124-l0036] [10.0pt] ity is a common metric for evaluating LLMs: it measures a model’s uncertainty when
[p0124-l0037] [10.0pt] predicting the next token in a sequence. It’s often assumed that lower is better, but a
[p0124-l0038] [10.0pt] sentence with high perplexity can still be correct.
[p0124-l0039] [10.0pt] We can implement a basic function that calculates perplexity:

[p0125-l0001] [9.0pt] 104
[p0125-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0125-l0003] [8.0pt] def calculate_perplexity(model, text, device):
[p0125-l0004] [8.0pt]     encodings = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt').to(device)
[p0125-l0005] [8.0pt]     input_ids = encodings.input_ids
[p0125-l0006] [8.0pt]     target_ids = input_ids.clone()
[p0125-l0007] [8.0pt]     with torch.no_grad():
[p0125-l0008] [8.0pt]         outputs = model(input_ids, labels=target_ids)
[p0125-l0009] [8.0pt]     neg_log_likelihood = outputs.loss
[p0125-l0010] [8.0pt]     perplexity = torch.exp(neg_log_likelihood)
[p0125-l0011] [8.0pt]     return perplexity
[p0125-l0012] [10.0pt] This function expects three arguments: a model, a text prompt, and the device to off­
[p0125-l0013] [10.0pt] load the model weights to. It encodes the input sequence, prepares the model inputs,
[p0125-l0014] [10.0pt] generates text, computes the loss, and uses it to calculate the perplexity score (which
[p0125-l0015] [10.0pt] is returned to the caller). We can apply this function to both models—the original and
[p0125-l0016] [10.0pt] the absmax-quantized one—using as the prompt the text each model generated a few
[p0125-l0017] [10.0pt] steps earlier:
[p0125-l0018] [8.0pt] perplexity = calculate_perplexity(model, original_text, device)
[p0125-l0019] [8.0pt] perplexity_absmax = calculate_perplexity(model_abs, absmax_text, device)
[p0125-l0020] [10.0pt] These are the measured perplexity scores:
[p0125-l0021] [8.0pt] Original perplexity:  18.66
[p0125-l0022] [8.0pt] Absmax perplexity:    8.20
[p0125-l0023] [10.0pt] In this example, the quantized model has lower perplexity than the original. But a
[p0125-l0024] [10.0pt] single run isn’t very reliable; you should repeat the experiment several times to under­
[p0125-l0025] [10.0pt] stand the differences between the models. This is easier if you first create two reusable
[p0125-l0026] [10.0pt] functions.
[p0125-l0027] [10.5pt] 6.2.2
[p0125-l0028] [10.5pt] LLM.int8() and quantization
[p0125-l0029] [10.0pt] In the previous example, for simplicity, we applied per-tensor quantization to all the
[p0125-l0030] [10.0pt] model layers. But you can quantize at different granularities. Quantizing the whole
[p0125-l0031] [10.0pt] model in one pass can seriously degrade performance, but quantizing individual val­
[p0125-l0032] [10.0pt] ues creates too much overhead. In practice, a good compromise is vector-wise quan­
[p0125-l0033] [10.0pt] tization, which accounts for variability across rows and columns within a tensor. This
[p0125-l0034] [10.0pt] is often sufficient for domain-specific models, since they’re typically under 7 billion
[p0125-l0035] [10.0pt] parameters. Above that threshold, you may see outlier features in any LLM layer. Even
[p0125-l0036] [10.0pt] a single outlier can significantly reduce precision for the other values, and you can’t
[p0125-l0037] [10.0pt] just discard outliers without a nontrivial hit to model performance.

=== PDF page 126 / printed label 105 ===
[p0126-l0001] [9.0pt] 105
[p0126-l0002] [9.0pt] 8-bit quantization
[p0126-l0003] [10.0pt] What can we do instead? Fortunately, there’s no need for custom implementations—
[p0126-l0004] [10.0pt] LLM.int8() already addresses this. First introduced in a 2022 paper (https://arxiv.org/
[p0126-l0005] [10.0pt] abs/2208.07339), it enables INT8 matrix multiplication for LLMs with no accuracy
[p0126-l0006] [10.0pt] loss. It cuts inference memory roughly in half while retaining full-precision perfor­
[p0126-l0007] [10.0pt] mance. It uses an absmax quantization scheme with mixed precision: outlier features
[p0126-l0008] [10.0pt] are processed in FP16 to preserve accuracy, while the remaining values use INT8. This
[p0126-l0009] [10.0pt] approach reduces an LLM’s memory footprint by nearly two times.
[p0126-l0010] [10.0pt] LLM.int8() performs matrix multiplication in three steps:
[p0126-l0011] [10.0pt] 1	 It extracts columns with outlier features (a small number of weights or activations
[p0126-l0012] [10.0pt] whose values are much larger in magnitude than the rest of the distribution)
[p0126-l0013] [10.0pt] from the input hidden states using a custom threshold.
[p0126-l0014] [10.0pt] 2	 Then it multiplies the outliers in FP16 and the rest in INT8 using vector-wise
[p0126-l0015] [10.0pt] quantization.
[p0126-l0016] [10.0pt] 3	 Finally, it dequantizes the non-outlier results (INT8 to FP16), adds them to the
[p0126-l0017] [10.0pt] outlier results, and produces the full FP16 result.
[p0126-l0018] [10.0pt] There’s more good news: LLM.int8() is integrated into the Hugging Face Transformers
[p0126-l0019] [10.0pt] API. It requires the Accelerate and bitsandbytes (https://github.com/bitsandbytes
[p0126-l0020] [10.0pt] -foundation/bitsandbytes) libraries; bitsandbytes implements LLM.int8() quantization
[p0126-l0021] [10.0pt] and runs on GPUs only.
[p0126-l0022] [10.0pt] A companion Colab notebook contains the full source code for this section and
[p0126-l0023] [10.0pt] requires GPU acceleration. The steps are similar to those in section 6.2.1, so only the
[p0126-l0024] [10.0pt] main parts are discussed here.
[p0126-l0025] [10.0pt] To load a quantized GPT-2 small model with this strategy, set load_in_8bit=True in
[p0126-l0026] [10.0pt] the Transformers auto class:
[p0126-l0027] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0126-l0028] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
[p0126-l0029] [8.0pt] device = torch.device('cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu')
[p0126-l0030] [8.0pt] model_id = 'openai-community/gpt2'
[p0126-l0031] [8.0pt] model_int8 = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id,
[p0126-l0032] [8.0pt]                                              device_map='auto',
[p0126-l0033] [8.0pt]                                              load_in_8bit=True,
[p0126-l0034] [8.0pt]                                              )
[p0126-l0035] [10.0pt] This model is about 176 MB—much smaller than the FP32 version. As in section 6.2.1,
[p0126-l0036] [10.0pt] we can plot the weight distributions for the original and quantized models to see how
[p0126-l0037] [10.0pt] closely they match (see figure 6.5).
[p0126-l0038] [10.0pt] Here we see spikes around certain values. They match parameters stored in INT8
[p0126-l0039] [10.0pt] format, so they’re not outliers. We can run inference with both models:
[p0126-l0040] [8.0pt] prompt = 'My favourite school subject is'
[p0126-l0041] [8.0pt] original_text = generate_text(model, prompt)
[p0126-l0042] [8.0pt] text_int8 = generate_text(model_int8, prompt)

=== PDF page 127 / printed label 106 ===
[p0127-l0001] [9.0pt] 106

[p0128-l0017] [12.5pt] 6.3
[p0128-l0018] [12.5pt] 8-bit quantization with ONNX
[p0128-l0019] [10.0pt] Let’s explore ONNX-based 8-bit PTQ using the bert-base-uncased model. The same
[p0128-l0020] [10.0pt] steps apply to any other transformer-based language models.
[p0128-l0021] [10.0pt] The Hugging Face API supports three approaches to LLM optimization, commonly
[p0128-l0022] [10.0pt] described in the literature as low-level, mid-level, and high-level. Let’s look at each.
[p0128-l0023] [10.0pt] The low-level approach uses PyTorch’s native torch.onnx module, which was used in
[p0128-l0024] [10.0pt] section 5.5 and 5.6 code examples. It provides the export method to convert a model
[p0128-l0025] [10.0pt] checkpoint to an ONNX graph. It’s considered low-level because it requires more man­
[p0128-l0026] [10.0pt] ual configuration and boilerplate code in the PyTorch API. While it’s a solid option for
[p0128-l0027] [10.0pt] model conversion and optimization, other quantization options are available.
[p0128-l0028] [10.0pt] The mid-level approach uses Transformers’ transformers.onnx package. Let’s use
[p0128-l0029] [10.0pt] the bert-base-uncased model (as in section 5.5) and look at the conversion and optimi­
[p0128-l0030] [10.0pt] zation process. First, load the model and tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0128-l0031] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification
[p0128-l0032] [8.0pt] model_id = 'google-bert/bert-base-uncased'
[p0128-l0033] [8.0pt] model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0128-l0034] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0128-l0035] [10.0pt] Next, load its configuration (via the transformer.onnx.FeaturesManager class), and
[p0128-l0036] [10.0pt] build the ONNX configuration:
[p0128-l0037] [8.0pt] from transformers.onnx import FeaturesManager
[p0128-l0038] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoConfig

=== PDF page 129 / printed label 108 ===
[p0129-l0001] [9.0pt] 108
[p0129-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0129-l0003] [8.0pt] feature = "sequence-classification"
[p0129-l0004] [8.0pt] model_kind, model_onnx_config =
[p0129-l0005] [10.0pt] ➥FeaturesManager.check_supported_model_or_raise(
[p0129-l0006] [8.0pt]                         model,
[p0129-l0007] [8.0pt]                         feature=feature)
[p0129-l0008] [8.0pt] onnx_config = model_onnx_config(model.config)
[p0129-l0009] [10.0pt] The conversion process could proceed as follows:
[p0129-l0010] [8.0pt] from pathlib import Path
[p0129-l0011] [8.0pt] from transformers.onnx import export
[p0129-l0012] [8.0pt] onnx_inputs, onnx_outputs = export(
[p0129-l0013] [8.0pt]         preprocessor=tokenizer,
[p0129-l0014] [8.0pt]         model=model,
[p0129-l0015] [8.0pt]         config=onnx_config,
[p0129-l0016] [8.0pt]         opset=14,
[p0129-l0017] [8.0pt]         output=Path("bert_uncased.onnx")
[p0129-l0018] [8.0pt] )
[p0129-l0019] [10.0pt] Like the native PyTorch package, the Transformers library includes an export method.
[p0129-l0020] [10.0pt] Compared with the example in section 5.5, it requires far fewer configuration settings.
[p0129-l0021] [10.0pt] The high-level approach uses Optimum (https://github.com/huggingface/
[p0129-l0022] [10.0pt] optimum), a Hugging Face Transformers extension that provides optimization tools for
[p0129-l0023] [10.0pt] training and running LLMs on target hardware efficiently. Optimum includes several
[p0129-l0024] [10.0pt] specialized packages; one supports graph optimization and quantization to speed up
[p0129-l0025] [10.0pt] training and inference with ONNX Runtime. You don’t need to install every package—
[p0129-l0026] [10.0pt] if you only need ONNX Runtime support, install that package, and skip the rest:
[p0129-l0027] [8.0pt] pip install optimum[onnxruntime]
[p0129-l0028] [10.0pt] Using the bert-base-uncased model, you can convert the model to ONNX format (a
[p0129-l0029] [10.0pt] graph) with Optimum in a single line of code:
[p0129-l0030] [8.0pt] from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification
[p0129-l0031] [8.0pt] model_id = 'bert-base-uncased'
[p0129-l0032] [8.0pt] model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id,
[p0129-l0033] [8.0pt]                                                     from_transformers=True)
[p0129-l0034] [10.0pt] Optimum for ONNX provides several ORTModelForXxx classes, each specialized for a
[p0129-l0035] [10.0pt] downstream task. In our example, we use ORTModelForSequenceClassification for
[p0129-l0036] [10.0pt] sequence-classification tasks. Optimum uses the transformers.onnx package behind
[p0129-l0037] [10.0pt] the scenes, transparently keeping the code high level. Note that Optimum does not
[p0129-l0038] [10.0pt] yet support all Transformer architectures (a popular unsupported LLM is shown in
[p0129-l0039] [10.0pt] chapter 7), so check the Hugging Face Hub for the latest list of supported models. For
[p0129-l0040] [10.0pt] unsupported models, you can use transformers.onnx directly or implement a custom
[p0129-l0041] [10.0pt] ONNX configuration, which we’ll cover later in the book.

=== PDF page 130 / printed label 109 ===
[p0130-l0001] [9.0pt] 109
[p0130-l0002] [9.0pt] 8-bit quantization with ONNX
[p0130-l0003] [10.0pt] Whatever technique you use, once you’ve converted an LLM to ONNX, the 8-bit
[p0130-l0004] [10.0pt] quantization process is the same. After you download it or save it to disk, you can use the
[p0130-l0005] [10.0pt] ONNX Runtime quantization API to dynamically quantize the converted model. Here’s
[p0130-l0006] [10.0pt] an example:
[p0130-l0007] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime.quantization import quantize_dynamic, QuantType
[p0130-l0008] [8.0pt] onnx_path = 'bert_uncased_model.onnx'
[p0130-l0009] [8.0pt] onnx_quantized_path = 'bert_uncased_quantized_model.onnx'
[p0130-l0010] [8.0pt] quantized_model = quantize_dynamic(onnx_path, onnx_quantized_path,
[p0130-l0011] [8.0pt]                                    weight_type=QuantType.QInt8)
[p0130-l0012] [10.0pt] The full-precision converted ONNX model is 417.91 MB (down from 440 MB before
[p0130-l0013] [10.0pt] conversion), while the quantized model is 105.22 MB.
[p0130-l0014] [10.0pt] The following end-to-end example performs 8-bit quantization with ONNX and eval­
[p0130-l0015] [10.0pt] uates its performance—this is a best-case scenario, where the domain-specific model
[p0130-l0016] [10.0pt] architecture is supported by Optimum. A companion Colab notebook includes the full
[p0130-l0017] [10.0pt] code. This example requires only Optimum (for ONNX Runtime) and Hugging Face’s
[p0130-l0018] [10.0pt] Evaluate library (https://github.com/huggingface/evaluate).
[p0130-l0019] [10.0pt] Because this section focuses on inference, we’ll use a model from the Hugging Face
[p0130-l0020] [10.0pt] Hub that has already been fine-tuned from distilbert-base-uncased: distilbert-base-­
[p0130-l0021] [10.0pt] uncased-finetuned-banking77. This model was fine-tuned for text classification on the
[p0130-l0022] [10.0pt] PolyAI/banking77 dataset (also on the Hugging Face Hub: https://huggingface.co/
[p0130-l0023] [10.0pt] datasets/PolyAI/banking77), which contains online banking queries annotated with
[p0130-l0024] [10.0pt] their corresponding intents. The dataset comprises 13,083 customer service queries
[p0130-l0025] [10.0pt] labeled with 77 intents, and it has two fields: text (the query) and label (the intent
[p0130-l0026] [10.0pt] label).
[p0130-l0027] [10.0pt] We’ll first download the fine-tuned FP32 model from the Hub and its tokenizer:
[p0130-l0028] [8.0pt] from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForSequenceClassification
[p0130-l0029] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer
[p0130-l0030] [8.0pt] model_id="optimum/distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-banking77"
[p0130-l0031] [8.0pt] model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id,
[p0130-l0032] [8.0pt]                                                         export=True)
[p0130-l0033] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0130-l0034] [10.0pt] We are using Optimum’s ORTModelForSequenceClassification to download the model
[p0130-l0035] [10.0pt] and automatically convert it to ONNX format. We are still using the Transformers’
[p0130-l0036] [10.0pt] AutoTokenizer to download the tokenizer for the baseline model. After the download
[p0130-l0037] [10.0pt] completes, we save both to disk (this step is required only for quantization):
[p0130-l0038] [8.0pt] from pathlib import Path
[p0130-l0039] [8.0pt] onnx_path = Path("onnx")
[p0130-l0040] [8.0pt] model.save_pretrained(onnx_path)
[p0130-l0041] [8.0pt] tokenizer.save_pretrained(onnx_path)

[p0131-l0001] [9.0pt] 110
[p0131-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0131-l0003] [10.0pt] Since Optimum downloaded the model, we can use the Transformers pipelines (sup­
[p0131-l0004] [10.0pt] ported by the library, unlike the native ONNX Runtime) to run inference and confirm
[p0131-l0005] [10.0pt] the model works:
[p0131-l0006] [8.0pt] from transformers import pipeline
[p0131-l0007] [8.0pt] vanilla_clf = pipeline("text-classification", model=model,
[p0131-l0008] [10.0pt] ➥tokenizer=tokenizer)
[p0131-l0009] [8.0pt] vanilla_clf("Could you assist me in checking my card validity?")
[p0131-l0010] [10.0pt] We now need to quantize the model to 8-bit precision, using dynamic quantization.
[p0131-l0011] [10.0pt] Unlike static quantization, dynamic quantization runs only on the CPU, not the GPU.
[p0131-l0012] [10.0pt] That’s not a problem, because quantization happens offline, and inference is still fast
[p0131-l0013] [10.0pt] without hardware acceleration (as you’ll see later in this section).
[p0131-l0014] [10.0pt] We’ll create an instance of ORTQuantizer (Optimum’s class for ONNX Runtime
[p0131-l0015] [10.0pt] quantization of models shared on the Hub) and define the quantization configuration.
[p0131-l0016] [10.0pt] Then we can apply it to the original model:
[p0131-l0017] [8.0pt] from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTQuantizer
[p0131-l0018] [8.0pt] from optimum.onnxruntime.configuration import AutoQuantizationConfig
[p0131-l0019] [8.0pt] dynamic_quantizer = ORTQuantizer.from_pretrained(model)
[p0131-l0020] [8.0pt] dqconfig = AutoQuantizationConfig.avx512_vnni(is_static=False,
[p0131-l0021] [8.0pt]                                               per_channel=False)
[p0131-l0022] [8.0pt] model_quantized_path = dynamic_quantizer.quantize(
[p0131-l0023] [8.0pt]     save_dir=onnx_path,
[p0131-l0024] [8.0pt]     quantization_config=dqconfig,
[p0131-l0025] [8.0pt] )
[p0131-l0026] [10.0pt] Once quantization is complete, we can compare model sizes: the original file is 255.76
[p0131-l0027] [10.0pt] MB, while the quantized version is 64.33 MB.
[p0131-l0028] [10.0pt] You can run inference on the quantized model the same way as on the original, using
[p0131-l0029] [10.0pt] a Transformers pipeline:
[p0131-l0030] [8.0pt] quantized_model_name = "model_quantized.onnx"
[p0131-l0031] [8.0pt] model = ORTModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(onnx_path,
[p0131-l0032] [8.0pt]                                             file_name=quantized_model_name)
[p0131-l0033] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(onnx_path)
[p0131-l0034] [8.0pt] q8_clf = pipeline("text-classification",model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer)
[p0131-l0035] [8.0pt] q8_clf("Could you assist me in checking my card validity?")
[p0131-l0036] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll evaluate model performance on the PolyAI/banking77 test set to see how
[p0131-l0037] [10.0pt] quantization affected accuracy. We can do this with Hugging Face’s high-level Evaluate
[p0131-l0038] [10.0pt] API: create an evaluator for the specific task (text classification in our example), load
[p0131-l0039] [10.0pt] the test set, and call the evaluator’s compute method, specifying the pipeline, the test

[p0132-l0003] [10.0pt] set (including which fields are inputs and labels), and the metric to compute (accuracy
[p0132-l0004] [10.0pt] here, though the code in the notebook also computes others):
[p0132-l0005] [8.0pt] from evaluate import evaluator
[p0132-l0006] [8.0pt] from datasets import load_dataset
[p0132-l0007] [8.0pt] dataset_id="PolyAI/banking77"

[p0132-l0017] [8.0pt]     strategy="simple",

[p0132-l0019] [10.0pt] According to the Hugging Face Hub, the original model’s accuracy is 92.5%. Running
[p0132-l0020] [10.0pt] the preceding code yields 92.34% for the quantized model (99.82% of the FP32 base­
[p0132-l0021] [10.0pt] line), a negligible loss. But what about latency? We can write a quick-and-dirty bench­
[p0132-l0022] [10.0pt] mark function to compare the two versions (chapters 7 and 10 show better ONNX
[p0132-l0023] [10.0pt] benchmarking approaches):
[p0132-l0024] [8.0pt] def measure_latency(payload_prompt, pipe):
[p0132-l0025] [8.0pt]     latencies = []
[p0132-l0026] [8.0pt]     for _ in range(10):
[p0132-l0027] [8.0pt]         _ = pipe(payload_prompt)
[p0132-l0028] [8.0pt]     for _ in range(300):
[p0132-l0029] [8.0pt]         start_time = perf_counter()
[p0132-l0030] [8.0pt]         _ =  pipe(payload_prompt)
[p0132-l0031] [8.0pt]         latency = perf_counter() - start_time
[p0132-l0032] [8.0pt]         latencies.append(latency)
[p0132-l0033] [8.0pt]     time_avg_ms = 1000 * np.mean(latencies)
[p0132-l0034] [8.0pt]     time_std_ms = 1000 * np.std(latencies)
[p0132-l0035] [8.0pt]     time_p95_ms = 1000 * np.percentile(latencies,95)
[p0132-l0036] [8.0pt]     return f"P95 latency (ms) - {time_p95_ms}; Average latency (ms)
[p0132-l0037] [10.0pt] ➥ - {time_avg_ms:.2f} +\- {time_std_ms:.2f};", time_p95_ms
[p0132-l0038] [10.0pt] This pipeline runs a short warmup (a few initial inference passes to stabilize caches
[p0132-l0039] [10.0pt] and compilation effects), benchmarks a set number of steps, then reports the average
[p0132-l0040] [10.0pt] latency and standard deviation. Running it on both the original and quantized model
[p0132-l0041] [10.0pt] pipelines with a 142-token prompt shows a 1.86x inference speedup with the quantized
[p0132-l0042] [10.0pt] model. With comparable performance, quantization significantly reduces latency.

[p0133-l0001] [9.0pt] 112
[p0133-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0133-l0003] [12.5pt] 6.4
[p0133-l0004] [12.5pt] 4-bit quantization
[p0133-l0005] [10.0pt] In the previous section, you saw practical examples of LLM quantization from single
[p0133-l0006] [10.0pt] precision to 8-bit integer format. Now let’s push further and reduce the model size by
[p0133-l0007] [10.0pt] quantizing to a lower precision, such as 4-bit integers.
[p0133-l0008] [10.5pt] 6.4.1
[p0133-l0009] [10.5pt] 4-bit quantization with GPTQ
[p0133-l0010] [10.0pt] After 8-bit quantization proved effective at shrinking LLMs with little loss in accuracy,
[p0133-l0011] [10.0pt] new techniques emerged for 4-bit integer quantization. The first was GPTQ, proposed
[p0133-l0012] [10.0pt] in 2022 in “GPTQ: Accurate Post-Training Quantization for Generative Pre-Trained
[p0133-l0013] [10.0pt] Transformers” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17323). GPTQ is a one-shot weight-­
[p0133-l0014] [10.0pt] quantization method based on approximate second-order information that is both
[p0133-l0015] [10.0pt] accurate and efficient. It can reduce GPT-based models to 3 or 4 bits per weight with
[p0133-l0016] [10.0pt] negligible accuracy loss compared to the uncompressed baseline. The paper reports
[p0133-l0017] [10.0pt] that even 175B-parameter models can run inference on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU
[p0133-l0018] [10.0pt] after quantization, and the method can also yield strong results on smaller models
[p0133-l0019] [10.0pt] and less powerful GPUs. The paper covers the math and methodology, but you don’t
[p0133-l0020] [10.0pt] need to master them to use GPTQ because a solid Python implementation is available
[p0133-l0021] [10.0pt] and integrated into major LLM libraries. The de facto standard implementation is the
[p0133-l0022] [10.0pt] AutoGPTQ package (https://github.com/AutoGPTQ/AutoGPTQ). Consult the asso­
[p0133-l0023] [10.0pt] ciated repository only if you want low-level implementation details—AutoGPTQ is also
[p0133-l0024] [10.0pt] integrated into the Hugging Face Transformers, Optimum, and PEFT libraries. In this
[p0133-l0025] [10.0pt] chapter, we’ll use the original implementation to make it easier to see how 4-bit quanti­
[p0133-l0026] [10.0pt] zation works (higher-level APIs hide many details).
[p0133-l0027] [10.0pt] In this section, you’ll learn how to use AutoGPTQ. A companion Colab notebook pro­
[p0133-l0028] [10.0pt] vides the full source code for the example. Along with AutoGPTQ, we’ll use the Hug­
[p0133-l0029] [10.0pt] ging Face Transformers library to apply 4-bit quantization to the GPT-2 XL model (1.5B
[p0133-l0030] [10.0pt] parameters, https://huggingface.co/openai-community/gpt2-xl). We’ll run with hard­
[p0133-l0031] [10.0pt] ware acceleration on a single NVIDIA Tesla T4 GPU.
[p0133-l0032] [10.0pt] After installing AutoGPTQ (see the package documentation; steps vary depending on
[p0133-l0033] [10.0pt] your PyTorch and CUDA driver versions), we can start implementing the model quanti­
[p0133-l0034] [10.0pt] zation code. First, download the GPT-2 XL tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0133-l0035] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer
[p0133-l0036] [8.0pt] model_id = "gpt2-xl"
[p0133-l0037] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0133-l0038] [10.0pt] Before loading the unquantized model, we need to define a base 4-bit quantization
[p0133-l0039] [10.0pt] configuration with AutoGPTQ’s BaseQuantizeConfig class:
[p0133-l0040] [8.0pt] from auto_gptq import BaseQuantizeConfig
[p0133-l0041] [8.0pt] quantize_config = BaseQuantizeConfig(
[p0133-l0042] [8.0pt]     bits=4,

=== PDF page 134 / printed label 113 ===
[p0134-l0001] [9.0pt] 113
[p0134-l0002] [9.0pt] 4-bit quantization
[p0134-l0003] [8.0pt]     group_size=128,
[p0134-l0004] [8.0pt]     desc_act=False,
[p0134-l0005] [8.0pt] )
[p0134-l0006] [10.0pt] We can now download the model:
[p0134-l0007] [8.0pt] from auto_gptq import AutoGPTQForCausalLM
[p0134-l0008] [8.0pt] model = AutoGPTQForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, quantize_config)
[p0134-l0009] [10.0pt] We can get the maximum sequence length from its configuration:
[p0134-l0010] [8.0pt] model_config = model.config.to_dict()
[p0134-l0011] [8.0pt] seq_len_keys = ["max_position_embeddings", "seq_length", "n_positions"]
[p0134-l0012] [8.0pt] if any(k in model_config for k in seq_len_keys):
[p0134-l0013] [8.0pt]     for key in seq_len_keys:
[p0134-l0014] [8.0pt]         if key in model_config:
[p0134-l0015] [8.0pt]             model.seqlen = model_config[key]
[p0134-l0016] [8.0pt]             break
[p0134-l0017] [8.0pt] else:
[p0134-l0018] [8.0pt]     print(
[p0134-l0019] [8.0pt]     "The model's sequence length cannot be retrieved from
[p0134-l0020] [8.0pt] its configuration. It will then be set to 2048."
[p0134-l0021] [8.0pt]     )
[p0134-l0022] [8.0pt]     model.seqlen = 2048
[p0134-l0023] [10.0pt] To perform one-shot weight quantization, we need some sample sequences. We’ll use
[p0134-l0024] [10.0pt] a few from the wikitext dataset on the Hugging Face Hub, which we used in section
[p0134-l0025] [10.0pt] 4.1.4:
[p0134-l0026] [8.0pt] import random
[p0134-l0027] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0134-l0028] [8.0pt] from datasets import load_dataset
[p0134-l0029] [8.0pt] seed = 0
[p0134-l0030] [8.0pt] random.seed(seed)
[p0134-l0031] [8.0pt] np.random.seed(seed)
[p0134-l0032] [8.0pt] torch.random.manual_seed(seed)
[p0134-l0033] [8.0pt] traindata = load_dataset("wikitext", "wikitext-2-raw-v1", split="train")
[p0134-l0034] [8.0pt] trainenc = tokenizer("\n\n".join(traindata["text"]), return_tensors="pt")
[p0134-l0035] [8.0pt] nsamples = 128
[p0134-l0036] [8.0pt] seqlen = model.seqlen
[p0134-l0037] [8.0pt] traindataset = []
[p0134-l0038] [8.0pt] for _ in range(nsamples):
[p0134-l0039] [8.0pt]     i = random.randint(0, trainenc.input_ids.shape[1] - seqlen - 1)
[p0134-l0040] [8.0pt]     j = i + seqlen
[p0134-l0041] [8.0pt]     inp = trainenc.input_ids[:, i:j]
[p0134-l0042] [8.0pt]     attention_mask = torch.ones_like(inp)
[p0134-l0043] [8.0pt]     traindataset.append({"input_ids": inp, "attention_mask":
[p0134-l0044] [10.0pt]    ➥attention_mask})

=== PDF page 135 / printed label 114 ===
[p0135-l0001] [9.0pt] 114
[p0135-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0135-l0003] [10.0pt] The preceding code snippet builds a small dataset of 128 samples from the wikitext
[p0135-l0004] [10.0pt] training set. Quantization quality depends on the samples used for conversion: more
[p0135-l0005] [10.0pt] samples can improve results. The number of samples to use depends on your use case,
[p0135-l0006] [10.0pt] model, and data—there’s no one-size-fits-all setting.
[p0135-l0007] [10.0pt] We can now start the quantization process. It will take a few minutes on the hardware
[p0135-l0008] [10.0pt] we’re using, but that’s fine because it runs offline:
[p0135-l0009] [8.0pt] model.quantize(traindataset, use_triton=False)
[p0135-l0010] [10.0pt] In this scenario, quantizing an LLM takes a single line of code once the training sam­
[p0135-l0011] [10.0pt] ples are prepared. We set use_triton to False because we’re using CUDA rather than
[p0135-l0012] [10.0pt] the NVIDIA Triton language and compiler (https://triton-lang.org/main/index
[p0135-l0013] [10.0pt] .html).
[p0135-l0014] [10.0pt] After quantization, save the 4-bit model to disk:
[p0135-l0015] [8.0pt] quantized_model_dir = "gpt2-xl-4bit"
[p0135-l0016] [8.0pt] model.save_quantized(quantized_model_dir)
[p0135-l0017] [10.0pt] You can optionally also upload it for sharing on the Hugging Face Hub. The original
[p0135-l0018] [10.0pt] model is 6.43 GB; the 4-bit quantized version is 1.02 GB.
[p0135-l0019] [10.0pt] The model is now ready for inference. Load it from where you saved it:
[p0135-l0020] [8.0pt] from auto_gptq import AutoGPTQForCausalLM
[p0135-l0021] [8.0pt] model = AutoGPTQForCausalLM.from_quantized(quantized_model_dir,
[p0135-l0022] [8.0pt]                                            device="cuda:0",
[p0135-l0023] [10.0pt]                                            ➥use_triton=False)
[p0135-l0024] [10.0pt] Currently, AutoGPTQ supports loading a quantized model only on CPUs or a single
[p0135-l0025] [10.0pt] GPU; multi-GPU setups aren’t supported. You can run inference by invoking the mod­
[p0135-l0026] [10.0pt] el’s generate method:
[p0135-l0027] [8.0pt] prompt = "Auto-GPTQ is"
[p0135-l0028] [8.0pt] output = tokenizer.decode(
[p0135-l0029] [8.0pt]     model.generate(**tokenizer(prompt,
[p0135-l0030] [10.0pt]     ➥return_tensors="pt").to("cuda:0"))[0])
[p0135-l0031] [8.0pt] print(output)
[p0135-l0032] [10.0pt] The same weight-analysis and model-evaluation considerations (perplexity calculation
[p0135-l0033] [10.0pt] in section 6.2 and inference benchmarking in section 6.3) apply here as well.
[p0135-l0034] [10.5pt] 6.4.2
[p0135-l0035] [10.5pt] 4-bit quantization with ggml
[p0135-l0036] [10.0pt] GPTQ isn’t the only way to get 4-bit post-training quantization for LLMs. Another
[p0135-l0037] [10.0pt] option is ggml (https://github.com/ggerganov/ggml), an open source C library that
[p0135-l0038] [10.0pt] supports several quantization levels (8-bit, 5-bit, and 4-bit). Models quantized with
[p0135-l0039] [10.0pt] ggml are typically saved in the GGML binary file format. Although it’s optimized for

=== PDF page 136 / printed label 115 ===
[p0136-l0001] [9.0pt] 115
[p0136-l0002] [9.0pt] 4-bit quantization
[p0136-l0003] [10.0pt] Apple Silicon, ggml-quantized models can also run on x86 (using AVX/AVX2 intrin­
[p0136-l0004] [10.0pt] sics), ppc64 (using VSX intrinsics), and Android. ggml is fast in part because it has no
[p0136-l0005] [10.0pt] third-party dependencies and does zero memory allocations at runtime.
[p0136-l0006] [10.0pt] ggml can also quantize other Transformer architectures (for example, image and
[p0136-l0007] [10.0pt] audio models), but in this chapter (and the next) we focus on LLMs and how to run
[p0136-l0008] [10.0pt] them efficiently on CPUs. GPTQ inference is optimized for GPUs, whereas ggml infer­
[p0136-l0009] [10.0pt] ence is optimized for CPUs, which makes it practical for many environments, including
[p0136-l0010] [10.0pt] typical laptops and personal computers. Recent releases also support limited GPU off­
[p0136-l0011] [10.0pt] loading at inference time—not to speed up inference, but to reduce power use and free
[p0136-l0012] [10.0pt] up CPU resources.
[p0136-l0013] [10.0pt] Later chapters return to ggml for more advanced optimization and quantization
[p0136-l0014] [10.0pt] techniques; unlike Hugging Face’s Python libraries, it requires more low-level program­
[p0136-l0015] [10.0pt] ming knowledge.
[p0136-l0016] [10.0pt] Scripts for converting some of the most popular open source LLMs to GGML format
[p0136-l0017] [10.0pt] are available in ggml’s official GitHub repository, and many quantized versions are
[p0136-l0018] [10.0pt] already available for download from the Hugging Face Hub. Although ggml is written in
[p0136-l0019] [10.0pt] C, you can load quantized models and run inference entirely in Python using Hugging
[p0136-l0020] [10.0pt] Face Transformers and CTransformers (https://github.com/marella/ctransformers).
[p0136-l0021] [10.0pt] CTransformers provides Python bindings for Transformer models implemented in
[p0136-l0022] [10.0pt] C/C++ via ggml.
[p0136-l0023] [10.0pt] The following example runs inference with a GGML-converted model using the
[p0136-l0024] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Transformers pipeline API:
[p0136-l0025] [8.0pt] from ctransformers import AutoModelForCausalLM
[p0136-l0026] [8.0pt] from transformers import pipeline, AutoTokenizer
[p0136-l0027] [8.0pt] model = AutoModelForCausalLM
[p0136-l0028] [10.0pt] ➥.from_pretrained("TheBloke/Llama-2-7B-Chat-GGML", hf=True)
[p0136-l0029] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("NousResearch/Llama-2-7b-chat-hf")
[p0136-l0030] [8.0pt] pipe = pipeline("text-generation", model=model, tokenizer=tokenizer)
[p0136-l0031] [8.0pt] print(pipe("AI is going to", max_new_tokens=256))
[p0136-l0032] [10.0pt] You can load a ggml-quantized model from the Hugging Face Hub with the
[p0136-l0033] [10.0pt] CTransformers AutoModelForCausalLM class. Load the tokenizer from the original
[p0136-l0034] [10.0pt] model as usual with the Transformers AutoTokenizer. You can then run inference
[p0136-l0035] [10.0pt] through a Transformers pipeline, just as you would with single- or half-precision
[p0136-l0036] [10.0pt] pretrained models.
[p0136-l0037] [10.0pt] ggml has two parent open source projects, llama.cpp and whisper.cpp, both under
[p0136-l0038] [10.0pt] active development. Llama.cpp (https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp) began
[p0136-l0039] [10.0pt] as a C/C++ port of Meta’s Llama model, but has since expanded to other popular
[p0136-l0040] [10.0pt] LLM and multimodal architectures. As part of llama.cpp, an alternative quantized-­
[p0136-l0041] [10.0pt] model format to GGML was introduced: GGUF, now the only format supported by
[p0136-l0042] [10.0pt] llama.cpp. Compared with GGML, GGUF makes it easier to distribute a quantized model

=== PDF page 137 / printed label 116 ===
[p0137-l0001] [9.0pt] 116
[p0137-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 6  Quantizing for your production environment
[p0137-l0003] [10.0pt] as a single file (there’s no external JSON file for the tokenizer) and stores hyperparame­
[p0137-l0004] [10.0pt] ters as key–value metadata, making it easier to add new fields without breaking compat­
[p0137-l0005] [10.0pt] ibility with existing GGUF models. GGUF is quickly becoming the de facto standard for
[p0137-l0006] [10.0pt] C/C++ quantized models. Future chapters present several examples of quantization in
[p0137-l0007] [10.0pt] GGML and GGUF formats.
[p0137-l0008] [10.0pt] This chapter and the previous one covered the ONNX framework’s capabilities,
[p0137-l0009] [10.0pt] focusing on LLM optimization, quantization, and inference. In the next two chapters,
[p0137-l0010] [10.0pt] we’ll apply these concepts to real-world projects.
[p0137-l0011] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0137-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Floating-point precision affects memory use and computational speed in lan­
[p0137-l0013] [10.0pt] guage model operations.
[p0137-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ A 32-bit float uses 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, and 23 mantissa bits.
[p0137-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ 16-bit floating point reduces memory requirements by half but can reduce
[p0137-l0016] [10.0pt] performance.
[p0137-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ Mixed-precision training switches between 32-bit and 16-bit operations during
[p0137-l0018] [10.0pt] training.
[p0137-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ BF16 offers a wider dynamic range than FP16, with less precision.
[p0137-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Quantization converts model weights from floating-point to low-bit integers.
[p0137-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Post-training quantization is applied after training; quantization-aware training
[p0137-l0022] [10.0pt] happens during training.
[p0137-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Zero-point quantization scales inputs by the total range divided by the difference
[p0137-l0024] [10.0pt] between maximum and minimum values.
[p0137-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Absmax quantization divides input values by their absolute maximum value and
[p0137-l0026] [10.0pt] then multiplies by a scaling factor.
[p0137-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ LLM.int8() uses mixed-precision quantization: outliers run in FP16 and the rest
[p0137-l0028] [10.0pt] in INT8.
[p0137-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ Vector-wise quantization accounts for variation across tensor rows and columns.
[p0137-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX Runtime provides three levels of quantization, from low-level PyTorch
[p0137-l0031] [10.0pt] APIs to the high-level Optimum.
[p0137-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ ONNX dynamic quantization greatly reduces model size with minimal perfor­
[p0137-l0033] [10.0pt] mance loss.
[p0137-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ GPTQ enables 4-bit quantization for GPT models with minimal accuracy loss.
[p0137-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ AutoGPTQ integrates with Hugging Face libraries for streamlined 4-bit
[p0137-l0036] [10.0pt] quantization.
[p0137-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ The GGML library provides CPU-optimized quantization at 8-, 5-, and 4-bit
[p0137-l0038] [10.0pt] precision.
[p0137-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ GGUF format lets you distribute quantized models as single files with embedded
[p0137-l0040] [10.0pt] metadata.

=== PDF page 138 / printed label 117 ===
[p0138-l0001] [9.0pt] 117
[p0138-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0138-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Quantization cuts a model’s memory footprint by two to four times while main­
[p0138-l0004] [10.0pt] taining comparable performance.
[p0138-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ Perplexity metrics evaluate quantized model performance by measuring predic­
[p0138-l0006] [10.0pt] tion uncertainty.

[p0142-l0001] [30.0pt] Generating
[p0142-l0002] [30.0pt] Python code
[p0142-l0003] [225.0pt] 7
[p0142-l0004] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0142-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ The role specialized open source LLMs play in
[p0142-l0006] [9.8pt] code generation
[p0142-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Optimizing and quantizing these LLMs to improve
[p0142-l0008] [9.8pt] inference performance
[p0142-l0009] [9.8pt] ¡ Running these LLMs on a laptop after 4-bit
[p0142-l0010] [9.8pt] quantization
[p0142-l0011] [10.0pt] In this chapter, we’ll apply the concepts covered so far to real-world, domain-specific
[p0142-l0012] [10.0pt] LLMs, including optimization and quantization. We’ll focus on models tuned for
[p0142-l0013] [10.0pt] Python code generation and programming assistance. Although most open source
[p0142-l0014] [10.0pt] models in this category support multiple languages, we’ll use Python so you can
[p0142-l0015] [10.0pt] readily judge the quality of the outputs.
[p0142-l0016] [12.5pt] 7.1
[p0142-l0017] [12.5pt] Using Transformers to generate code
[p0142-l0018] [10.0pt] Beyond closed-source, proprietary LLM-based code assistants, several popular open-
[p0142-l0019] [10.0pt] source LLMs designed for coding tasks have been released. In this chapter, we’ll get into
[p0142-l0020] [10.0pt] hands-on experimentation with some of these options, look at their pros and cons, and
[p0142-l0021] [9.0pt] 121

=== PDF page 143 / printed label 122 ===
[p0143-l0001] [9.0pt] 122
[p0143-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0143-l0003] [10.0pt] see how to optimize and, if needed, quantize them to run inference on commodity hard­
[p0143-l0004] [10.0pt] ware (ideally on our laptops) while maintaining good performance. First, though, we’ll
[p0143-l0005] [10.0pt] consider the present and future of human programmers in this era of coding assistants.
[p0143-l0006] [10.0pt] Given the availability of commercial and open-source copilots, many CEOs and other
[p0143-l0007] [10.0pt] executives have predicted the obsolescence of programmers in favor of prompt engi­
[p0143-l0008] [10.0pt] neers, or claimed that everyone (whatever their background) will become a software
[p0143-l0009] [10.0pt] architect. How true is that? Let’s start with large generalist models. Several research
[p0143-l0010] [10.0pt] efforts, such as SWE-bench (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770), evaluate large com­
[p0143-l0011] [10.0pt] mercial models such as GPT-4 and Claude 2 on real-world programming challenges
[p0143-l0012] [10.0pt] based on real code. The paper focuses on Python (2,294 issues and related pull requests
[p0143-l0013] [10.0pt] from GitHub repositories), but many benchmarks for other languages can be found
[p0143-l0014] [10.0pt] online. Neither model scored well on these problems, even with knowledge retrieval.
[p0143-l0015] [10.0pt] More prompt engineering helps little: even with a larger context, results can still be con­
[p0143-l0016] [10.0pt] fused or random, at the cost of more processing power and the user’s time. Since the
[p0143-l0017] [10.0pt] paper’s publication, many large and small models, with or without retrieval-­augmented
[p0143-l0018] [10.0pt] generation (RAG), have been benchmarked. The updated leaderboard is available at
[p0143-l0019] [10.0pt] https://www.swebench.com/ (updated every Monday). Over time, new models and
[p0143-l0020] [10.0pt] supporting techniques have improved results, but none of the benchmarked models
[p0143-l0021] [10.0pt] can yet be used without expert human supervision (see figure 7.1).
[p0143-l0022] [8.0pt] Figure 7.1  SWE-bench leaderboard (early 2025 snapshot)

=== PDF page 144 / printed label 123 ===
[p0144-l0001] [9.0pt] 123
[p0144-l0002] [9.0pt] Generating Python code with a Transformer architecture
[p0144-l0003] [10.0pt] Several factors explain the modest performance. Resolving software engineering prob­
[p0144-l0004] [10.0pt] lems often requires coordinating changes across multiple functions, classes, and files,
[p0144-l0005] [10.0pt] interacting with execution environments, and reasoning well beyond straightforward
[p0144-l0006] [10.0pt] code generation. These are areas where humans still outperform ML models. And
[p0144-l0007] [10.0pt] because these models are trained as generalists, they rarely match the depth of exper­
[p0144-l0008] [10.0pt] tise that professional software engineers bring to complex programming tasks.
[p0144-l0009] [10.0pt] Dedicated models for programming tasks, such as Microsoft Copilot, are often more
[p0144-l0010] [10.0pt] accurate and can handle more complex work than general-purpose models. Still, they
[p0144-l0011] [10.0pt] can be costly for some organizations and require human oversight and guardrails to
[p0144-l0012] [10.0pt] prevent data leakage. They may also lack transparency about where their training data
[p0144-l0013] [10.0pt] comes from. These tools raise the same privacy, IP, and safety concerns discussed earlier
[p0144-l0014] [10.0pt] in this book, especially when they rely on large, closed models.
[p0144-l0015] [10.0pt] Luckily for us, LLMs specialized for this kind of task are available, and specialization
[p0144-l0016] [10.0pt] drastically reduces model size. We can see this in the industry’s growing move toward
[p0144-l0017] [10.0pt] smaller, more focused coding LLMs that, despite having only a few billion parameters,
[p0144-l0018] [10.0pt] match, and sometimes outperform, larger models on evaluation benchmarks. This isn’t
[p0144-l0019] [10.0pt] surprising: if the main task is coding in one or a few programming languages, you can
[p0144-l0020] [10.0pt] remove much of the irrelevant knowledge in large generalist models. A smaller, more
[p0144-l0021] [10.0pt] focused data pool is easier to keep relevant, cheaper to train, and less likely to inadver­
[p0144-l0022] [10.0pt] tently include copyrighted or unauthorized data.
[p0144-l0023] [10.0pt] Back to the main question: Will generative AI replace human programmers? Prob­
[p0144-l0024] [10.0pt] ably not, even if models reach 98% to 100% accuracy on coding tasks. Coding is only
[p0144-l0025] [10.0pt] one part of software development. It also involves investing in new things, understand­
[p0144-l0026] [10.0pt] ing users’ requirements and needs, translating ideas into something buildable, and
[p0144-l0027] [10.0pt] polishing the result. These steps require human judgment and cannot be reduced
[p0144-l0028] [10.0pt] to next-token generation. In my opinion, software engineers will not shift into roles
[p0144-l0029] [10.0pt] focused mainly on reviewing and verifying AI-generated code, even if generative mod­
[p0144-l0030] [10.0pt] els become highly accurate. These models can still be a big help, and I wouldn’t dis­
[p0144-l0031] [10.0pt] courage professionals from using them. But domain knowledge is always needed to
[p0144-l0032] [10.0pt] use them well: a good software engineer can become a better software engineer using a
[p0144-l0033] [10.0pt] code assistant, but someone with little or no software engineering knowledge will not.
[p0144-l0034] [10.0pt] Software engineering isn’t different from other domains when it comes to support from
[p0144-l0035] [10.0pt] AI-based assistants.
[p0144-l0036] [12.5pt] 7.2
[p0144-l0037] [12.5pt] Generating Python code with a Transformer architecture
[p0144-l0038] [10.0pt] Let’s get started. We’ll use an open source, pretrained code-generation model as our
[p0144-l0039] [10.0pt] baseline and see what we get.
[p0144-l0040] [10.5pt] 7.2.1
[p0144-l0041] [10.5pt] Python code generation with CodeGen
[p0144-l0042] [10.0pt] The first open source pretrained model we’ll consider is Salesforce’s CodeGen
[p0144-l0043] [10.0pt] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.13474). It uses a standard Transformer architecture for
[p0144-l0044] [10.0pt] conversational program synthesis: each problem is solved interactively in multiple

=== PDF page 145 / printed label 124 ===
[p0145-l0001] [9.0pt] 124
[p0145-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0145-l0003] [10.0pt] steps, each consisting of a natural-language specification from the user and a synthe­
[p0145-l0004] [10.0pt] sized subprogram from the system. Although better open source coding models are
[p0145-l0005] [10.0pt] available, including CodeGen 2.0 and 2.5, CodeGen is still a useful example for this
[p0145-l0006] [10.0pt] class of specialized LLMs because it highlights architectural choices that can require
[p0145-l0007] [10.0pt] extra work beyond the typical use of Hugging Face Transformers, ONNX, and related
[p0145-l0008] [10.0pt] libraries.
[p0145-l0009] [10.0pt] CodeGen is conceptually comparable to OpenAI’s Codex, the model that was behind
[p0145-l0010] [10.0pt] GitHub Copilot when Salesforce released its own proposal. It offers two families of pre­
[p0145-l0011] [10.0pt] trained models: multi, trained to generate code in six languages (C, C++, Go, Java, JavaS­
[p0145-l0012] [10.0pt] cript, and Python), and mono, trained to generate Python only. Each family includes
[p0145-l0013] [10.0pt] four sizes: 350M (350 million parameters), 2B (2.7 billion parameters), 6B (6.1 billion
[p0145-l0014] [10.0pt] parameters), and 16B (16.1 billion parameters). To show CodeGen’s scale at release,
[p0145-l0015] [10.0pt] figure 7.2 compares the largest model with other open or closed source LLMs for the
[p0145-l0016] [10.0pt] same task available at the time.
[p0145-l0017] [8.0pt] Figure 7.2  Comparing the most popular code assistant LLMs’ sizes when CodeGen was released
[p0145-l0018] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier in this chapter, we are focusing only on Python code generation,
[p0145-l0019] [10.0pt] so any reference to CodeGen models in this section refers to the mono family.
[p0145-l0020] [10.0pt] Inference with the 350M pretrained model is fast, even before optimization. Bench­
[p0145-l0021] [10.0pt] marks on a single NVIDIA T4 GPU average 0.8 s for requests that generate fewer than 50
[p0145-l0022] [10.0pt] tokens and 0.9 s for requests that generate 50 to 250 tokens. Still, the 350M model isn’t suit­
[p0145-l0023] [10.0pt] able for production; later in this chapter, we’ll discuss the quality of the generated results.

[p0146-l0003] [10.0pt] The 2B model is a more robust candidate (as are the larger versions). This model
[p0146-l0004] [10.0pt] family can generate code that uses not only Python’s standard library but also third-
[p0146-l0005] [10.0pt] party open source libraries. Even so, the 350M version is a good choice for explaining
[p0146-l0006] [10.0pt] the concepts covered in this chapter.
[p0146-l0007] [10.0pt] The first Colab notebook for this chapter contains a complete, end-to-end example
[p0146-l0008] [10.0pt] of optimizing inference for CodeGen 350M mono. We’ll use this smaller model to show
[p0146-l0009] [10.0pt] that even a few hundred million–parameter model leaves room for inference optimiza­
[p0146-l0010] [10.0pt] tion, and the same ideas apply to the larger mono models.
[p0146-l0011] [10.0pt] All the CodeGen checkpoints (mono and multi) are available on the Hugging Face
[p0146-l0012] [10.0pt] Hub and via the Transformers library, so we can download the pretrained model and its
[p0146-l0013] [10.0pt] tokenizer as usual:
[p0146-l0014] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0146-l0015] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer, CodeGenForCausalLM
[p0146-l0016] [8.0pt] device = "cpu"
[p0146-l0017] [8.0pt] model_id = "Salesforce/codegen-350M-mono"
[p0146-l0018] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0146-l0019] [8.0pt] model = CodeGenForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id).to(device)
[p0146-l0020] [8.0pt] model.eval()
[p0146-l0021] [10.0pt] The only difference here is the use of CodeGenForCausalLM, Hugging Face Transform­
[p0146-l0022] [10.0pt] ers’ auto class for CodeGen models.
[p0146-l0023] [10.0pt] This example doesn’t require hardware acceleration. We’ll assume the model and
[p0146-l0024] [10.0pt] data are loaded and running on CPUs. The small CodeGen mono model works as
[p0146-l0025] [10.0pt] follows:
[p0146-l0026] [8.0pt] prompt = "def hello_world():"

[p0146-l0028] [8.0pt] generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=12)
[p0146-l0029] [8.0pt] print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0],
[p0146-l0030] [8.0pt]                        skip_special_tokens=True,
[p0146-l0031] [8.0pt]                        pad_token_id=50256))
[p0146-l0032] [10.0pt] Given a prompt with a descriptively named function definition, it generates the func­
[p0146-l0033] [10.0pt] tion body as follows:
[p0146-l0034] [8.0pt] def hello_world():

[p0149-l0019] [10.0pt] Based on what you learned in chapter 6, you might expect to use Optimum to convert
[p0149-l0020] [10.0pt] this model to ONNX and then quantize it. That’s correct now, but until early 2024,
[p0149-l0021] [10.0pt] the CodeGen architecture wasn’t supported in Optimum—it was added only recently.
[p0149-l0022] [10.0pt] Let’s first use Optimum to export the CodeGen model to ONNX and quantize it; later,
[p0149-l0023] [10.0pt] we’ll look at an alternative approach for cases where Optimum doesn’t support a mod­
[p0149-l0024] [10.0pt] el’s architecture.
[p0149-l0025] [10.0pt] With Optimum installed for ONNX Runtime, the model can be downloaded from
[p0149-l0026] [10.0pt] the Hugging Face Hub and converted to ONNX automatically:
[p0149-l0027] [8.0pt] from optimum.onnxruntime import ORTModelForCausalLM
[p0149-l0028] [8.0pt] model_id = 'Salesforce/codegen-350M-mono'
[p0149-l0029] [8.0pt] model = ORTModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id,
[p0149-l0030] [8.0pt]                                             export=True,
[p0149-l0031] [8.0pt]                                             provider="CPUExecutionProvider"
[p0149-l0032] [8.0pt] )
[p0149-l0033] [10.0pt] We are using the Optimum ORTModelForCausalLM class because CodeGen is a causal
[p0149-l0034] [10.0pt] LM. We also specified the ONNX execution provider (CPUExecutionProvider in this
[p0149-l0035] [10.0pt] example) at download time.

[p0150-l0036] [10.0pt] We also need to implement two simple utility functions to collect metrics during bench­
[p0150-l0037] [10.0pt] mark execution for all three model versions. First, we define the track_infer_time
[p0150-l0038] [10.0pt] function, which measures the duration of a single inference run and is applied across
[p0150-l0039] [10.0pt] the full benchmark cycle:

[p0151-l0003] [8.0pt] from contextlib import contextmanager
[p0151-l0004] [8.0pt] from time import perf_counter
[p0151-l0005] [8.0pt] @contextmanager
[p0151-l0006] [8.0pt] def track_infer_time(time_buffer):
[p0151-l0007] [8.0pt]     start_time = perf_counter()
[p0151-l0008] [8.0pt]     yield
[p0151-l0009] [8.0pt]     end_time = perf_counter()
[p0151-l0010] [8.0pt]     time_buffer.append(end_time - start_time)
[p0151-l0011] [10.0pt] The second utility is the BenchmarkInferenceResult class, used to collect metrics across

[p0154-l0014] [10.0pt] izations in this section is available in the accompanying Colab notebook.
[p0154-l0015] [10.0pt] We’ve seen that exporting a model to ONNX and/or an ONNX-quantized version can
[p0154-l0016] [10.0pt] significantly improve latency and throughput, even for small language models. But
[p0154-l0017] [10.0pt] how do we assess how optimization and quantization affect the quality of the generated
[p0154-l0018] [10.0pt] code? Section 7.2.3 will explore strategies for evaluating language model output for
[p0154-l0019] [10.0pt] Python code generation.
[p0154-l0020] [10.5pt] 7.2.2
[p0154-l0021] [10.5pt] Using ONNX with models not supported by Optimum
[p0154-l0022] [10.0pt] Some LLM architectures aren’t yet supported by the Optimum package (for example,
[p0154-l0023] [10.0pt] CodeGen models were still unsupported as of early 2024). In those cases, you can use
[p0154-l0024] [10.0pt] the mid-level approach for ONNX quantization. After downloading a model from the
[p0154-l0025] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Hub and saving it to disk, run the transformers.onnx script from the
[p0154-l0026] [10.0pt] Transformers library as follows:
[p0154-l0027] [8.0pt] !python -m transformers.onnx --feature "causal-lm" --framework pt
[p0154-l0028] [10.0pt] ➥-export_with_transformers --model=local-pt-checkpoint onnx/
[p0154-l0029] [10.0pt] The --feature option sets the model category (causal-lm for CodeGen models; see
[p0154-l0030] [10.0pt] the Transformers documentation for other models). The --model option specifies the
[p0154-l0031] [10.0pt] directory where the downloaded checkpoints are saved.

=== PDF page 155 / printed label 134 ===
[p0155-l0001] [9.0pt] 134
[p0155-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0155-l0003] [10.0pt] After conversion, you can perform 8-bit quantization using the ONNX Runtime API:
[p0155-l0004] [8.0pt] import os
[p0155-l0005] [8.0pt] import onnx
[p0155-l0006] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime.quantization import quantize_dynamic, QuantType
[p0155-l0007] [8.0pt] def quantize_onnx_model(onnx_model_path, quantized_model_path):
[p0155-l0008] [8.0pt]     onnx_opt_model = onnx.load(onnx_model_path)
[p0155-l0009] [8.0pt]     quantize_dynamic(onnx_model_path,
[p0155-l0010] [8.0pt]                      quantized_model_path,
[p0155-l0011] [8.0pt]                      weight_type=QuantType.QInt8)
[p0155-l0012] [8.0pt] quantize_onnx_model(onnx_model_path, quantized_model_path)
[p0155-l0013] [10.5pt] 7.2.3
[p0155-l0014] [10.5pt] Model evaluation
[p0155-l0015] [10.0pt] Several open source Python packages, such as Hugging Face’s Evaluate and EleutherAI’s
[p0155-l0016] [10.0pt] LLM Evaluation Harness (discussed in chapters 6 and 4, respectively), plus public
[p0155-l0017] [10.0pt] datasets, are available for LLM evaluation. But generating unstructured outputs such as
[p0155-l0018] [10.0pt] Python (or other) code calls for extra choices to make evaluation robust and meaningful.
[p0155-l0019] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ll walk through an approach based on the CodeGen 350M
[p0155-l0020] [10.0pt] mono model and its ONNX-converted, 8-bit-quantized variants introduced in sec­
[p0155-l0021] [10.0pt] tion 7.2.1, and which you can also apply to other LLMs specialized on Python code
[p0155-l0022] [10.0pt] generation. The code comes from Amazon Science’s ReCode paper (https://arxiv
[p0155-l0023] [10.0pt] .org/abs/2212.10264) and is shared in a Colab notebook for this chapter. I chose this
[p0155-l0024] [10.0pt] approach because ReCode defines robustness metrics for code generation models by
[p0155-l0025] [10.0pt] measuring worst-case behavior under different prompt perturbations (language mod­
[p0155-l0026] [10.0pt] els are sensitive to prompt changes). This provides a practical way to assess code quality
[p0155-l0027] [10.0pt] for production use.
[p0155-l0028] [10.0pt] We’ll use OpenAI’s HumanEval evaluation dataset (https://github.com/openai/
[p0155-l0029] [10.0pt] human-eval), introduced in “Evaluating Large Language Models Trained on Code”
[p0155-l0030] [10.0pt] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.03374). HumanEval is also available on the Hugging Face
[p0155-l0031] [10.0pt] Hub (https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/openai_humaneval). It contains 164
[p0155-l0032] [10.0pt] Python programming problems, each with a function signature, docstring, body, and
[p0155-l0033] [10.0pt] several unit tests. The comments and docstrings are in English. The dataset fields are as
[p0155-l0034] [10.0pt] follows:
[p0155-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ task_id—The identifier of the data sample
[p0155-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ prompt—The input for the model, containing function header and docstrings
[p0155-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ canonical_solution—A code solution for the problem in the prompt
[p0155-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ test—A test function to validate the generated code for correctness
[p0155-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ entry_point—The starting point for the tests
[p0155-l0040] [10.0pt] You can download this dataset via the Hugging Face Datasets API and then transform
[p0155-l0041] [10.0pt] it into the format expected by the ReCode evaluation. Alternatively, you can download
[p0155-l0042] [10.0pt] a ready-to-use JSON copy from the ReCode GitHub repo:

=== PDF page 156 / printed label 135 ===
[p0156-l0001] [9.0pt] 135
[p0156-l0002] [9.0pt] Generating Python code with a Transformer architecture
[p0156-l0003] [8.0pt] !mkdir -p datasets/nominal/
[p0156-l0004] [8.0pt] %cd ./datasets/nominal/
[p0156-l0005] [8.0pt] !wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/amazon-

[p0156-l0008] [10.0pt] You can run the end-to-end evaluation on this test set with or without a GPU, but hard­
[p0156-l0009] [10.0pt] ware acceleration is recommended. On an NVIDIA T4 GPU, the vanilla CodeGen
[p0156-l0010] [10.0pt] 350M mono model takes more than an hour to run on all 164 test samples (adding the
[p0156-l0011] [10.0pt] prompt to the answer and setting large maximum generation length). Because the full
[p0156-l0012] [10.0pt] code is lengthy, we don’t include it here; instead, this section walks through the work­
[p0156-l0013] [10.0pt] flow so you can see how generated code is evaluated.
[p0156-l0014] [10.0pt] After downloading the CodeGen 340M mono model and its tokenizer from the Hug­
[p0156-l0015] [10.0pt] ging Face Hub, split the HumanEval JSON samples into individual JSON files, each contain­
[p0156-l0016] [10.0pt] ing the prompt for a single generation run. For each sample, first tokenize the prompt
[p0156-l0017] [10.0pt] with the CodeGen tokenizer. Then generate code using the following configuration:
[p0156-l0018] [8.0pt] from transformers import GenerationConfig
[p0156-l0019] [8.0pt] generation_config = GenerationConfig(
[p0156-l0020] [8.0pt]     pad_token_id=50256,
[p0156-l0021] [8.0pt]     truncation=True,
[p0156-l0022] [8.0pt]     max_length=1000,
[p0156-l0023] [8.0pt]     max_context_length=1000,
[p0156-l0024] [8.0pt]     use_cache=True,
[p0156-l0025] [8.0pt]     return_dict_in_generate=True,
[p0156-l0026] [8.0pt]     output_scores=True
[p0156-l0027] [8.0pt] )
[p0156-l0028] [10.0pt] After generating the code for a sample, we need to check that it is valid Python. Results
[p0156-l0029] [10.0pt] that fail validation are not written to the results file. For this check, we use Python’s
[p0156-l0030] [10.0pt] built-in ast package to parse the generated code into an abstract syntax tree (AST), as
[p0156-l0031] [10.0pt] Python does before compiling to bytecode.
[p0156-l0032] [10.0pt] To see what an AST looks like, consider this simple example. Suppose the prompt for
[p0156-l0033] [10.0pt] the generative model is
[p0156-l0034] [8.0pt] def hello_world():
[p0156-l0035] [10.0pt] and the generated body for this function is
[p0156-l0036] [8.0pt] print('Hello world')
[p0156-l0037] [10.0pt] You can get the latter’s AST via the ast class’s  method. In the Colab code, it’s called
[p0156-l0038] [10.0pt] from is_valid_python:
[p0156-l0039] [8.0pt] import ast
[p0156-l0040] [8.0pt] def is_valid_python(code):

[p0157-l0037] [10.0pt] In this case, there are six nodes in the tree. Generating an AST is a standard step in
[p0157-l0038] [10.0pt] Python compilation. When you run a .py file, Python first converts the source to an
[p0157-l0039] [10.0pt] AST and then to bytecode (a .pyc file). The Python virtual machine then interprets
[p0157-l0040] [10.0pt] that bytecode. ASTs are also used for other purposes; for example, popular Python
[p0157-l0041] [10.0pt] IDEs use them to parse files and understand code structure to power editor features.
[p0157-l0042] [10.0pt] We can use ASTs in the same way to validate code generated by our LLMs.
[p0157-l0043] [10.0pt] After validating the generated Python code with an AST, we collect the results in a
[p0157-l0044] [10.0pt] single JSON file to simplify evaluation. The final step depends on the HumanEval package,
[p0157-l0045] [10.0pt] so we install it from source because it isn’t available through a Python package manager:
