[p0158-l0002] [9.0pt] Generating Python code with a Transformer architecture
[p0158-l0003] [10.0pt] For each generated sample, we assess its correctness by executing the code and running
[p0158-l0004] [10.0pt] its HumanEval test. As a safety measure to prevent malicious code execution, HumanEval
[p0158-l0005] [10.0pt] comments out the line in execution.py that runs the generated code. In our Colab
[p0158-l0006] [10.0pt] notebook, we override part of that code to enable the evaluation of code generated by
[p0158-l0007] [10.0pt] our model. Use caution when running these evaluations.
[p0158-l0008] [10.0pt] We aggregate the results and save them to a JSON file along with the generated code.
[p0158-l0009] [10.0pt] We also add a passed attribute with the value true or false.
[p0158-l0010] [10.0pt] Although the Colab notebook covers only the vanilla CodeGen 350M mono model,
[p0158-l0011] [10.0pt] you can repeat the same evaluation process and code for its ONNX-exported and 8-bit
[p0158-l0012] [10.0pt] quantized versions, and for other open source small language models for Python code
[p0158-l0013] [10.0pt] generation.
[p0158-l0014] [10.5pt] 7.2.4
[p0158-l0015] [10.5pt] Python code generation with better models
[p0158-l0016] [10.0pt] When Salesforce released version 2.0 of the CodeGen models, it again offered the
[p0158-l0017] [10.0pt] mono and multi families in four sizes each, roughly matching the first-generation
[p0158-l0018] [10.0pt] sizes.
[p0158-l0019] [10.0pt] The latest generation is CodeGen 2.5, which comes in a single size—7 billion param­
[p0158-l0020] [10.0pt] eters for both the mono and multi versions. It features robust infill sampling (it can
[p0158-l0021] [10.0pt] read text on both the left and right side of the current position), and it is optimized
[p0158-l0022] [10.0pt] for fast sampling with FlashAttention, making it suitable for efficient serving and local
[p0158-l0023] [10.0pt] deployment, including on personal machines. FlashAttention is an alternative to tradi­
[p0158-l0024] [10.0pt] tional self-attention that makes LLMs more efficient, enabling faster training and infer­
[p0158-l0025] [10.0pt] ence. Instead of repeatedly reading and writing keys, queries, and values from GPU
[p0158-l0026] [10.0pt] HBM (large but relatively slow), it loads them once into SRAM (smaller but faster),
[p0158-l0027] [10.0pt] fuses the attention operations, and then writes the results back.
[p0158-l0028] [10.0pt] All the CodeGen 1 and 2 models were released under the permissive Apache 2.0
[p0158-l0029] [10.0pt] license, and CodeGen 2.5 multi and mono use the same license. Note that the Code­
[p0158-l0030] [10.0pt] Gen 2.5 instruct model is available for research only, not for commercial use.
[p0158-l0031] [10.0pt] Generating Python code with the CodeGen 2.5 mono model works the same way as
[p0158-l0032] [10.0pt] with the CodeGen 1 mono model discussed earlier in this chapter. First, download the
[p0158-l0033] [10.0pt] model and tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0158-l0034] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
[p0158-l0035] [8.0pt] model_id = "Salesforce/codegen25-7b-mono"
[p0158-l0036] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, trust_remote_code=True)
[p0158-l0037] [8.0pt] model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained model_id)
[p0158-l0038] [10.0pt] You can then generate code by invoking the generate method on the tokenized prompt:
[p0158-l0039] [8.0pt] text = "def hello_world():"
[p0158-l0040] [8.0pt] input_ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
[p0158-l0041] [8.0pt] generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=128)
[p0158-l0042] [8.0pt] print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0], skip_special_tokens=True)

[p0159-l0001] [9.0pt] 138
[p0159-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0159-l0003] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier, CodeGen 2.5 also works well for code infilling—filling in missing
[p0159-l0004] [10.0pt] parts of an incomplete code snippet. It requires the prompt to follow this formatting
[p0159-l0005] [10.0pt] convention:
[p0159-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Insert a <mask_1> token at the cursor.
[p0159-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ Add a <sep> token to mark the boundary.
[p0159-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Insert another <mask_1> token to specify which mask to infill.
[p0159-l0009] [10.0pt] Here’s an example:
[p0159-l0010] [8.0pt] def format(prefix, suffix):
[p0159-l0011] [8.0pt]   return prefix + "<mask_1>" + suffix + "<|endoftext|>"
[p0159-l0012] [10.0pt]   ➥+ "<sep>" + "<mask_1>"
[p0159-l0013] [10.0pt] Then generate the body of a Python function, as in the following example:
[p0159-l0014] [8.0pt] prefix = "def hello_world():\n    "
[p0159-l0015] [8.0pt] suffix = "    return greeting_message"
[p0159-l0016] [10.0pt] We need to format the prompt with our custom format function, tokenize it, and then
[p0159-l0017] [10.0pt] invoke the model’s generate method:
[p0159-l0018] [8.0pt] text = format(prefix, suffix)
[p0159-l0019] [8.0pt] input_ids = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt").input_ids
[p0159-l0020] [8.0pt] generated_ids = model.generate(input_ids, max_length=128)
[p0159-l0021] [8.0pt] print(tokenizer.decode(generated_ids[0],
[p0159-l0022] [10.0pt] ➥ skip_special_tokens=False)[len(text):])
[p0159-l0023] [10.0pt] Other small language models for code generation have been proposed. One strong
[p0159-l0024] [10.0pt] example is StarCoder2 (https://huggingface.co/bigcode/starcoder2-3b), a 3 billion–
[p0159-l0025] [10.0pt] parameter model developed by BigCode, an open scientific collaboration focused on
[p0159-l0026] [10.0pt] the responsible development and use of large language models for code, supported by
[p0159-l0027] [10.0pt] ServiceNow, Hugging Face, and NVIDIA. Introduced in a 2024 paper (https://arxiv
[p0159-l0028] [10.0pt] .org/abs/2402.19173), it was trained on 3+ trillion tokens from the Stack v2 dataset
[p0159-l0029] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/datasets/bigcode/the-stack-v2), covering code in 17 pro­
[p0159-l0030] [10.0pt] gramming languages (including Python) plus curated natural language text from Wiki­
[p0159-l0031] [10.0pt] pedia, arXiv, and GitHub issues. StarCoder2 uses grouped-query attention (proposed
[p0159-l0032] [10.0pt] in a 2023 paper; https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245v3) to speed inference, and it has a
[p0159-l0033] [10.0pt] 16,384-token context window with a 4,096-token sliding-window attention. Because it is
[p0159-l0034] [10.0pt] not instruction-tuned, it is best suited to generating a function body when the function
[p0159-l0035] [10.0pt] header is specified in the prompt, but the official GitHub repo (https://github.com/
[p0159-l0036] [10.0pt] bigcode-project/starcoder2) includes tuning scripts.
[p0159-l0037] [10.0pt] You can generate code with StarCoder2 using Hugging Face packages in the usual
[p0159-l0038] [10.0pt] way. First, download the model and tokenizer from the Hub:

[p0161-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0161-l0003] [10.0pt] It is possible to make a 4-bit quantized version of the model the same way, just replac­
[p0161-l0004] [10.0pt] ing the second line with the following:
[p0161-l0005] [8.0pt] quantization_config = BitsAndBytesConfig(load_in_4bit=True)
[p0161-l0006] [10.0pt] The companion Colab notebook for this chapter benchmarks inference performance
[p0161-l0007] [10.0pt] for BF16 and 8-bit quantized versions of the StarCoder v2 3B model. The benchmark
[p0161-l0008] [10.0pt] code is similar to the CodeGen example shown earlier, so I haven’t repeated it here.
[p0161-l0009] [10.0pt] When you run the benchmark on a GPU, you’ll see that (thanks to the grouped-query
[p0161-l0010] [10.0pt] attention implementation) the model delivers better throughput and latency than the
[p0161-l0011] [10.0pt] CodeGen 350M and 2B mono models.
[p0161-l0012] [12.5pt] 7.3
[p0161-l0013] [12.5pt] Coding assistance on commodity hardware
[p0161-l0014] [10.0pt] The CodeGen and StarCoder models discussed in section 7.2 showed good inference
[p0161-l0015] [10.0pt] performance (with room for further optimization), making them suitable for deploy­
[p0161-l0016] [10.0pt] ment behind an API to enable code generation from client applications. It would also
[p0161-l0017] [10.0pt] be useful to have one of these models running smoothly on a laptop as a coding assis­
[p0161-l0018] [10.0pt] tant. In this section, we’ll verify an optimized small language model to run locally as a
[p0161-l0019] [10.0pt] code assistant with acceptable performance. Our target laptop is a MacBook Air with
[p0161-l0020] [10.0pt] an Apple M1 chip and 8 GB of unified memory. I chose one of the less powerful Apple
[p0161-l0021] [10.0pt] M-series laptops to make things more challenging and to show that, even with this
[p0161-l0022] [10.0pt] hardware, you can optimize inference and run useful, domain-specific SLMs smoothly.
[p0161-l0023] [10.0pt] Our reference model will be StarCoder v2 3B.
[p0161-l0024] [10.0pt] If you browse the Hugging Face Hub, you’ll find several LLMs (including StarCoder
[p0161-l0025] [10.0pt] v2 3B) already available in GGUF format. A natural way to try one of these quantized
[p0161-l0026] [10.0pt] models for laptop inference is to use the Transformers API, just as you would with a
[p0161-l0027] [10.0pt] standard FP32 or FP16 model:
[p0161-l0028] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM
[p0161-l0029] [8.0pt] model_id = "second-state/StarCoder2-3B-GGUF"
[p0161-l0030] [8.0pt] filename = "starcoder2-3b-Q2_K.gguf"
[p0161-l0031] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, gguf_file=filename)
[p0161-l0032] [8.0pt] model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, gguf_file=filename)
[p0161-l0033] [10.0pt] The only difference here is the filename of the quantized model checkpoint to down­
[p0161-l0034] [10.0pt] load. GGUF offers multiple quantization options, so several quantized versions of the
[p0161-l0035] [10.0pt] same model may be available.
[p0161-l0036] [10.0pt] Although the Hugging Face Hub can host GGUF models, and the Transformers
[p0161-l0037] [10.0pt] library can download them, Transformers still can’t use models in quantized GGUF for­
[p0161-l0038] [10.0pt] mat. After a GGUF download completes, the model is automatically unquantized, and
[p0161-l0039] [10.0pt] inference can run only in the original format. That puts us back at the start, because the
[p0161-l0040] [10.0pt] original model is typically too large to run locally with limited CPU/GPU and memory.

=== PDF page 162 / printed label 141 ===
[p0162-l0001] [9.0pt] 141
[p0162-l0002] [9.0pt] Coding assistance on commodity hardware
[p0162-l0003] [10.0pt] The only workaround, if we want to go through the Transformers API, is to save the
[p0162-l0004] [10.0pt] model to disk after downloading:
[p0162-l0005] [8.0pt] model_checkpoint_dir = 'starcoderv2-checkpoint-dir'
[p0162-l0006] [8.0pt] tokenizer.save_pretrained(model_checkpoint_dir)
[p0162-l0007] [8.0pt] model.save_pretrained(model_checkpoint_dir)
[p0162-l0008] [10.0pt] We can then apply a quantization technique to it.
[p0162-l0009] [10.0pt] But there are smarter options. llama.cpp (https://github.com/ggerganov/llama
[p0162-l0010] [10.0pt] .cpp) is an open source C/C++ library and project that enables inference for several
[p0162-l0011] [10.0pt] LLMs on a wide range of hardware, including devices without a GPU (such as laptops
[p0162-l0012] [10.0pt] and mobile phones). GGUF is the binary file format used by llama.cpp.
[p0162-l0013] [10.0pt] To keep things simple, we will use llama-cpp-python (https://github.com/abetlen/
[p0162-l0014] [10.0pt] llama-cpp-python), which provides Python bindings for llama.cpp and supports Apple’s
[p0162-l0015] [10.0pt] Metal (MPS, Metal Performance Shaders) backend. To install it, you need Python 3.8+
[p0162-l0016] [10.0pt] and a C compiler for your machine (for example, Xcode on macOS). After creating a
[p0162-l0017] [10.0pt] virtual environment, you can install llama-cpp-python from PyPI:
[p0162-l0018] [8.0pt] CMAKE_ARGS="-DGGML_METAL=on" pip install llama-cpp-python
[p0162-l0019] [10.0pt] The preceding command builds and installs the library, including building and install­
[p0162-l0020] [10.0pt] ing llama.cpp. You’ll also need the huggingface-hub library to download the model:
[p0162-l0021] [8.0pt] !pip install huggingface-hub
[p0162-l0022] [10.0pt] Now that everything is set up, we can start coding to make the model available for local
[p0162-l0023] [10.0pt] inference. First, we’ll import the required dependencies:
[p0162-l0024] [8.0pt] from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
[p0162-l0025] [8.0pt] from llama_cpp import Llama
[p0162-l0026] [10.0pt] Then we can download the model from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0162-l0027] [8.0pt] model_name = "second-state/StarCoder2-3B-GGUF "
[p0162-l0028] [8.0pt] model_file = "starcoder2-3b-Q4_K_M.gguf "
[p0162-l0029] [8.0pt] model_path = hf_hub_download(model_name, filename=model_file)
[p0162-l0030] [10.0pt] The GGUF-converted model used in this example is Second State’s 4-bit K_M-quantized
[p0162-l0031] [10.0pt] version of StarCoder v2 3B (https://huggingface.co/second-state/StarCoder2-3B
[p0162-l0032] [10.0pt] -GGUF). After downloading it to your laptop, you can load it into memory using the
[p0162-l0033] [10.0pt] llama-cpp-python library’s Llama class, as follows:
[p0162-l0034] [8.0pt] llm = Llama(
[p0162-l0035] [8.0pt]     model_path=model_path,
[p0162-l0036] [8.0pt]     n_ctx=3072,
[p0162-l0037] [8.0pt]     n_threads=4
[p0162-l0038] [8.0pt]     n_gpu_layers=0
[p0162-l0039] [8.0pt] )

[p0163-l0001] [9.0pt] 142
[p0163-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 7  Generating Python code
[p0163-l0003] [10.0pt] We’ve specified the local path to the model checkpoints, the context size (3,072 for
[p0163-l0004] [10.0pt] StarCoder v2 3B), the number of CPU cores to use, and how many model layers to
[p0163-l0005] [10.0pt] offload to the GPU (none in this example, since we want to run inference on the CPU
[p0163-l0006] [10.0pt] only).
[p0163-l0007] [10.0pt] Next, we can set arguments for code generation, such as the maximum number of
[p0163-l0008] [10.0pt] new tokens, a stop policy, whether to echo the prompt in the output, the decoding strat­
[p0163-l0009] [10.0pt] egy, and other inference options:
[p0163-l0010] [8.0pt] generation_kwargs = {
[p0163-l0011] [8.0pt]     "max_tokens":20,
[p0163-l0012] [8.0pt]     "stop":["</s>"],
[p0163-l0013] [8.0pt]     "echo":False,
[p0163-l0014] [8.0pt]     "top_k":1
[p0163-l0015] [8.0pt] }
[p0163-l0016] [10.0pt] Now we can set a prompt and run inference:
[p0163-l0017] [8.0pt] prompt = "def hello_world():"
[p0163-l0018] [8.0pt] res = llm(prompt, **generation_kwargs)
[p0163-l0019] [10.0pt] The preceding command outputs a dictionary in an OpenAI-compatible format:
[p0163-l0020] [8.0pt] {
[p0163-l0021] [8.0pt]   "id": "cmpl-xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx",
[p0163-l0022] [8.0pt]   "object": "text_completion",
[p0163-l0023] [8.0pt]   "created": xxxxxxxxxx,
[p0163-l0024] [8.0pt]   "model": "./models/starcoder2-3b-Q4_K_M.gguf",
[p0163-l0025] [8.0pt]   "choices": [
[p0163-l0026] [8.0pt]     {
[p0163-l0027] [8.0pt]       "text": "\n    return 'Hello World!\n\n",
[p0163-l0028] [8.0pt]       "index": 0,
[p0163-l0029] [8.0pt]       "logprobs": None,
[p0163-l0030] [8.0pt]       "finish_reason": "length"
[p0163-l0031] [8.0pt]     }
[p0163-l0032] [8.0pt]   ],
[p0163-l0033] [8.0pt]   "usage": {
[p0163-l0034] [8.0pt]     "prompt_tokens": 5,
[p0163-l0035] [8.0pt]     "completion_tokens": 20,
[p0163-l0036] [8.0pt]     "total_tokens": 25
[p0163-l0037] [8.0pt]   }
[p0163-l0038] [8.0pt] }
[p0163-l0039] [10.0pt] To return only the generated text and omit the other response fields, use this
[p0163-l0040] [10.0pt] command:
[p0163-l0041] [8.0pt] print(res["choices"][0]["text"])
[p0163-l0042] [10.0pt] The first time you run this code, it will be slower because it must download the model
[p0163-l0043] [10.0pt] checkpoints locally. After that first run, you can generate code completely offline.

[p0164-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0164-l0003] [10.0pt] You can benchmark this local model’s performance the same way you did for the
[p0164-l0004] [10.0pt] CodeGen models. Repeat the inference tests with the same configuration used for the
[p0164-l0005] [10.0pt] smaller models, and you’ll see latency and throughput results like the following:
[p0164-l0006] [8.0pt]              GGUF 4-bit K_M
[p0164-l0007] [8.0pt] Average_latency (ms) 432.545684
[p0164-l0008] [8.0pt] Latency_P50          432.409188
[p0164-l0009] [8.0pt] Latency_P75          436.077177
[p0164-l0010] [8.0pt] Latency_P90          438.191962
[p0164-l0011] [8.0pt] Latency_P95          438.622171
[p0164-l0012] [8.0pt] Latency_P99          440.215217
[p0164-l0013] [8.0pt] Throughput               2.311895
[p0164-l0014] [10.0pt] The overall performance (using only four threads and no GPU) is comparable to the
[p0164-l0015] [10.0pt] 4-bit quantized CodeGen model, which is acceptable for local use. You can evaluate the
[p0164-l0016] [10.0pt] generated code as explained in section 7.2.3.
[p0164-l0017] [10.0pt] So far, we’ve run inference from the CLI by executing a Python script with a prompt.
[p0164-l0018] [10.0pt] You can also run in chat mode (llama-cpp-python provides an API for this). The library
[p0164-l0019] [10.0pt] also includes a web server, so you can use llama.cpp-compatible models with any
[p0164-l0020] [10.0pt] OpenAI-compatible client. This mode makes local models easy to integrate with an IDE
[p0164-l0021] [10.0pt] for code completion and suggestions.
[p0164-l0022] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ve assumed the code-generation model we need is available from
[p0164-l0023] [10.0pt] the Hugging Face Hub in GGUF format. But what if the model you want is available
[p0164-l0024] [10.0pt] only in single or half precision, or it’s available in GGUF but the performance isn’t
[p0164-l0025] [10.0pt] great? In those cases, after you’ve downloaded the source model checkpoints and
[p0164-l0026] [10.0pt] supporting files locally, you can quantize the model and convert it to GGUF using the
[p0164-l0027] [10.0pt] convert_hf_to_gguf.py script in the llama.cpp GitHub repo:
[p0164-l0028] [8.0pt] python llama.cpp/convert-hf-to-gguf.py <checkpoints_dir> --outfile
[p0164-l0029] [10.0pt] ➥<output_file_name>.gguf --outtype <quantization_type>
[p0164-l0030] [10.0pt] The script requires the directory for the downloaded model checkpoints and files, a
[p0164-l0031] [10.0pt] name for the target GGUF file, and the quantization type (see the llama.cpp docs for
[p0164-l0032] [10.0pt] options). You can also upload the resulting GGUF model to the Hugging Face Hub.
[p0164-l0033] [10.0pt] After quantization, repeat the steps from earlier in this section to generate code locally.
[p0164-l0034] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0164-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Specialized open source code-generation models can match generalist perfor­
[p0164-l0036] [10.0pt] mance with fewer parameters.
[p0164-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ CodeGen models support multiple programming languages, including Python-
[p0164-l0038] [10.0pt] only code generation via the mono family.
[p0164-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Converting code generation models to ONNX can reduce average inference
[p0164-l0040] [10.0pt] time by about 19% compared to standard PyTorch implementations.
[p0164-l0041] [10.0pt] ¡ 8-bit quantization of ONNX models can cut inference time by an additional 60%
[p0164-l0042] [10.0pt] without sacrificing quality.

[p0166-l0013] [12.5pt] 8.1
[p0166-l0014] [12.5pt] Applying Transformers in chemistry
[p0166-l0015] [10.0pt] In chapter 7, you saw how to overcome inference challenges using the tips and
[p0166-l0016] [10.0pt] tricks introduced in the first part of this book. Before we move on to more advanced
[p0166-l0017] [10.0pt] inference optimization and model quantization in the following chapters, we’ll
[p0166-l0018] [10.0pt] apply these techniques to specialized SLMs in the chemistry domain to show that
[p0166-l0019] [10.0pt] they aren’t limited to creating coding assistants. If chemistry is new to you, don’t
[p0166-l0020] [9.0pt] 145

[p0167-l0001] [9.0pt] 146
[p0167-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 8  Generating protein structures
[p0167-l0003] [10.0pt] worry—we’ll keep it high level and cover only what you need to follow the model
[p0167-l0004] [10.0pt] descriptions and inference optimization strategies we’ll apply.
[p0167-l0005] [10.0pt] Chemistry is one of the fields that has benefited most from advances in natural
[p0167-l0006] [10.0pt] language processing (NLP). Researchers have reframed many chemistry tasks as text-­
[p0167-l0007] [10.0pt] sequence problems. Combined with open datasets, this has sparked a wave of work
[p0167-l0008] [10.0pt] starting with clearly defined fundamental challenges. Early models were single-modal,
[p0167-l0009] [10.0pt] using molecules as both input and output. More recent work is multimodal, adding
[p0167-l0010] [10.0pt] data such as spectra from analytical techniques and human language (such as synthesis
[p0167-l0011] [10.0pt] procedures) to bridge the gap between chemical and natural-language modeling.
[p0167-l0012] [10.5pt] Some chemistry terms
[p0167-l0013] [9.5pt] Amino acid—Organic molecule used by living organisms to build proteins
[p0167-l0014] [9.5pt] Antibody—Immune-system protein that helps fight pathogens such as bacteria and
[p0167-l0015] [9.5pt] viruses
[p0167-l0016] [9.5pt] Oligomer—Molecule made of a small number of repeating units called monomers
[p0167-l0017] [9.5pt] Protein—Molecule made of amino acids that supports growth, tissue repair, and
[p0167-l0018] [9.5pt] other body functions
[p0167-l0019] [9.5pt] Reactant—Substance that is changed or consumed in a chemical reaction
[p0167-l0020] [9.5pt] Reagent—Substance added to trigger a reaction or test for one (or for a specific
[p0167-l0021] [9.5pt] chemical)
[p0167-l0022] [9.5pt] SMILES—The Simplified Molecular Input Line Entry System, a chemical notation for
[p0167-l0023] [9.5pt] representing molecular structures in computer-readable form (https://biocyc.org/
[p0167-l0024] [9.5pt] help.html?object=smiles)
[p0167-l0025] [10.0pt] One early and notable effort is the Molecular Transformer (https://pubs.acs.org/
[p0167-l0026] [10.0pt] doi/10.1021/acscentsci.9b00576). Organic synthesis is a key building block in medic­
[p0167-l0027] [10.0pt] inal chemistry, and a necessary but still unsolved step in synthesis planning is prod­
[p0167-l0028] [10.0pt] uct prediction: given reactants and reagents, what will the final products be? In this
[p0167-l0029] [10.0pt] work, reaction prediction is treated as machine translation between SMILES strings for
[p0167-l0030] [10.0pt] reactants, reagents, and products. The model outperforms earlier methods, achieving
[p0167-l0031] [10.0pt] top-1 accuracy above 90% on a common benchmark dataset. The Molecular Trans­
[p0167-l0032] [10.0pt] former learns correlations between the presence or absence of chemical motifs in the
[p0167-l0033] [10.0pt] reactants, reagents, and products in the dataset, and it requires no handcrafted rules.
[p0167-l0034] [10.0pt] Drug discovery is the area where adopting language models has delivered the biggest
[p0167-l0035] [10.0pt] gains so far. As mentioned in chapter 1, because they’re trained mostly on data scraped
[p0167-l0036] [10.0pt] from the web, large commercial language models underperform on tasks that require
[p0167-l0037] [10.0pt] specialized knowledge—knowledge that typically requires domain-specific, often
[p0167-l0038] [10.0pt] proprietary data that isn’t available to tech companies. In other cases, a model needs
[p0167-l0039] [10.0pt] task-specific tuning, or the data’s structure is too complex for large general-purpose

=== PDF page 168 / printed label 147 ===
[p0168-l0001] [9.0pt] 147
[p0168-l0002] [9.0pt] From natural language to protein structures
[p0168-l0003] [10.0pt] models to be useful. In all these scenarios, the closed nature of large commercial mod­
[p0168-l0004] [10.0pt] els and the high cost of fine-tuning them make it impossible to achieve the performance
[p0168-l0005] [10.0pt] needed for drug discovery.
[p0168-l0006] [10.0pt] For these reasons, academia and industry have turned to smaller open source pre­
[p0168-l0007] [10.0pt] trained language models. These models provide full control and make it possible to
[p0168-l0008] [10.0pt] release production-ready models for a diverse set of drug discovery tasks. Each month
[p0168-l0009] [10.0pt] brings new specialized models, many under permissive open source licenses that often
[p0168-l0010] [10.0pt] cover not only the source code and model checkpoints, but also the training and test
[p0168-l0011] [10.0pt] datasets. I maintain a GitHub repo that tracks major fully open source initiatives in this
[p0168-l0012] [10.0pt] area (https://github.com/virtualramblas/awesome-deep-learning-4-life-sciences).
[p0168-l0013] [10.0pt] This chapter will look at notable examples of domain-specific SLMs for protein and
[p0168-l0014] [10.0pt] crystal structure generation, along with ML/AI engineering considerations and sugges­
[p0168-l0015] [10.0pt] tions for improving inference performance.
[p0168-l0016] [12.5pt] 8.2
[p0168-l0017] [12.5pt] From natural language to protein structures
[p0168-l0018] [10.0pt] The first SLM we’ll explore is ProtGPT2 (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467
[p0168-l0019] [10.0pt] -022-32007-7), a model that “speaks” the protein language and can be used for novel
[p0168-l0020] [10.0pt] protein design and engineering. Sequences generated by ProtGPT2 preserve key fea­
[p0168-l0021] [10.0pt] tures of natural proteins (amino acid propensities, secondary structure content, and
[p0168-l0022] [10.0pt] globularity) while exploring previously unseen regions of protein space.
[p0168-l0023] [10.0pt] ProtGPT2 is a decoder-only GPT-2 model with 738 million parameters. It was pre­
[p0168-l0024] [10.0pt] trained in a self-supervised fashion to predict the next token (oligomer) in a sequence,
[p0168-l0025] [10.0pt] using 87,162 raw protein sequences from the UniRef50 database (https://www.uniprot
[p0168-l0026] [10.0pt] .org/help/uniref) and without including the corresponding annotations. The pre­
[p0168-l0027] [10.0pt] processed training set is available on the Hugging Face Hub (https://huggingface
[p0168-l0028] [10.0pt] .co/datasets/nferruz/UR50_2021_04). Given a natural-language prompt, it can gen­
[p0168-l0029] [10.0pt] erate protein sequences. The pretrained model is available on the Hugging Face Hub
[p0168-l0030] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/nferruz/ProtGPT2).
[p0168-l0031] [10.0pt] Let’s look at how this model works and use it to generate de novo proteins in a zero-
[p0168-l0032] [10.0pt] shot setting. A companion Colab notebook is provided for this example. Because the

[p0168-l0040] [8.0pt]                     do_sample=True, top_k=950,

[p0170-l0026] [12.5pt] 8.3
[p0170-l0027] [12.5pt] Antibody generation with an SLM
[p0170-l0028] [10.0pt] Our second SLM in this chapter is the Antibody Generator (also referred to as
[p0170-l0029] [10.0pt] Antibody­GPT), a specialized protein generation model for creating therapeutic anti­
[p0170-l0030] [10.0pt] body sequences for use in immunology, vaccine development, and medical treatments.
[p0170-l0031] [10.0pt] Antibodies are proteins that protect us when a foreign substance (called an antigen)
[p0170-l0032] [10.0pt] enters the body. Produced by the immune system, antibodies bind to these substances
[p0170-l0033] [10.0pt] to help eliminate them. The Antibody Generator is based on ProGen2, an advanced
[p0170-l0034] [10.0pt] language model developed by Salesforce and trained on more than 280 million pro­
[p0170-l0035] [10.0pt] tein sequences–it was introduced in the paper “ProGen2: Exploring the Boundaries of
[p0170-l0036] [10.0pt] Protein Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.13517).
[p0170-l0037] [10.0pt] The ProGen2 family follows a decoder-only architecture and includes four model
[p0170-l0038] [10.0pt] sizes: small (151 million parameters), medium (765 million parameters), large (2.7 bil­
[p0170-l0039] [10.0pt] lion parameters), and extra-large (6.4 billion parameters). The Antibody Generator
[p0170-l0040] [10.0pt] models were built using the ProGen2 small, medium, and large variants as a baseline
[p0170-l0041] [10.0pt] and were fine-tuned on 5,000 experimentally resolved crystal structures of antibodies
[p0170-l0042] [10.0pt] and their antigens (see figure 8.1). All three Antibody Generator model options are
[p0170-l0043] [10.0pt] available on the Hugging Face Hub.
[p0170-l0044] [10.0pt] Let’s run inference with AntibodyGPT, starting with the small model. A companion
[p0170-l0045] [10.0pt] Colab notebook is provided for this example, and it requires GPU acceleration.

[p0171-l0004] [10.0pt] To download checkpoints for this model (or either of the other two versions) from the
[p0171-l0005] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Hub and load them into memory, you’ll need a custom auto class, Pro­
[p0171-l0006] [10.0pt] GenForCausalLM. It’s implemented in a public GitHub repo by Joseph Roberts (a coau­
[p0171-l0007] [10.0pt] thor of AntibodyGPT): https://github.com/joethequant/docker_protein_generator.
[p0171-l0008] [10.0pt] First, clone the repo:

[p0171-l0025] [8.0pt] ELDFQWREKTPEPPVPCVPEQTEYATIVFPSGMGTSSPARRGSADGPRSAQPLRPEDGHCSWPL'

[p0172-l0017] [10.0pt] Although this model is smaller than ProtGPT, generating just two target sequences

[p0172-l0034] [10.0pt] Before optimizing this model, let’s look at how we can validate its generated results.
[p0172-l0035] [10.0pt] Perplexity and similar statistical metrics make little sense on their own in cases like
[p0172-l0036] [10.0pt] this. A more reliable option is the ANARCI tool (https://opig.stats.ox.ac.uk/webapps/
[p0172-l0037] [10.0pt] sabdab-sabpred/sabpred/anarci/), developed and maintained by the Oxford Pro­
[p0172-l0038] [10.0pt] tein Informatics Group (OPIG), for antibody numbering and receptor classification.

=== PDF page 173 / printed label 152 ===
[p0173-l0001] [9.0pt] 152
[p0173-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 8  Generating protein structures
[p0173-l0003] [10.0pt] ANARCI checks whether generated antibody sequences conform to known patterns and
[p0173-l0004] [10.0pt] structures, helping us assess structural viability and alignment with established frame­
[p0173-l0005] [10.0pt] works. The goal is for sequences to be not only novel but also biologically relevant and
[p0173-l0006] [10.0pt] potentially functional. You can submit a generated antibody sequence to the ANARCI
[p0173-l0007] [10.0pt] online tool; figure 8.2 shows the results for one of the sequences from our example.
[p0173-l0008] [8.0pt] Figure 8.2  The output of the online ANARCI tool for one of the antibody sequences generated in our example
[p0173-l0009] [10.0pt] In many domains, it’s common to validate generated content with a dedicated tool.
[p0173-l0010] [10.0pt] Subject matter experts should always review it. You can also perform this validation
[p0173-l0011] [10.0pt] programmatically using the Python ANARCI API (https://github.com/oxpig/ANARCI/
[p0173-l0012] [10.0pt] tree/master).
[p0173-l0013] [10.0pt] Next, let’s see whether the model benefits from quantization. Using the Bitsandbytes

[p0173-l0015] [8.0pt] from transformers import BitsAndBytesConfig

[p0173-l0017] [8.0pt]   load_in_8bit=True,
[p0173-l0018] [8.0pt] )

[p0174-l0017] [12.5pt] 8.4
[p0174-l0018] [12.5pt] From CIF files to crystal structures
[p0174-l0019] [10.0pt] The third SLM we’ll explore is CrystaLLM from the “Crystal Structure Generation with
[p0174-l0020] [10.0pt] Autoregressive Large Language Modeling” paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.04340).
[p0174-l0021] [10.0pt] It’s a Transformer-based, decoder-only LLM built to generate crystal structures. Pre­
[p0174-l0022] [10.0pt] viously, crystal structure-prediction methods—often based on computationally inten­
[p0174-l0023] [10.0pt] sive ab initio techniques—typically relied on dedicated tools to optimize candidate
[p0174-l0024] [10.0pt] structures.
[p0174-l0025] [10.0pt] CrystaLLM is the first model trained on textual representations of crystallographic
[p0174-l0026] [10.0pt] information files (CIFs), rather than traditional chemical representations. The authors
[p0174-l0027] [10.0pt] argue that symbol sequences can represent complex chemical structures and that LLMs
[p0174-l0028] [10.0pt] can learn deeper causal relationships beyond simple correlations. Trained on extensive
[p0174-l0029] [10.0pt] CIF data, the model can generate physically plausible inorganic crystal structures. The
[p0174-l0030] [10.0pt] authors also added Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) and a graph-based neural network
[p0174-l0031] [10.0pt] to improve structural sampling.
[p0174-l0032] [10.0pt] During training, the model is given token sequences from a corpus of CIF files and
[p0174-l0033] [10.0pt] learns to predict the next token. After training, it can generate new CIF files condi­
[p0174-l0034] [10.0pt] tioned on a starting token sequence. Generating a CIF file involves repeatedly sampling
[p0174-l0035] [10.0pt] tokens from the model, conditioning on the accumulated generated content, until a
[p0174-l0036] [10.0pt] terminating condition is reached.
[p0174-l0037] [10.0pt] Figure 8.3 (from the previously cited paper) provides a high-level view of CrystaLLM’s
[p0174-l0038] [10.0pt] training and inference processes. As you can see, during training, a CIF file is tokenized
[p0174-l0039] [10.0pt] into a symbol sequence. The model processes the sequence, and it outputs, for
[p0174-l0040] [10.0pt] each input symbol, a probability distribution over the vocabulary. These predicted
[p0174-l0041] [10.0pt] distributions are compared with the target distributions (all the probability mass on the
[p0174-l0042] [10.0pt] correct next token) using the cross-entropy loss metric. The targets are the input tokens

[p0175-l0001] [9.0pt] 154
[p0175-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 8  Generating protein structures
[p0175-l0003] [7.0pt] Target
[p0175-l0004] [7.0pt] Cross-entropy loss
[p0175-l0005] [7.0pt] Output
[p0175-l0006] [7.0pt] Input
[p0175-l0007] [7.0pt] Tokenization
[p0175-l0008] [7.0pt] Repeat until terminating
[p0175-l0009] [7.0pt] condition is true
[p0175-l0010] [8.0pt] Figure 8.3  The CrystaLLM training process (a) and the generation process with MCTS decoding (b)
[p0175-l0011] [10.0pt] shifted one position left, since the task is to predict the next token from the preceding
[p0175-l0012] [10.0pt] tokens (as in many LLM content-generation tasks). The tokens are grouped into CIF
[p0175-l0013] [10.0pt] tags, atoms, numeric digits, and punctuation. The output tokens (not sampled during
[p0175-l0014] [10.0pt] training) represent those with the highest assigned probability. Underlined tokens
[p0175-l0015] [10.0pt] indicate cases where the correct next token receives relatively low probability.
[p0175-l0016] [10.0pt] Once the model is trained, it generates a CIF file from a prompt. The prompt is
[p0175-l0017] [10.0pt] built by concatenating the symbol data with the target cell composition, and it’s then
[p0175-l0018] [10.0pt] tokenized and fed to the model. At each step, the model samples the next token from
[p0175-l0019] [10.0pt] the predicted distribution and appends it to the CIF contents. This repeats until a pre­
[p0175-l0020] [10.0pt] defined stopping condition is reached. The model is based on GPT-2; the model defi­
[p0175-l0021] [10.0pt] nition, training, and inference code are adapted from Andrej Karpathy’s nanoGPT
[p0175-l0022] [10.0pt] repository (https://github.com/karpathy/nanoGPT).
[p0175-l0023] [10.0pt] CrystaLLM can generate plausible crystal structures for a wide range of inorganic
[p0175-l0024] [10.0pt] compounds, including ones it didn’t see during training. It generates syntactically
[p0175-l0025] [10.0pt] valid, physically plausible structures and can predict crystal structures given chemical

=== PDF page 176 / printed label 155 ===
[p0176-l0001] [9.0pt] 155
[p0176-l0002] [9.0pt] From CIF files to crystal structures
[p0176-l0003] [10.0pt] composition and symmetry information. It also generalizes to unseen inorganic struc­
[p0176-l0004] [10.0pt] tures, achieving structural matches in up to 40% of cases, and can extrapolate structural
[p0176-l0005] [10.0pt] motifs to new compositions. This work is important because it has shown potential to
[p0176-l0006] [10.0pt] accelerate material discovery by generating candidate crystal structures for downstream
[p0176-l0007] [10.0pt] optimization.
[p0176-l0008] [10.0pt] We’ll skip the remaining training details. In this chapter, we’ll use the pretrained
[p0176-l0009] [10.0pt] model and focus only on the inference process. A companion Colab notebook is pro­
[p0176-l0010] [10.0pt] vided for this section.
[p0176-l0011] [10.0pt] To set up the environment, we’ll first clone the CrystaLLM GitHub repository:
[p0176-l0012] [8.0pt] !git clone https://github.com/lantunes/CrystaLLM.git
[p0176-l0013] [8.0pt] %cd CrystaLLM
[p0176-l0014] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll make the cloned source code directories part of the Python path:
[p0176-l0015] [8.0pt] import sys
[p0176-l0016] [8.0pt] import os
[p0176-l0017] [8.0pt] sys.path.append('/content/CrystaLLM')
[p0176-l0018] [8.0pt] os.environ["PYTHONPATH"] += (":/content/CrystaLLM")
[p0176-l0019] [10.0pt] Once you’ve installed the missing requirements, download the pretrained model
[p0176-l0020] [10.0pt] weights. Two versions of CrystaLLM are available: small (25 million parameters) and
[p0176-l0021] [10.0pt] large (200 million parameters). These weights aren’t available on the Hugging Face
[p0176-l0022] [10.0pt] Hub, so download them using the following Python script (here we’re requesting the
[p0176-l0023] [10.0pt] small version):
[p0176-l0024] [8.0pt] !python bin/download.py crystallm_v1_small.tar.gz
[p0176-l0025] [8.0pt] !tar xvf crystallm_v1_small.tar.gz
[p0176-l0026] [10.0pt] We’re now ready to use it to generate crystal structures. First, we need to create a
[p0176-l0027] [10.0pt] prompt, which in this case is the partial contents of a preprocessed CIF file. Typically,
[p0176-l0028] [10.0pt] the prompt contains the cell composition: a formula specifying the total count of each
[p0176-l0029] [10.0pt] atom type in the unit cell. For example, we can specify Na2Cl2 (disodium dichloride),
[p0176-l0030] [10.0pt] which indicates four atoms in the unit cell, and use the provided make_prompt_file.py
[p0176-l0031] [10.0pt] script to prepare and save the prompt for later use:
[p0176-l0032] [8.0pt] !python bin/make_prompt_file.py Na2Cl2 my_prompt.txt
[p0176-l0033] [10.0pt] To prompt the model with a cell composition, the format should use the data_ prefix
[p0176-l0034] [10.0pt] and a newline character at the end of the line:
[p0176-l0035] [8.0pt] data_<cell_composition>\n
[p0176-l0036] [10.0pt] The make_prompt_file.py script handles this formatting convention (and more). In
[p0176-l0037] [10.0pt] our example, the model is prompted with data_Na2Cl2\n.

[p0177-l0003] [10.0pt] We can now generate the CIF files; we’ll use the provided sample.py script:
[p0177-l0004] [8.0pt] !python bin/sample.py \
[p0177-l0005] [8.0pt] out_dir=crystallm_v1_small \
[p0177-l0006] [8.0pt] start=FILE:sample_prompt.txt \
[p0177-l0007] [8.0pt] num_samples=2 \
[p0177-l0008] [8.0pt] top_k=10 \
[p0177-l0009] [8.0pt] max_new_tokens=3000 \
[p0177-l0010] [8.0pt] device=cpu \
[p0177-l0011] [8.0pt] target=file
[p0177-l0012] [10.0pt] This script takes the following arguments:
[p0177-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ out_dir—The directory containing the downloaded model checkpoints.
[p0177-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ start—Either a prompt in the required format or the path to a file containing
[p0177-l0015] [10.0pt] the prompt.
[p0177-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ num_samples—The number of samples to generate.
[p0177-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ top_k—The maximum number of most likely tokens to keep.
[p0177-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ max_new_tokens—The maximum number of tokens to generate per sample.
[p0177-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ device—Where to offload the model weights: CPU or GPU.
[p0177-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ target—Where the generated content should be sent. In our example, it’s file.
[p0177-l0021] [10.0pt] Alternatively, it can be console.
[p0177-l0022] [10.0pt] These are some other arguments we haven’t used here:
[p0177-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ temperature—This has the same meaning as in any Transformer model.
[p0177-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ seed—Sets the random seed for reproducibility; defaults to 1,337.
[p0177-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ dtype—Model precision; defaults to bfloat16.
[p0177-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ compile—Boolean flag indicating whether to compile the model with PyTorch
[p0177-l0027] [10.0pt] before CIF generation for faster execution. Defaults to False.
[p0177-l0028] [10.0pt] No hardware acceleration is needed for this small model. With the chosen configura­
[p0177-l0029] [10.0pt] tion (3,000 tokens max per sequence), generating two CIF files on a Colab CPU VM

[p0180-l0021] [10.0pt] If you want to upload a CrystaLLM pretrained model (or your fine-tuned version) to
[p0180-l0022] [10.0pt] a Hugging Face Hub repository and use it with the Transformers library, follow these
[p0180-l0023] [10.0pt] steps. We show the small model here; the large model follows the same steps but uses

[p0180-l0025] [10.0pt] First, create a configuration file, config.json, as required by the Transformers

[p0180-l0027] [10.0pt] CrystaLLM GitHub repository (there is a similar file for the large model).
[p0180-l0028] [8.0pt] crystall_small_config = """{
[p0180-l0029] [8.0pt]   "bias": true,
[p0180-l0030] [8.0pt]   "model_type": "gpt2",
[p0180-l0031] [8.0pt]   "block_size": 1024,
[p0180-l0032] [8.0pt]   "dropout": 0.1,
[p0180-l0033] [8.0pt]   "n_embd": 512,
[p0180-l0034] [8.0pt]   "n_head": 8,
[p0180-l0035] [8.0pt]   "n_layer": 8,
[p0180-l0036] [8.0pt]   "vocab_size": 50257
[p0180-l0037] [8.0pt] }"""
[p0180-l0038] [8.0pt] with open('/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small/config.json', 'a') as f:
[p0180-l0039] [8.0pt]     f.write(crystall_small_config)
[p0180-l0040] [10.0pt] Next, convert the model checkpoint from .pt to .bin, which is required to load it into
[p0180-l0041] [10.0pt] an auto class:
[p0180-l0042] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0180-l0043] [8.0pt] checkpoint = torch.load("/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small/ckpt.pt",
[p0180-l0044] [8.0pt]                     map_location=torch.device('cpu'))
[p0180-l0045] [8.0pt] params = checkpoint["model"]
[p0180-l0046] [8.0pt] torch.save(params,
[p0180-l0047] [10.0pt] ➥"/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small/pytorch_model.bin")

[p0181-l0003] [10.0pt] Note that instead of accessing the model_state_dict key, we access the model key
[p0181-l0004] [10.0pt] directly, because this pretrained model stores its weights under that key in the check­
[p0181-l0005] [10.0pt] point dictionary.
[p0181-l0006] [10.0pt] Now we can wrap the model in a Model class, provide the generated configuration,
[p0181-l0007] [10.0pt] and make it available through the Transformers library:
[p0181-l0008] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoConfig, AutoModelForCausalLM
[p0181-l0009] [8.0pt] config = AutoConfig.from_pretrained(
[p0181-l0010] [8.0pt]             '/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small/config.json')
[p0181-l0011] [8.0pt] transformer_model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
[p0181-l0012] [8.0pt]             '/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small', config=config)
[p0181-l0013] [10.0pt] Then we save the Model to disk (to generate the remaining files):
[p0181-l0014] [8.0pt] transformer_model.save_pretrained
[p0181-l0015] [10.0pt] ➥("/content/CrystaLLM/crystallm_v1_small_hf")
[p0181-l0016] [10.0pt] It can also be uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub if needed. First, in Colab, create a
[p0181-l0017] [10.0pt] new secret with the name HF_TOKEN. Copy your access token key from your Hugging
[p0181-l0018] [10.0pt] Face Hub profile settings, and paste it into the Value field of the HF_TOKEN. Then tog­
[p0181-l0019] [10.0pt] gle the key icon on the left side of the Colab UI to let the notebook access the secret.
[p0181-l0020] [10.0pt] Finally, load the token programmatically:
[p0181-l0021] [8.0pt] import os
[p0181-l0022] [8.0pt] from google.colab import userdata
[p0181-l0023] [8.0pt] os.environ["HF_TOKEN"] = userdata.get("HF_TOKEN")
[p0181-l0024] [10.0pt] You can then use it to log in to the Hugging Face Hub (this requires the huggingface_hub
[p0181-l0025] [10.0pt] package to be installed):
[p0181-l0026] [8.0pt] from huggingface_hub import login
[p0181-l0027] [8.0pt] login(os.environ["HF_TOKEN"])
[p0181-l0028] [10.0pt] You can now push the model to the Hub:
[p0181-l0029] [8.0pt] transformer_model.push_to_hub("crystallm_v1_small_hf")

[p0182-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0182-l0003] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0182-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Chemistry language models use NLP techniques to represent molecular struc­
[p0182-l0005] [10.0pt] tures as text sequences for drug discovery.
[p0182-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ ProtGPT2 generates protein sequences with a decoder-only GPT-2 model trained

[p0187-l0003] [10.0pt] in a final model size that exceeds the available inference hardware capacity, even after
[p0187-l0004] [10.0pt] quantization.
[p0187-l0005] [10.0pt] This chapter introduces advanced LLM quantization techniques that can help you
[p0187-l0006] [10.0pt] run such specialized models efficiently in target environments, balancing quality and
[p0187-l0007] [10.0pt] speed. The sections that follow describe these strategies and compare their pros and
[p0187-l0008] [10.0pt] cons. You’ll also find detailed code examples and benchmarks.
[p0187-l0009] [10.0pt] NOTE  This chapter covers advanced LMM quantization techniques for cases
[p0187-l0010] [10.0pt] where the methods in chapter 6 can’t meet performance or compute con­
[p0187-l0011] [10.0pt] straints. Before continuing, make sure you understand chapter 6.
[p0187-l0012] [12.5pt] 9.1
[p0187-l0013] [12.5pt] FlexGen
[p0187-l0014] [10.0pt] FlexGen is a high-throughput inference engine for running LLMs in situations where
[p0187-l0015] [10.0pt] GPU memory is limited. Introduced in the 2023 paper “FlexGen: High-Throughput
[p0187-l0016] [10.0pt] Generative Inference of Large Language Models with a Single GPU” (https://arxiv
[p0187-l0017] [10.0pt] .org/abs/2303.06865), FlexGen can be configured for different hardware constraints
[p0187-l0018] [10.0pt] by pooling memory and compute across the GPU, CPU, and disk. It searches for effi­
[p0187-l0019] [10.0pt] cient ways to store and access tensors by solving a linear programming problem, and it
[p0187-l0020] [10.0pt] further compresses the weights and attention cache to 4 bits with negligible accuracy
[p0187-l0021] [10.0pt] loss. This expands the feasible batch-size range and increases the maximum through­
[p0187-l0022] [10.0pt] put for a model. The paper reports substantially higher throughput than with tradi­
[p0187-l0023] [10.0pt] tional offloading methods.
[p0187-l0024] [10.0pt] To give you an idea of what FlexGen enables, consider a GPT-3–sized model with
[p0187-l0025] [10.0pt] 175 billion parameters. Using the formula in section 4.2, the VRAM required to load
[p0187-l0026] [10.0pt] it is 840 GB in FP32 or 420 GB in FP16. This means that to load the model and make it
[p0187-l0027] [10.0pt] available for inference, you’d need, for example, six NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPUs
[p0187-l0028] [10.0pt] (see figure 9.1).
[p0187-l0029] [7.0pt] (4 × P)
[p0187-l0030] [7.0pt] Required_memory = ---------- × 1.2 = 840 GB (fp32) or 420 GB (fp16)
[p0187-l0031] [7.0pt] (32 ÷ F)
[p0187-l0032] [8.0pt] 6 NVIDIA A100 Tensor Core GPU!
[p0187-l0033] [8.0pt] Figure 9.1  The hardware needed to load a 175 billion–parameter language model into memory

=== PDF page 188 / printed label 167 ===
[p0188-l0001] [9.0pt] 167
[p0188-l0002] [9.0pt] FlexGen
[p0188-l0003] [10.0pt] Given the price of the hardware, running a single model this way can be very
[p0188-l0004] [10.0pt] expensive—­often beyond the budget of small and mid-sized organizations and even
[p0188-l0005] [10.0pt] some large non-tech ones. Assume a node with one consumer GPU (16 GB DRAM)
[p0188-l0006] [10.0pt] but more RAM and disk space, which are cheaper and more available than GPUs. The
[p0188-l0007] [10.0pt] FlexGen linear programming optimizer finds the best way to store and access the mod­
[p0188-l0008] [10.0pt] el’s weights, activations, and attention KV cache across the GPU, CPU, and disk. As a
[p0188-l0009] [10.0pt] result, parts of the model are offloaded, as shown in figure 9.2 (assuming the model is
[p0188-l0010] [10.0pt] loaded in FP16 format). This approach is definitely cheaper than buying or renting six
[p0188-l0011] [10.0pt] NVIDIA A100 GPUs.
[p0188-l0012] [7.0pt] 175B model: 420 GB VRAM → 16 GB VRAM + 200 GB DRAM + 204 GB disk
[p0188-l0013] [8.0pt] Cheaper than 6 A100 GPUs!
[p0188-l0014] [8.0pt] Figure 9.2  Loading a 175 billion–parameter language model with FlexGen across GPU, CPU, and disk
[p0188-l0015] [10.0pt] This kind of offloading lets us deploy a very large model in a hardware-constrained
[p0188-l0016] [10.0pt] environment, but it increases latency and reduces throughput. That’s expected: CPUs
[p0188-l0017] [10.0pt] and disks are slower than GPUs, and offloading adds extra I/O.
[p0188-l0018] [10.0pt] FlexGen goes beyond basic offloading: during generative inference, it decides which
[p0188-l0019] [10.0pt] tensors (weights, activations, and KV cache) to offload, where to place them, and when
[p0188-l0020] [10.0pt] to move them to improve throughput while keeping I/O efficient. It further boosts
[p0188-l0021] [10.0pt] inference performance by compressing both weights and the KV cache to 4 bits with
[p0188-l0022] [10.0pt] negligible accuracy loss. This is an extreme example using a very large model—when
[p0188-l0023] [10.0pt] you fine-tune a model for domain-specific tasks, you typically won’t reach this size—but
[p0188-l0024] [10.0pt] it illustrates the benefits of the FlexGen approach in simple terms.
[p0188-l0025] [10.0pt] NOTE  FlexGen supports only NVIDIA GPUs via CUDA and has no plans to
[p0188-l0026] [10.0pt] support other vendors’ hardware acceleration.
[p0188-l0027] [10.0pt] Let’s look at how FlexGen works in practice and see whether it delivers on the paper’s
[p0188-l0028] [10.0pt] claims. A companion Colab notebook includes the code for this section.
[p0188-l0029] [10.0pt] FlexGen is open source and available on GitHub (the repository is named Flex­
[p0188-l0030] [10.0pt] LLMGen; https://github.com/FMInference/FlexLLMGen/tree/main), and you
[p0188-l0031] [10.0pt] can install it from PyPI without building from source. It includes prebuilt imple­
[p0188-l0032] [10.0pt] mentations for Facebook’s OPT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01068) and Galactica

[p0189-l0003] [10.0pt] (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.09085) models and BigScience’s BLOOM (https://
[p0189-l0004] [10.0pt] arxiv.org/abs/2211.05100), plus models fine-tuned from these baselines. In this sec­
[p0189-l0005] [10.0pt] tion, we focus on OPT, a suite of decoder-only pretrained transformers ranging from
[p0189-l0006] [10.0pt] 125M to 175B parameters. The paper reports that OPT-175B is comparable to GPT-3

[p0190-l0008] [10.0pt] The CLI is a quick way to evaluate FlexGen. For models that run inference as part of a
[p0190-l0009] [10.0pt] larger ecosystem, however, it’s usually better to call the FlexGen API programmatically
[p0190-l0010] [10.0pt] alongside the Hugging Face Transformers API. For example, to run a text completion
[p0190-l0011] [10.0pt] task with a model that doesn’t fit on your GPU, start by importing the required Flex­
[p0190-l0012] [10.0pt] Gen classes (which will be discussed as we use them):
[p0190-l0013] [8.0pt] from flexgen.flex_opt import (Policy, OptLM, ExecutionEnv,
[p0190-l0014] [10.0pt] ➥CompressionConfig, str2bool)
[p0190-l0015] [10.0pt] Next, download the target model’s tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:
[p0190-l0016] [8.0pt] from transformers import AutoTokenizer
[p0190-l0017] [8.0pt] model_id = "facebook/opt-6.7b"
[p0190-l0018] [8.0pt] tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id, padding_side="left")
[p0190-l0019] [8.0pt] tokenizer.add_bos_token = False

[p0190-l0023] [10.0pt] and its create method. This method takes the name of the directory where FlexGen
[p0190-l0024] [10.0pt] can offload data that shouldn’t go in GPU memory or RAM:
[p0190-l0025] [8.0pt] offload_dir = './flexgen_offload'
[p0190-l0026] [8.0pt] env = ExecutionEnv.create(offload_dir)
[p0190-l0027] [10.0pt] We also need to set up FlexGen offloading and compression policies. The Policy class
[p0190-l0028] [10.0pt] handles both. Here’s how to use it to set up everything we need:
[p0190-l0029] [8.0pt] policy = Policy(len(prompts), 1,
[p0190-l0030] [8.0pt]                 50, 50, 50, 50, 100, 0,
[p0190-l0031] [8.0pt]                 overlap=True, sep_layer=True, pin_weight=True,
[p0190-l0032] [8.0pt]                 cpu_cache_compute=True, attn_sparsity=1.0,
[p0190-l0033] [8.0pt]                 compress_weight=True,

[p0191-l0003] [10.0pt] When creating an instance of the Policy class, we pass the offloading percentages (as
[p0191-l0004] [10.0pt] with the CLI command) and specify whether to compress weights and the weight com­
[p0191-l0005] [10.0pt] pression settings, whether to compress the cache, and the cache compression settings.

[p0191-l0007] [10.0pt] Face Hub model ID, the execution-environment instance, the local cache path (after

[p0191-l0012] [10.0pt] The FlexGen-prepared model is now ready for few-shot text-completion tasks. After
[p0191-l0013] [10.0pt] you set up a list of example prompts, you can run completion as follows:

[p0191-l0016] [8.0pt]     inputs.input_ids,
[p0191-l0017] [8.0pt]     do_sample=True,

[p0191-l0019] [8.0pt]     max_new_tokens=32,

[p0191-l0025] [8.0pt]     print("-" * 70)
[p0191-l0026] [10.0pt] LLMs prepared for FlexGen are fully supported by the Hugging Face’s Transformers
[p0191-l0027] [10.0pt] library. When you’re done generating text completions, you can shut down the execu­
[p0191-l0028] [10.0pt] tion environment:
[p0191-l0029] [8.0pt] env.close_copy_threads()
[p0191-l0030] [10.0pt] FlexGen also supports multiple GPUs, which helps when the model you need to run
[p0191-l0031] [10.0pt] might not fit in VRAM on your available hardware.
[p0191-l0032] [10.0pt] To support other families of open source LLMs, you can create a new Python script
[p0191-l0033] [10.0pt] that follows the structure of flexgen.opt_config.py. In it, specify the target model
[p0191-l0034] [10.0pt] architecture configuration, and implement utilities to download its weights from the
[p0191-l0035] [10.0pt] Hub.
[p0191-l0036] [10.0pt] FlexGen provides advanced offloading and compression out of the box, and it deliv­
[p0191-l0037] [10.0pt] ers higher throughput on large batches than other approaches covered so far in this
[p0191-l0038] [10.0pt] book, such as Accelerate and DeepSpeed. But it’s optimized for throughput-focused
[p0191-l0039] [10.0pt] scenarios (LLM applications running inference on millions of tokens per batch). If
[p0191-l0040] [10.0pt] latency is your main KPI, FlexGen isn’t the best way to run a larger model on budget
[p0191-l0041] [10.0pt] hardware; you’ll need to consider other optimization options instead.

[p0192-l0001] [9.0pt] 171
[p0192-l0002] [9.0pt] SmoothQuant
[p0192-l0003] [12.5pt] 9.2
[p0192-l0004] [12.5pt] SmoothQuant
[p0192-l0005] [10.0pt] SmoothQuant is a post-training quantization method that improves LLM efficiency
[p0192-l0006] [10.0pt] while preserving accuracy. Traditional quantization methods often focus on weights
[p0192-l0007] [10.0pt] and can struggle with activation outliers, especially in larger models. These outliers can
[p0192-l0008] [10.0pt] hurt performance after quantization. SmoothQuant (introduced in the paper of the
[p0192-l0009] [10.0pt] same name; https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10438) addresses this by enabling 8-bit weight
[p0192-l0010] [10.0pt] and activation quantization without additional training. It does so by smoothing activa­
[p0192-l0011] [10.0pt] tion outliers via a mathematical transformation, effectively shifting quantization diffi­
[p0192-l0012] [10.0pt] culties from activations to weights. This makes it possible to quantize a range of LLM
[p0192-l0013] [10.0pt] architectures successfully. According to experiments in the paper, SmoothQuant can
[p0192-l0014] [10.0pt] deliver up to 1.56 times speed increases and a 50% reduction in memory usage with
[p0192-l0015] [10.0pt] minimal accuracy loss. This can enable the deployment of extremely large models,
[p0192-l0016] [10.0pt] potentially even on a single node, depending on the node’s hardware specs. Smooth­
[p0192-l0017] [10.0pt] Quant is compatible with the PyTorch framework.
[p0192-l0018] [10.0pt] Before going hands-on with SmoothQuant, let’s look at the main quantization chal­
[p0192-l0019] [10.0pt] lenge it addresses. The techniques described in chapter 6 work well for LLMs up to about
[p0192-l0020] [10.0pt] 6 or 7 billion parameters. Beyond that threshold, systematic activation outliers often
[p0192-l0021] [10.0pt] appear, which can degrade accuracy after quantization. In section 6.2.2, I introduced
[p0192-l0022] [10.0pt] the LLM.int8() technique, which mitigates this problem with a mixed-precision decom­
[p0192-l0023] [10.0pt] position (it keeps outliers in FP16 while using INT8 for the remaining activations). This
[p0192-l0024] [10.0pt] technique is already integrated into popular Python libraries, including some we use
[p0192-l0025] [10.0pt] throughout this book. But for larger models, this decomposition is difficult to imple­
[p0192-l0026] [10.0pt] ment efficiently on hardware accelerators. In those cases, it’s better to use a different
[p0192-l0027] [10.0pt] training-free quantization scheme that uses INT8 for all compute-intensive operations.
[p0192-l0028] [10.0pt] SmoothQuant migrates the quantization difficulty from activations to weights by apply­
[p0192-l0029] [10.0pt] ing a mathematically equivalent, per-channel scaling transformation that smooths mag­
[p0192-l0030] [10.0pt] nitudes across channels and makes
[p0192-l0031] [10.0pt] the
[p0192-l0032] [10.0pt] model
[p0192-l0033] [10.0pt] more
[p0192-l0034] [10.0pt] quantization-­
[p0192-l0035] [10.0pt] friendly. Figure 9.3, taken from the
[p0192-l0036] [10.0pt] original SmoothQuant paper, illus­
[p0192-l0037] [10.0pt] trates the idea.
[p0192-l0038] [10.0pt] Figure 9.3 (top) shows activation
[p0192-l0039] [10.0pt] (left) and weight (right) distribu­
[p0192-l0040] [10.0pt] tions for an LLM with a large acti­
[p0192-l0041] [10.0pt] vation outlier. This outlier stretches
[p0192-l0042] [10.0pt] the quantization range, making
[p0192-l0043] [10.0pt] quantization difficult. Figure 9.3
[p0192-l0044] [10.0pt] (bottom) shows the same model
[p0192-l0045] [10.0pt] after SmoothQuant shifts scale vari­
[p0192-l0046] [10.0pt] ance from activations to weights
[p0192-l0047] [10.0pt] offline (before inference). The
[p0192-l0048] [10.0pt] activations are smoothed and the
[p0192-l0049] [8.0pt] Figure 9.3  A high-level explanation of SmoothQuant

=== PDF page 193 / printed label 172 ===
[p0193-l0001] [9.0pt] 172
[p0193-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 9  Advanced quantization techniques
[p0193-l0003] [10.0pt] weights adjusted, making both easier to quantize. SmoothQuant can preserve accuracy
[p0193-l0004] [10.0pt] after quantization while reducing serving costs.
[p0193-l0005] [10.0pt] Let’s look at an example; the complete code is available in a companion Colab note­
[p0193-l0006] [10.0pt] book. We’ll see that, for a given LLM, SmoothQuant can use INT8 for both activations
[p0193-l0007] [10.0pt] and weights while achieving accuracy comparable to FP16 on the same model. Smooth­
[p0193-l0008] [10.0pt] Quant has been tested on diverse LLM families, including Llama, OPT, Mistral, Mixtral,
[p0193-l0009] [10.0pt] and Falcon. For PyTorch, SmoothQuant provides INT8 inference with CUTLASS INT8
[p0193-l0010] [10.0pt] GEMM kernels, wrapped as PyTorch modules in the torch-int (https://github.com/
[p0193-l0011] [10.0pt] Guangxuan-Xiao/torch-int) Python package. SmoothQuant has also been integrated
[p0193-l0012] [10.0pt] into inference engines such as Intel’s Neural Compressor, NVIDIA’s TensorRT-LLM,
[p0193-l0013] [10.0pt] and Amazon SageMaker (we’ll cover LLM inference engines in chapter 11). To keep
[p0193-l0014] [10.0pt] the focus on how SmoothQuant works in code, we’ll simulate 8-bit dynamic per-tensor
[p0193-l0015] [10.0pt] quantization of weights and activations using FP16. All examples in this section require
[p0193-l0016] [10.0pt] hardware acceleration.
[p0193-l0017] [10.0pt] Our first target model is Facebook’s OPT-2.7b (https://huggingface.co/facebook/
[p0193-l0018] [10.0pt] opt-2.7b). We’ll start with a model that has fewer than 6 billion parameters to see
[p0193-l0019] [10.0pt] whether the SmoothQuant strategy benefits smaller models.
[p0193-l0020] [10.0pt] Let’s first install SmoothQuant from the source code:
[p0193-l0021] [8.0pt] pip install git+https://github.com/mit-han-lab/smoothquant.git
[p0193-l0022] [10.0pt] Next, download the model’s FP16 weights and its tokenizer from the Hugging Face
[p0193-l0023] [10.0pt] Hub:

[p0196-l0024] [10.0pt] The smooth_lm function takes as input the original model, the model scales (available
[p0196-l0025] [10.0pt] for this and many other models on the Hugging Face Hub; https://huggingface.co/
[p0196-l0026] [10.0pt] mit-han-lab/smoothquant-scales/tree/main), and alpha, a hyperparameter that con­
[p0196-l0027] [10.0pt] trols the migration strength, that is, how much quantization difficulty is shifted from
[p0196-l0028] [10.0pt] activations to weights. The SmoothQuant paper defines the smoothing factor sj for a
[p0196-l0029] [10.0pt] given activation Xj and weight Wj as a function of alpha:
[p0196-l0030] [10.0pt] For this example—and for models under 100 billion parameters in general—we can
[p0196-l0031] [10.0pt] keep alpha = 0.5.

[p0197-l0009] [8.0pt] SmoothQuant W8A8 quantized model accuracy: 0.799
[p0197-l0010] [10.0pt] As you’ve seen, SmoothQuant is a powerful strategy for reducing compute costs with­
[p0197-l0011] [10.0pt] out affecting model performance, especially once specialized models exceed 6 to 7 bil­
[p0197-l0012] [10.0pt] lion parameters. As mentioned earlier, several LLM families are supported out of the
[p0197-l0013] [10.0pt] box; others require some code customization to adapt the smoothing and quantization
[p0197-l0014] [10.0pt] steps to the architecture.
[p0197-l0015] [12.5pt] 9.3
[p0197-l0016] [12.5pt] BitNet
[p0197-l0017] [10.0pt] BitNet is a scalable 1-bit Transformer architecture designed to reduce the cost and
[p0197-l0018] [10.0pt] energy use of large language models. It replaces traditional linear layers with a com­
[p0197-l0019] [10.0pt] ponent called BitLinear, which allows the training of 1-bit weights from scratch. Exper­
[p0197-l0020] [10.0pt] imental findings indicate that BitNet, proposed for the first time in “BitNet: Scaling
[p0197-l0021] [10.0pt] 1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11453),
[p0197-l0022] [10.0pt] shows competitive language-modeling performance with much lower memory use and
[p0197-l0023] [10.0pt] energy consumption than leading 8-bit quantization methods and FP16 transformer
[p0197-l0024] [10.0pt] benchmarks. BitNet preserves high precision for optimizer states and gradients to
[p0197-l0025] [10.0pt] maintain training stability, and it scales to larger models, adhering to a scaling law like
[p0197-l0026] [10.0pt] full-precision transformers. The paper also describes group quantization for model
[p0197-l0027] [10.0pt] parallelism, improving efficiency without additional communication overhead. Over­
[p0197-l0028] [10.0pt] all, BitNet has the potential to lower inference costs and improve performance, mak­
[p0197-l0029] [10.0pt] ing it a promising alternative to other quantization methods.
[p0197-l0030] [10.0pt] Figure 9.4, from the original BitNet paper, shows the BitLinear component (left)
[p0197-l0031] [10.0pt] and the BitNet architecture (right), which uses BitLinear in the attention layers. As you
[p0197-l0032] [10.0pt] can see, the BitNet architecture has the same layout as a transformer. The main differ­
[p0197-l0033] [10.0pt] ence is that it uses BitLinear in the attention layers instead of matrix multiplication. This
[p0197-l0034] [10.0pt] binarizes the attention weights (1-bit), while the rest of the model uses higher precision
[p0197-l0035] [10.0pt] (8-bit). This reduces computational costs while preserving precision for the input/out­
[p0197-l0036] [10.0pt] put embeddings, since the model still uses high-precision probabilities for sampling.
[p0197-l0037] [10.0pt] The BitNet paper also reports on several comparison experiments. Figure 9.5 com­
[p0197-l0038] [10.0pt] pares the scaling curves of BitNet and FP16 transformers.
[p0197-l0039] [10.0pt] For smaller models, traditional FP16 transformers achieve lower loss than BitNet. As
[p0197-l0040] [10.0pt] model size increases, the gap narrows: the loss delta is already small at around 30 billion
[p0197-l0041] [10.0pt] parameters and drops to 0.09 near 100 billion.

=== PDF page 198 / printed label 177 ===
[p0198-l0001] [9.0pt] 177
[p0198-l0002] [9.0pt] BitNet
[p0198-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 9.4  The BitLinear component (left) and the BitNet architecture (right)
[p0198-l0004] [8.0pt] Figure 9.5  Comparing the scaling curves for BitNet and FP16 transformers
[p0198-l0005] [10.0pt] The biggest challenge in training low-bit transformers is optimization stability. The
[p0198-l0006] [10.0pt] paper’s authors tested both BitNet and an FP16 baseline by training a series of models
[p0198-l0007] [10.0pt] with varying peak learning rates. Figure 9.6 shows the results.
[p0198-l0008] [10.0pt] On the left of figure 9.6, BitNet converges with a high learning rate, whereas FP16
[p0198-l0009] [10.0pt] transformers fail to converge, indicating better training stability. On the right, BitNet
[p0198-l0010] [10.0pt] converges when training with different learning rates—its perplexity improves as the
[p0198-l0011] [10.0pt] learning rate increases.
[p0198-l0012] [10.0pt] The BitNet paper also compares this architecture with other post-training quanti­
[p0198-l0013] [10.0pt] zation (PTQ) methods, including Absmax, SmoothQuant, GPTQ, and QuIP (a 2-bit
[p0198-l0014] [10.0pt] method described in “QuIP: 2-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models With
[p0198-l0015] [10.0pt] Guarantees,” https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13304). Figure 9.7, from the BitNet paper,
[p0198-l0016] [10.0pt] compares the accuracy of an FP16 transformer with the same model after PTQ using
[p0198-l0017] [10.0pt] different techniques, including BitNet, on zero-shot (left) and few-shot (right) down­
[p0198-l0018] [10.0pt] stream tasks.

[p0199-l0005] [8.0pt] Figure 9.6  The results of the stability tests for BitNet and FP16 transformers
[p0199-l0006] [7.0pt] (a)
[p0199-l0007] [7.0pt] (b)
[p0199-l0008] [8.0pt] Figure 9.7  Average accuracy on downstream tasks in zero-shot (a) and few-shot (b) settings for vanilla
[p0199-l0009] [8.0pt] FP16 transformers, BitNet, and various PTQ methods
[p0199-l0010] [10.0pt] The different techniques have been evaluated on multiple datasets; the table in figure
[p0199-l0011] [10.0pt] 9.8 (from the BitNet paper) summarizes the zero-shot results.
[p0199-l0012] [10.0pt] The graphs and table in figures 9.7 and 9.8 show that BitNet’s average performance
[p0199-l0013] [10.0pt] (accuracy and perplexity) is slightly lower than the FP16 Transformer baseline, but it’s
[p0199-l0014] [10.0pt] much better than any other PTQ scenario.

[p0200-l0001] [9.0pt] 179
[p0200-l0002] [9.0pt] BitNet and Python
[p0200-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 9.8  Zero-shot results for BitNet and a baseline Transformer (FP16), plus results after applying
[p0200-l0004] [8.0pt] various quantization techniques
[p0200-l0005] [12.5pt] 9.4
[p0200-l0006] [12.5pt] BitNet and Python
[p0200-l0007] [10.0pt] The BitNet framework is based on llama.cpp (introduced in chapter 6), and its core
[p0200-l0008] [10.0pt] is implemented in C++. It provides optimized kernels for fast, energy-efficient, lossless
[p0200-l0009] [10.0pt] inference for 1-bit models on CPUs. It doesn’t yet support GPUs, but that’s planned.
[p0200-l0010] [10.0pt] You can install BitNet from source; follow the instructions for your OS in the official
[p0200-l0011] [10.0pt] Microsoft GitHub repository (https://github.com/microsoft/BitNet).
[p0200-l0012] [10.0pt] BitNet also provides Python bindings, so you can run inference in Python on BitNet-­
[p0200-l0013] [10.0pt] quantized models hosted on the Hugging Face Hub. The main Python script, run_
[p0200-l0014] [10.0pt] inference.py, uses the following syntax:
[p0200-l0015] [8.0pt] python run_inference.py -m models/
[p0200-l0016] [10.0pt] ➥Falcon3-7B-Instruct-1.58bit/ggml-model-i2_s.gguf -p "You are a helpful
[p0200-l0017] [10.0pt] ➥assistant" -cnv
[p0200-l0018] [10.0pt] In its basic form, it takes as arguments the ID of the target model in the Hugging Face
[p0200-l0019] [10.0pt] Hub, a prompt, and a flag to enable or disable chat mode (valid for instructed models
[p0200-l0020] [10.0pt] only). You can also pass other arguments to set the temperature, the maximum num­
[p0200-l0021] [10.0pt] ber of tokens to generate, the number of threads to use, and the prompt context size.
[p0200-l0022] [10.0pt] At the time of writing, BitNet supports its native models (0.7B and 3.3B parameters)
[p0200-l0023] [10.0pt] and the Llama and Falcon families. If you’d rather not use C++ and port pretrained
[p0200-l0024] [10.0pt] models yourself, you can use a full Python alternative: a PyTorch port with CUDA sup­
[p0200-l0025] [10.0pt] port. The source code is available on GitHub: https://github.com/kyegomez/BitNet.
[p0200-l0026] [10.0pt] It’s also available on PyPI and can be installed from there:
[p0200-l0027] [8.0pt] pip install bitnet

=== PDF page 201 / printed label 180 ===
[p0201-l0001] [9.0pt] 180
[p0201-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 9  Advanced quantization techniques
[p0201-l0003] [10.0pt] This package provides PyTorch implementations of BitLinear, the BitNet Transformer,
[p0201-l0004] [10.0pt] and BitNet Attention and FeedForward.
[p0201-l0005] [10.0pt] With this API, you can create a simple BitNet Transformer as follows:
[p0201-l0006] [8.0pt] from bitnet import BitNetTransformer
[p0201-l0007] [8.0pt] bitnet = BitNetTransformer(
[p0201-l0008] [8.0pt]     num_tokens=20000,
[p0201-l0009] [8.0pt]     dim=1024,
[p0201-l0010] [8.0pt]     depth=6,
[p0201-l0011] [8.0pt]     heads=8,
[p0201-l0012] [8.0pt]     ff_mult=4,
[p0201-l0013] [8.0pt] )
[p0201-l0014] [10.0pt] We use the BitNetTransformer class and specify the number of unique input tokens,
[p0201-l0015] [10.0pt] the embedding dimension, the number of layers and attention heads, and the feed-­
[p0201-l0016] [10.0pt] forward hidden-dimension multiplier. The resulting model architecture follows:
[p0201-l0017] [8.0pt] BitNetTransformer(
[p0201-l0018] [8.0pt]   (emb): Embedding(20000, 1024)
[p0201-l0019] [8.0pt]   (transformer): Transformer(
[p0201-l0020] [8.0pt]     (layers): ModuleList(
[p0201-l0021] [8.0pt]       (0-5): 6 x BitMGQA(
[p0201-l0022] [8.0pt]         (q_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=1024, bias=True)
[p0201-l0023] [8.0pt]         (k_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=512, bias=True)
[p0201-l0024] [8.0pt]         (v_proj): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=512, bias=True)
[p0201-l0025] [8.0pt]         (norm): LayerNorm((512,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
[p0201-l0026] [8.0pt]         (out_proj): BitLinear(in_features=512, out_features=1024, bias=True)
[p0201-l0027] [8.0pt]       )
[p0201-l0028] [8.0pt]     )
[p0201-l0029] [8.0pt]     (ffn_layers): ModuleList(
[p0201-l0030] [8.0pt]       (0-5): 6 x BitFeedForward(
[p0201-l0031] [8.0pt]         (ff): Sequential(
[p0201-l0032] [8.0pt]           (0): Sequential(
[p0201-l0033] [8.0pt]             (0): BitLinear(in_features=1024, out_features=4096, bias=True)
[p0201-l0034] [8.0pt]             (1): SiLU()
[p0201-l0035] [8.0pt]           )
[p0201-l0036] [8.0pt]           (1): LayerNorm((4096,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
[p0201-l0037] [8.0pt]           (2): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
[p0201-l0038] [8.0pt]           (3): BitLinear(in_features=4096, out_features=1024, bias=True)
[p0201-l0039] [8.0pt]         )
[p0201-l0040] [8.0pt]       )
[p0201-l0041] [8.0pt]     )
[p0201-l0042] [8.0pt]   )
[p0201-l0043] [8.0pt]   (to_logits): Sequential(
[p0201-l0044] [8.0pt]     (0): RMSNorm()
[p0201-l0045] [8.0pt]     (1): Linear(in_features=1024, out_features=20000, bias=True)
[p0201-l0046] [8.0pt]   )
[p0201-l0047] [8.0pt] )
[p0201-l0048] [10.0pt] We can easily identify all the PyTorch implementations provided by this package.
[p0201-l0049] [10.0pt] This package integrates with the Hugging Face Transformers library and supports

[p0202-l0027] [8.0pt]           (c_proj): Conv1D()
[p0202-l0028] [8.0pt]           (attn_dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
[p0202-l0029] [8.0pt]           (resid_dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
[p0202-l0030] [8.0pt]         )
[p0202-l0031] [8.0pt]         (ln_2): LayerNorm((1280,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
[p0202-l0032] [8.0pt]         (mlp): GPT2MLP(

[p0202-l0036] [8.0pt]           (dropout): Dropout(p=0.1, inplace=False)
[p0202-l0037] [8.0pt]         )
[p0202-l0038] [8.0pt]       )
[p0202-l0039] [8.0pt]     )
[p0202-l0040] [8.0pt]     (ln_f): LayerNorm((1280,), eps=1e-05, elementwise_affine=True)
[p0202-l0041] [8.0pt]   )
[p0202-l0042] [8.0pt]   (lm_head): BitLinear(in_features=1280, out_features=50257, bias=False)

[p0203-l0016] [10.0pt] The Python BitNet package also provides a drop-in replacement for PyTorch models:
[p0203-l0017] [8.0pt] import torch

[p0203-l0026] [10.0pt] In the preceding example, all the PyTorch linear layers have been replaced with BitNet

[p0203-l0028] [10.0pt] It is also possible to run inference with existing PyTorch checkpoints:
[p0203-l0029] [8.0pt] from bitnet import BitNetInference

[p0203-l0032] [8.0pt] output_str = bitnet.generate("The dog jumped over the ", 512)
[p0203-l0033] [10.0pt] BitNet could be a viable alternative to other quantization strategies when there are
[p0203-l0034] [10.0pt] computational or sustainability constraints.
[p0203-l0035] [10.0pt] This concludes our look at advanced model-quantization techniques. For many pro­
[p0203-l0036] [10.0pt] duction use cases with local small language models, traditional quantization methods
[p0203-l0037] [10.0pt] are a good fit. But for niche tasks involving more complex, unstructured content, you
[p0203-l0038] [10.0pt] may want to use one of these advanced strategies.

=== PDF page 204 / printed label 183 ===
[p0204-l0001] [9.0pt] 183
[p0204-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0204-l0003] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0204-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ FlexGen distributes model weights, activations, and the attention cache across
[p0204-l0005] [10.0pt] the GPU, CPU, and disk, enabling large-model inference on limited hardware.
[p0204-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ FlexGen uses linear programming to find efficient patterns for storing and
[p0204-l0007] [10.0pt] accessing tensors across different storage types.
[p0204-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ FlexGen compresses weights and the attention cache to 4 bits, increasing
[p0204-l0009] [10.0pt] throughput with minimal accuracy loss.
[p0204-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ In FlexGen, the Policy class sets offloading percentages and compression for
[p0204-l0011] [10.0pt] weights, cache, and activations.
[p0204-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ FlexGen prioritizes throughput over latency, making it best for batch processing
[p0204-l0013] [10.0pt] with millions of tokens.
[p0204-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ SmoothQuant addresses activation outliers in large language models by shifting
[p0204-l0015] [10.0pt] the hard part of quantization from activations to weights.
[p0204-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ SmoothQuant uses mathematical transformations to smooth activation magni­
[p0204-l0017] [10.0pt] tudes across channels before quantization.
[p0204-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Models larger than 6 to 7 billion parameters develop systematic activation outli­
[p0204-l0019] [10.0pt] ers that degrade quantization performance.
[p0204-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ SmoothQuant preserves accuracy when 8-bit quantizing weights and activations
[p0204-l0021] [10.0pt] in large models.
[p0204-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ SmoothQuant replaces standard linear layers to enable 8-bit weight and activa­
[p0204-l0023] [10.0pt] tion quantization.
[p0204-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ BitNet introduces BitLinear components that replace traditional linear layers
[p0204-l0025] [10.0pt] with 1-bit weights.
[p0204-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ BitNet keeps optimizer states and gradients in high precision while using 1-bit
[p0204-l0027] [10.0pt] weights in its attention layers.
[p0204-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ BitLinear components cut computational costs while preserving precision for
[p0204-l0029] [10.0pt] input/output embeddings.
[p0204-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ BitNet trains more stably and converges more reliably than traditional FP16
[p0204-l0031] [10.0pt] transformers at high learning rates.
[p0204-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ BitNet achieves competitive performance while using far less memory and
[p0204-l0033] [10.0pt] energy than 8-bit quantization.
[p0204-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Python BitNet implementations offer PyTorch-compatible replacements for lin­
[p0204-l0035] [10.0pt] ear layers in existing models.
