[p0205-l0001] [30.0pt] Profiling insights
[p0205-l0002] [225.0pt] 10
[p0205-l0003] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0205-l0004] [9.8pt] ¡ Profiling ONNX ported models
[p0205-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ Transforming raw ONNX profiling data into
[p0205-l0006] [9.8pt] insights
[p0205-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Optimizing ONNX graphs for LLMs
[p0205-l0008] [10.0pt] Chapter 5 introduced the ONNX format and ONNX Runtime capabilities, first in
[p0205-l0009] [10.0pt] general and then for LLMs. Chapter 6 covered several approaches, including 8-bit
[p0205-l0010] [10.0pt] quantization through the ONNX API. This chapter will explore other ONNX fea­
[p0205-l0011] [10.0pt] tures, such as profiling the performance of LLMs ported to ONNX format and tools
[p0205-l0012] [10.0pt] you can use to extract useful insights from the profiling data.
[p0205-l0013] [12.5pt] 10.1	 Profiling ONNX-ported LLMs
[p0205-l0014] [10.0pt] The ONNX Runtime (ORT) delivers high performance for running machine learn­
[p0205-l0015] [10.0pt] ing (ML) and deep learning (DL) models across a wide range of hardware. Still, to
[p0205-l0016] [10.0pt] meet specific key performance indicators (KPIs) for latency, throughput, and mem­
[p0205-l0017] [10.0pt] ory use, you may need additional model optimizations and runtime configuration
[p0205-l0018] [10.0pt] for a given use case, model, and device.
[p0205-l0019] [9.0pt] 184

=== PDF page 206 / printed label 185 ===
[p0206-l0001] [9.0pt] 185
[p0206-l0002] [9.0pt] Profiling ONNX-ported LLMs
[p0206-l0003] [10.0pt] The ORT supports in-code performance profiling. It’s disabled by default, but you
[p0206-l0004] [10.0pt] can enable it during debugging by setting the enable_profiling option to True in an
[p0206-l0005] [10.0pt] ORT inference session:
[p0206-l0006] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0206-l0007] [8.0pt] sess_options = rt.SessionOptions()
[p0206-l0008] [8.0pt] sess_options.enable_profiling = True
[p0206-l0009] [10.0pt] At runtime, ORT generates a JSON file with performance data such as threading and
[p0206-l0010] [10.0pt] per-operator latency.
[p0206-l0011] [10.0pt] Let’s take a look at what’s in this profiling file, starting with a simple model and then
[p0206-l0012] [10.0pt] moving on to LLMs. We’ll reuse the linear regression example from section 5.2:
[p0206-l0013] [8.0pt] from onnx import TensorProto
[p0206-l0014] [8.0pt] from onnx.helper import (
[p0206-l0015] [8.0pt]     make_model, make_node, make_graph,
[p0206-l0016] [8.0pt]     make_tensor_value_info)
[p0206-l0017] [8.0pt] from onnx.checker import check_model
[p0206-l0018] [8.0pt] X = make_tensor_value_info('X', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
[p0206-l0019] [8.0pt] A = make_tensor_value_info('A', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
[p0206-l0020] [8.0pt] B = make_tensor_value_info('B', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None, None])
[p0206-l0021] [8.0pt] Y = make_tensor_value_info('Y', TensorProto.FLOAT, [None])
[p0206-l0022] [8.0pt] node1 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A'], ['XA'])
[p0206-l0023] [8.0pt] node2 = make_node('Add', ['XA', 'B'], ['Y'])
[p0206-l0024] [8.0pt] graph = make_graph([node1, node2], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
[p0206-l0025] [8.0pt] onnx_model = make_model(graph)
[p0206-l0026] [8.0pt] check_model(onnx_model)
[p0206-l0027] [10.0pt] To run inference with this model, we need to create an inference session and specify
[p0206-l0028] [10.0pt] the execution provider (CPU; no hardware acceleration needed):
[p0206-l0029] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime import InferenceSession
[p0206-l0030] [8.0pt] sess = InferenceSession(onnx_model.SerializeToString(),
[p0206-l0031] [8.0pt]                         providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
[p0206-l0032] [10.0pt] We’ll test it with three input arrays of random values:
[p0206-l0033] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0206-l0034] [8.0pt] res = sess.run(None, {
[p0206-l0035] [8.0pt]     'X': np.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32),
[p0206-l0036] [8.0pt]     'A': nup.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32),
[p0206-l0037] [8.0pt]     'B': np.random.randn(2, 2).astype(np.float32)
[p0206-l0038] [8.0pt]   }
[p0206-l0039] [8.0pt] )

=== PDF page 207 / printed label 186 ===
[p0207-l0001] [9.0pt] 186
[p0207-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 10  Profiling insights
[p0207-l0003] [10.0pt] To measure this model’s performance (and spot areas for improvement), we’ll run
[p0207-l0004] [10.0pt] inference with profiling enabled. There are no other code changes:
[p0207-l0005] [8.0pt] import onnxruntime as rt
[p0207-l0006] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime import InferenceSession
[p0207-l0007] [8.0pt] sess_options = rt.SessionOptions()
[p0207-l0008] [8.0pt] sess_options.enable_profiling = True
[p0207-l0009] [8.0pt] sess = InferenceSession(onnx_model.SerializeToString(),
[p0207-l0010] [8.0pt]                         sess_options,
[p0207-l0011] [8.0pt]                         providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"])
[p0207-l0012] [10.0pt] To access the generated profiling data, we need to use the end_profiling method:
[p0207-l0013] [8.0pt] prof = sess.end_profiling()
[p0207-l0014] [10.0pt] This method returns the name of the generated JSON file, which follows the
[p0207-l0015] [10.0pt] onnxruntime­_­profile__YYYY-MM-DD_hh-mm-ss.json naming convention. The file con­
[p0207-l0016] [10.0pt] tents look like this:
[p0207-l0017] [8.0pt] [
[p0207-l0018] [8.0pt] {"cat" : "Session","pid" :21460,"tid" :14412,"dur" :36164,"ts" :7,
[p0207-l0019] [8.0pt] "ph" : "X","name" :"model_loading_array","args" : {}},
[p0207-l0020] [8.0pt] {"cat" : "Session","pid" :21460,"tid" :14412,"dur" :1430,"ts" :36425,
[p0207-l0021] [8.0pt] "ph" : "X","name" :"session_initialization","args" : {}},
[p0207-l0022] [8.0pt] {"cat" : "Node","pid" :21460,"tid" :14412,"dur" :2,"ts" :34744604,
[p0207-l0023] [8.0pt] "ph" : "X","name" :"MatMul_0_fence_before","args" : {"op_name" : "MatMul"}},

[p0208-l0008] [10.0pt] The JSON profiling file contains raw data for an ONNX inference session, broken
[p0208-l0009] [10.0pt] down by operator and execution provider. On its own, this data provides little insight,
[p0208-l0010] [10.0pt] so you need to aggregate and transform it to understand the model’s performance.
[p0208-l0011] [10.0pt] ONNX Runtime includes Ort_perf_view, which reads this profiling JSON file, renders
[p0208-l0012] [10.0pt] summarized statistics as treemaps, and computes latency per ONNX operator (for
[p0208-l0013] [10.0pt] both CPU and GPU). For small models, such as the linear regressor in this example,
[p0208-l0014] [10.0pt] the view is clean (as shown in figure 10.1) because we use only two ONNX operators.
[p0208-l0015] [8.0pt] Figure 10.1  Ort_perf_view rendering of performance stats for inference on a linear regression ONNX model
[p0208-l0016] [10.0pt] The Ort_perf_view visualizations show one square per operator, labeled with the oper­
[p0208-l0017] [10.0pt] ator name and call count for the profiled run. The box size reflects the proportion
[p0208-l0018] [10.0pt] of operator calls. For larger models, this view is less useful for performance analysis,
[p0208-l0019] [10.0pt] though it still provides a 10,000-foot overview of aggregated operator calls (see figure
[p0208-l0020] [10.0pt] 10.2).
[p0208-l0021] [10.0pt] In figure 10.2, you can see that there are thousands of calls for each operator in the
[p0208-l0022] [10.0pt] ONNX graph for the model under test. Clicking an operator’s box expands that section
[p0208-l0023] [10.0pt] to show details for each call (input and output values and duration in microseconds), as
[p0208-l0024] [10.0pt] shown in figure 10.3.
[p0208-l0025] [10.0pt] This visualization isn’t very helpful; it just shows raw data without insights. Let’s
[p0208-l0026] [10.0pt] switch to something better.

=== PDF page 209 / printed label 188 ===
[p0209-l0001] [9.0pt] 188
[p0209-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 10  Profiling insights
[p0209-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 10.2  Ort_perf_view output showing performance stats for inference run on a large ONNX model
[p0209-l0004] [8.0pt] Figure 10.3  Ort_perf_view expanded view of all Sqrt operator calls during inference for the model under test
[p0209-l0005] [12.5pt] 10.2	 Transforming raw ONNX profiling data into insights
[p0209-l0006] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ll look at a custom implementation that extracts insights from raw
[p0209-l0007] [10.0pt] ONNX profiling data and presents them in a user-friendly way. To keep this example
[p0209-l0008] [10.0pt] simple and easy to follow, we’ll use a linear regression model trained in scikit-learn and
[p0209-l0009] [10.0pt] then converted to ONNX format. The same profiling process, data transformation,
[p0209-l0010] [10.0pt] and visualization code apply to any ONNX-converted model, including LLMs.

[p0210-l0002] [9.0pt] Transforming raw ONNX profiling data into insights
[p0210-l0003] [10.0pt] We’ll use scikit-learn’s diabetes dataset for the training and test sets. It contains 442
[p0210-l0004] [10.0pt] samples with 10 features each (age, sex, body mass index, average blood pressure, and
[p0210-l0005] [10.0pt] six blood serum measurements). The target variable is a quantitative measure of disease
[p0210-l0006] [10.0pt] progression one year after the baseline.
[p0210-l0007] [10.0pt] Let’s download the dataset:
[p0210-l0008] [8.0pt] from sklearn.datasets import load_diabetes
[p0210-l0009] [8.0pt] data = load_diabetes()
[p0210-l0010] [10.0pt] Next, split the data into training and test sets:
[p0210-l0011] [8.0pt] from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
[p0210-l0012] [8.0pt] X, y = data.data, data.target
[p0210-l0013] [8.0pt] X_train, X_test, y_train, __ = train_test_split(X, y, random_state=11)
[p0210-l0014] [10.0pt] We can now train the model using the scikit-learn API:
[p0210-l0015] [8.0pt] from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
[p0210-l0016] [8.0pt] clr = LinearRegression()
[p0210-l0017] [8.0pt] clr.fit(X_train, y_train)
[p0210-l0018] [10.0pt] We can convert the trained model to ONNX format using the sklearn-onnx package
[p0210-l0019] [10.0pt] (https://github.com/onnx/sklearn-onnx):
[p0210-l0020] [8.0pt] from skl2onnx import to_onnx
[p0210-l0021] [8.0pt] model_def = to_onnx(clr, X_train)
[p0210-l0022] [10.0pt] The converted model graph will look like this:

[p0212-l0026] [10.0pt] We can profile this converted model by creating an inference session with profiling
[p0212-l0027] [10.0pt] enabled, as explained in section 9.1:
[p0212-l0028] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime import InferenceSession, SessionOptions
[p0212-l0029] [8.0pt] so = SessionOptions()
[p0212-l0030] [8.0pt] so.enable_profiling = True
[p0212-l0031] [8.0pt] sess = InferenceSession(model_def.SerializeToString(), so)
[p0212-l0032] [10.0pt] We’ll run inference over the test set (111 samples) and stop profiling at the end:
[p0212-l0033] [8.0pt] sess.run(None, {'X': X_test})
[p0212-l0034] [8.0pt] prof = sess.end_profiling()
[p0212-l0035] [10.0pt] The raw profiling data can now be loaded from the JSON file:
[p0212-l0036] [8.0pt] import json
[p0212-l0037] [8.0pt] with open(prof, "r") as f:
[p0212-l0038] [8.0pt]     js = json.load(f)
[p0212-l0039] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll create a pandas DataFrame from them:
[p0212-l0040] [8.0pt] from mlprodict.onnxrt.ops_whole.session import OnnxWholeSession
[p0212-l0041] [8.0pt] df = pd.DataFrame(OnnxWholeSession.process_profiling(js))

[p0213-l0003] [10.0pt] We used the OnnxWholeSession class from the mlprodict Python library (https://
[p0213-l0004] [10.0pt] github.com/sdpython/mlprodict/) to convert the JSON content into a cleaner tabu­
[p0213-l0005] [10.0pt] lar format (see figure 10.4).
[p0213-l0006] [8.0pt] Figure 10.4  The head rows of the profiling data for the regression model example in tabular format
[p0213-l0007] [10.0pt] Starting with this cleaner data representation, it’s easier to build visualizations and
[p0213-l0008] [10.0pt] extract insights. We’ll use the Plotly Express Python charting library (https://plotly
[p0213-l0009] [10.0pt] .com/python/plotly-express/). For performance analysis, we want to compare the
[p0213-l0010] [10.0pt] total duration for each ONNX operator in the model graph. To do that, we’ll first
[p0213-l0011] [10.0pt] group operators by type and calculate the total duration for each one:
[p0213-l0012] [8.0pt] gr_dur = df[['dur', "args_op_name"]].groupby("args_op_name")
[p0213-l0013] [10.0pt] ➥.sum().sort_values('dur')
[p0213-l0014] [10.0pt] This data can then be displayed in a horizontal bar chart, where the x-axis is total dura­
[p0213-l0015] [10.0pt] tion (in milliseconds), and the y-axis is the ONNX operator type (see figure 10.5):
[p0213-l0016] [8.0pt] fig = px.bar(gr_dur, x='dur',
[p0213-l0017] [8.0pt]              labels={
[p0213-l0018] [8.0pt]                      "dur": "Duration (ms)",
[p0213-l0019] [8.0pt]                      "args_op_name": "Operation type",
[p0213-l0020] [8.0pt]                  },
[p0213-l0021] [8.0pt]              title='Duration')
[p0213-l0022] [8.0pt] fig.show()

[p0214-l0018] [10.0pt] This visualization quickly shows which operators take the most time during a model’s
[p0214-l0019] [10.0pt] inference. Another useful metric is how often each operator is called. To visualize that,
[p0214-l0020] [10.0pt] first aggregate by operator type, and then count occurrences for each type, ordering by
[p0214-l0021] [10.0pt] duration so the chart matches the total-duration view:
[p0214-l0022] [8.0pt] gr_n = df[['dur', "args_op_name"]].groupby("args_op_name")
[p0214-l0023] [10.0pt] ➥.count().sort_values('dur')
[p0214-l0024] [8.0pt] gr_n = gr_n.loc[gr_dur.index, :]
[p0214-l0025] [10.0pt] This information can then be shown in a horizontal bar chart, where the x-axis is the
[p0214-l0026] [10.0pt] count of occurrences for a given operator, and the y-axis is the ONNX operator type
[p0214-l0027] [10.0pt] (see figure 10.6):
[p0214-l0028] [8.0pt] fig = px.bar(gr_n, x='dur',
[p0214-l0029] [8.0pt]              labels={
[p0214-l0030] [8.0pt]                      "dur": "Op count",
[p0214-l0031] [8.0pt]                      "args_op_name": "Operation type",
[p0214-l0032] [8.0pt]                  },
[p0214-l0033] [8.0pt]              title='Occurrences')
[p0214-l0034] [8.0pt] fig.show()
[p0214-l0035] [10.0pt] For a more complete performance analysis, it’s useful to show not only how often each

[p0214-l0037] [10.0pt] we’ll first calculate each operator’s percentage of the total inference time:
[p0214-l0038] [8.0pt] gr_dur /= gr_dur['dur'].sum()

[p0215-l0027] [10.0pt] For LLMs, we can reuse the same data-cleaning, aggregation, and visualization code
[p0215-l0028] [10.0pt] unchanged; a companion Colab notebook is provided. The notebook covers converting
[p0215-l0029] [10.0pt] the GPT-2 small model to ONNX, running inline profiling, and analyzing and visualiz­
[p0215-l0030] [10.0pt] ing the profiling data. We won’t repeat the code for loading the model and tokenizer
[p0215-l0031] [10.0pt] or converting to ONNX because we covered them in earlier chapters. Instead, we’ll
[p0215-l0032] [10.0pt] just look at the charts produced by profiling the ONNX GPT-2 small model (figures
[p0215-l0033] [10.0pt] 10.8–10.10).
[p0215-l0034] [10.0pt] In figure 10.8, the x-axis shows duration (ms), and the y-axis lists the ONNX opera­
[p0215-l0035] [10.0pt] tion types in the profiled run.
[p0215-l0036] [10.0pt] In figure 10.9, the x-axis shows how many times each ONNX operator was called, and
[p0215-l0037] [10.0pt] the y-axis lists the operator types used in the profiled run.

[p0215-l0039] [10.0pt] lists the ONNX operation types in the profiled run.

[p0218-l0001] [9.0pt] 197
[p0218-l0002] [9.0pt] Optimization of ONNX graphs for LLMs
[p0218-l0003] [12.5pt] 10.3	 Optimization of ONNX graphs for LLMs
[p0218-l0004] [10.0pt] The ORT for Python can evaluate models converted to ONNX—not only the full
[p0218-l0005] [10.0pt] graph, but also individual nodes (including custom ones). It can also capture inter­
[p0218-l0006] [10.0pt] mediate results within a graph or node. Converting to a new model version or moving
[p0218-l0007] [10.0pt] from a Python ML/DL framework to an ONNX graph can introduce inefficiencies,
[p0218-l0008] [10.0pt] and evaluating one or more nodes can help you find and fix them.
[p0218-l0009] [10.0pt] Let’s first consider the simple linear regression example model from section 10.1. To
[p0218-l0010] [10.0pt] evaluate the model’s full ONNX graph, we can use ONNX’s ReferenceEvaluator class:
[p0218-l0011] [8.0pt] from onnx.reference import ReferenceEvaluator
[p0218-l0012] [8.0pt] sess = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_model)
[p0218-l0013] [10.0pt] We’ll prepare the model’s input arrays as usual:
[p0218-l0014] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0218-l0015] [8.0pt] x = np.random.randn(4, 2).astype(np.float32)
[p0218-l0016] [8.0pt] a = np.random.randn(2, 1).astype(np.float32)
[p0218-l0017] [8.0pt] b = np.random.randn(1, 1).astype(np.float32)
[p0218-l0018] [8.0pt] feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a, 'B': b}
[p0218-l0019] [10.0pt] Then we’ll run the model using the previously created ReferenceEvaluator instance:
[p0218-l0020] [8.0pt] evaluation = sess.run(None, feeds)
[p0218-l0021] [10.0pt] We can also evaluate a single node in the graph. For the MatMul node in our regression
[p0218-l0022] [10.0pt] model, do the following:
[p0218-l0023] [8.0pt] node_sess = ReferenceEvaluator(node1)
[p0218-l0024] [8.0pt] feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a}
[p0218-l0025] [8.0pt] node_evaluation = node_sess.run(None, feeds)
[p0218-l0026] [10.0pt] We can enable step-to-step evaluation by setting the verbose argument on a Reference­
[p0218-l0027] [10.0pt] Evaluator instance to different levels of verbosity:
[p0218-l0028] [8.0pt] sess = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_model, verbose=verbose)
[p0218-l0029] [10.0pt] The verbose argument accepts integer values from 1 (the default, less verbose) to 4
[p0218-l0030] [10.0pt] (the most verbose, step-by-step evaluation). For our linear regression model, the fol­
[p0218-l0031] [10.0pt] lowing output displays the different verbosity levels:
[p0218-l0032] [8.0pt] ------ verbose=1
[p0218-l0033] [8.0pt] [array([[0.9837985],
[p0218-l0034] [8.0pt]        [1.126987 ],
[p0218-l0035] [8.0pt]        [0.8049259],
[p0218-l0036] [8.0pt]        [1.6867123]], dtype=float32)]

[p0219-l0038] [10.0pt] As the previous code shows, verbosity level 1 displays only the model’s output, level 2
[p0219-l0039] [10.0pt] also shows the sequence of operations between inputs, level 3 also includes input values
[p0219-l0040] [10.0pt] and intermediate outputs, and level 4 includes the inputs to the intermediate steps.
[p0219-l0041] [10.0pt] The linear regression in this example follows this formula:
[p0219-l0042] [8.0pt] y = Add(MatMul(X, A), B)
[p0219-l0043] [10.0pt] Another way to implement linear regression is to use a similar formula, adding the
[p0219-l0044] [10.0pt] identity matrix to matrix A:
[p0219-l0045] [8.0pt] y = Add(MatMul(X, Add(A, I)), B)

=== PDF page 220 / printed label 199 ===
[p0220-l0001] [9.0pt] 199
[p0220-l0002] [9.0pt] Optimization of ONNX graphs for LLMs
[p0220-l0003] [10.0pt] To implement it, you’ll need to modify the original code that builds the model with
[p0220-l0004] [10.0pt] ONNX operators:
[p0220-l0005] [8.0pt] node0 = make_node('EyeLike', ['A'], ['Eye'])
[p0220-l0006] [8.0pt] node1 = make_node('Add', ['A', 'Eye'], ['A1'])
[p0220-l0007] [8.0pt] node2 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A1'], ['XA1'])
[p0220-l0008] [8.0pt] node3 = make_node('Add', ['XA1', 'B'], ['Y'])
[p0220-l0009] [8.0pt] graph = make_graph([node0, node1, node2, node3], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
[p0220-l0010] [10.0pt] In this example, we use the EyeLike operator, ONNX’s implementation of the identity
[p0220-l0011] [10.0pt] matrix (a square matrix with ones on the main diagonal and zeros elsewhere), and
[p0220-l0012] [10.0pt] combine the nodes to build the final graph for the updated linear regression formula.
[p0220-l0013] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier in this section, you can also evaluate custom ONNX nodes. For
[p0220-l0014] [10.0pt] example, in the following code, we’ll create a custom node that combines the EyeLike
[p0220-l0015] [10.0pt] and Add operators and then see whether the model runs more efficiently:
[p0220-l0016] [8.0pt] node01 = make_node('AddEyeLike', ['A'], ['A1'], domain='combined')
[p0220-l0017] [10.0pt] We can then rebuild the graph:
[p0220-l0018] [8.0pt] node2 = make_node('MatMul', ['X', 'A1'], ['XA1'])
[p0220-l0019] [8.0pt] node3 = make_node('Add', ['XA1', 'B'], ['Y'])
[p0220-l0020] [8.0pt] graph = make_graph([node01, node2, node3], 'lr', [X, A, B], [Y])
[p0220-l0021] [10.0pt] Let’s rebuild the model and recheck it:
[p0220-l0022] [8.0pt] from onnx.helper import make_opsetid
[p0220-l0023] [8.0pt] onnx_optimized_model = make_model(graph, opset_imports=[
[p0220-l0024] [8.0pt]     make_opsetid('', 18), make_opsetid('combined', 1)
[p0220-l0025] [8.0pt] ])
[p0220-l0026] [8.0pt] check_model(onnx_optimized_model)
[p0220-l0027] [10.0pt] This kind of optimization—combining two operators into a single optimized operator
[p0220-l0028] [10.0pt] (AddEyeLike)—is called fusion. To evaluate the custom node (or a model whose graph
[p0220-l0029] [10.0pt] includes it), you must implement a custom class, because ReferenceEvaluator natively
[p0220-l0030] [10.0pt] supports only built-in ONNX operators. However, it can also accept custom operator
[p0220-l0031] [10.0pt] implementations. You can implement custom operators by extending the ONNX OpRun
[p0220-l0032] [10.0pt] class and implementing its _run method:
[p0220-l0033] [8.0pt] from onnx.reference.op_run import OpRun
[p0220-l0034] [8.0pt] class AddEyeLike(OpRun):
[p0220-l0035] [8.0pt]     op_domain = "combined"
[p0220-l0036] [8.0pt]     def _run(self, X, alpha=1.):
[p0220-l0037] [8.0pt]         assert len(X.shape) == 2

=== PDF page 221 / printed label 200 ===
[p0221-l0001] [9.0pt] 200
[p0221-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 10  Profiling insights
[p0221-l0003] [8.0pt]         assert X.shape[0] == X.shape[1]
[p0221-l0004] [8.0pt]         X = X.copy()
[p0221-l0005] [8.0pt]         ind = numpy.diag_indices(X.shape[0])
[p0221-l0006] [8.0pt]         X[ind] += alpha
[p0221-l0007] [8.0pt]         return (X,)
[p0221-l0008] [10.0pt] You can now evaluate the model as usual. The only difference is that when you create
[p0221-l0009] [10.0pt] a ReferenceEvaluator instance, you also need to pass a list of the custom node imple­
[p0221-l0010] [10.0pt] mentations included in the model’s ONNX graph:
[p0221-l0011] [8.0pt] sess = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_optimized_model, verbose=2,
[p0221-l0012] [10.0pt] ➥ new_ops=[AddEyeLike])
[p0221-l0013] [10.0pt] Evaluation for the given inputs proceeds the same way as for models without custom
[p0221-l0014] [10.0pt] operators:
[p0221-l0015] [8.0pt] x = numpy.random.randn(4, 2).astype(numpy.float32)
[p0221-l0016] [8.0pt] a = numpy.random.randn(2, 2).astype(numpy.float32) / 10
[p0221-l0017] [8.0pt] b = numpy.random.randn(1, 2).astype(numpy.float32)
[p0221-l0018] [8.0pt] feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a, 'B': b}
[p0221-l0019] [8.0pt] sess.run(None, feeds)
[p0221-l0020] [10.0pt] Before measuring any execution speedup, let’s confirm that the optimization didn’t
[p0221-l0021] [10.0pt] reduce prediction quality. We’ll evaluate both model versions (the original and the
[p0221-l0022] [10.0pt] one after fusing the two operators):
[p0221-l0023] [8.0pt] sess_original = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_model)
[p0221-l0024] [8.0pt] sess_optimized = ReferenceEvaluator(onnx_optimized_model,
[p0221-l0025] [10.0pt] ➥ new_ops=[AddEyeLike])
[p0221-l0026] [8.0pt] y_original = sess_original.run(None, feeds)[0]
[p0221-l0027] [8.0pt] y_optimized = sess_optimized.run(None, feeds)[0]
[p0221-l0028] [8.0pt] print(f"output from original model: {y_original}")
[p0221-l0029] [8.0pt] print(f"output from optimized model: {y_optimized}")
[p0221-l0030] [8.0pt] print(f"difference: {numpy.abs(y_original - y_optimized).max()}")
[p0221-l0031] [10.0pt] There is no difference:
[p0221-l0032] [8.0pt] output from original model: [[-1.3435526   0.11092019]
[p0221-l0033] [8.0pt]  [ 0.8220897   0.18847765]
[p0221-l0034] [8.0pt]  [-1.29872     0.882055  ]
[p0221-l0035] [8.0pt]  [-0.10433175 -0.30559355]]
[p0221-l0036] [8.0pt] output from optimized model: [[-1.3435526   0.11092019]
[p0221-l0037] [8.0pt]  [ 0.8220897   0.18847765]
[p0221-l0038] [8.0pt]  [-1.29872     0.882055  ]
[p0221-l0039] [8.0pt]  [-0.10433175 -0.30559355]]
[p0221-l0040] [8.0pt] difference: 0.0

=== PDF page 222 / printed label 201 ===
[p0222-l0001] [9.0pt] 201
[p0222-l0002] [9.0pt] Optimization of ONNX graphs for LLMs
[p0222-l0003] [10.0pt] Let’s now benchmark both model versions on larger matrices, timing 10,000 runs with
[p0222-l0004] [10.0pt] Python’s timeit package:
[p0222-l0005] [8.0pt] x = numpy.random.randn(4, 100).astype(numpy.float32)
[p0222-l0006] [8.0pt] a = numpy.random.randn(100, 100).astype(numpy.float32) / 10
[p0222-l0007] [8.0pt] b = numpy.random.randn(1, 100).astype(numpy.float32)
[p0222-l0008] [8.0pt] feeds = {'X': x, 'A': a, 'B': b}
[p0222-l0009] [8.0pt] import timeit
[p0222-l0010] [8.0pt] print(f"time with EyeLike+Add: {timeit.timeit(lambda:
[p0222-l0011] [10.0pt] ➥ sess_original.run(None, feeds), number=10000)}")
[p0222-l0012] [8.0pt] print(f"time with AddEyeLike: {timeit.timeit(lambda:
[p0222-l0013] [10.0pt] ➥ sess_optimized.run(None, feeds), number=10000)}")
[p0222-l0014] [10.0pt] There is a clear improvement with the optimized model:
[p0222-l0015] [8.0pt] time with EyeLike+Add: 1.1427911999999196
[p0222-l0016] [8.0pt] time with AddEyeLike: 0.8636034999999538
[p0222-l0017] [10.0pt] You can also evaluate and profile by following the directions in sections 7.1 and 7.2. I
[p0222-l0018] [10.0pt] ran the benchmarks on a PC with two Intel Core i5-7300U CPUs (2.6 GHz) and 8 GB
[p0222-l0019] [10.0pt] of RAM.
[p0222-l0020] [10.0pt] In section 5.6.1, I described ONNX Runtime (ORT) optimization levels and how
[p0222-l0021] [10.0pt] they apply to LLMs. You also saw that graph optimization can be done offline or inline,
[p0222-l0022] [10.0pt] and that ORT provides two optimization sets: basic (including the operator fusion
[p0222-l0023] [10.0pt] introduced in this section) and extended. I also introduced the built-in optimizer class
[p0222-l0024] [10.0pt] for Transformer models in the ORT API, which automates offline graph optimization
[p0222-l0025] [10.0pt] for an ONNX model (or a model converted to ONNX format). Now let’s see how the
[p0222-l0026] [10.0pt] ONNX graph for an LLM changes after optimization.
[p0222-l0027] [10.0pt] In this example, we’ll use the GPT-2 small model; the complete code is in the Colab
[p0222-l0028] [10.0pt] notebook for section 10.2. No hardware acceleration is required; all optimization con­
[p0222-l0029] [10.0pt] siderations are for CPUs only. After downloading the GPT-2 small weights and tokenizer
[p0222-l0030] [10.0pt] from the Hugging Face Hub and converting the model to ONNX, we can optimize it
[p0222-l0031] [10.0pt] offline programmatically with the ORT optimizer:
[p0222-l0032] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime.transformers import optimizer
[p0222-l0033] [8.0pt] num_layer = model.config.n_layer
[p0222-l0034] [8.0pt] num_attention_heads = model.config.n_head
[p0222-l0035] [8.0pt] hidden_size = model.config.n_embd
[p0222-l0036] [8.0pt] onnx_model_path='gpt2onnx.onnx'
[p0222-l0037] [8.0pt] onnx_optim_model_path="gpt2onnx-opt.onnx"
[p0222-l0038] [8.0pt] optimized_model = optimizer.optimize_model(onnx_model_path,
[p0222-l0039] [8.0pt]                                            model_type='gpt2',
[p0222-l0040] [8.0pt]                                            num_heads=num_attention_heads,

[p0222-l0042] [8.0pt]                                            use_gpu=False,

[p0226-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0226-l0003] [10.0pt] Analyzing the automated ONNX optimizations for LLMs is a great way to learn when
[p0226-l0004] [10.0pt] and how to apply them manually to custom models.
[p0226-l0005] [10.0pt] This chapter wraps up our exploration of the ONNX format and ORT. The next two
[p0226-l0006] [10.0pt] chapters show how you can combine these and other techniques from earlier chapters
[p0226-l0007] [10.0pt] with SLM deployment in diverse environments to make the most of available computa­
[p0226-l0008] [10.0pt] tional power without sacrificing too much quality.
[p0226-l0009] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0226-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Enable performance profiling in ONNX Runtime (ORT) by setting enable_
[p0226-l0011] [10.0pt] profiling to True in SessionOptions.
[p0226-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Raw profiling data is stored in JSON files with timing information for each oper­
[p0226-l0013] [10.0pt] ator execution.
[p0226-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ OnnxWholeSession.process_profiling converts messy JSON profiling output
[p0226-l0015] [10.0pt] into a clean, tabular DataFrame format.
[p0226-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Plotly Express can create interactive bar charts of operator duration, call counts,
[p0226-l0017] [10.0pt] and execution percentages for performance analysis.
[p0226-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ The ReferenceEvaluator class evaluates entire ONNX models or individual
[p0226-l0019] [10.0pt] nodes for debugging and optimization.
[p0226-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Verbosity levels 1 to 4 control how much step-by-step evaluation detail you see
[p0226-l0021] [10.0pt] when debugging.
[p0226-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Operator fusion combines consecutive operators into single optimized nodes to
[p0226-l0023] [10.0pt] speed execution.
[p0226-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ To evaluate custom operators, extend the OpRun class, and implement _run.
[p0226-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ The ORT optimizer automatically applies basic and extended optimizations to
[p0226-l0026] [10.0pt] transformer models.
[p0226-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Graph optimization reduces model size by removing unnecessary nodes, such as
[p0226-l0028] [10.0pt] redundant Reshape operations.
[p0226-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ Skip Layer Normalization Fusion combines bias layers, skip connections, and
[p0226-l0030] [10.0pt] layer normalizations into single operations.
[p0226-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ Fast GELU Fusion optimization is applied automatically when you specify the
[p0226-l0032] [10.0pt] model’s architecture type.
[p0226-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ The Netron tool lets you visually inspect ONNX graphs to see which optimiza­
[p0226-l0034] [10.0pt] tions were applied.
[p0226-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Model evaluation ensures optimizations don’t hurt prediction quality or
[p0226-l0036] [10.0pt] accuracy.
[p0226-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ Basic optimizations include constant folding, eliminating redundant nodes, and
[p0226-l0038] [10.0pt] semantics-preserving fusions.
[p0226-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Extended optimizations perform complex node fusions specific to CPU, CUDA,
[p0226-l0040] [10.0pt] or ROCm execution providers.

[p0227-l0001] [30.0pt] Deployment
[p0227-l0002] [30.0pt] and serving
[p0227-l0003] [225.0pt] 11
[p0227-l0004] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0227-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ SLM serving and inference with vLLM
[p0227-l0006] [9.8pt] ¡ SLM serving with FastAPI
[p0227-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ SLM deployment and serving on devices with
[p0227-l0008] [9.8pt] MLC LLM
[p0227-l0009] [9.8pt] ¡ Options for SLM deployment and inference on
[p0227-l0010] [9.8pt] Android devices
[p0227-l0011] [10.0pt] It’s time to look at some of the most common environments and tools for deploying
[p0227-l0012] [10.0pt] and serving small, customized language models. We won’t cover them all: the closer
[p0227-l0013] [10.0pt] you get to local or edge deployments, the more hardware options and frameworks
[p0227-l0014] [10.0pt] you’ll encounter. I’ve focused on the options that are currently most popular across
[p0227-l0015] [10.0pt] operating systems and hardware combinations.
[p0227-l0016] [12.5pt] 11.1	 vLLM
[p0227-l0017] [10.0pt] vLLM is an open source library for LLM serving and inference (https://github.com/
[p0227-l0018] [10.0pt] vllm-project/vllm). vLLM was introduced in the September 2023 paper “Efficient
[p0227-l0019] [10.0pt] Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention”
[p0227-l0020] [9.0pt] 206

=== PDF page 228 / printed label 207 ===
[p0228-l0001] [9.0pt] 207
[p0228-l0002] [9.0pt] vLLM
[p0228-l0003] [10.0pt] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06180). The paper introduces PagedAttention, an atten­
[p0228-l0004] [10.0pt] tion algorithm that improves memory management for LLMs by addressing issues
[p0228-l0005] [10.0pt] of memory fragmentation and redundancy in the key–value (KV) cache. It does this
[p0228-l0006] [10.0pt] by storing KV-cache blocks noncontiguously, which increases memory flexibility and
[p0228-l0007] [10.0pt] reduces fragmentation—key to improving throughput and batch size in LLM serving
[p0228-l0008] [10.0pt] systems. vLLM uses a centralized scheduler and KV-cache manager, similar to a virtual
[p0228-l0009] [10.0pt] memory system, and emphasizes batching during autoregressive generation to opti­
[p0228-l0010] [10.0pt] mize throughput. The paper critiques existing LLM serving systems for not meeting
[p0228-l0011] [10.0pt] LLM-specific needs, and it highlights vLLM’s dynamic memory allocation and block
[p0228-l0012] [10.0pt] management as key improvements for efficient memory use in complex applications.
[p0228-l0013] [10.0pt] Overall, it is the first effort to focus on serving LLMs specifically, rather than ML mod­
[p0228-l0014] [10.0pt] els in general.
[p0228-l0015] [10.0pt] The paper notes several inefficiencies and challenges in how earlier systems man­
[p0228-l0016] [10.0pt] aged memory:
[p0228-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ Contiguous memory allocation—Most systems store a request’s KV cache in contig­
[p0228-l0018] [10.0pt] uous memory space. This can cause significant internal and external fragmen­
[p0228-l0019] [10.0pt] tation. Internal fragmentation occurs when the actual request is shorter than its
[p0228-l0020] [10.0pt] reserved maximum length, leaving unused space. External fragmentation occurs
[p0228-l0021] [10.0pt] when different requests reserve different block sizes, leaving gaps that other
[p0228-l0022] [10.0pt] requests can’t use.
[p0228-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Preallocation of memory—Existing systems preallocate memory for a request
[p0228-l0024] [10.0pt] based on its maximum possible sequence length, regardless of the actual input
[p0228-l0025] [10.0pt] or output length. This static allocation wastes memory because reserved space
[p0228-l0026] [10.0pt] for future tokens and internal fragmentation goes unused until the request
[p0228-l0027] [10.0pt] completes.
[p0228-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Inefficient memory sharing—Advanced decoding algorithms such as parallel sam­
[p0228-l0029] [10.0pt] pling and beam search generate multiple outputs per request, but existing sys­
[p0228-l0030] [10.0pt] tems can’t share memory because each sequence’s KV cache is stored in its own
[p0228-l0031] [10.0pt] contiguous space.
[p0228-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Scheduling and preemption—Existing systems struggle to schedule and preempt
[p0228-l0033] [10.0pt] requests because input and output lengths vary. They must decide when to delete
[p0228-l0034] [10.0pt] or swap some requests’ KV caches from GPU memory to make room for new
[p0228-l0035] [10.0pt] requests or continued generation for existing prompts.
[p0228-l0036] [10.0pt] vLLM addresses the memory-management inefficiencies because it limits batch size
[p0228-l0037] [10.0pt] and throughput in LLM serving systems.
[p0228-l0038] [10.0pt] This paper led to the open source vLLM project, released under the Apache 2.0
[p0228-l0039] [10.0pt] license. It’s a community-driven initiative with contributions from both academia and
[p0228-l0040] [10.0pt] industry. Today, vLLM is a mature project with the following features and capabilities:
[p0228-l0041] [10.0pt] ¡ State-of-the-art serving throughput
[p0228-l0042] [10.0pt] ¡ Efficient management of attention key and value memory through Paged­Attention

=== PDF page 229 / printed label 208 ===
[p0229-l0001] [9.0pt] 208
[p0229-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0229-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Continuous batching of incoming requests
[p0229-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Support for the most popular CPUs and GPUS (NVIDIA GPUs, AMD CPUs and
[p0229-l0005] [10.0pt] GPUs, Intel CPUs, Gaudi accelerators and GPUs, PowerPC CPUs, TPU, and AWS
[p0229-l0006] [10.0pt] Trainium and Inferentia Accelerators)
[p0229-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ Optimized CUDA kernels, including integration with FlashAttention and
[p0229-l0008] [10.0pt] FlashInfer
[p0229-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ Fast model execution with CUDA/HIP graph
[p0229-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Support for quantization (GPTQ, AWQ, INT4, INT8, and FP8)
[p0229-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ High throughput serving with various decoding algorithms
[p0229-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Speculative decoding
[p0229-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ Chunked prefill
[p0229-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ Distributed inference (tensor and pipeline parallelism)
[p0229-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ Streaming outputs
[p0229-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Prefix caching support
[p0229-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ Integration with Hugging Face models (Transformers, MoEs, embedding mod­
[p0229-l0018] [10.0pt] els, multimodal LLMs)
[p0229-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ Compatibility with the OpenAI API
[p0229-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Multi-LoRA support
[p0229-l0021] [10.0pt] Let’s look at how we can use vLLM to serve SLMs.
[p0229-l0022] [10.5pt] 11.1.1	 Offline serving
[p0229-l0023] [10.0pt] vLLM supports offline and online serving. We’ll first look at offline serving—it’s a
[p0229-l0024] [10.0pt] good starting point for getting familiar with the library. A companion Colab notebook
[p0229-l0025] [10.0pt] is provided.
[p0229-l0026] [10.0pt] In most cases, you can install vLLM as a Python library:
[p0229-l0027] [8.0pt] pip install vllm
[p0229-l0028] [10.0pt] For supported hardware architectures without a prebuilt wheel, you’ll need to build it
[p0229-l0029] [10.0pt] from source. Check the official documentation before installing it in your environment.
[p0229-l0030] [10.0pt] In this first example, you’ll get familiar with the main vLLM API in a text-generation
[p0229-l0031] [10.0pt] use case. We’ll then build on that with a chat use case and a quantized model. We’ll use
[p0229-l0032] [10.0pt] hardware acceleration with an NVIDIA GPU.
[p0229-l0033] [10.0pt] First, we’ll download a pretrained model from the Hugging Face Hub (GPT-2 small
[p0229-l0034] [10.0pt] in this example):
[p0229-l0035] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0229-l0036] [8.0pt] from vllm import LLM
[p0229-l0037] [8.0pt] model_id = "openai-community/gpt2"
[p0229-l0038] [8.0pt] device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"
[p0229-l0039] [8.0pt] vllm_model = LLM(model_id, device=device)

=== PDF page 230 / printed label 209 ===
[p0230-l0001] [9.0pt] 209
[p0230-l0002] [9.0pt] vLLM
[p0230-l0003] [10.0pt] You’ll notice that the code for this part is cleaner than the equivalent based on Hug­
[p0230-l0004] [10.0pt] ging Face’s Transformers API. The single line that creates the LLM class performs sev­
[p0230-l0005] [10.0pt] eral actions (rather than just downloading the model checkpoints):
[p0230-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ It downloads the model configuration file.
[p0230-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ It analyzes the model configuration and prepares the model setup accordingly.
[p0230-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ It downloads the model’s tokenizer.
[p0230-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ It downloads the model’s checkpoints.
[p0230-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ It loads the checkpoints in the destination device (GPU memory in this example).
[p0230-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ It profiles the memory.
[p0230-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ It initializes the KV cache.
[p0230-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ It warms up the model.
[p0230-l0014] [10.0pt] The model is now ready for inference. Because we didn’t specify a task, vLLM defaulted
[p0230-l0015] [10.0pt] to generate (it also supports classify, score, reward, and embed), so the selected GPT-2
[p0230-l0016] [10.0pt] model is ready to generate text. Provide a prompt, and start text completion with the
[p0230-l0017] [10.0pt] generate method:
[p0230-l0018] [8.0pt] prompt = "Once upon a time in a land far away"
[p0230-l0019] [8.0pt] output = vllm_model.generate(prompt)
[p0230-l0020] [8.0pt] print(output[0].outputs[0].text)
[p0230-l0021] [10.0pt] The generate method also accepts an argument that specifies the sampling strategy.
[p0230-l0022] [10.0pt] vLLM provides SamplingParams, a class for configuring sampling configuration
[p0230-l0023] [10.0pt] (temperature, top_p, top_k, and other options supported by libraries such as Hugging
[p0230-l0024] [10.0pt] Face’s Transformers):
[p0230-l0025] [8.0pt] from vllm import SamplingParams
[p0230-l0026] [8.0pt] sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.1, top_p=0.95)
[p0230-l0027] [8.0pt] output = vllm_model.generate(prompt, sampling_params)
[p0230-l0028] [10.0pt] This is the simplest, most general way to use vLLM for inference with any of the sup­
[p0230-l0029] [10.0pt] ported models. You can see how clean the vLLM API is, which was a design goal for its
[p0230-l0030] [10.0pt] authors and maintainers from the start.
[p0230-l0031] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll make things slightly more complex with a chat use case. We’ll switch
[p0230-l0032] [10.0pt] to a different model—the instruction-tuned Microsoft Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model
[p0230-l0033] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct)—and set up a chat app,
[p0230-l0034] [10.0pt] mostly reusing the code from the previous example. The setup code for chatting looks
[p0230-l0035] [10.0pt] the same as for text generation:
[p0230-l0036] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0230-l0037] [8.0pt] from vllm import LLM, SamplingParams
[p0230-l0038] [8.0pt] model_id = "microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct"
[p0230-l0039] [8.0pt] device = "cuda" if torch.cuda.is_available() else "cpu"

=== PDF page 231 / printed label 210 ===
[p0231-l0001] [9.0pt] 210
[p0231-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0231-l0003] [8.0pt] llm = LLM(model=model_id, device=device, dtype=torch.half)
[p0231-l0004] [8.0pt] sampling_params = SamplingParams(temperature=0.5)
[p0231-l0005] [10.0pt] The only thing that changes is the method we call. Given a conversation prompt like
[p0231-l0006] [10.0pt] the following
[p0231-l0007] [8.0pt] conversation = [
[p0231-l0008] [8.0pt]     {
[p0231-l0009] [8.0pt]         "role": "system",
[p0231-l0010] [8.0pt]         "content": "You are a helpful assistant"
[p0231-l0011] [8.0pt]     },
[p0231-l0012] [8.0pt]     {
[p0231-l0013] [8.0pt]         "role": "user",
[p0231-l0014] [8.0pt]         "content": "Hi"
[p0231-l0015] [8.0pt]     },
[p0231-l0016] [8.0pt]     {
[p0231-l0017] [8.0pt]         "role": "assistant",
[p0231-l0018] [8.0pt]         "content": "Hi! How can I assist you today?"
[p0231-l0019] [8.0pt]     },
[p0231-l0020] [8.0pt]     {
[p0231-l0021] [8.0pt]         "role": "user",
[p0231-l0022] [8.0pt]         "content": "Write an essay about the Monte Carlo Tree Search
[p0231-l0023] [10.0pt]         ➥ algorithm.",
[p0231-l0024] [8.0pt]     },
[p0231-l0025] [8.0pt] ]
[p0231-l0026] [10.0pt] the method we’ll use is chat:
[p0231-l0027] [8.0pt] outputs = llm.chat(conversation,
[p0231-l0028] [8.0pt]                    sampling_params=sampling_params,
[p0231-l0029] [8.0pt]                    use_tqdm=False)
[p0231-l0030] [10.0pt] The chat method works for both single and batch inference:
[p0231-l0031] [8.0pt] conversations = [conversation for _ in range(10)]
[p0231-l0032] [8.0pt] outputs = llm.chat(messages=conversations,
[p0231-l0033] [8.0pt]                    sampling_params=sampling_params,
[p0231-l0034] [8.0pt]                    use_tqdm=True)

[p0233-l0030] [10.5pt] 11.1.2	 Online serving
[p0233-l0031] [10.0pt] vLLM also provides an HTTP server compatible with the OpenAI API (https://github
[p0233-l0032] [10.0pt] .com/openai/openai-python), the de facto standard for online LLM serving. After you
[p0233-l0033] [10.0pt] install vLLM, you can start a server with the serve CLI command. In its simplest form,
[p0233-l0034] [10.0pt] the command expects the following arguments:
[p0233-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ The ID of an LLM in the Hugging Face Hub
[p0233-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ The precision format for the model
[p0233-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ An authorization token to access the server’s API
[p0233-l0038] [10.0pt] The following example uses Microsoft’s Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model:
[p0233-l0039] [8.0pt] vllm serve microsoft/Phi-3-mini-4k-instruct --dtype
[p0233-l0040] [8.0pt] float16 --api-key token-abc123

[p0234-l0002] [9.0pt] vLLM
[p0234-l0003] [10.0pt] After the server has ramped up, you can call it with an HTTP client built with the
[p0234-l0004] [10.0pt] OpenAI Python client API (as you would with any other framework that supports this
[p0234-l0005] [10.0pt] library and format). The vLLM server supports the OpenAI API for completions, chat
[p0234-l0006] [10.0pt] completions, and embeddings, and it provides further extensions for tokenizing/­
[p0234-l0007] [10.0pt] detokenizing, pooling, scoring, and reranking. The following example shows an HTTP

[p0234-l0017] [8.0pt]     {"role": "user", "content": "Hello!"}
[p0234-l0018] [8.0pt]   ]
[p0234-l0019] [8.0pt] )

[p0234-l0021] [8.0pt] ChatCompletionMessage(content=' Hello! How can I assist you today?',

[p0234-l0023] [8.0pt] tool_calls=[], reasoning_content=None)
[p0234-l0024] [10.0pt] For a full list of OpenAI API configurations and options, see the OpenAI Python SDK
[p0234-l0025] [10.0pt] documentation at https://github.com/openai/openai-python. You can serve vLLM
[p0234-l0026] [10.0pt] offline or online using Docker containers and deploy it on Kubernetes, Nginx, or
[p0234-l0027] [10.0pt] AWS.
[p0234-l0028] [10.0pt] Because of vLLM’s many implementation optimizations, SLM inference is very fast
[p0234-l0029] [10.0pt] compared to other frameworks and runtimes. But once a model is deployed behind
[p0234-l0030] [10.0pt] an HTTP endpoint, you should benchmark its real serving performance before open­
[p0234-l0031] [10.0pt] ing access to client applications. The official vLLM GitHub repository provides several
[p0234-l0032] [10.0pt] Python scripts to automate benchmarks for any model served through the framework’s
[p0234-l0033] [10.0pt] API. The scripts are in the benchmarks folder, and they cover metrics such as latency
[p0234-l0034] [10.0pt] and throughput. Two benchmarking datasets are also available on the Hugging Face
[p0234-l0035] [10.0pt] Hub: ShareGPT (text only) and ShareGPT4V (multimodal).
[p0234-l0036] [10.0pt] To benchmark models served online, we first need to clone the vLLM GitHub repo
[p0234-l0037] [10.0pt] and install its requirements. Then download the ShareGPT dataset in JSON format, such
[p0234-l0038] [10.0pt] as by using wget:
[p0234-l0039] [8.0pt] wget https://huggingface.co/datasets/anon8231489123

[p0234-l0041] [10.0pt] ➥/ShareGPT_V3_unfiltered_cleaned_split.json

[p0236-l0002] [9.0pt] FastAPI
[p0236-l0003] [12.5pt] 11.2	 FastAPI
[p0236-l0004] [10.0pt] FastAPI (https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/) is a modern, open source web framework for
[p0236-l0005] [10.0pt] building APIs with standard Python type hints. It aims to be performant, easy to use,
[p0236-l0006] [10.0pt] and easy to learn. FastAPI is built on Starlette (https://www.starlette.io/) for the web
[p0236-l0007] [10.0pt] layer and Pydantic (https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/) for data modeling and vali­
[p0236-l0008] [10.0pt] dation. It uses Python’s async features for nonblocking operations and good perfor­
[p0236-l0009] [10.0pt] mance under load, and its straightforward syntax helps developers get started quickly.
[p0236-l0010] [10.0pt] FastAPI also generates live, interactive API documentation automatically, with either
[p0236-l0011] [10.0pt] Swagger UI (https://swagger.io/) or ReDoc (https://github.com/Redocly/redoc) as
[p0236-l0012] [10.0pt] the documentation interface (they offer different user experiences for exploring and
[p0236-l0013] [10.0pt] testing the same REST API). This documentation is derived from your code and type
[p0236-l0014] [10.0pt] hints, making the API easy to understand and test. FastAPI is well suited for data-driven
[p0236-l0015] [10.0pt] APIs, microservices, and ML APIs.
[p0236-l0016] [10.0pt] Before we serve LLMs with this framework, let’s review the basic FastAPI syntax. After
[p0236-l0017] [10.0pt] installing the library, we need to import the main requirement:
[p0236-l0018] [8.0pt] from fastapi import FastAPI
[p0236-l0019] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll create an instance of the FastAPI app:
[p0236-l0020] [8.0pt] app = FastAPI()
[p0236-l0021] [10.0pt] Now we can start building routes. Routes define how incoming HTTP requests are
[p0236-l0022] [10.0pt] handled. Each route is tied to a URL path and specifies the function that processes the
[p0236-l0023] [10.0pt] request. For example, to accept HTTP GET requests, we’ll define a function and deco­
[p0236-l0024] [10.0pt] rate it with the FastAPI get annotation:
[p0236-l0025] [8.0pt] @app.get("/")
[p0236-l0026] [8.0pt] def read_root():
[p0236-l0027] [8.0pt]     return {"Hello": "Friend"}
[p0236-l0028] [10.0pt] To accept HTTP POST requests, we can define a custom function and decorate it with
[p0236-l0029] [10.0pt] FastAPI’s post annotation:
[p0236-l0030] [8.0pt] from typing import Union
[p0236-l0031] [8.0pt] @app.post("/items/")
[p0236-l0032] [8.0pt] async def create_item(item_id: int, q: Union[str, None] = None):
[p0236-l0033] [8.0pt]     return {"item_id": item_id, "q": q}
[p0236-l0034] [10.0pt] Now we can start the web server from the CLI:
[p0236-l0035] [8.0pt] fastapi <environment> <python_web_app_name>.py
[p0236-l0036] [10.0pt] Here <environment> can take the values dev (for development/testing) or run (for pro­
[p0236-l0037] [10.0pt] duction). After the server starts, the implemented APIs are available at the hostname

=== PDF page 237 / printed label 216 ===
[p0237-l0001] [9.0pt] 216
[p0237-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0237-l0003] [10.0pt] (default localhost) and port (default 8000) specified at the server’ startup. You can
[p0237-l0004] [10.0pt] set the host and port with the --host and --port options of the fastapi command-line
[p0237-l0005] [10.0pt] application.
[p0237-l0006] [10.0pt] Because this framework uses Swagger UI and ReDoc, it automatically generates
[p0237-l0007] [10.0pt] online documentation for our custom API at the /docs GET endpoint (see figure 11.1).
[p0237-l0008] [8.0pt] Figure 11.1  Online documentation for our FastAPI web application’s custom API
[p0237-l0009] [10.0pt] Alternatively, you can use the /redoc GET route (see figure 11.2).
[p0237-l0010] [10.0pt] That’s it, regardless of the complexity or scope of your functions or API.
[p0237-l0011] [10.0pt] Now let’s see how to use FastAPI to serve LLMs. The server code is straightforward,
[p0237-l0012] [10.0pt] since its structure is the same as any for other FastAPI app. What are specific to LLMs are
[p0237-l0013] [10.0pt] the inference handling function and any supporting code for model initialization. The
[p0237-l0014] [10.0pt] Hugging Face libraries we’ve used throughout this book integrate easily into FastAPI
[p0237-l0015] [10.0pt] apps. As in the previous example, we’ll start by creating an instance of the FastAPI app
[p0237-l0016] [10.0pt] class:
[p0237-l0017] [8.0pt] from fastapi import FastAPI
[p0237-l0018] [8.0pt] app = FastAPI()

=== PDF page 238 / printed label 217 ===
[p0238-l0001] [9.0pt] 217
[p0238-l0002] [9.0pt] FastAPI
[p0238-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 11.2  Online ReDoc documentation for our sample FastAPI web application’s custom API
[p0238-l0004] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll create two classes—one for the model’s input and one for its output:
[p0238-l0005] [8.0pt] from pydantic import BaseModel
[p0238-l0006] [8.0pt] class InputData(BaseModel):
[p0238-l0007] [8.0pt]  prompt: str
[p0238-l0008] [8.0pt] class OutputData(BaseModel):
[p0238-l0009] [8.0pt]  response: str
[p0238-l0010] [10.0pt] We’ll initialize the model pipeline at application startup. Hugging Face pipelines are
[p0238-l0011] [10.0pt] supported, and we can also use the Transformers auto classes. For example, for the
[p0238-l0012] [10.0pt] GPT-2 small model for text generation, the syntax is as follows:
[p0238-l0013] [8.0pt] model = pipeline("text-generation", model="openai-community/gpt2")
[p0238-l0014] [10.0pt] Finally, we need to create a route that uses the model to generate text based on a
[p0238-l0015] [10.0pt] prompt through the request:
[p0238-l0016] [8.0pt] @app.post("/generate", response_model=OutputData)
[p0238-l0017] [8.0pt] def generate(request: Request, input_data: InputData):
[p0238-l0018] [8.0pt]  prompt = input_data.prompt
[p0238-l0019] [8.0pt]  response = model(prompt)[0]["generated_text"]
[p0238-l0020] [8.0pt]  return OutputData(response=response)

=== PDF page 239 / printed label 218 ===
[p0239-l0001] [9.0pt] 218
[p0239-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0239-l0003] [10.0pt] The preceding route returns the generated text in response to an HTTP POST request.
[p0239-l0004] [10.0pt] You can package FastAPI applications for serving LLMs in Docker containers and
[p0239-l0005] [10.0pt] deploy them to container platforms such as Kubernetes or cloud services like AWS and
[p0239-l0006] [10.0pt] Azure. For our simple GPT-2 text-generation app, the Dockerfile looks like this:
[p0239-l0007] [8.0pt] FROM python:3.10-slim
[p0239-l0008] [8.0pt] WORKDIR /fastapi-demo
[p0239-l0009] [8.0pt] COPY requirements.txt .
[p0239-l0010] [8.0pt] COPY ./src ./src
[p0239-l0011] [8.0pt] RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
[p0239-l0012] [8.0pt] EXPOSE 8000
[p0239-l0013] [8.0pt] CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:main", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]
[p0239-l0014] [10.0pt] In the preceding Dockerfile, we start from an official Python runtime image, set the root
[p0239-l0015] [10.0pt] directory in the container, copy in the requirements file and source code, install depen­
[p0239-l0016] [10.0pt] dencies, expose the listening port, and start the web server when the container starts.
[p0239-l0017] [10.5pt] 11.2.1	 Benchmarking various models
[p0239-l0018] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier, FastAPI delivers strong performance. When serving LLMs with
[p0239-l0019] [10.0pt] FastAPI, focus your benchmarking on model inference, since it has the biggest effect
[p0239-l0020] [10.0pt] on overall performance.
[p0239-l0021] [10.0pt] For this subsection, a companion Colab notebook provides code to benchmark a
[p0239-l0022] [10.0pt] model you’ll serve through a FastAPI route. The notebook doesn’t include the serving
[p0239-l0023] [10.0pt] code because it requires tunneling, and Colab policies can change in ways that block
[p0239-l0024] [10.0pt] tunneling techniques and third-party services. Still, you can use the notebook to bench­
[p0239-l0025] [10.0pt] mark different model versions, identify the fastest option, and choose a deployment
[p0239-l0026] [10.0pt] candidate. Afterward, benchmark the FastAPI web application in a separate environ­
[p0239-l0027] [10.0pt] ment, as you would for any other web application.
[p0239-l0028] [10.0pt] This example uses the GPT-2 small model, but you can benchmark any GPT-2 size
[p0239-l0029] [10.0pt] (including fine-tuned or PEFT variants) by swapping the model ID on the Hugging Face
[p0239-l0030] [10.0pt] Hub. With minor changes to the auto classes and input preparation, the same approach
[p0239-l0031] [10.0pt] works for other decoder-only architectures. GPT-2 small needs no hardware accelera­
[p0239-l0032] [10.0pt] tion, but larger models or running all benchmarks at once will likely require a GPU.
[p0239-l0033] [10.0pt] Let’s download the model and tokenizer from the Hugging Face Hub:

[p0241-l0006] [10.0pt] By applying techniques from earlier chapters, we now have four versions of the same
[p0241-l0007] [10.0pt] model. We’ll benchmark them and choose one to serve through a FastAPI web app.
[p0241-l0008] [10.0pt] Let’s define a simple helper function we can reuse to benchmark any of these models:
[p0241-l0009] [8.0pt] import timeit
[p0241-l0010] [8.0pt] def benchmark_llm(f, name=""):
[p0241-l0011] [8.0pt]     for _ in range(10):
[p0241-l0012] [8.0pt]         f()
[p0241-l0013] [8.0pt]     seconds_per_iter = timeit.timeit(f, number=100) / 100
[p0241-l0014] [8.0pt]     print(
[p0241-l0015] [8.0pt]         f"{name}:",
[p0241-l0016] [8.0pt]         f"{seconds_per_iter * 1000:.3f} ms",
[p0241-l0017] [8.0pt]     )
[p0241-l0018] [10.0pt] This function expects two input values: a function f that runs inference for a given
[p0241-l0019] [10.0pt] model and a benchmark name (useful for building reports and visualizations). After
[p0241-l0020] [10.0pt] an initial warmup, it runs the model 100 times and returns the average latency.
[p0241-l0021] [10.0pt] Before running the benchmarks, we need to prepare the inputs expected by each
[p0241-l0022] [10.0pt] model version, along with the inference function to pass to benchmark_llm. We will use
[p0241-l0023] [10.0pt] the following test prompt:
[p0241-l0024] [8.0pt] text = "Today is Saturday and"

[p0241-l0027] [10.0pt] The benchmark execution is then quite straightforward:
[p0241-l0028] [8.0pt] benchmark_llm(lambda: model(**inputs_base), "PyTorch")
[p0241-l0029] [10.0pt] The other three versions of the model are in ONNX format, so we need a bit of setup

[p0243-l0012] [10.5pt] 11.2.2	 Deploying the best-performing model with FastAPI
[p0243-l0013] [10.0pt] To deploy the selected model version behind a FastAPI route, we can follow the usual
[p0243-l0014] [10.0pt] pattern for implementing routes in the framework. In addition, we need to implement
[p0243-l0015] [10.0pt] a custom function to generate text with the ONNX-optimized GPT-2 small model:
[p0243-l0016] [8.0pt] import numpy as np
[p0243-l0017] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0243-l0018] [8.0pt] from onnxruntime import InferenceSession
[p0243-l0019] [8.0pt] async def generate(prompt, max_length, device):
[p0243-l0020] [8.0pt]   pt_inputs_base = tokenizer(prompt,
[p0243-l0021] [8.0pt]                             max_length=max_length,
[p0243-l0022] [8.0pt]                             return_tensors="pt").to(device)
[p0243-l0023] [8.0pt]   pt_inputs = tokenizer(prompt,
[p0243-l0024] [8.0pt]                         max_length=max_length,
[p0243-l0025] [8.0pt]                         return_tensors="pt").to(device)
[p0243-l0026] [8.0pt]   ort_inputs = dict(tokenizer(prompt,
[p0243-l0027] [8.0pt]                             max_length=max_length,
[p0243-l0028] [8.0pt]                             return_tensors="np",
[p0243-l0029] [8.0pt]                             return_attention_mask=False))
[p0243-l0030] [8.0pt]   ort_inputs['input_ids'] = ort_inputs['input_ids'].astype(np.int32)
[p0243-l0031] [8.0pt]   optimized_onnx_path = "gpt2_optimized.onnx"
[p0243-l0032] [8.0pt]   providers=["CPUExecutionProvider"]
[p0243-l0033] [8.0pt]   optimized_sess = InferenceSession(optimized_onnx_path,
[p0243-l0034] [8.0pt]                                   providers=providers)
[p0243-l0035] [8.0pt]   logits = optimized_sess.run(None, ort_inputs)
[p0243-l0036] [8.0pt]   np_logits = logits[0]
[p0243-l0037] [8.0pt]   output = torch.from_numpy(np_logits)
[p0243-l0038] [8.0pt]   predicted_ids = np.argmax(output[0], axis=-1)
[p0243-l0039] [8.0pt]   return output
[p0243-l0040] [10.0pt] The custom generate function takes as input the user prompt, maximum token count,
[p0243-l0041] [10.0pt] and device to use (CPU in our example). In the body of the function, we prepare the
[p0243-l0042] [10.0pt] input for the ONNX model, create an ORT inference session, run text generation,
[p0243-l0043] [10.0pt] and decode the output to return the generated text in natural language. The generate
[p0243-l0044] [10.0pt] function is declared async because, when the model is exposed through a web API,
[p0243-l0045] [10.0pt] server performance can vary based on factors such as network speed and bandwidth or

=== PDF page 244 / printed label 223 ===
[p0244-l0001] [9.0pt] 223
[p0244-l0002] [9.0pt] MLC LLM
[p0244-l0003] [10.0pt] the output size (which affects LLM latency). Making the function calls asynchronous
[p0244-l0004] [10.0pt] frees the CPU to do other work while inference completes.
[p0244-l0005] [10.0pt] On the web app’s side, we first need to create a class to handle the inputs for the gen­
[p0244-l0006] [10.0pt] eration. The GenerateRequest class extends Pydantic’s BaseModel class and defines two
[p0244-l0007] [10.0pt] fields—the user prompt and the maximum length:
[p0244-l0008] [8.0pt] from pydantic import BaseModel
[p0244-l0009] [8.0pt] class GenerateRequest(BaseModel):
[p0244-l0010] [8.0pt]     prompt: str
[p0244-l0011] [8.0pt]     max_length: int = 64
[p0244-l0012] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll create the FastAPI app and implement a route that generates a sentence
[p0244-l0013] [10.0pt] from a prompt and maximum length:
[p0244-l0014] [8.0pt] from fastapi import FastAPI
[p0244-l0015] [8.0pt] app = FastAPI()
[p0244-l0016] [8.0pt] @app.post("/generate")
[p0244-l0017] [8.0pt] async def generate_text(request: GenerateRequest):
[p0244-l0018] [8.0pt]     device = "cpu"
[p0244-l0019] [8.0pt]     generated_sentence = await generate(request.prompt,
[p0244-l0020] [8.0pt]                                         request.max_length,
[p0244-l0021] [8.0pt]                                         device)
[p0244-l0022] [8.0pt]     return {"Generated sentence = ": generated_sentence}
[p0244-l0023] [10.0pt] In this section, you’ve seen how to deploy an SLM behind FastAPI, which is a good fit
[p0244-l0024] [10.0pt] for most local and cloud deployments. The next sections cover a different scenario:
[p0244-l0025] [10.0pt] deploying and serving SLMs on the edge.
[p0244-l0026] [12.5pt] 11.3	 MLC LLM
[p0244-l0027] [10.0pt] So far in this chapter, we’ve explored two ways to deploy and serve SLMs behind tradi­
[p0244-l0028] [10.0pt] tional REST APIs. In this section and the next, we’ll move closer to the edge and look
[p0244-l0029] [10.0pt] at options for on-device deployment and serving.
[p0244-l0030] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ll look at MLC LLM (https://github.com/mlc-ai/mlc-llm/tree/
[p0244-l0031] [10.0pt] main), an open source ML compiler and high-performance deployment engine for
[p0244-l0032] [10.0pt] LLMs. It compiles and runs code on the MLCEngine, a unified high-performance LLM
[p0244-l0033] [10.0pt] inference engine across multiple platforms. MLCEngine also provides an OpenAI-­
[p0244-l0034] [10.0pt] compatible API via a REST server and through Python, JavaScript, iOS, and Android,
[p0244-l0035] [10.0pt] all backed by the same engine and compiler. Figure 11.3 shows the end-to-end workflow
[p0244-l0036] [10.0pt] for MLC LLM.
[p0244-l0037] [10.0pt] Figure 11.4 lists the supported operating systems, CPUs, and GPUs at the time of
[p0244-l0038] [10.0pt] writing.

[p0245-l0033] [10.0pt] Key strengths of the MLC LLM framework include cross-platform performance—­
[p0245-l0034] [10.0pt] especially on mobile and edge devices—universal deployment with a single engine, a famil­
[p0245-l0035] [10.0pt] iar OpenAI-style API, and support for high concurrency, batching, and prompt caching.
[p0245-l0036] [10.0pt] Let’s get familiar with the MLC LLM API. A companion Colab notebook provides the
[p0245-l0037] [10.0pt] code example for this section, and it uses an NVIDIA GPU for hardware acceleration.
[p0245-l0038] [10.0pt] The steps in this example apply to any LLM hosted on the Hugging Face Hub (a require­
[p0245-l0039] [10.0pt] ment), and they show how to prepare the model for inference on Linux-based devices.
[p0245-l0040] [10.0pt] First, we need to install the library for Linux and the available CUDA drivers:
[p0245-l0041] [8.0pt] python -m pip install --pre -U -f https://mlc.ai
[p0245-l0042] [10.0pt] ➥/wheels mlc-llm-nightly-cu122 mlc-ai-nightly-cu122

[p0246-l0001] [9.0pt] 225
[p0246-l0002] [9.0pt] MLC LLM
[p0246-l0003] [10.0pt] After verifying the installation, we can download the target model weights and configu­
[p0246-l0004] [10.0pt] ration files from the Hugging Face Hub.
[p0246-l0005] [10.0pt] We need to install Git LFS (https://github.com/git-lfs/git-lfs), a Git extension for
[p0246-l0006] [10.0pt] versioning large files. Then we can create the destination directory for the converted
[p0246-l0007] [10.0pt] weights and configuration and clone the target model repo from the Hub (in this
[p0246-l0008] [10.0pt] example, RedPajama INCITE Instruct 3B, trained by Together AI in collaboration with
[p0246-l0009] [10.0pt] several open source communities):
[p0246-l0010] [8.0pt] !mkdir -p dist/models
[p0246-l0011] [8.0pt] !git lfs install
[p0246-l0012] [8.0pt] !git clone https://huggingface.co/togethercomputer
[p0246-l0013] [10.0pt] ➥/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1
[p0246-l0014] [10.0pt] To convert the model’s weights to MLC LLM format, we’ll use the mlc_llm_convert_
[p0246-l0015] [10.0pt] weights command. It takes as input the path to the directory where the model weights
[p0246-l0016] [10.0pt] have been cloned, the quantization type, the target device (an NVIDIA GPU in our
[p0246-l0017] [10.0pt] case), and the output directory that will store the converted weights:
[p0246-l0018] [8.0pt] mlc_llm convert_weight ./RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1/ \
[p0246-l0019] [8.0pt]     --quantization q4f16_1 \
[p0246-l0020] [8.0pt]     --device cuda \
[p0246-l0021] [8.0pt]     -o dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC
[p0246-l0022] [10.0pt] Once the conversion is completed, the next step is to generate the chat configuration
[p0246-l0023] [10.0pt] for the selected model. This can be done using mlc_llm_gen_config, another com­
[p0246-l0024] [10.0pt] mand file provided by MLC LLM. It expects the path to the directory where you cloned
[p0246-l0025] [10.0pt] the model weights (and configuration), the quantization type, the model chat tem­
[p0246-l0026] [10.0pt] plate, and the output directory for the generated configuration (the same one used for
[p0246-l0027] [10.0pt] the converted model weights):
[p0246-l0028] [8.0pt] mlc_llm gen_config ./RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1/ \
[p0246-l0029] [8.0pt]     --quantization q4f16_1 --conv-template redpajama_chat \
[p0246-l0030] [8.0pt]     -o dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC/
[p0246-l0031] [10.0pt] After the previous two steps, the content of the RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1
[p0246-l0032] [10.0pt] -q4f16_1-MLC directory should look like this:
[p0246-l0033] [8.0pt] mlc-chat-config.json    params_shard_1.bin   params_shard_32.bin
[p0246-l0034] [8.0pt] params_shard_45.bin

[p0247-l0021] [10.0pt] The chat configuration file (mlc-chat-config.json), model weight metadata (ndarray
[p0247-l0022] [10.0pt] -­cache.json, ndarray-cache-b16.json), model shards, and tokenizer files (tokenizer
[p0247-l0023] [10.0pt] .json, tokenizer_config.json) must be present for conversion and chat configuration
[p0247-l0024] [10.0pt] to succeed.
[p0247-l0025] [10.0pt] We’re not done yet. At this stage, the model is prepared (and can optionally be
[p0247-l0026] [10.0pt] uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub), but to run it on a target platform or device, we
[p0247-l0027] [10.0pt] still need to compile the model library according to the specifications in the generated
[p0247-l0028] [10.0pt] mlc-chat-config.json file. In our Colab notebook example, the target for inference is
[p0247-l0029] [10.0pt] a Linux device. (See the official MLC LLM documentation for the steps to compile the
[p0247-l0030] [10.0pt] model for other operating systems.)
[p0247-l0031] [10.0pt] Our next step is to create the destination directory for the compiled model:
[p0247-l0032] [8.0pt] mkdir ./dist/libs
[p0247-l0033] [10.0pt] Now we’ll compile the model with the mlc_llm_compile command. It takes as input
[p0247-l0034] [10.0pt] the path to the directory containing the model chat configuration file, the target
[p0247-l0035] [10.0pt] device type (NVIDIA GPU), and the output path and filename for the compiled
[p0247-l0036] [10.0pt] model:
[p0247-l0037] [8.0pt] mlc_llm compile ./dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC
[p0247-l0038] [10.0pt] ➥/mlc-chat-config.json \
[p0247-l0039] [8.0pt]     --device cuda -o dist/libs
[p0247-l0040] [10.0pt]     ➥/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-cuda.so
[p0247-l0041] [10.0pt] Now that the model is ready, we can use the MLC LLM Python API to create an
[p0247-l0042] [10.0pt] MLCEngine instance for OpenAI-compatible chat completions in Python with MLC
[p0247-l0043] [10.0pt] LLM ported models. It takes the model configuration path and the compiled model
[p0247-l0044] [10.0pt] path as input:

[p0248-l0002] [9.0pt] MLC LLM
[p0248-l0003] [8.0pt] from mlc_llm import MLCEngine
[p0248-l0004] [8.0pt] engine = MLCEngine(
[p0248-l0005] [8.0pt]    model="./dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC",

[p0248-l0008] [8.0pt] response = engine.chat.completions.create(
[p0248-l0009] [8.0pt]     messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "What is the meaning of life?"}],

[p0248-l0011] [8.0pt]     stream=False,
[p0248-l0012] [8.0pt] )

[p0248-l0014] [8.0pt] for response in engine.chat.completions.create(

[p0248-l0021] [10.0pt] The MLCEngine class handles only synchronous chat completions. For concurrent, asyn­
[p0248-l0022] [10.0pt] chronous generation, use AsyncMLCEngine. If you’ve uploaded a converted, compiled
[p0248-l0023] [10.0pt] model to the Hugging Face Hub, these engine classes can download it; just specify the
[p0248-l0024] [10.0pt] model location in the following format:
[p0248-l0025] [8.0pt] HF://<model_id_in_the_hf_hub>
[p0248-l0026] [10.0pt] The chat-completion code for asynchronous generation via AsyncMLCEngine mirrors
[p0248-l0027] [10.0pt] that of MLCEngine.
[p0248-l0028] [10.0pt] Besides using the Python API and CLI to run ported SLMs and the MLCEngine, you
[p0248-l0029] [10.0pt] can also serve them through MLC LLM’s REST API. The server is available automati­
[p0248-l0030] [10.0pt] cally after you install MLC LLM. For the ported model in this section’s example, we’ll
[p0248-l0031] [10.0pt] start the server from the command line as follows:
[p0248-l0032] [8.0pt] mlc_llm serve MODEL --model-lib ./dist
[p0248-l0033] [10.0pt] ➥/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC
[p0248-l0034] [10.0pt] We’ll use the same command-line tool we used to convert and compile the model, but
[p0248-l0035] [10.0pt] this time, we’ll specify a different action (serve) and provide the compiled model’s loca­
[p0248-l0036] [10.0pt] tion with the --model-lib option. The other options for this command are as follows:
[p0248-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ --additional-models—Serves multiple models.
[p0248-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ --speculative-mode—Specifies whether speculative decoding is enabled (and
[p0248-l0039] [10.0pt] which type to use: small draft, eagle, or medusa) or disabled (default).

=== PDF page 249 / printed label 228 ===
[p0249-l0001] [9.0pt] 228
[p0249-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0249-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ --device—Specifies the device on which to run the model. By default, it’s set to
[p0249-l0004] [10.0pt] auto, which lets MLC LLM detect available devices and choose the best one. To
[p0249-l0005] [10.0pt] target a specific device, use device_name:device_id or device_name (in the latter
[p0249-l0006] [10.0pt] case, the device ID defaults to 0).
[p0249-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ --mode—Specifies the engine mode. Use local (low request concurrency),
[p0249-l0008] [10.0pt] interactive (up to one concurrent request), or server (many concurrent
[p0249-l0009] [10.0pt] requests; this uses as much GPU as possible).
[p0249-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ --overrides—Specifies values for one or more engine configuration parameters,
[p0249-l0011] [10.0pt] such as maximum GPU utilization, enabling tensor parallelism, and context-­
[p0249-l0012] [10.0pt] window size.
[p0249-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ --enable-tracing—Enables request logging.
[p0249-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ --host—Specifies a host name.
[p0249-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ --port—Changes the port the server listens on. Default is 8000.
[p0249-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ --allow-credentials—Indicates whether the server should allow credentials.
[p0249-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ --allowed-origins—Specifies the allowed origins.
[p0249-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ --allowed-methods—Restricts the allowed HTTP methods.
[p0249-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ --allowed-headers—Specifies the allowed headers.
[p0249-l0020] [10.0pt] NOTE  Speculative decoding is an inference-time optimization that lets an
[p0249-l0021] [10.0pt] LLM predict multiple future tokens in parallel instead of generating one at a
[p0249-l0022] [10.0pt] time. It’s covered in chapter 12.
[p0249-l0023] [10.0pt] Once the server is running, you can access it at the hostname and port you specified at
[p0249-l0024] [10.0pt] startup. The /docs endpoint lists all supported endpoints. A GET request to /v1/models
[p0249-l0025] [10.0pt] returns the available models.
[p0249-l0026] [10.0pt] To interact with the server from any Python application (to run inference with a
[p0249-l0027] [10.0pt] hosted model), implement a client as follows using the Requests package (https://
[p0249-l0028] [10.0pt] github.com/psf/requests):
[p0249-l0029] [8.0pt] import requests
[p0249-l0030] [8.0pt] import json
[p0249-l0031] [8.0pt] payload = {
[p0249-l0032] [8.0pt]  "model": "./dist/RedPajama-INCITE-Instruct-3B-v1-q4f16_1-MLC/",
[p0249-l0033] [8.0pt]  "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "Write a poem about Python"}],
[p0249-l0034] [8.0pt]  "stream": True,
[p0249-l0035] [8.0pt] }
[p0249-l0036] [8.0pt] with requests.post("http://127.0.0.1:8080/v1/chat
[p0249-l0037] [10.0pt] ➥/completions", json=payload, stream=True) as r:
[p0249-l0038] [8.0pt]    for chunk in r.iter_content(chunk_size=None):

[p0249-l0040] [8.0pt]       if "[DONE]" in chunk[6:]:
[p0249-l0041] [8.0pt]          break
