[p0250-l0006] [10.0pt] MLC LLM applications for SLM serving can also be managed as Docker containers
[p0250-l0007] [10.0pt] and deployed on devices that support containerization.
[p0250-l0008] [12.5pt] 11.4	 Deployment and inference on Android devices
[p0250-l0009] [10.0pt] There are several options for deploying private, offline SLMs on Android devices
[p0250-l0010] [10.0pt] (https://www.android.com/intl/en_ie/). Many online examples use TensorFlow Lite
[p0250-l0011] [10.0pt] or MediaPipe, which require developing SLMs in TensorFlow or converting PyTorch
[p0250-l0012] [10.0pt] weights to TensorFlow via ONNX. This section focuses on PyTorch alternatives.
[p0250-l0013] [10.5pt] 11.4.1	 MLC LLM framework
[p0250-l0014] [10.0pt] One option for deploying to Android is to use the MLC LLM framework discussed
[p0250-l0015] [10.0pt] in section 11.3. The MLC LLM documentation includes an end-to-end tutorial for
[p0250-l0016] [10.0pt] building and deploying apps and SLMs on Android (https://llm.mlc.ai/docs/deploy/
[p0250-l0017] [10.0pt] android.html). I won’t repeat the steps here because the linked page explains them
[p0250-l0018] [10.0pt] well. Here’s a summary:
[p0250-l0019] [10.0pt] 1	 Install the prerequisites to build the model and app locally.
[p0250-l0020] [10.0pt] 2	 Build the runtime and the selected model libraries. This step is the same as for
[p0250-l0021] [10.0pt] compiling and building a model for any other destination platform, as detailed
[p0250-l0022] [10.0pt] in section 11.3.
[p0250-l0023] [10.0pt] 3	 Customize and build the template Android app available in the MLC LLM
[p0250-l0024] [10.0pt] GitHub repository.
[p0250-l0025] [10.0pt] 4	 Bundle the app with the model weights.
[p0250-l0026] [10.0pt] 5	 Install the APK and weights on the target Android phone.
[p0250-l0027] [10.0pt] The MLC LLM documentation tutorial uses a Samsung S23 with a Snapdragon 8 Gen
[p0250-l0028] [10.0pt] 2 chip, but the workflow is the same for other Android devices. Focus on the target
[p0250-l0029] [10.0pt] device’s hardware specs, benchmark performance, and optimize the model as needed.
[p0250-l0030] [10.0pt] This approach has the advantages of porting and serving an SLM through the MLC
[p0250-l0031] [10.0pt] LLM framework, but it also requires installing many third-party, non-Python compo­
[p0250-l0032] [10.0pt] nents (Android Studio, rustc, the Java Development Kit, the NDK, and more) in your
[p0250-l0033] [10.0pt] development environment, in addition to model conversion and compilation. Let’s
[p0250-l0034] [10.0pt] look at some other alternatives.
[p0250-l0035] [10.5pt] 11.4.2	 MLLM framework
[p0250-l0036] [10.0pt] Another potential open source option is mllm (https://ubiquitouslearning.github
[p0250-l0037] [10.0pt] .io/mllm_website/), a lightweight, fast LLM engine for mobile and edge devices that
[p0250-l0038] [10.0pt] supports text and multimodal inputs. It’s implemented in plain C++ with no depen­
[p0250-l0039] [10.0pt] dencies and supports a range of mobile hardware and quantization strategies. At the
[p0250-l0040] [10.0pt] time of writing, mllm runs on Android, Linux, and macOS on x86_64 and arm64. You

=== PDF page 251 / printed label 230 ===
[p0251-l0001] [9.0pt] 230
[p0251-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0251-l0003] [10.0pt] must build it from source. On Linux and macOS, you’ll need gcc 11.4+ and CMake
[p0251-l0004] [10.0pt] 3.19+. On Android, you’ll need Android NDK toolchain 26+.
[p0251-l0005] [10.0pt] First, you’ll need to clone the official GitHub repo:
[p0251-l0006] [8.0pt] git clone https://github.com/UbiquitousLearning/mllm
[p0251-l0007] [10.0pt] mllm can be built with one of the provided scripts. On Linux/macOS, use build.sh:
[p0251-l0008] [8.0pt] cd ./scripts && ./build.sh
[p0251-l0009] [10.0pt] Several text and multimodal models are available in mllm format on the Hugging Face
[p0251-l0010] [10.0pt] Hub and can be used as soon as the library build completes. Models are provided in
[p0251-l0011] [10.0pt] FP32 and INT4 (CPU-optimized); a few are also optimized for the Hexagon NPU in
[p0251-l0012] [10.0pt] INT8. See the mllm GitHub repo for the latest list.
[p0251-l0013] [10.0pt] During the build, a dedicated bash script for running inference is created in the bin
[p0251-l0014] [10.0pt] directory for each model. For example, to run Llama 2 7B, download the already con­
[p0251-l0015] [10.0pt] verted model from the Hub:
[p0251-l0016] [8.0pt] !mkdir ../models && cd ../models
[p0251-l0017] [8.0pt] !wget https://huggingface.co/mllmTeam/llama-2-7b-mllm/resolve
[p0251-l0018] [10.0pt] ➥/main/llama-2-7b-chat-q4_k.mllm?download
[p0251-l0019] [10.0pt] ➥=true  -O llama-2-7b-chat-q4_k.mllm
[p0251-l0020] [10.0pt] Then run the following script to start a chat session:
[p0251-l0021] [8.0pt] cd ./bin
[p0251-l0022] [8.0pt] ./demo_llama -m ../models/llama-2-7b-chat-q4_k.mllm -v
[p0251-l0023] [8.0pt]  ../vocab/llama2_vocab.mllm
[p0251-l0024] [10.0pt] On Android devices, you’ll need to use a different build script to build mllm, and you’ll
[p0251-l0025] [10.0pt] need to specify the Android NDK path:
[p0251-l0026] [8.0pt] export ANDROID_NDK=/path/to/your/ndk
[p0251-l0027] [8.0pt] cd ./scripts
[p0251-l0028] [8.0pt] ./build_android.sh
[p0251-l0029] [10.0pt] Then, after downloading one of the available converted models from the Hugging
[p0251-l0030] [10.0pt] Face Hub, you can start a chat session using the script for that model. Here’s an exam­
[p0251-l0031] [10.0pt] ple for the Llama 2 7B model:
[p0251-l0032] [8.0pt] cd ../script
[p0251-l0033] [8.0pt] ./run_llama.sh
[p0251-l0034] [10.0pt] If the model you want to use isn’t yet available in mllm, or if it’s a custom model, the
[p0251-l0035] [10.0pt] mllm repo includes a Python script, convert.py, that converts PyTorch or safetensors
[p0251-l0036] [10.0pt] weights (single-file or sharded). You’ll find it in tools/convertor. Before running it, set
[p0251-l0037] [10.0pt] up a Python environment, and install the converter requirements:

=== PDF page 252 / printed label 231 ===
[p0252-l0001] [9.0pt] 231
[p0252-l0002] [9.0pt] Deployment and inference on Android devices
[p0252-l0003] [8.0pt] cd ./tools/convertor
[p0252-l0004] [8.0pt] pip install -r ./requirements.txt
[p0252-l0005] [10.0pt] You can then use the script for a given model as follows for PyTorch-format checkpoints:
[p0252-l0006] [8.0pt] python convert.py --input_model=<model_name>.pth
[p0252-l0007] [8.0pt] --output_model=<model_name>.mllm --type=torch
[p0252-l0008] [10.0pt] Or like this, for checkpoints in safetensors format:
[p0252-l0009] [8.0pt] python convert.py --input_model=<model_name>.safetensors
[p0252-l0010] [8.0pt] --output_model=<model_name>.mllm --type=safetensor
[p0252-l0011] [10.0pt] Because device memory, storage, and computational resources are often limited, mllm
[p0252-l0012] [10.0pt] supports INT4 quantization for mllm models, including custom models converted to
[p0252-l0013] [10.0pt] the format this library requires. Only two quantization modes are supported: Q4_0
[p0252-l0014] [10.0pt] and Q4_K. After you build the mllm library, the quantize script is available in the bin
[p0252-l0015] [10.0pt] directory:
[p0252-l0016] [8.0pt] cd ./bin
[p0252-l0017] [8.0pt] ./quantize <model_name>.mllm model_q4_0.mllm Q4_K
[p0252-l0018] [10.5pt] 11.4.3	 Hugging Face Transformers
[p0252-l0019] [10.0pt] Another alternative, fully Python-based, is to deploy and run SLMs for on-device infer­
[p0252-l0020] [10.0pt] ence directly with the Hugging Face Transformers library. This method requires devel­
[p0252-l0021] [10.0pt] oper options to be enabled on the target device.
[p0252-l0022] [10.0pt] To check if developer options are enabled, open the device’s Settings section, and
[p0252-l0023] [10.0pt] confirm that Developer Options appears in the list. If not, go to Settings > About phone
[p0252-l0024] [10.0pt] > Software Information, find the phone’s Build Number, and tap it seven times.
[p0252-l0025] [10.0pt] Once that’s done, you’ll need to install the Termux app (https://termux.dev/en/)
[p0252-l0026] [10.0pt] from the Google Play Store. Termux is an open source terminal emulator for Android
[p0252-l0027] [10.0pt] that runs a Debian-based Linux environment. No rooting is required to install it or add
[p0252-l0028] [10.0pt] packages through its package manager. Termux is essentially a portable Linux distri­
[p0252-l0029] [10.0pt] bution, so you can also install compilers and interpreters for popular programming
[p0252-l0030] [10.0pt] languages. This means you can install Python and create virtual environments to run
[p0252-l0031] [10.0pt] your own SLMs.
[p0252-l0032] [10.0pt] After starting Termux, you can install Python from the command line. First, update
[p0252-l0033] [10.0pt] the package list:
[p0252-l0034] [8.0pt] pkg update && pkg upgrade
[p0252-l0035] [10.0pt] Then proceed with the main installation:
[p0252-l0036] [8.0pt] pkg install python

[p0253-l0001] [9.0pt] 232
[p0253-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 11  Deployment and serving
[p0253-l0003] [10.0pt] After installation, install the Python package manager and a virtual environment
[p0253-l0004] [10.0pt] manager:
[p0253-l0005] [8.0pt] pkg install python-pip
[p0253-l0006] [8.0pt] pip install virtualenv
[p0253-l0007] [10.0pt] You’ll need to create a virtual environment to isolate the dependencies for SLM
[p0253-l0008] [10.0pt] deployment and inference. Choose a destination directory on the device, and create
[p0253-l0009] [10.0pt] the environment as you would on a laptop or server:
[p0253-l0010] [8.0pt] python -m venv slm-env
[p0253-l0011] [10.0pt] Now activate the virtual environment:
[p0253-l0012] [8.0pt] source slm-env/bin/activate
[p0253-l0013] [10.0pt] Finally, install the required PyTorch and Transformers packages (and any others
[p0253-l0014] [10.0pt] needed to implement our Python inference script):
[p0253-l0015] [8.0pt] pip install torch transformers
[p0253-l0016] [10.0pt] We can now implement inference code for the selected model. The simple example
[p0253-l0017] [10.0pt] that follows uses a bert-base-uncased model for a classification task, but you can use any
[p0253-l0018] [10.0pt] model supported by the Transformers library:
[p0253-l0019] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0253-l0020] [8.0pt] from transformers import BertTokenizer, BertForSequenceClassification
[p0253-l0021] [8.0pt] model_id = 'google-bert/bert-base-uncased'
[p0253-l0022] [8.0pt] tokenizer = BertTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0253-l0023] [8.0pt] model = BertForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_id)
[p0253-l0024] [8.0pt] <h1>Sample text</h1>
[p0253-l0025] [8.0pt] text = "That movie is a blockbuster"
[p0253-l0026] [8.0pt] <h1>Tokenize the text</h1>
[p0253-l0027] [8.0pt] inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors='pt')
[p0253-l0028] [8.0pt] <h1>Perform classification</h1>
[p0253-l0029] [8.0pt] with torch.no_grad():
[p0253-l0030] [8.0pt]  outputs = model(<strong>inputs)
[p0253-l0031] [8.0pt] <h1>Get the predicted class</h1>
[p0253-l0032] [8.0pt] predicted_class = torch.argmax(outputs.logits)
[p0253-l0033] [8.0pt] print(f"Predicted class: {predicted_class}")
[p0253-l0034] [10.0pt] We’ll now save the script on the device and run it for inference like any other Python
[p0253-l0035] [10.0pt] application. Assuming the script is named bert_classification.py, run it like this:
[p0253-l0036] [8.0pt] python bert_classification.py

=== PDF page 254 / printed label 233 ===
[p0254-l0001] [9.0pt] 233
[p0254-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0254-l0003] [10.0pt] That’s it.
[p0254-l0004] [10.0pt] Running LLMs locally can be resource-intensive, so choose a model your Android
[p0254-l0005] [10.0pt] device can handle in terms of memory, CPU (or GPU), and storage. After benchmark­
[p0254-l0006] [10.0pt] ing on-device performance, try the optimization techniques from earlier chapters
[p0254-l0007] [10.0pt] (including quantization) to speed up inference while maintaining acceptable output
[p0254-l0008] [10.0pt] quality.
[p0254-l0009] [10.0pt] That concludes our survey of options for deploying and serving SLMs. The frame­
[p0254-l0010] [10.0pt] works we covered share two key traits: an easy-to-use API and strong, out-of-the-box
[p0254-l0011] [10.0pt] performance. The next chapter continues with local SLM deployment and serving,
[p0254-l0012] [10.0pt] focusing on user-friendly ways to build powerful SLM-based assistants on a laptop.
[p0254-l0013] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0254-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ vLLM uses PagedAttention to manage memory efficiently by storing key–value

[p0257-l0001] [9.0pt] 236
[p0257-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 12  Running on your laptop
[p0257-l0003] [12.5pt] 12.1	 Why use a personal local assistant
[p0257-l0004] [10.0pt] Platforms that expose commercial LLMs through a chat interface or API—such as
[p0257-l0005] [10.0pt] those from OpenAI, xAI, Anthropic, and Google—can learn about their users in ways
[p0257-l0006] [10.0pt] we can’t fully realize. They collect data from user interactions and turn that informa­
[p0257-l0007] [10.0pt] tion into assets. Even when platforms let users opt out of data collection or the use of
[p0257-l0008] [10.0pt] prompts, generated responses, and other sensitive data for model tuning, their closed
[p0257-l0009] [10.0pt] nature makes it hard to know how consistently those choices are honored. This mat­
[p0257-l0010] [10.0pt] ters because information can be unintentionally exposed, not only through third-party
[p0257-l0011] [10.0pt] chat systems and APIs, but also via client laptops and smartphones connected to the
[p0257-l0012] [10.0pt] internet. This is critical not only at the enterprise level, but also for personal use. LLMs
[p0257-l0013] [10.0pt] can boost productivity, but privacy and safety concerns can’t be ignored.
[p0257-l0014] [10.0pt] Fortunately, as you’ve seen in earlier chapters, there are alternatives to third-party
[p0257-l0015] [10.0pt] online models and services, both for individuals who want private AI assistants and for
[p0257-l0016] [10.0pt] companies that need secure tools for employees. These alternatives extend beyond
[p0257-l0017] [10.0pt] open source small language models; there are also ways to serve models on a user’s lap­
[p0257-l0018] [10.0pt] top and higher-level tools to interact with them.
[p0257-l0019] [10.0pt] This chapter explores options for running SLMs locally, safely, and offline on a lap­
[p0257-l0020] [10.0pt] top using only open source components. This doesn’t just apply to running chatbots
[p0257-l0021] [10.0pt] but also to running SLMs for broader tasks, including complex systems such as RAG
[p0257-l0022] [10.0pt] applications.
[p0257-l0023] [12.5pt] 12.2	 Running an LLM locally with Ollama
[p0257-l0024] [10.0pt] We’ll start with Ollama (https://ollama.com/), an application based on llama.cpp
[p0257-l0025] [10.0pt] (a C/C++ library introduced in chapter 6) that lets you interact with LLMs on your
[p0257-l0026] [10.0pt] local computer. You can use any community-created GGUF-format quantized model
[p0257-l0027] [10.0pt] available on the Hugging Face Hub (at the time of writing, more than 45,000 are
[p0257-l0028] [10.0pt] hosted there). You can also convert your own models to the format Ollama expects, as
[p0257-l0029] [10.0pt] explained later in this section. Ollama bundles model weights, configuration, and data
[p0257-l0030] [10.0pt] into a single package defined by a Modelfile, and it optimizes setup details, including
[p0257-l0031] [10.0pt] GPU usage.
[p0257-l0032] [10.0pt] Installing Ollama is straightforward: download the version for your operating sys­
[p0257-l0033] [10.0pt] tem (Windows, macOS, or Linux) from the official website. A Docker image, ollama/
[p0257-l0034] [10.0pt] ollama, is also available on Docker Hub. Once installed, Ollama exposes an API that
[p0257-l0035] [10.0pt] serves the model, so users can interact with it locally, either directly or through a client
[p0257-l0036] [10.0pt] application.
[p0257-l0037] [10.0pt] To run a model, use the run command in a terminal. If the model isn’t installed
[p0257-l0038] [10.0pt] yet, Ollama downloads it first. You can browse the long list of available models on the
[p0257-l0039] [10.0pt] Ollama website (see figure 12.1).
[p0257-l0040] [10.0pt] The list includes not only text models but also vision, multimodal, and embedding
[p0257-l0041] [10.0pt] models. For example, to run the DeepSeek-R1 8B model, use the following command:
[p0257-l0042] [8.0pt] ollama run deepseek-r1:8B

=== PDF page 258 / printed label 237 ===
[p0258-l0001] [9.0pt] 237
[p0258-l0002] [9.0pt] Running an LLM locally with Ollama
[p0258-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 12.1  Ollama’s online model catalog
[p0258-l0004] [10.0pt] The first time you run a model with run, Ollama downloads it from the Ollama repo.
[p0258-l0005] [10.0pt] Subsequent runs start the CLI chat immediately. Figure 12.2 shows an active chat ses­
[p0258-l0006] [10.0pt] sion with the DeepSeek-R1 8B model on macOS.
[p0258-l0007] [10.0pt] All the models in the Ollama repository are quantized, which reduces memory and
[p0258-l0008] [10.0pt] compute requirements compared to the originals. Many can run on a laptop without
[p0258-l0009] [10.0pt] hardware acceleration because they’re optimized for CPUs (assuming you have enough
[p0258-l0010] [10.0pt] RAM). As a rule of thumb, you’ll typically need at least 8 GB of RAM for 7B or 8B mod­
[p0258-l0011] [10.0pt] els, 14 to 16 GB for 13B models, and 32 GB for 33B models.
[p0258-l0012] [10.0pt] If a model isn’t in the Ollama catalog but is hosted on the Hugging Face Hub, you
[p0258-l0013] [10.0pt] can still use the run command to download and run it locally. Just provide the model’s
[p0258-l0014] [10.0pt] Hub URL:
[p0258-l0015] [8.0pt] ollama run hf.co/mlabonne/Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct-abliterated-GGUF

[p0259-l0012] [10.0pt] speed will depend on your laptop’s hardware. To remove models you no longer need,

[p0259-l0018] [10.0pt] accepts HTTP GET requests and returns the list of installed models, such as the CLI

[p0260-l0025] [10.0pt] So far, we’ve seen SLMs served through Ollama from the CLI, which is a suitable option

[p0260-l0027] [10.0pt] to more people, the Ollama open source community has developed an ecosystem of

[p0260-l0033] [10.0pt] ers, interpreters, or related configuration. LocalLLM is a minimal, user-friendly web

[p0260-l0036] [10.0pt] a young project, LocalLLM includes useful features such as switching between local
[p0260-l0037] [10.0pt] models in the UI, support for streaming responses, Markdown and code-block render­
[p0260-l0038] [10.0pt] ing, and a raw-text debug view (particularly helpful when interacting with models such
[p0260-l0039] [10.0pt] as DeepSeek-R1 that use test-time compute). A prerequisite is a local instance of Ollama
[p0260-l0040] [10.0pt] serving the SLMs you want to use.

[p0261-l0016] [10.5pt] 12.2.1	 Importing a custom model into Ollama
[p0261-l0017] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier, there are plenty of GGUF models on the Hugging Face Hub and
[p0261-l0018] [10.0pt] in the Ollama catalog. You may well find a model that fits your needs there, but you

=== PDF page 262 / printed label 241 ===
[p0262-l0001] [9.0pt] 241
[p0262-l0002] [9.0pt] Running an LLM locally with Ollama
[p0262-l0003] [10.0pt] may also want to fine-tune a baseline model on your own private data and make it avail­
[p0262-l0004] [10.0pt] able for chat on your laptop or to a broader group in your organization. Through the
[p0262-l0005] [10.0pt] llama.cpp library, Ollama can convert custom SLMs to the GGUF format and add them
[p0262-l0006] [10.0pt] to a local server for use via the CLI or REST API.
[p0262-l0007] [10.0pt] To convert and import a model, first build llama.cpp locally. Clone the official
[p0262-l0008] [10.0pt] GitHub repo, and install its requirements:
[p0262-l0009] [8.0pt] git clone https://github.com/ggerganov/llama.cpp.git
[p0262-l0010] [8.0pt] cd ./llama.cpp
[p0262-l0011] [8.0pt] pip install -r requirements.txt
[p0262-l0012] [10.0pt] In this example, we assume our custom model is uploaded to the Hugging Face Hub
[p0262-l0013] [10.0pt] and under version control. If the model is only local, you can skip the next step. Install
[p0262-l0014] [10.0pt] Git LFS, and clone the Hugging Face Hub repo that hosts the model and its associated
[p0262-l0015] [10.0pt] files:
[p0262-l0016] [8.0pt] cd ..
[p0262-l0017] [8.0pt] git lfs install
[p0262-l0018] [8.0pt] git clone https://huggingface.co/TechXGenus/starcoder2-3b-instruct
[p0262-l0019] [10.0pt] The model in this example is a version of BigCode’s StarCoder2 3B (an SLM special­
[p0262-l0020] [10.0pt] ized for code generation), fine-tuned on an additional 0.7 billion high-quality code-­
[p0262-l0021] [10.0pt] related tokens.
[p0262-l0022] [10.0pt] After cloning it locally, convert the model to GGUF format using convert_hf_to_
[p0262-l0023] [10.0pt] gguf.py, a Python script in the llama.cpp source code repository:
[p0262-l0024] [8.0pt] mkdir gguf_model
[p0262-l0025] [8.0pt] cd ./llama.cpp
[p0262-l0026] [8.0pt] python convert_hf_to_gguf.py ../starcoder2-3b-instruct/
[p0262-l0027] [10.0pt] ➥--outfile ../gguf_model/starcoder2-3b_instruct.gguf
[p0262-l0028] [10.0pt] This script takes two arguments: the path to the directory where you cloned the origi­
[p0262-l0029] [10.0pt] nal model, and the path and filename for the converted model. After conversion, we
[p0262-l0030] [10.0pt] need to create a Modelfile. A Modelfile describes how to deploy the converted custom
[p0262-l0031] [10.0pt] model to a local Ollama server and serve it for inference. In this case, our Modelfile
[p0262-l0032] [10.0pt] would look like this:
[p0262-l0033] [8.0pt] FROM starcoder2-3b_instruct.gguf
[p0262-l0034] [8.0pt] PARAMETER num_ctx 4096
[p0262-l0035] [8.0pt] TEMPLATE """<|endoftext|>You are an exceptionally intelligent coding
[p0262-l0036] [8.0pt] assistant that consistently delivers accurate and reliable responses to user

[p0264-l0014] [10.5pt] 12.2.2	 User privacy in Ollama
[p0264-l0015] [10.0pt] Once a model has been downloaded locally, Ollama can run completely offline, so
[p0264-l0016] [10.0pt] the user’s laptop doesn’t need to be connected to the internet or a LAN. That’s strong
[p0264-l0017] [10.0pt] evidence for privacy preservation. But what happens if you chat locally with an SLM in
[p0264-l0018] [10.0pt] Ollama while the hosting laptop is online? Does the Ollama server send any informa­
[p0264-l0019] [10.0pt] tion out, and is there anything you should watch for to keep your privacy intact? The
[p0264-l0020] [10.0pt] considerations in this section reflect the latest release available when this chapter was
[p0264-l0021] [10.0pt] written (0.5.13). Please verify it yourself, since future versions of Ollama may behave
[p0264-l0022] [10.0pt] differently.
[p0264-l0023] [10.0pt] A review of Ollama’s current source code, along with packet sniffing of a running
[p0264-l0024] [10.0pt] local instance, shows nothing suspicious. Everything happens on a locally hosted server.
[p0264-l0025] [10.0pt] Still, a few things are worth watching in case they change in the future. The first is
[p0264-l0026] [10.0pt] the updater.go file. The body of the IsNewReleaseAvailable function calls the external
[p0264-l0027] [10.0pt] endpoint https://ollama.com/api/update every 60 minutes, sending anonymized infor­
[p0264-l0028] [10.0pt] mation about the laptop’s operating system, version, and architecture, along with the
[p0264-l0029] [10.0pt] current timestamp. This function runs as part of the regular update check to see whether
[p0264-l0030] [10.0pt] a new release is available for the local configuration. There seems to be no way to dis­
[p0264-l0031] [10.0pt] able this through the local server configuration. The only option is to clone the Ollama
[p0264-l0032] [10.0pt] source code repository locally and comment out the following line in lifecycle.go:
[p0264-l0033] [8.0pt] StartBackgroundUpdaterChecker(ctx, t.UpdateAvailable)
[p0264-l0034] [10.0pt] Then you can build the application locally.
[p0264-l0035] [10.0pt] Another thing to pay attention to is the history file. It’s created in your local Ollama
[p0264-l0036] [10.0pt] installation directory and is updated with every prompt sent to the local models during
[p0264-l0037] [10.0pt] chats. It stores only prompt text, but because prompts may contain sensitive informa­
[p0264-l0038] [10.0pt] tion, you should protect this plaintext (not encrypted) file from unauthorized access by
[p0264-l0039] [10.0pt] intruders or malware.
[p0264-l0040] [10.0pt] You should similarly pay special attention to the Ollama server log file. It’s created
[p0264-l0041] [10.0pt] and updated in the logs subdirectory of your local Ollama installation. It records REST

=== PDF page 265 / printed label 244 ===
[p0265-l0001] [9.0pt] 244
[p0265-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 12  Running on your laptop
[p0265-l0003] [10.0pt] API calls and model use, but it doesn’t include sensitive information. Even so, it’s good
[p0265-l0004] [10.0pt] practice to apply security measures to prevent unauthorized access, because the file
[p0265-l0005] [10.0pt] isn’t encrypted.
[p0265-l0006] [10.0pt] In short, Ollama seems to preserve user privacy during local-model inference and
[p0265-l0007] [10.0pt] chat, even when the laptop is connected to the web.
[p0265-l0008] [10.0pt] That concludes our look at the Ollama tool. We’ll return to it in the next chapter
[p0265-l0009] [10.0pt] where we’ll explore end-to-end solutions that use small language models.

[p0267-l0016] [10.0pt] need connectivity to download the model.
[p0267-l0017] [10.0pt] LM Studio 0.3.10 introduced speculative decoding (for models in GGUF or MLX for­
[p0267-l0018] [10.0pt] mats). This inference optimization was proposed in the “Fast Inference from Trans­
[p0267-l0019] [10.0pt] formers via Speculative Decoding” paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.17192). In
[p0267-l0020] [10.0pt] LLMs, it speeds up generation by drafting multiple future tokens in parallel and then
[p0267-l0021] [10.0pt] having a larger model verify them.

=== PDF page 268 / printed label 247 ===
[p0268-l0001] [9.0pt] 247
[p0268-l0002] [9.0pt] Running an LLM locally with LM Studio
[p0268-l0003] [10.0pt] Speculative decoding runs two models side by side: a large target LLM and a smaller,
[p0268-l0004] [10.0pt] faster draft model. Both models must use the same tokenizer. The draft model gener­
[p0268-l0005] [10.0pt] ates candidate text, and the target model accepts or rejects those tokens to produce
[p0268-l0006] [10.0pt] the final output. Because Transformer models can evaluate many tokens at once while
[p0268-l0007] [10.0pt] predicting the next one, speculative decoding uses that capability to reduce generation
[p0268-l0008] [10.0pt] time while preserving quality.
[p0268-l0009] [10.0pt] In LM Studio, speculative decoding works like this:
[p0268-l0010] [10.0pt] 1	 The draft model runs, quickly predicting the next few tokens as a draft.
[p0268-l0011] [10.0pt] 2	 The target model confirms or rejects each draft token, accepting only those it
[p0268-l0012] [10.0pt] would have generated itself.
[p0268-l0013] [10.0pt] This can speed up generation (when enough tokens are accepted) without degrading
[p0268-l0014] [10.0pt] quality. But if tokens are often rejected, total generation will likely slow down. Model
[p0268-l0015] [10.0pt] choice matters: besides sharing a tokenizer, the draft model should be much smaller
[p0268-l0016] [10.0pt] than the target model and from the same family.
[p0268-l0017] [10.0pt] Let’s walk through an example of speculative decoding in LM Studio. We’ll use
[p0268-l0018] [10.0pt] Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (4-bit quantized) as the target model and Llama 3.2 1B Instruct
[p0268-l0019] [10.0pt] (4-bit quantized) as the draft model. If you’ve downloaded them locally (via the lms CLI
[p0268-l0020] [10.0pt] or the Mission Control panel in the LM Studio desktop app), you can select them in the
[p0268-l0021] [10.0pt] Speculative Decoding panel at the bottom right of the chat view (see figure 12.7).
[p0268-l0022] [8.0pt] Figure 12.7  The LM Studio’s Speculative Decoding panel
[p0268-l0023] [10.0pt] Once both models have been selected, turn on the Visualize Accepted Draft Tokens
[p0268-l0024] [10.0pt] switch in the Speculative Decoding panel to see colored tokens showing whether they
[p0268-l0025] [10.0pt] were generated by the draft model or the target model. You can then start a chat as
[p0268-l0026] [10.0pt] usual in the user view. The only changes you’ll notice are draft-model tokens high­
[p0268-l0027] [10.0pt] lighted in green (see figure 12.8) and faster content generation.

=== PDF page 269 / printed label 248 ===
[p0269-l0001] [9.0pt] 248
[p0269-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 12  Running on your laptop
[p0269-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 12.8  Speculative Decoding in action with the Llama 3.2 3B Instruct (target) and Llama 3.2 1B Instruct
[p0269-l0004] [8.0pt] (draft) models in LM Studio
[p0269-l0005] [10.0pt] Benchmarks with these models on a MacBook Air M1 show a slower ramp-up: first-­
[p0269-l0006] [10.0pt] token generation with the larger model takes almost twice as long. Still, the average
[p0269-l0007] [10.0pt] time only increases from about 1.5 seconds to 3 seconds, and generating 500 tokens is
[p0269-l0008] [10.0pt] faster overall. With speculative decoding, you can cut total time by about 30% (roughly
[p0269-l0009] [10.0pt] 9 to 10 seconds). Speculative decoding can be used through the REST API or program­
[p0269-l0010] [10.0pt] matically via LM Studio’s Python SDK.
[p0269-l0011] [12.5pt] 12.4	 The LM Studio Python SDK
[p0269-l0012] [10.0pt] LM Studio’s Python SDK is an open source library (https://github.com/lmstudio-ai/
[p0269-l0013] [10.0pt] lmstudio-python), and it’s available on PyPI:
[p0269-l0014] [8.0pt] pip install lmstudio
[p0269-l0015] [10.0pt] This library lets you interact with models served by the LM Studio server from Python
[p0269-l0016] [10.0pt] clients, Jupyter notebooks, or the Python REPL. Anything you can do in the UI, you

=== PDF page 270 / printed label 249 ===
[p0270-l0001] [9.0pt] 249
[p0270-l0002] [9.0pt] The LM Studio Python SDK
[p0270-l0003] [10.0pt] can do programmatically with this SDK. It provides a synchronous convenience API
[p0270-l0004] [10.0pt] and a scoped resource API that uses with statements for deterministic cleanup of net­
[p0270-l0005] [10.0pt] work resources. The convenience API works well for a CLI or notebook cells. For larger
[p0270-l0006] [10.0pt] applications, use the scoped API so context managers reliably close connections and
[p0270-l0007] [10.0pt] other allocated resources.
[p0270-l0008] [10.0pt] Let’s see how this API works by walking through examples for chat, text completion,
[p0270-l0009] [10.0pt] embedding generation, and agentic flow. For the code examples in this section, we’ll
[p0270-l0010] [10.0pt] assume an LM Studio API server is running locally and a model is loaded and ready to
[p0270-l0011] [10.0pt] accept requests (here, the Llama 3.2 3B Instruct 4-bit quantized version from the LM
[p0270-l0012] [10.0pt] Studio online catalog). You can chat with the loaded model using the API with the fol­
[p0270-l0013] [10.0pt] lowing very high-level code:
[p0270-l0014] [8.0pt] import lmstudio as lms
[p0270-l0015] [8.0pt] model = lms.llm('llama-3.2-3b-instruct')
[p0270-l0016] [8.0pt] print(model.respond("What is the meaning of life?"))
[p0270-l0017] [10.0pt] As you can see, we specified the model ID and then called its respond method. The
[p0270-l0018] [10.0pt] returned value is a PredictionResult instance whose content attribute contains the
[p0270-l0019] [10.0pt] generated text.
[p0270-l0020] [10.0pt] You can do the same through the scoped resource API as follows:
[p0270-l0021] [8.0pt] import lmstudio as lms
[p0270-l0022] [8.0pt] with lms.Client() as client:
[p0270-l0023] [8.0pt]     model = client.llm.model("llama-3.2-3b-instruct")
[p0270-l0024] [8.0pt]     result = model.respond("What is the meaning of life?")
[p0270-l0025] [8.0pt]     print(result)
[p0270-l0026] [8.0pt] Inferencing parameters can be passed to the respond method. Example:
[p0270-l0027] [8.0pt] result = model.respond("What is the meaning of life?", config={
[p0270-l0028] [8.0pt]     "temperature": 0.2,
[p0270-l0029] [8.0pt]     "maxTokens": 200,
[p0270-l0030] [8.0pt] })
[p0270-l0031] [10.0pt] With either approach, you can stream the chat response by calling respond_stream
[p0270-l0032] [10.0pt] instead of respond.
[p0270-l0033] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll manage a chat context. The model receives a multiturn conversation as
[p0270-l0034] [10.0pt] input and predicts the assistant’s response. First, create a chat with an initial system
[p0270-l0035] [10.0pt] prompt using the Chat helper class:
[p0270-l0036] [8.0pt] chat = lms.Chat("You are a helpful assistant.")
[p0270-l0037] [10.0pt] Then, within an infinite while loop, we’ll implement the code that handles chat turns
[p0270-l0038] [10.0pt] between the model and a human user.

=== PDF page 271 / printed label 250 ===
[p0271-l0001] [9.0pt] 250
[p0271-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 12  Running on your laptop
[p0271-l0003] [9.0pt] Listing 12.1  Managing a chat context with the LM Studio Python API
[p0271-l0004] [8.0pt] while True:
[p0271-l0005] [8.0pt]     try:
[p0271-l0006] [8.0pt]         user_input = input("You (leave blank to exit): ")
[p0271-l0007] [8.0pt]     except EOFError:
[p0271-l0008] [8.0pt]         print()
[p0271-l0009] [8.0pt]         break

[p0271-l0011] [8.0pt]         break
[p0271-l0012] [8.0pt]     chat.add_user_message(user_input)
[p0271-l0013] [8.0pt]     prediction_stream = model.respond_stream(
[p0271-l0014] [8.0pt]         chat,

[p0271-l0016] [8.0pt]     )
[p0271-l0017] [8.0pt]     print("Bot: ", end="", flush=True)

[p0271-l0019] [8.0pt]         print(fragment.content, end="", flush=True)
[p0271-l0020] [8.0pt]     print()
[p0271-l0021] [10.0pt] When it’s your turn, the script pauses for input. The model’s responses are streamed
[p0271-l0022] [10.0pt] via the respond_stream method. To end the chat and stop the script, press Enter on an
[p0271-l0023] [10.0pt] empty prompt.
[p0271-l0024] [10.0pt] This SDK also supports text completion. To do this, call complete on your chosen
[p0271-l0025] [10.0pt] model, as shown here:
[p0271-l0026] [8.0pt] result = model.complete("Today is Friday and", config={"maxTokens": 200})
[p0271-l0027] [10.0pt] You can generate embeddings for input text programmatically with this SDK. First,
[p0271-l0028] [10.0pt] you need an embedding model downloaded locally and served. By default, LM Studio
[p0271-l0029] [10.0pt] Server includes Nomic AI’s Nomic Embed Text v1.5, but you can choose a different
[p0271-l0030] [10.0pt] embedding model.
[p0271-l0031] [10.0pt] To convert a prompt into a vector, pass it to the embed method on the appropriate
[p0271-l0032] [10.0pt] embedding model handle:
[p0271-l0033] [8.0pt] import lmstudio as lms
[p0271-l0034] [8.0pt] model = lms.embedding_model("nomic-embed-text-v1.5")
[p0271-l0035] [8.0pt] embedding = model.embed("A fancy prompt!")
[p0271-l0036] [10.0pt] One interesting feature of this Python SDK is the ability to set up an agentic flow.
[p0271-l0037] [10.0pt] Instead of using an SLM in a simple text-in/text-out fashion, you can ask the model
[p0271-l0038] [10.0pt] to call a tool (or a set of tools) and handle the returned output. The LM Studio SDK
[p0271-l0039] [10.0pt] introduced the concept of execution rounds, which describe the cycle of running a tool,
[p0271-l0040] [10.0pt] passing its output to an LLM, and letting the LLM choose the next step. The model
[p0271-l0041] [10.0pt] can repeat this cycle multiple times before returning a final result.
[p0271-l0042] [10.0pt] The act function in the LM Studio SDK implements automatic, multi-round tool
[p0271-l0043] [10.0pt] calling. Let’s look at a basic example. Assume we’ve implemented a regular Python

=== PDF page 272 / printed label 251 ===
[p0272-l0001] [9.0pt] 251
[p0272-l0002] [9.0pt] Running an LLM locally with Jan
[p0272-l0003] [10.0pt] function that performs some actions, given inputs, and returns a result. For example,
[p0272-l0004] [10.0pt] the function could take two floats as input, multiply them, and return the result:
[p0272-l0005] [8.0pt] def multiply(a: float, b: float) → float:
[p0272-l0006] [8.0pt]     return a * b
[p0272-l0007] [10.0pt] We pick up a model available in the local server as usual:
[p0272-l0008] [8.0pt] import lmstudio as lms
[p0272-l0009] [8.0pt] model = lms.llm("llama-3.2-3b-instruct")
[p0272-l0010] [10.0pt] We can then call the act function for it, passing a prompt and the tool function
[p0272-l0011] [10.0pt] (multiply):
[p0272-l0012] [8.0pt] model.act(
[p0272-l0013] [8.0pt]   "What is the result of 123 multiplied by 456?",
[p0272-l0014] [8.0pt]   [multiply],
[p0272-l0015] [8.0pt]   on_message=print,
[p0272-l0016] [8.0pt] )
[p0272-l0017] [10.0pt] In the preceding code, we pass a list of tools, so you can provide multiple tool functions
[p0272-l0018] [10.0pt] for a single act call. Based on the prompt, the model decides which tool(s) to use.
[p0272-l0019] [10.0pt] Our example tool is intentionally simple, but a tool function can run any Python code,
[p0272-l0020] [10.0pt] including access to the web, local files and applications, and databases. Design tools
[p0272-l0021] [10.0pt] defensively: validate inputs, handle failures, and plan for misuse.
[p0272-l0022] [10.0pt] An agentic workflow’s performance depends on the model you choose, so evaluate
[p0272-l0023] [10.0pt] candidate SLMs (or create evaluation tasks for custom-tuned SLMs) before you make
[p0272-l0024] [10.0pt] your final choice. We’ll discuss agentic workflows further in chapters 13 and 14.
[p0272-l0025] [12.5pt] 12.5	 Running an LLM locally with Jan
[p0272-l0026] [10.0pt] The third tool we’ll explore is Jan (https://github.com/janhq/jan). Like Ollama, it’s
[p0272-l0027] [10.0pt] 100% open source and shares most of the same features as Ollama and LM Studio. Like
[p0272-l0028] [10.0pt] LM Studio, Jan provides a desktop app (macOS, Linux, and Windows) that lets you
[p0272-l0029] [10.0pt] chat with local models and models hosted behind major commercial APIs (OpenAI,
[p0272-l0030] [10.0pt] ­Anthropic, Groq, Google, OpenRouter, and others). We’ll focus on local models here.
[p0272-l0031] [10.0pt] As with the other tools we’ve looked at, you don’t need to be online to chat with local
[p0272-l0032] [10.0pt] LLMs. You only need an internet connection to download a model the first time or to
[p0272-l0033] [10.0pt] connect the Jan desktop app to a cloud API.
[p0272-l0034] [10.0pt] The Jan UI is simpler than the LM Studio’s UI. After downloading and installing the
[p0272-l0035] [10.0pt] version for your operating system, start the app to see the chat view (see figure 12.9).
[p0272-l0036] [10.0pt] The center pane is the chat area: the prompt box (and an area for optional RAG file
[p0272-l0037] [10.0pt] uploads) is at the bottom, and the message history is above. As shown in the figure,
[p0272-l0038] [10.0pt] responses are well formatted, and generated code includes syntax highlighting and
[p0272-l0039] [10.0pt] allows easy copy-and-paste.

[p0273-l0007] [10.0pt] You can download local models from the Jan Hub, the default online catalog, or the
[p0273-l0008] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Hub. Models must be in GGUF format, which is the only format Jan sup­

[p0273-l0013] [10.0pt] models that will run slowly or need more memory than you have. At the top of the

[p0273-l0017] [10.0pt] click Import Model, select the local GGUF file, choose whether to create a symbolic link
[p0273-l0018] [10.0pt] or copy the file into Jan’s directory, and click Import.
[p0273-l0019] [10.0pt] Like Ollama and LM Studio, Jan includes a built-in API server that’s compatible with
[p0273-l0020] [10.0pt] the OpenAI API specification, so you can interact with local models over HTTP. The
[p0273-l0021] [10.0pt] server isn’t started by default: in the Jan desktop app, open the Local API Server view, and
[p0273-l0022] [10.0pt] click Start Server to expose the REST API to other local client applications. The server
[p0273-l0023] [10.0pt] listens on port 1337 by default, but you can change it (and other settings) in the UI.

[p0274-l0002] [9.0pt] The Cortex local LLM engine
[p0274-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 12.10  The model selection panel in the Jan desktop app
[p0274-l0004] [10.0pt] Unlike LM Studio (or Ollama when using a third-party frontend), Jan can’t run the
[p0274-l0005] [10.0pt] API server while you chat with a model in the UI; the two modes are mutually exclusive.
[p0274-l0006] [12.5pt] 12.6	 The Cortex local LLM engine
[p0274-l0007] [10.0pt] The Jan application and its built-in API server are powered by Cortex (https://github
[p0274-l0008] [10.0pt] .com/janhq/cortex.cpp), an open source local AI engine written in C++. Cortex lets
[p0274-l0009] [10.0pt] you switch inference backends (llama.cpp by default, or ONNX Runtime). It supports
[p0274-l0010] [10.0pt] GPUs and tries to use one by default when running a model (NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel
[p0274-l0011] [10.0pt] are supported). Quantized models are available from the Hugging Face Hub or bun­
[p0274-l0012] [10.0pt] dled with Cortex; the supported model list is the same as Jan’s (see https://cortex.so/
[p0274-l0013] [10.0pt] models/). Cortex supports multiple quantization modes per model, so several versions
[p0274-l0014] [10.0pt] of the same SLM may be available. TypeScript and Python client libraries are in prog­
[p0274-l0015] [10.0pt] ress; the Python client isn’t released yet.
[p0274-l0016] [10.0pt] You can install the Cortex engine as a standalone local LLM engine or as part of Jan.
[p0274-l0017] [10.0pt] After Cortex is installed, use the cortex CLI to start the server:
[p0274-l0018] [8.0pt] cortex start
[p0274-l0019] [10.0pt] The default port is 39281. The API documentation is available from a web browser at
[p0274-l0020] [10.0pt] http://127.0.0.1:39281. An HTTP GET request to the engines endpoint displays the
[p0274-l0021] [10.0pt] list of installed engines:

[p0275-l0004] [8.0pt]   --url http://127.0.0.1:39281/v1/engines
[p0275-l0005] [10.0pt] The output of the request would look like this:
[p0275-l0006] [8.0pt] {"llama-cpp":[{"engine":"llama-cpp",

[p0275-l0014] [10.0pt] When you start the server for the first time, no LLM is installed by default. You’ll need

[p0275-l0022] [8.0pt]   --data '{"model": "tinyllama:1b"}'
[p0275-l0023] [10.0pt] Once the model finishes downloading, it’s ready to chat. Start a chat session with the

[p0277-l0057] [10.0pt] ports GGUF and Apple MLX models for local inference.

[p0279-l0001] [30.0pt] Creating end-to-end
[p0279-l0002] [30.0pt] LLM applications
[p0279-l0003] [225.0pt] 13
[p0279-l0004] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0279-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ Why standalone SLMs/LLMs aren’t always
[p0279-l0006] [9.8pt] enough
[p0279-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Building a RAG system that uses only SLMs
[p0279-l0008] [9.8pt] ¡ Building an agentic AI with SLMs
[p0279-l0009] [10.0pt] So far, we’ve looked at strategies for optimizing small language models (SLMs) to
[p0279-l0010] [10.0pt] run on available hardware while maintaining acceptable quality. Throughout, we
[p0279-l0011] [10.0pt] have focused on a common pattern: an SLM receives a prompt, generates task-­
[p0279-l0012] [10.0pt] specific output, and returns a result to the client application or user. This is a fre­
[p0279-l0013] [10.0pt] quent scenario, but it’s not the only way to use language models. They often deliver
[p0279-l0014] [10.0pt] more business value as part of a larger system.
[p0279-l0015] [10.0pt] In this chapter, we’ll explore two popular LLM-based system paradigms: retrieval-­
[p0279-l0016] [10.0pt] augmented generation (RAG) and agentic AI. The difference here is that we’ll build
[p0279-l0017] [10.0pt] on domain-specific small models only, which offers benefits for privacy, safety, secu­
[p0279-l0018] [10.0pt] rity, specificity, and cost savings.
[p0279-l0019] [9.0pt] 258

=== PDF page 280 / printed label 259 ===
[p0280-l0001] [9.0pt] 259
[p0280-l0002] [9.0pt] Why LLMs alone aren’t enough
[p0280-l0003] [12.5pt] 13.1	 Why LLMs alone aren’t enough
[p0280-l0004] [10.0pt] In early 2023, large tech organizations started rushing to “win” the LLM race and reach
[p0280-l0005] [10.0pt] so-called AGI (artificial general intelligence), fueled by daily hype. That push contin­
[p0280-l0006] [10.0pt] ued through 2024 and early 2025 and led to larger and larger language models, based
[p0280-l0007] [10.0pt] on the assumption that more data and more compute (and lately also time-scale com­
[p0280-l0008] [10.0pt] pute) would make these models reason like humans across a wide range of tasks, rather
[p0280-l0009] [10.0pt] than excel at a single narrow task (or a small set), as with today’s ML/AI. The reality
[p0280-l0010] [10.0pt] is that, because of their architecture, language models based on Transformer variants
[p0280-l0011] [10.0pt] won’t converge to AGI. They are, however, useful for narrow but nontrivial tasks when
[p0280-l0012] [10.0pt] tuned on high-quality domain-specific datasets or integrated into a broader system.
[p0280-l0013] [10.0pt] For example, imagine we are a Formula 1 racing team. Our goal is to design and
[p0280-l0014] [10.0pt] build a car that can compete in the Formula 1 World Championship, win races, and
[p0280-l0015] [10.0pt] possibly win the drivers’ or constructors’ title. The engine is a core component, but at
[p0280-l0016] [10.0pt] design time, we don’t try to build the best engine possible; we choose the best fit for the
[p0280-l0017] [10.0pt] car we have in mind. We need to consider many other factors, such as the mechanical
[p0280-l0018] [10.0pt] parts, electronics, and tires, because how well these work together is key to success (see
[p0280-l0019] [10.0pt] figure 13.1). We also need to follow the official rules established by the FIA (Fédération
[p0280-l0020] [10.0pt] Internationale de l’Automobile) for Formula 1 constructors.
[p0280-l0021] [10.0pt] NOTE  Figures 13.1 and 13.2 were generated using the Ikea Instructions LoRA
[p0280-l0022] [10.0pt] for the Stable Diffusion XL Base model. The LoRA weights are available in Hug­
[p0280-l0023] [10.0pt] ging Face Hub at https://huggingface.co/ostris/ikea-instructions-lora-sdxl.
[p0280-l0024] [8.0pt] Figure 13.1  A sample
[p0280-l0025] [8.0pt] business goal for our imaginary
[p0280-l0026] [8.0pt] Formula 1 racing team: build
[p0280-l0027] [8.0pt] a competitive car, where the
[p0280-l0028] [8.0pt] engine is important but not the
[p0280-l0029] [8.0pt] only component

=== PDF page 281 / printed label 260 ===
[p0281-l0001] [9.0pt] 260
[p0281-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 13  Creating end-to-end LLM applications
[p0281-l0003] [10.0pt] Now think of the engine as a language model and the car as the final system built
[p0281-l0004] [10.0pt] around it to meet a business goal. The model takes user inputs through an interface
[p0281-l0005] [10.0pt] (web or desktop). Those inputs are often enriched with data from other sources (for
[p0281-l0006] [10.0pt] example, a database or document management system) to provide context. The model
[p0281-l0007] [10.0pt] then generates content that may need postprocessing with external tools so it can be
[p0281-l0008] [10.0pt] formatted and delivered to users or downstream systems. When designing such a sys­
[p0281-l0009] [10.0pt] tem, we’ll also consider scalability, reliability, and security. The business value doesn’t
[p0281-l0010] [10.0pt] come from the model alone, but from the system as a whole. That’s one reason to
[p0281-l0011] [10.0pt] choose smaller models that can be specialized for the goal and work well with the other
[p0281-l0012] [10.0pt] components. In many industries, as in Formula 1, real-world tech projects (including
[p0281-l0013] [10.0pt] those with ML/AI components) must meet regulations. Compliance is easier when we
[p0281-l0014] [10.0pt] control the full stack, including a tailored SLM bundled into the system.
[p0281-l0015] [10.0pt] The preceding scenario resonates with professionals in any industry, not just tech­
[p0281-l0016] [10.0pt] nology. Since ChatGPT’s release, companies such as OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI,
[p0281-l0017] [10.0pt] and Meta have followed a pattern that, to continue the Formula 1 analogy, resembles
[p0281-l0018] [10.0pt] the one shown in figure 13.2.
[p0281-l0019] [8.0pt] Figure 13.2  A pattern that’s sure to fail in Formula 1: building a mammoth engine, putting it on wheels,
[p0281-l0020] [8.0pt] and ignoring integration with other components and the team’s core scope

=== PDF page 282 / printed label 261 ===
[p0282-l0001] [9.0pt] 261
[p0282-l0002] [9.0pt] Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
[p0282-l0003] [10.0pt] In this scenario, the Formula 1 team focuses only on the engine and may even out­
[p0282-l0004] [10.0pt] source its design to an organization that ignores the rest of the car. It delivers a huge,
[p0282-l0005] [10.0pt] powerful engine that doesn’t fit, and integration with the other components becomes
[p0282-l0006] [10.0pt] a nightmare. This car will not compete for the world championship, and you can’t
[p0282-l0007] [10.0pt] blame FIA regulations for the failure. This is what many big tech companies have done
[p0282-l0008] [10.0pt] (and are still doing): training ever-larger models, pouring money and compute into a
[p0282-l0009] [10.0pt] race toward AGI on the wrong architecture.
[p0282-l0010] [10.0pt] Don’t get me wrong: large models work well for general-domain, routine tasks such
[p0282-l0011] [10.0pt] as text classification and summarization. But to improve performance, prompt engi­
[p0282-l0012] [10.0pt] neering can’t be the only answer. We also need to integrate external knowledge, and
[p0282-l0013] [10.0pt] that integration can be costly and difficult because of safety, privacy, security, and other
[p0282-l0014] [10.0pt] industry-specific regulations, even for trivial tasks.
[p0282-l0015] [12.5pt] 13.2	 Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
[p0282-l0016] [10.0pt] I briefly introduced retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) in chapter 2, but in this
[p0282-l0017] [10.0pt] section (and the next chapter), we’ll go deeper, looking at it from different angles and
[p0282-l0018] [10.0pt] seeing how we can avoid common pitfalls. All the examples in this section will use open
[p0282-l0019] [10.0pt] source SLMs for both retrieval and generation.
[p0282-l0020] [10.0pt] More than one Python framework is available for implementing RAG. In this first
[p0282-l0021] [10.0pt] example, we’ll implement it using specific packages for different tasks (PDF parsing
[p0282-l0022] [10.0pt] and content extraction, embedding and generator model handling, vector storage,
[p0282-l0023] [10.0pt] etc.) without a dedicated RAG framework, so we can focus on understanding the vari­
[p0282-l0024] [10.0pt] ous steps and their challenges. We’ll make things more complex in later examples.
[p0282-l0025] [10.0pt] RAG enhances language models by integrating external knowledge bases. Although
[p0282-l0026] [10.0pt] large models are powerful, they bring significant cost and integration challenges. SLMs
[p0282-l0027] [10.0pt] are a more resource-efficient alternative, especially for industry-specific tasks. In a RAG
[p0282-l0028] [10.0pt] system, language models not only generate content but also convert large volumes of
[p0282-l0029] [10.0pt] unstructured text and user prompts into embeddings (see figure 13.3). Using smaller
[p0282-l0030] [10.0pt] models drastically reduces the cost of these conversions.
[p0282-l0031] [10.0pt] In figure 13.3, we can see two phases in a RAG system: offline and online. Offline,
[p0282-l0032] [10.0pt] the raw document corpus is chunked into smaller text segments and transformed into
[p0282-l0033] [10.0pt] embeddings by an embedding model. Those embeddings are stored in a vector data­
[p0282-l0034] [10.0pt] base, with indexes built on top to speed up search. This phase runs when you first set
[p0282-l0035] [10.0pt] up the RAG system and whenever documents are added, removed, or updated in the
[p0282-l0036] [10.0pt] knowledge base. Online, whenever a user submits a query, the query is embedded and
[p0282-l0037] [10.0pt] used to look up semantically similar document chunks in the vector database. The
[p0282-l0038] [10.0pt] retrieved chunks add context to the query and are passed to the generator model,
[p0282-l0039] [10.0pt] which produces an answer.
[p0282-l0040] [10.0pt] Let’s start with a simple use case where we have a single PDF document to query.
[p0282-l0041] [10.0pt] To extract content from the PDF, we’ll use PyMuPDF (https://github.com/pymupdf/
[p0282-l0042] [10.0pt] PyMuPDF), an open source Python library for extracting data from PDF documents
[p0282-l0043] [10.0pt] as well as analyzing, converting, and manipulating them (recent versions also handle

[p0287-l0046] [8.0pt] of tasks like open-ended text generation have become the bottleneck for
[p0287-l0047] [8.0pt] inference throughput in existing systems. To this end, frameworks like vLLM
[p0287-l0048] [8.0pt] [4] powered by PagedAttention and research systems like Orca [5] have
[p0287-l0049] [8.0pt] significantly improved the performance of inference for LLMs. However,
[p0287-l0050] [8.0pt] these systems still struggle to provide consistent quality of service,
[p0287-l0051] [8.0pt] particularly for workloads with longer prompts. These long prompt workloads
[p0287-l0052] [8.0pt] are becoming increasingly important as more and more models, like MPT-
[p0287-l0053] [8.0pt] StoryWriter [6], and systems, such as DeepSpeed Ulysses [7], 1
[p0287-l0054] [8.0pt] arXiv:2401.08671v1 [cs. PF] 9 Jan 2024',

[p0288-l0002] [9.0pt] Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
[p0288-l0003] [8.0pt]   'chunk_char_count': 1022,
[p0288-l0004] [8.0pt]   'chunk_word_count': 150,
[p0288-l0005] [8.0pt]   'chunk_token_count': 255.5}]
[p0288-l0006] [10.0pt] The embedding process (shown  in figure 13.3) uses sentence-transformers (https://
[p0288-l0007] [10.0pt] github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers/), a Python open source library that
[p0288-l0008] [10.0pt] computes dense vector representations for sentences, paragraphs, and images. It pro­
[p0288-l0009] [10.0pt] vides BERT-family models (encoder-only Transformer architecture) hosted on the
[p0288-l0010] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Hub. The model embeds text into a vector space so that similar texts are
[p0288-l0011] [10.0pt] close together, which makes retrieval more efficient using cosine similarity or another
[p0288-l0012] [10.0pt] metric.
[p0288-l0013] [10.0pt] First, we need to download the chosen embedding model:
[p0288-l0014] [8.0pt] from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
[p0288-l0015] [8.0pt] embedding_model = SentenceTransformer(
[p0288-l0016] [8.0pt]             model_name_or_path="all-mpnet-base-v2",
[p0288-l0017] [8.0pt]             device="cpu")
[p0288-l0018] [10.0pt] In this example, we’ve selected all-mpnet-base-v2 (https://huggingface.co/sentence
[p0288-l0019] [10.0pt] -transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2), a sentence-embedding model that maps sentences
[p0288-l0020] [10.0pt] and paragraphs to a 768-dimensional vector space. The model is fine-tuned on a 1B
[p0288-l0021] [10.0pt] sentence-pair dataset using a contrastive learning objective for tasks such as cluster­
[p0288-l0022] [10.0pt] ing and semantic search. If they aren’t already on disk, the model checkpoints are
[p0288-l0023] [10.0pt] downloaded from the Hugging Face Hub and loaded into memory; this code example
[p0288-l0024] [10.0pt] doesn’t require hardware acceleration.
[p0288-l0025] [10.0pt] NOTE  With contrastive learning, the model is trained to maximize the similar­
[p0288-l0026] [10.0pt] ity between positive pairs and minimize it between negative pairs. Positive pairs
[p0288-l0027] [10.0pt] are two different views of the same instance, while negative pairs are views from
[p0288-l0028] [10.0pt] different instances. This is becoming a new trend for specializing small embed­
[p0288-l0029] [10.0pt] ding models used in RAG systems.
[p0288-l0030] [10.0pt] Finally, we can apply the model to each chunk to generate embeddings (the embed­
[p0288-l0031] [10.0pt] dings block in figure 13.3) and store them under a new dictionary key named
[p0288-l0032] [10.0pt] embedding:
[p0288-l0033] [8.0pt] embedding_model.to("cpu")
[p0288-l0034] [8.0pt] for item in tqdm(pages_and_chunks):
[p0288-l0035] [8.0pt]     item["embedding"] = embedding_model.encode(item["sentence_chunk"])
[p0288-l0036] [10.0pt] A RAG system typically uses a vector database (the vector store in figure 13.3) to store
[p0288-l0037] [10.0pt] and index document embeddings for faster, scalable search. We’ll cover vector storage
[p0288-l0038] [10.0pt] later in this section.

[p0290-l0002] [9.0pt] Combining a domain-specific SLM with RAG
[p0290-l0003] [10.0pt] We’ll use the all-mpnet-base-v2 embedding model to embed the query in the same
[p0290-l0004] [10.0pt] vector space as the document text (see the query embedding block in figure 13.3). We
[p0290-l0005] [10.0pt] must embed the prompts with the same model we used to build the knowledge base:
[p0290-l0006] [8.0pt] query_embedding = embedding_model.encode(query, convert_to_tensor=True)
[p0290-l0007] [10.0pt] Given this query, the ideal results should include information about the blocked
[p0290-l0008] [10.0pt] KV-caching strategy described in the original paper. We’ll use similarity search. Unlike
[p0290-l0009] [10.0pt] keyword-­based text search, similarity search compares vectors, so the final results
[p0290-l0010] [10.0pt] include not only the words in the query string but also other text that matches the
[p0290-l0011] [10.0pt] query’s meaning. Both the Sentence Transformers library and the PyTorch framework
[p0290-l0012] [10.0pt] include built-in methods for finding similar vectors.
[p0290-l0013] [10.0pt] In this example, we’ll use the Sentence Transformers API, since we’re already using
[p0290-l0014] [10.0pt] this library for embedding text. The most popular algorithms for this type of search
[p0290-l0015] [10.0pt] (also built into most vector databases) are
[p0290-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Dot product—The dot product measures the magnitude and direction between
[p0290-l0017] [10.0pt] two vectors. Vectors aligned in direction and magnitude have a higher positive
[p0290-l0018] [10.0pt] value, while opposite vectors have a higher negative value.
[p0290-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ Cosine similarity—With cosine similarity, vectors are normalized by magnitude,
[p0290-l0020] [10.0pt] Euclidean norm, or L2 norm, so that they have unit length, and they are com­
[p0290-l0021] [10.0pt] pared by direction. Vectors aligned in direction score close to 1, while vectors in
[p0290-l0022] [10.0pt] opposite directions score close to -1.
[p0290-l0023] [10.0pt] Cosine similarity is typically used for text similarity because it measures semantic
[p0290-l0024] [10.0pt] similarity (via direction). But because we embedded our document with the all-mpnet
[p0290-l0025] [10.0pt] -base-v2 model, which always returns normalized outputs, cosine similarity and dot
[p0290-l0026] [10.0pt] product return the same results.
[p0290-l0027] [10.0pt] Let’s try cosine similarity and take the top five scores:
[p0290-l0028] [8.0pt] import torch
[p0290-l0029] [8.0pt] from sentence_transformers import util
[p0290-l0030] [8.0pt] cosine_scores = util.cos_sim(a=query_embedding, b=embeddings)[0]
[p0290-l0031] [8.0pt] top_results_cosine_sim = torch.topk(cosine_scores, k=5)
[p0290-l0032] [10.0pt] This query returns the following results:
[p0290-l0033] [8.0pt] torch.return_types.topk(
[p0290-l0034] [8.0pt] values=tensor([0.2963, 0.1960, 0.1868, 0.1395, 0.1132]),
[p0290-l0035] [8.0pt] indices=tensor([ 3,  5, 11, 13, 27]))
[p0290-l0036] [10.0pt] The values here are relevance scores, and the indices are the page numbers for the top
[p0290-l0037] [10.0pt] five returned chunks. The top two results (the highest-scoring ones) relate directly to
[p0290-l0038] [10.0pt] the blocked KV-caching strategy:

[p0291-l0011] [8.0pt] gingFace TGI [9] and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM [10].2.2 Continuous Batching In
[p0291-l0012] [8.0pt] the
[p0291-l0013] [8.0pt] past, dynamic batching, in which a server would wait for multiple requests
[p0291-l0014] [8.0pt] to
[p0291-l0015] [8.0pt] process in phase with each other, was used to improve GPU utilization.
[p0291-l0016] [8.0pt] However,
[p0291-l0017] [8.0pt] this approach has drawbacks, as it typically requires padding inputs to
[p0291-l0018] [8.0pt] identical lengths or stalling the system to wait to construct a larger
[p0291-l0019] [8.0pt] batch.
[p0291-l0020] [8.0pt] Recent advancement in large language model (LLM) inference and serving has
[p0291-l0021] [8.0pt] been
[p0291-l0022] [8.0pt] fo- cusing on fine granularity scheduling and optimizing memory efficiency.
[p0291-l0023] [8.0pt] For
[p0291-l0024] [8.0pt] instance, Orca proposes iteration-level scheduling (also known as
[p0291-l0025] [8.0pt] continuous
[p0291-l0026] [8.0pt] batching) which makes distinct scheduling decisions at each forward pass of
[p0291-l0027] [8.0pt] the
[p0291-l0028] [8.0pt] model. This allows requests to join/leave the batch as needed, eliminating
[p0291-l0029] [8.0pt] the
[p0291-l0030] [8.0pt] need for padding requests thus improving the overall through- put. In addition
[p0291-l0031] [8.0pt] to Orca, continuous batching has been implemented in NVIDIA TRT-LLM,
[p0291-l0032] [8.0pt] HuggingFace
[p0291-l0033] [8.0pt] TGI, and vLLM. In current systems, there are two primary approaches to
[p0291-l0034] [8.0pt] implement
[p0291-l0035] [8.0pt] continuous batching. In TGI and vLLM, the generation phase is preempted to
[p0291-l0036] [8.0pt] perform prompt processing (called infill in TGI) before continuing with
[p0291-l0037] [8.0pt] generation.
[p0291-l0038] [8.0pt] Page number: 2
[p0291-l0039] [8.0pt] Score: 0.1960
[p0291-l0040] [8.0pt] Text:
[p0291-l0041] [8.0pt] doesn't reach a fixed bound. These approaches to varying degrees need to
[p0291-l0042] [8.0pt] stall
[p0291-l0043] [8.0pt] generation to process long prompts (see Section 3.2). We propose a novel
[p0291-l0044] [8.0pt] prompt

[p0294-l0037] [8.0pt]                                           add_generation_prompt=True)
[p0294-l0038] [8.0pt]     return prompt

[p0294-l0041] [10.0pt] them into the base prompt with the user query, applies the model’s chat template, and

[p0295-l0019] [8.0pt] - The blocked KV-cache increases system throughput by increasing the amount
[p0295-l0020] [8.0pt] of potential sequence concurrency by eliminating KV-cache induced memory
[p0295-l0021] [8.0pt] fragmentation. Non-contiguous KV cache implementations are also included in
[p0295-l0022] [8.0pt] Hug- gingFace TGI [9] and NVIDIA TensorRT-LLM [10].2.2 Continuous Batching
[p0295-l0023] [8.0pt] In the past, dynamic batching, in which a server would wait for multiple
[p0295-l0024] [8.0pt] requests to process in phase with each other, was used to improve GPU
[p0295-l0025] [8.0pt] utilization. However, this approach has drawbacks, as it typically requires
[p0295-l0026] [8.0pt] padding inputs to identical lengths or stalling the system to wait to
[p0295-l0027] [8.0pt] construct a larger batch. Recent advancement in large language model (LLM)
[p0295-l0028] [8.0pt] inference and serving has been fo- cusing on fine granularity scheduling
[p0295-l0029] [8.0pt] and optimizing memory efficiency. For instance, Orca proposes iteration-
[p0295-l0030] [8.0pt] level scheduling (also known as continuous batching) which makes distinct
[p0295-l0031] [8.0pt] scheduling decisions at each forward pass of the model. This allows
[p0295-l0032] [8.0pt] requests to join/leave the batch as needed, eliminating the need for
[p0295-l0033] [8.0pt] padding requests thus improving the overall through- put. In addition to
[p0295-l0034] [8.0pt] Orca, continuous batching has been implemented in NVIDIA TRT-LLM,
[p0295-l0035] [8.0pt] HuggingFace TGI, and vLLM. In current systems, there are two primary
[p0295-l0036] [8.0pt] approaches to implement continuous batching. In TGI and vLLM, the
[p0295-l0037] [8.0pt] generation phase is preempted to perform prompt processing (called infill
[p0295-l0038] [8.0pt] in TGI) before continuing with generation.
[p0295-l0039] [8.0pt] - doesn't reach a fixed bound. These approaches to varying degrees need to
[p0295-l0040] [8.0pt] stall generation to process long prompts (see Section 3.2). We propose a
[p0295-l0041] [8.0pt] novel prompt and generation composition strategy, Dynamic SplitFuse dis-
[p0295-l0042] [8.0pt] cussed at length in the next section.3 Dynamic SplitFuse: A Novel Prompt
[p0295-l0043] [8.0pt] and Generation Composition Strategy DeepSpeed-FastGen is built to leverage
[p0295-l0044] [8.0pt] continuous batching and non-contiguous KV caches to enable increased
[p0295-l0045] [8.0pt] occupancy and higher responsivity for serving LLMs in the data center,
[p0295-l0046] [8.0pt] similar to existing frameworks such as TRT-LLM, TGI, and vLLM.iIn order to
[p0295-l0047] [8.0pt] achieve a new level of performance, DeepSpeed-FastGen introduces SplitFuse

[p0296-l0031] [12.5pt] 13.3	 Using a vector database
[p0296-l0032] [10.0pt] In the previous section, we explored a RAG example in which the knowledge base
[p0296-l0033] [10.0pt] was built from a single PDF. In local deployments, where you typically have only a few
[p0296-l0034] [10.0pt] documents—represented by at most a few hundred thousand embeddings—it’s fine
[p0296-l0035] [10.0pt] to persist the embeddings to disk. But to scale up, you’ll want a vector database (often
[p0296-l0036] [10.0pt] called a vector store).
[p0296-l0037] [10.0pt] A vector database stores vectors (fixed-length lists of numbers) along with other data.
[p0296-l0038] [10.0pt] It typically implements one or more approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) algorithms,
[p0296-l0039] [10.0pt] enabling you to search with a query vector and retrieve the closest-matching records.
[p0296-l0040] [10.0pt] These databases have many applications, but since 2024, they’ve become a key compo­
[p0296-l0041] [10.0pt] nent of most RAG systems.
[p0296-l0042] [10.0pt] Many implementations are available, both open source and commercial. These are
[p0296-l0043] [10.0pt] some popular open source vector databases:

[p0297-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Weaviate (https://github.com/weaviate/weaviate)
[p0297-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Milvus (https://github.com/milvus-io/milvus)
[p0297-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ OpenSearch (https://github.com/opensearch-project/OpenSearch)
[p0297-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Chroma (https://github.com/chroma-core/chroma)
[p0297-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ LanceDB (https://github.com/lancedb/lancedb)
[p0297-l0008] [10.0pt] For the examples in this section, we’ll use LanceDB because it’s easy to set up and
[p0297-l0009] [10.0pt] maintain locally, and it scales well when you move to a distributed environment. It’s a
[p0297-l0010] [10.0pt] serverless vector search database with persistent storage that simplifies retrieval, filter­
[p0297-l0011] [10.0pt] ing, and embedding management. It supports vector similarity search, full-text search,
[p0297-l0012] [10.0pt] and SQL, with native Python and JavaScript/TypeScript support. It also supports zero-
[p0297-l0013] [10.0pt] copy data access and automatic versioning without extra infrastructure, and it inte­
[p0297-l0014] [10.0pt] grates with popular LLM frameworks like LangChain and LlamaIndex, as well as data
[p0297-l0015] [10.0pt] libraries such as Apache Arrow, pandas, and Polars.

[p0300-l0016] [8.0pt] Benchmarking Methodology We use two primary quantitative schemes for
[p0300-l0017] [8.0pt] measuring performance.4.1.1 Throughput-Latency Curves Two key metrics for
[p0300-l0018] [8.0pt] production readiness are throughput (measured in requests per second) and
[p0300-l0019] [8.0pt] latency (the responsiveness of each request). To measure this, we
[p0300-l0020] [8.0pt] instantiate multiple clients (ranging from 1 to 32) concurrently and send
[p0300-l0021] [8.0pt] requests (512 in total) to the server. The resulting latency of each
[p0300-l0022] [8.0pt] request is measured at the endpoint and throughput is measured by the end-
[p0300-l0023] [8.0pt] to-end time to complete the experiment.4.1.2 Effective Throughput
[p0300-l0024] [8.0pt] Interactive applications, such as chat applications, can have more

[p0300-l0046] [12.5pt] 13.4	 Building an agent
[p0300-l0047] [10.0pt] Agentic AI was 2025’s big buzzword in the generative AI hype, primarily driven by big
[p0300-l0048] [10.0pt] tech, large consulting firms, and self-proclaimed AI gurus. Although agentic AI is an

=== PDF page 301 / printed label 280 ===
[p0301-l0001] [9.0pt] 280
[p0301-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 13  Creating end-to-end LLM applications
[p0301-l0003] [10.0pt] important way to use language models, many so-called agentic systems are really just
[p0301-l0004] [10.0pt] RPA (robotic process automation) applications that use a model in the usual way: a
[p0301-l0005] [10.0pt] prompt goes in, the model generates output, and the rest of the solution consumes it.
[p0301-l0006] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ll clarify the topic and cover the basics of building an agent locally
[p0301-l0007] [10.0pt] using open source components. Agentic AI is a big subject, so this is a hands-on intro­
[p0301-l0008] [10.0pt] duction; we’ll look at more advanced concepts in the next chapter.
[p0301-l0009] [10.0pt] A language model, large or small, predicts the most likely next token for a given
[p0301-l0010] [10.0pt] prompt. By sampling tokens repeatedly, it can carry on a conversation and handle
[p0301-l0011] [10.0pt] many tasks, especially when specialized to a narrow domain with high-quality data. Still,
[p0301-l0012] [10.0pt] this approach has limitations. As a chat continues, the model can lose earlier context
[p0301-l0013] [10.0pt] because of the limitations of its context window. Language models also often struggle
[p0301-l0014] [10.0pt] with tasks such as math (even basic multiplication and division) and logic, which is
[p0301-l0015] [10.0pt] expected given how these models work. In addition, because transformers generate the
[p0301-l0016] [10.0pt] best next token for the text they are given, if the input has been enriched with outdated
[p0301-l0017] [10.0pt] or incorrect context, the output may fit that input perfectly while still being wrong for
[p0301-l0018] [10.0pt] the original question. These limitations highlight the need for short- and long-term
[p0301-l0019] [10.0pt] memory management, access to external tools, more accurate, up-to-date informa­
[p0301-l0020] [10.0pt] tion (including from the web), and ways to break problems into steps and refine initial
[p0301-l0021] [10.0pt] answers. This is a scenario that fits the idea of an AI agent.
[p0301-l0022] [10.0pt] A software system can be defined as an AI agent when it can autonomously perform
[p0301-l0023] [10.0pt] tasks and make decisions on a user’s behalf, using AI to learn, adapt, and pursue
[p0301-l0024] [10.0pt] specific goals. An AI agent must be able to reason (analyze the prompt and related
[p0301-l0025] [10.0pt] context, if provided, and determine next steps), act (execute tasks by calling exter­
[p0301-l0026] [10.0pt] nal tools or APIs), and interact (communicate with other agents or users to solve
[p0301-l0027] [10.0pt] problems collaboratively). Agents fall into different categories, but before we get to
[p0301-l0028] [10.0pt] that classification, we’ll expand on these capabilities and start implementing our first
[p0301-l0029] [10.0pt] agent system.
[p0301-l0030] [10.0pt] Imagine asking a specialized language model to plan a weeklong trip from Dublin to
[p0301-l0031] [10.0pt] New York. The workflow might look like this:
[p0301-l0032] [10.0pt] 1	 A user asks the model for a list of accommodation options.
[p0301-l0033] [10.0pt] 2	 The model returns a list of options (hotels, B&Bs, and short-stay apartments).
[p0301-l0034] [10.0pt] 3	 The user asks for a list of return flights from Dublin to New York for specific
[p0301-l0035] [10.0pt] dates.
[p0301-l0036] [10.0pt] 4	 The model returns round-trip flight options from Dublin to New York.
[p0301-l0037] [10.0pt] 5	 The user manages everything using information provided by the model.
[p0301-l0038] [10.0pt] Now let’s look at the same scenario in an agentic system:
[p0301-l0039] [10.0pt] 1	 A user gives the model a trip-planning request prompt (Dublin to New York).
[p0301-l0040] [10.0pt] 2	 The agent searches various sites for hotels, B&Bs, and short-stay apartment
[p0301-l0041] [10.0pt] options in the destination city.

=== PDF page 302 / printed label 281 ===
[p0302-l0001] [9.0pt] 281
[p0302-l0002] [9.0pt] Building an agent
[p0302-l0003] [10.0pt] 3	 The agent queries multiple online sources for return flights from Dublin to New
[p0302-l0004] [10.0pt] York for the given period.
[p0302-l0005] [10.0pt] 4	 The agent determines the best combination of flights and accommodations.
[p0302-l0006] [10.0pt] 5	 The agent also suggests other trip options, such as car rentals, local travel cards,
[p0302-l0007] [10.0pt] and places to visit.
[p0302-l0008] [10.0pt] 6	 The agent listens to the user’s feedback.
[p0302-l0009] [10.0pt] 7	 Once the user is satisfied with the agent’s suggestions, the agent makes the
[p0302-l0010] [10.0pt] bookings.
[p0302-l0011] [10.0pt] Comparing the two systems highlights the agents’ reasoning, action, and interaction
[p0302-l0012] [10.0pt] capabilities. In the agentic scenario, we can see the core traits of agentic AI: a plan (the
[p0302-l0013] [10.0pt] user prompt to organize a trip), reasoning that breaks the plan into steps, tool selec­
[p0302-l0014] [10.0pt] tions (such as a web browser and an online booking system), and actions (using those
[p0302-l0015] [10.0pt] tools and their outputs).
[p0302-l0016] [10.0pt] Implementing an AI agent doesn’t require coding everything from scratch because
[p0302-l0017] [10.0pt] many open-source frameworks are already available. In this section, we’ll use Hugging
[p0302-l0018] [10.0pt] Face’s smolagents (https://github.com/huggingface/smolagents). It’s a small library
[p0302-l0019] [10.0pt] (just over 1,000 lines of code at the time of writing), and its API is easy to learn and use.
[p0302-l0020] [10.0pt] smolagents integrates with other Hugging Face libraries we’ve used in this book,
[p0302-l0021] [10.0pt] such as Transformers. It’s not limited to models hosted on the Hugging Face Hub
[p0302-l0022] [10.0pt] or Hugging Face endpoints; it also supports OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and Together
[p0302-l0023] [10.0pt] AI endpoints; OpenAI-compatible servers; and LiteLLM and Ollama servers. smol­
[p0302-l0024] [10.0pt] agents supports models that handle multiple types of content (text, images, video,
[p0302-l0025] [10.0pt] and audio), but we’ll focus on text only. Implemented in Python, smolagents also
[p0302-l0026] [10.0pt] integrates easily with other LLM frameworks such as LangChain, LangGraph, and
[p0302-l0027] [10.0pt] Anthropic’s MCP.
[p0302-l0028] [10.0pt] smolagents comes with two built-in agent implementations: CodeAgent and
[p0302-l0029] [10.0pt] ­ToolCallingAgent. CodeAgent is the default and is recommended by the framework’s
[p0302-l0030] [10.0pt] authors. At each step, it writes and executes Python snippets. By default, execution hap­
[p0302-l0031] [10.0pt] pens in your local environment. This is generally safe because the agent can call only
[p0302-l0032] [10.0pt] its configured tools plus a predefined set of safe functions from native modules, and
[p0302-l0033] [10.0pt] the Python interpreter blocks imports by default except from a safe list. For produc­
[p0302-l0034] [10.0pt] tion (anything beyond your laptop or phone), smolagents supports safer execution in
[p0302-l0035] [10.0pt] Docker or E2B (https://github.com/e2b-dev) sandboxes.
[p0302-l0036] [10.0pt] CodeAgent largely follows the classic ReAct (reasoning and acting) pattern, a frame­
[p0302-l0037] [10.0pt] work for building AI agents that interleave reasoning and tool use to execute tasks
[p0302-l0038] [10.0pt] (matching the definition of an agent introduced earlier in this section). ReAct agents
[p0302-l0039] [10.0pt] use LLMs to analyze problems, choose tools, and iterate toward a solution. In Code­
[p0302-l0040] [10.0pt] Agent, the model expresses its actions as Python code snippets.
[p0302-l0041] [10.0pt] Figure 13.5 shows the CodeAgent workflow. As you can see, building an agent requires
[p0302-l0042] [10.0pt] at least one LLM, a memory manager, and a set of tools.
