[p0303-l0023] [10.0pt] Let’s configure these components and build a CodeAgent programmatically. First, we’ll
[p0303-l0024] [10.0pt] install the smolagents package:
[p0303-l0025] [8.0pt] pip install smolagents
[p0303-l0026] [10.0pt] In its simplest form, a CodeAgent looks like this:
[p0303-l0027] [8.0pt] from smolagents import CodeAgent, HfApiModel
[p0303-l0028] [8.0pt] model_id = "<model_id>"
[p0303-l0029] [8.0pt] model = HfApiModel(model_id=model_id, token="<huggingface_api_token>")
[p0303-l0030] [8.0pt] agent = CodeAgent(tools=[], model=model, add_base_tools=True)

=== PDF page 304 / printed label 283 ===
[p0304-l0001] [9.0pt] 283
[p0304-l0002] [9.0pt] Building an agent
[p0304-l0003] [10.0pt] The HfApiModel class indicates that the LLM is served through a Hugging Face end­
[p0304-l0004] [10.0pt] point. We pass the model ID from the Hugging Face Hub and the Hugging Face API
[p0304-l0005] [10.0pt] token for authentication. We then define the agent with the CodeAgent class, providing
[p0304-l0006] [10.0pt] the model and the list of tools the agent is allowed to use. Setting add_base_tools to
[p0304-l0007] [10.0pt] True adds the default toolbox on top of the tools listed in tools.
[p0304-l0008] [10.0pt] To start the agent, we call the run method on the CodeAgent instance:
[p0304-l0009] [8.0pt] agent.run("<user_task>")
[p0304-l0010] [10.0pt] Execution stops if the agent generates code that attempts an illegal operation, tries to
[p0304-l0011] [10.0pt] install an unauthorized package, or triggers a Python error.
[p0304-l0012] [10.0pt] The framework provides a default toolbox, which we added at initialization using the
[p0304-l0013] [10.0pt] add_base_tools argument. It includes the following tools:
[p0304-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ DuckDuckGo web search—Performs web searches with DuckDuckGo (https://
[p0304-l0015] [10.0pt] duckduckgo.com/).
[p0304-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Google web search—Performs web searches using the Google Search API.
[p0304-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ Python code interpreter—Runs LLM-generated Python code in a secure environ­
[p0304-l0018] [10.0pt] ment. Add this tool only to the ToolCallingAgent, since code-based agents can
[p0304-l0019] [10.0pt] execute Python natively.
[p0304-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ Speech-to-text—A Whisper-Turbo–based pipeline that transcribes audio to text.
[p0304-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ User input—Asks for user input on a specific question.
[p0304-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Visit web page—Visits a URL and returns the web page content as a Markdown
[p0304-l0023] [10.0pt] string.
[p0304-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Final answer—Called by an agent to return the final answer after it completes
[p0304-l0025] [10.0pt] planning and execution.
[p0304-l0026] [10.0pt] smolagents agents aren’t limited to using the default tool set. You can add new tools
[p0304-l0027] [10.0pt] programmatically in two ways. First, you can use the @tool function decorator:
[p0304-l0028] [8.0pt] from smolagents import tool
[p0304-l0029] [8.0pt] @tool
[p0304-l0030] [8.0pt] def find_accomodation_options(query: str):
[p0304-l0031] [8.0pt]     ...
[p0304-l0032] [10.0pt] You can also implement them as Python classes:
[p0304-l0033] [8.0pt] from smolagents import Tool
[p0304-l0034] [8.0pt] class FindAccomodationoptionsTool(Tool):
[p0304-l0035] [8.0pt]    ...
[p0304-l0036] [10.0pt] Before we get hands-on with agents, let’s first look at the other built-in agent class,
[p0304-l0037] [10.0pt] ToolCallingAgent. This implementation writes actions as JSON-like blobs. That was the

=== PDF page 305 / printed label 284 ===
[p0305-l0001] [9.0pt] 284
[p0305-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 13  Creating end-to-end LLM applications
[p0305-l0003] [10.0pt] original approach in early LLM-based agents: they were prompted to generate actions
[p0305-l0004] [10.0pt] as JSON (or other predefined text formats). The downside is a constrained action
[p0305-l0005] [10.0pt] space (the set of predefined tools) and limited flexibility. The paper “Executable Code
[p0305-l0006] [10.0pt] Actions Elicit Better LLM Agents” (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01030) was the first to
[p0305-l0007] [10.0pt] propose using executable Python code to unify an agent’s action space. Its experiments
[p0305-l0008] [10.0pt] suggest that when agents act by executing interpretable code and collaborate with users
[p0305-l0009] [10.0pt] in natural language, they can address these limits and perform better (see figure 13.6,
[p0305-l0010] [10.0pt] from the paper). This is a valid reason to follow Hugging Face’s recommendation to use
[p0305-l0011] [10.0pt] CodeAgent rather than ToolCallingAgent for your custom agent implementations.
[p0305-l0012] [8.0pt] Figure 13.6  Comparing text, JSON, and a code interpreter as actions on the same example task. At the top are
[p0305-l0013] [8.0pt] the generated steps, and below are the quantitative results across LLMs.
[p0305-l0014] [10.0pt] Let’s now build a custom local agent and tools with this framework. A companion
[p0305-l0015] [10.0pt] Colab notebook includes the full code. To run it on Colab’s free-tier VM, you’ll need
[p0305-l0016] [10.0pt] GPU acceleration.
[p0305-l0017] [10.0pt] We’ll build an agent that can book flights, managing the full flow from a single
[p0305-l0018] [10.0pt] prompt. Because we’re using a small local model, we’ll use smolagents’ Transformers­
[p0305-l0019] [10.0pt] Model class to download models from the Hugging Face Hub and run them locally:

[p0306-l0010] [10.0pt] HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-1.7B-Instruct), the largest model in the SmolLM2 family
[p0306-l0011] [10.0pt] pretrained by Hugging Face for the smolagents framework. The first time you run

[p0306-l0016] [10.0pt] Now that we have the model, we can start implementing the tools we’ll add to the
[p0306-l0017] [10.0pt] agent toolbox so it can complete its assigned tasks. In this example, we’ll implement
[p0306-l0018] [10.0pt] tools as functions and decorate them with @tool.
[p0306-l0019] [10.0pt] The first function, search_for_flights, will search for and select a flight between the
[p0306-l0020] [10.0pt] origin and destination airports. It will parse a mock web page to find flights that match
[p0306-l0021] [10.0pt] the user-provided origin and destination, though you could adapt it to browse a real
[p0306-l0022] [10.0pt] web page. Since this function only mocks a real search, and our goal is to understand
[p0306-l0023] [10.0pt] the workflow of agents in smolagents, I won’t reproduce the code here. The compan­
[p0306-l0024] [10.0pt] ion notebook includes the full implementation along with a mock website (a multiline
[p0306-l0025] [10.0pt] string) that lists flight information in the following schema:
[p0306-l0026] [8.0pt] 1. Flight DUB-BOS123
[p0306-l0027] [8.0pt] - Price: $350
[p0306-l0028] [8.0pt] - Origin: Dublin Airport (DUB)
[p0306-l0029] [8.0pt] - Destination: Boston Logan International Airport (BOS)
[p0306-l0030] [8.0pt] - Date: January 10, 2025
[p0306-l0031] [8.0pt] 2. Flight DUB-EWR456
[p0306-l0032] [8.0pt] - Price: $370
[p0306-l0033] [8.0pt] - Origin: Dublin Airport (DUB)
[p0306-l0034] [8.0pt] - Destination: Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR)
[p0306-l0035] [8.0pt] - Date: January 10, 2025
[p0306-l0036] [8.0pt] ...
[p0306-l0037] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll implement a function that selects a seat for a given flight.
[p0306-l0038] [9.0pt] Listing 13.3  Tool for finding a seat for a flight

[p0306-l0040] [8.0pt] @tool
[p0306-l0041] [8.0pt] def find_seat(flight: str, seat_class: str='Economy') -> str:
[p0306-l0042] [8.0pt]   """Finds a seat within a given flight.

[p0307-l0019] [10.0pt] The preceding function can pick a seat based on the specified class (business or econ­

[p0307-l0024] [10.0pt] With our model and custom tools in place, we can build our flight-booking agent:
[p0307-l0025] [8.0pt] from smolagents import CodeAgent
[p0307-l0026] [8.0pt] custom_tools = [search_for_flights, find_seat]
[p0307-l0027] [8.0pt] agent = CodeAgent(tools=custom_tools, model=model,
[p0307-l0028] [8.0pt]                   verbosity_level=2, max_steps=2)
[p0307-l0029] [10.0pt] The preceding code is a CodeAgent. We’ve added tools to its default toolbox, selected
[p0307-l0030] [10.0pt] the local SLM, set verbosity to 2 (info), and limited it to two steps (for now). We can
[p0307-l0031] [10.0pt] provide a task and have the agent do the rest:
[p0307-l0032] [8.0pt] user_task = "Find a flight from Dublin to New York and then select a seat."
[p0307-l0033] [8.0pt] agent.run(user_task)
[p0307-l0034] [10.0pt] The agent first reasons about the assigned task and then splits it into steps. For each
[p0307-l0035] [10.0pt] step, the agent selects the appropriate tool to search for a flight from Dublin to New
[p0307-l0036] [10.0pt] York and choose a seat. It then generates Python code to execute each step and returns
[p0307-l0037] [10.0pt] the results to the user. The logs from this run show the following two steps:
[p0307-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ I will use the search_for_flights tool to find a flight from Dublin to New York.
[p0307-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ I will use the find_seat tool to find a seat on the flight from Dublin to New York.

[p0308-l0001] [9.0pt] 287
[p0308-l0002] [9.0pt] Building an agent
[p0308-l0003] [10.0pt] These steps include the tool that the agent has identified as the best fit for the action.
[p0308-l0004] [10.0pt] In the first step, it generated the following Python code using the SLM:
[p0308-l0005] [8.0pt] ```py
[p0308-l0006] [8.0pt] origin = 'DUB'
[p0308-l0007] [8.0pt] destination = 'JFK'
[p0308-l0008] [8.0pt] date = '2023-01-01'
[p0308-l0009] [8.0pt] web_page = 'https://www.google.com/search?q
[p0308-l0010] [10.0pt] ➥=flights+from+Dublin+to+New+York+on+2023-01-01'
[p0308-l0011] [8.0pt] answer = search_for_flights(origin=origin, destination=destination,
[p0308-l0012] [10.0pt] ➥ date=date, web_page=web_page)
[p0308-l0013] [8.0pt] print(answer)
[p0308-l0014] [8.0pt] ```
[p0308-l0015] [10.0pt] It calls the search_for_flights tool, passes the Dublin and JFK IATA codes (derived
[p0308-l0016] [10.0pt] from the origin and destination city names), and attempts a web search (which won’t
[p0308-l0017] [10.0pt] run here because the tool is restricted to a mock web page). This step returns two
[p0308-l0018] [10.0pt] results because the page lists two flights for the same route on different dates:
[p0308-l0019] [8.0pt] [{'Flight Code': 'DUB-JFK789', 'Price': '400', 'Origin': 'dublin airport
[p0308-l0020] [8.0pt] (dub)', 'Destination': 'john f. kennedy
[p0308-l0021] [8.0pt] international airport (jfk)', 'Date': 'January 20, 2025'}, {'Flight Code':
[p0308-l0022] [8.0pt] 'DUB-JFK101', 'Price': '450', 'Origin':
[p0308-l0023] [8.0pt] 'dublin airport (dub)', 'Destination': 'john f. kennedy international
[p0308-l0024] [8.0pt] airport (jfk)', 'Date': 'January 10, 2025'}]
[p0308-l0025] [10.0pt] Because the task doesn’t specify which flight to choose, the agent selects the first result
[p0308-l0026] [10.0pt] returned by the search.
[p0308-l0027] [10.0pt] Here’s the Python code generated for the second step:
[p0308-l0028] [8.0pt] ```py
[p0308-l0029] [8.0pt] flight_code = 'DUB-JFK789'
[p0308-l0030] [8.0pt] answer = find_seat(flight=flight_code)
[p0308-l0031] [8.0pt] print(answer)
[p0308-l0032] [8.0pt] ``
[p0308-l0033] [10.0pt] The agent calls the find_seat tool using the code for the first flight returned in the
[p0308-l0034] [10.0pt] previous step. Since the user didn’t specify a class, the agent defaults to economy. In
[p0308-l0035] [10.0pt] this run, the tool returned seat D24.
[p0308-l0036] [10.0pt] Let’s make things a bit more complicated for the agent. We’ll add a third tool and see
[p0308-l0037] [10.0pt] whether it affects the planning phase. The agent is still responsible for booking flights,
[p0308-l0038] [10.0pt] but we’re introducing fibonacci, a tool unrelated to its main duties. It returns the nth
[p0308-l0039] [10.0pt] Fibonacci number (a sequence in which each number is the sum of the two preceding
[p0308-l0040] [10.0pt] numbers, starting with 0 and 1). You can find the full code in the notebook. Let’s add it
[p0308-l0041] [10.0pt] to the agent’s tool list:
[p0308-l0042] [8.0pt] custom_tools = [search_for_flights, find_seat, fibonacci]
[p0308-l0043] [8.0pt] agent = CodeAgent(tools=custom_tools, model=model,
[p0308-l0044] [8.0pt]                   verbosity_level=2, max_steps=2)

=== PDF page 309 / printed label 288 ===
[p0309-l0001] [9.0pt] 288
[p0309-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 13  Creating end-to-end LLM applications
[p0309-l0003] [10.0pt] Now we’ll run the previous task again. When the agent receives the task, it identifies
[p0309-l0004] [10.0pt] the same steps as it did when no fibonacci tool was available, and it produces the same
[p0309-l0005] [10.0pt] Python code to execute them. Here we added only one unnecessary, task-unrelated
[p0309-l0006] [10.0pt] tool for readability, but you should see the same behavior with a larger tool pool, where
[p0309-l0007] [10.0pt] only a few tools are pertinent (assuming you’ve applied the tool-naming and typing
[p0309-l0008] [10.0pt] guidance discussed earlier in this section).
[p0309-l0009] [10.0pt] We can extend this custom agent’s workflow by adding a tool that books the selected
[p0309-l0010] [10.0pt] flight ticket (it’s a mock booking for now, but it will let us test how the agent plans a
[p0309-l0011] [10.0pt] task).
[p0309-l0012] [9.0pt] Listing 13.4  Tool for mocking the flight ticket booking
[p0309-l0013] [8.0pt] @tool
[p0309-l0014] [8.0pt] def book_flight_ticket(flight: str, seat: str) -> str:
[p0309-l0015] [8.0pt]   """Books a flight ticket.
[p0309-l0016] [8.0pt]   Args:
[p0309-l0017] [8.0pt]     flight: The flight code.
[p0309-l0018] [8.0pt]     seat: The seat number.
[p0309-l0019] [8.0pt]   Returns:
[p0309-l0020] [8.0pt]     The ticket number.
[p0309-l0021] [8.0pt]   """
[p0309-l0022] [8.0pt]   ticket_number = random.randint(100000, 999999)
[p0309-l0023] [8.0pt]   return f"Ticket booked for flight {flight} and seat {seat}
[p0309-l0024] [10.0pt] ➥. Ticket number: {ticket_number}"
[p0309-l0025] [10.0pt] We’ll add this tool to the agent’s toolbox and set the maximum number of steps to 3:
[p0309-l0026] [8.0pt] custom_tools = [search_for_flights, find_seat, book_flight_ticket]
[p0309-l0027] [8.0pt] agent = CodeAgent(tools=custom_tools, model=model,
[p0309-l0028] [8.0pt]                   verbosity_level=2, max_steps=3)
[p0309-l0029] [10.0pt] Now we’ll run the same tasks as in the previous examples:
[p0309-l0030] [8.0pt] user_task = "Find a flight from Dublin to New York and then select a seat."
[p0309-l0031] [8.0pt] agent.run(user_task)
[p0309-l0032] [10.0pt] The agent autonomously identifies three steps—searching for the ticket, selecting
[p0309-l0033] [10.0pt] a seat, and booking the flight—even though the user doesn’t explicitly ask for these
[p0309-l0034] [10.0pt] tasks. This is the final output from the model for this run:
[p0309-l0035] [8.0pt] Out: Ticket booked for flight DUB-JFK789 and seat B26. Ticket number: 798158
[p0309-l0036] [10.0pt] In this section, we’ve built a single agent that can use multiple tools. smolagents also
[p0309-l0037] [10.0pt] supports multi-agent systems, where multiple agents interact and collaborate to solve
[p0309-l0038] [10.0pt] more complex tasks. We’ll cover this in chapter 14.

[p0310-l0001] [9.0pt] 289
[p0310-l0002] [9.0pt] Building an agent
[p0310-l0003] [10.0pt] Note that when implementing a local custom agent with smolagents, Transformers­
[p0310-l0004] [10.0pt] Model isn’t your only option for loading SLMs. You can also use models hosted on an
[p0310-l0005] [10.0pt] Ollama server (covered in chapter 12). The overall workflow is the same.
[p0310-l0006] [10.0pt] In our flight-booking example, almost everything stays the same except for the
[p0310-l0007] [10.0pt] model serving. First, we install a local Ollama server and start it running:
[p0310-l0008] [8.0pt] ollama serve
[p0310-l0009] [10.0pt] We can now download a quantized Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model:
[p0310-l0010] [8.0pt] ollama pull phi3:mini
[p0310-l0011] [10.0pt] The only code change required to switch the agent to this model is as follows:
[p0310-l0012] [8.0pt] from smolagents import LiteLLMModel
[p0310-l0013] [8.0pt] model = LiteLLMModel(
[p0310-l0014] [8.0pt]         model_id="phi3:mini",
[p0310-l0015] [8.0pt]         api_base="http://localhost:11434",
[p0310-l0016] [8.0pt]         api_key="<your-api-key>",
[p0310-l0017] [8.0pt]         num_ctx=4096
[p0310-l0018] [8.0pt] )
[p0310-l0019] [10.0pt] We’ll use the LiteLLMModel class, which requires the model ID from the Ollama
[p0310-l0020] [10.0pt] server, the base URL (specifying the correct port if we are not using the default),
[p0310-l0021] [10.0pt] the local API key, and the context size. Then we pass this model when creating the
[p0310-l0022] [10.0pt] CodeAgent, as usual:
[p0310-l0023] [8.0pt] custom_tools = [search_for_flights, find_seat, book_flight_ticket]
[p0310-l0024] [8.0pt] agent = CodeAgent(tools=custom_tools, model=model,
[p0310-l0025] [8.0pt]                   verbosity_level=2, max_steps=3)
[p0310-l0026] [10.0pt] Here are a few best practices for building higher-quality agents with this framework;
[p0310-l0027] [10.0pt] many of them apply to agentic AI development in general:
[p0310-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Use only instructed models.
[p0310-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ Performance often depends on model size. For agentic API applications, very
[p0310-l0030] [10.0pt] small models tend to underperform, unlike what we see in other applications.
[p0310-l0031] [10.0pt] That doesn’t mean you can’t use SLMs, but models under 3 billion parameters
[p0310-l0032] [10.0pt] may not deliver satisfactory results. Use an evaluation strategy appropriate for
[p0310-l0033] [10.0pt] your chosen models.
[p0310-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Keep your agentic AI workflow design as simple as possible to reduce risk, cost,
[p0310-l0035] [10.0pt] and latency.
[p0310-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ Agentic systems combine deterministic components with probabilistic ones (the
[p0310-l0037] [10.0pt] SLMs). Although these models can self-correct, a best practice is to make the
[p0310-l0038] [10.0pt] system as deterministic as possible: give the model only tasks it can reliably com­
[p0310-l0039] [10.0pt] plete, and shift any deterministic work to other parts of the architecture.

[p0311-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Whenever possible, combine two or more tools into one. This reduces the num­
[p0311-l0004] [10.0pt] ber of calls to SLMs, which lowers costs.
[p0311-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ Keep tasks for SLMs simple and clear.
[p0311-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Ensure that for any data types the model handles through custom tools, you val­
[p0311-l0007] [10.0pt] idate formats and value ranges. This reduces the chance of errors and simplifies

[p0311-l0011] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0311-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Language models alone provide limited business value without being integrated
[p0311-l0013] [10.0pt] into complex systems that add external knowledge and tools.
[p0311-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ RAG systems enhance language models by retrieving information from external
[p0311-l0015] [10.0pt] knowledge bases and generating text.
[p0311-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Document chunking splits large texts into smaller segments to avoid exceeding
[p0311-l0017] [10.0pt] embedding and generator model capacity limits.
[p0311-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ PyMuPDF extracts PDF content, and spaCy detects sentence boundaries for
[p0311-l0019] [10.0pt] preprocessing.
[p0311-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ The Sentence Transformers library converts text into dense vectors using
[p0311-l0021] [10.0pt] encoder-­only Transformer architectures.
[p0311-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Cosine similarity measures semantic relationships between query and document
[p0311-l0023] [10.0pt] embeddings to retrieve relevant content.
[p0311-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Vector databases such as LanceDB store embeddings and use approximate near­
[p0311-l0025] [10.0pt] est neighbor algorithms for fast similarity search.
[p0311-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ LanceDB offers serverless vector storage with automatic versioning and zero-
[p0311-l0027] [10.0pt] copy embedding management.
[p0311-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Embedding models must be identical for both creating a knowledge base and
[p0311-l0029] [10.0pt] processing queries so the vectors share a consistent space.
[p0311-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Generator models receive enriched prompts containing user queries and
[p0311-l0031] [10.0pt] retrieved context to produce informed responses.
[p0311-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Prompt-formatting functions combine user queries with retrieved context using
[p0311-l0033] [10.0pt] model-specific chat templates.
[p0311-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ AI agents autonomously perform tasks and make decisions by reasoning about
[p0311-l0035] [10.0pt] problems and acting through external tools.
[p0311-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ The smolagents framework lets you build local agents using small language mod­
[p0311-l0037] [10.0pt] els and Python-based tools.
[p0311-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ CodeAgent writes and runs Python snippets for each step instead of generating
[p0311-l0039] [10.0pt] JSON instructions.
[p0311-l0040] [10.0pt] ¡ Tool functions need docstrings and type hints so they’re automatically available
[p0311-l0041] [10.0pt] as agent-usable capabilities.

[p0313-l0001] [30.0pt] Advanced components
[p0313-l0002] [30.0pt] for LLM applications
[p0313-l0003] [225.0pt] 14
[p0313-l0004] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0313-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ RAG on a knowledge graph
[p0313-l0006] [9.8pt] ¡ Combining RAG and agentic AI using only SLMs
[p0313-l0007] [9.8pt] ¡ Managing short- and long-term memory for
[p0313-l0008] [9.8pt] chatbots and AI agents
[p0313-l0009] [10.0pt] In chapter 13, you learned about two key paradigms for language models: retrieval­
[p0313-l0010] [10.0pt] -augmented generation (RAG) and agentic AI. We built a RAG system from scratch,
[p0313-l0011] [10.0pt] introduced vector databases for these applications, and implemented an AI agent
[p0313-l0012] [10.0pt] using the open source smolagents framework. In this chapter, we’ll cover some new
[p0313-l0013] [10.0pt] concepts and tools that can make RAG systems and agents more robust, and you’ll
[p0313-l0014] [10.0pt] learn how to combine them.
[p0313-l0015] [12.5pt] 14.1	 GraphRAG
[p0313-l0016] [10.0pt] In the previous chapter, you learned that RAG connects language models to exter­
[p0313-l0017] [10.0pt] nal data sources, giving them access to private or domain-specific information and
[p0313-l0018] [10.0pt] reducing hallucinations. A baseline RAG typically combines a vector database with
[p0313-l0019] [10.0pt] two language models; the vector database stores embeddings, one model retrieves
[p0313-l0020] [9.0pt] 292

=== PDF page 314 / printed label 293 ===
[p0314-l0001] [9.0pt] 293
[p0314-l0002] [9.0pt] GraphRAG
[p0314-l0003] [10.0pt] context for a user query, and the other model generates an answer from that context.
[p0314-l0004] [10.0pt] This approach works well in many cases, but it can struggle with complex tasks that
[p0314-l0005] [10.0pt] require multihop reasoning or connecting information from multiple sources. The
[p0314-l0006] [10.0pt] core challenge is that baseline RAG retrieves text by semantic similarity, which does not
[p0314-l0007] [10.0pt] reliably surface specific details needed to answer complex questions, especially when
[p0314-l0008] [10.0pt] those details are not stated explicitly in the knowledge base. As a result, finding the
[p0314-l0009] [10.0pt] right information can be difficult, sometimes leading to costly workarounds, such as
[p0314-l0010] [10.0pt] manually creating Q&A pairs for common queries.
[p0314-l0011] [10.0pt] One way to address these challenges is to augment RAG retrieval and generation
[p0314-l0012] [10.0pt] with knowledge graphs (KGs). A KG is a structured representation of knowledge that
[p0314-l0013] [10.0pt] captures entities, their attributes, and the relationships between them. KGs consist of
[p0314-l0014] [10.0pt] nodes (entities such as people, places, or concepts) and edges (relationships between
[p0314-l0015] [10.0pt] entities), which help machines better represent context and meaning and can improve
[p0314-l0016] [10.0pt] search, data integration, and reasoning. This is the definition of GraphRAG.
[p0314-l0017] [10.0pt] NOTE  For an in-depth look at knowledge graphs and LLMs, see Knowledge
[p0314-l0018] [10.0pt] Graphs and LLMs in Action by Alessandro Negro et al. (2025; https://www
[p0314-l0019] [10.0pt] .manning.com/books/knowledge-graphs-and-llms-in-action).
[p0314-l0020] [10.0pt] One of the best approaches to implementing GraphRAG comes from Microsoft’s
[p0314-l0021] [10.0pt] paper “From Local to Global: A GraphRAG Approach to Query-Focused Summari­
[p0314-l0022] [10.0pt] zation” (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2404.16130). It presents a graph-based approach to
[p0314-l0023] [10.0pt] question-answering over private text corpora that scales with both the breadth of user
[p0314-l0024] [10.0pt] questions and the amount of source text. It uses an LLM to build a graph index in two
[p0314-l0025] [10.0pt] stages:
[p0314-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ Derive an entity knowledge graph from the source documents.
[p0314-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Pregenerate community summaries for groups of closely related entities.
[p0314-l0028] [10.0pt] Given a question, each community summary is used to generate a partial response;
[p0314-l0029] [10.0pt] these partial responses are then summarized into a final response for the user. This
[p0314-l0030] [10.0pt] approach, named GraphRAG, substantially improves on a conventional RAG baseline
[p0314-l0031] [10.0pt] in both the comprehensiveness and the diversity of generated answers.
[p0314-l0032] [10.0pt] Figure 14.1, adapted from the Microsoft paper, shows the general GraphRAG work­
[p0314-l0033] [10.0pt] flow. Blocks on the left represent tasks in the indexing phase; blocks on the right
[p0314-l0034] [10.0pt] represent tasks in the query phase. Some artifacts (such as graph communities and
[p0314-l0035] [10.0pt] community summaries) are generated during indexing but used at query time, which
[p0314-l0036] [10.0pt] is why they are shown in a different color. Indexing typically runs offline and produces
[p0314-l0037] [10.0pt] a KG on top of the knowledge base. Input documents must be selected and prepro­
[p0314-l0038] [10.0pt] cessed outside the indexing pipeline, because the quality of the KG depends on the
[p0314-l0039] [10.0pt] quality of the source documents. The extracted text is chunked and sent to an LLM,
[p0314-l0040] [10.0pt] which extracts domain-specific entities and relationships (the KG’s nodes and edges)
[p0314-l0041] [10.0pt] and then detects and summarizes graph communities. Here, a community is a group
[p0314-l0042] [10.0pt] of nodes that are more densely connected to one another than to the rest of the graph.

[p0315-l0028] [8.0pt] Figure 14.1  The logical blocks and workflow of Microsoft’s GraphRAG proposal
[p0315-l0029] [10.0pt] Imagine a KG representing a movie database with entities such as movies, actors, direc­
[p0315-l0030] [10.0pt] tors, genres, and production companies. In this setting, communities emerge from
[p0315-l0031] [10.0pt] relationships between entities. For example, consider the Action Movies community,
[p0315-l0032] [10.0pt] made up of the following entities (nodes):
[p0315-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ Movies—”Mad Max: Fury Road,” “Die Hard,” “Mission: Impossible – Fallout”
[p0315-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ Actors—”Tom Cruise,” “Bruce Willis,” “Charlize Theron”
[p0315-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Directors—”George Miller,” “John McTiernan,” “Christopher McQuarrie”
[p0315-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ Genres—“Action”
[p0315-l0037] [10.0pt] It will have the following relationships (edges):
[p0315-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ “Mad Max: Fury Road” is of genre “Action.”
[p0315-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ “Die Hard” features actor “Bruce Willis.”
[p0315-l0040] [10.0pt] ¡ “Mission: Impossible – Fallout” features actor “Tom Cruise”
[p0315-l0041] [10.0pt] ¡ “Mad Max: Fury Road” is directed by “George Miller.”
[p0315-l0042] [10.0pt] ¡ “Die Hard” is directed by “John McTiernan.”
[p0315-l0043] [10.0pt] ¡ “Mission: Impossible – Fallout” is directed by “Christopher McQuarrie.”
[p0315-l0044] [10.0pt] Figure 14.2 shows the same data as a graph.
[p0315-l0045] [10.0pt] These are the characteristics of this community:
[p0315-l0046] [10.0pt] ¡ The movies, actors, and directors in this community are interconnected through
[p0315-l0047] [10.0pt] multiple relationships (for example, actors appear in multiple action movies).

=== PDF page 316 / printed label 295 ===
[p0316-l0001] [9.0pt] 295
[p0316-l0002] [9.0pt] GraphRAG
[p0316-l0003] [8.0pt] Figure 14.2  The action movie graph for the preceding example data
[p0316-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ All entities in this community belong to the “Action” genre, forming a distinct
[p0316-l0005] [10.0pt] cluster in the KG.
[p0316-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ This community makes some downstream tasks easier, such as analyzing trends
[p0316-l0007] [10.0pt] in action movies, studying actor-director collaborations, and generating recom­
[p0316-l0008] [10.0pt] mendations for action-movie fans.
[p0316-l0009] [10.0pt] During the query phase, a user prompt is enriched with retrieved content (entities
[p0316-l0010] [10.0pt] and relationships) and community summaries, and then it is passed to the generator
[p0316-l0011] [10.0pt] model to produce the final answer.
[p0316-l0012] [10.0pt] After the GraphRAG paper was published, Microsoft also released an official open
[p0316-l0013] [10.0pt] source implementation (https://github.com/microsoft/graphrag) under the MIT
[p0316-l0014] [10.0pt] license. Following the concepts introduced earlier in this section, we’ll build a naive
[p0316-l0015] [10.0pt] Python implementation that’s framework- and vendor-agnostic. We’ll use a minimal
[p0316-l0016] [10.0pt] set of Python packages because our goal is to understand the concepts and how they
[p0316-l0017] [10.0pt] can benefit a RAG system, not to learn a specific implementation. Unlike Microsoft’s
[p0316-l0018] [10.0pt] GraphRAG implementation, which supports only OpenAI and Azure OpenAI end­
[p0316-l0019] [10.0pt] points, we’ll use small, local, open source models. A companion Colab notebook is pro­
[p0316-l0020] [10.0pt] vided for this section, and we’ll refer to figure 14.1 throughout the implementation.

=== PDF page 317 / printed label 296 ===
[p0317-l0001] [9.0pt] 296
[p0317-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0317-l0003] [10.0pt] For this example, we’ll use the quantized Mistral 7B model from the Ollama library
[p0317-l0004] [10.0pt] (https://ollama.com/library/mistral), hosted on a local Ollama server. I chose it
[p0317-l0005] [10.0pt] because it performs well at extracting entities and relationships from unstructured
[p0317-l0006] [10.0pt] text, outperforming other smaller open source models, performing nearly as well as
[p0317-l0007] [10.0pt] the larger models supported by the MS implementation. The code runs without hard­
[p0317-l0008] [10.0pt] ware acceleration, but a GPU is recommended to speed up model tasks, especially when
[p0317-l0009] [10.0pt] working with a large knowledge base corpus.
[p0317-l0010] [10.0pt] The Colab notebook downloads three PDF papers on 8-bit quantization for LLMs—
[p0317-l0011] [10.0pt] these will serve as our knowledge base. For simplicity, we’ll focus on one of the papers,
[p0317-l0012] [10.0pt] “On-Device LLMs for Home Assistant: Dual Role in Intent Detection and Response
[p0317-l0013] [10.0pt] Generation” (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2502.12923), but you can run the notebook with
[p0317-l0014] [10.0pt] all the documents at any time.
[p0317-l0015] [10.0pt] After downloading the PDF, we’ll extract its text and save it to a file for chunking.
[p0317-l0016] [10.0pt] The notebook provides the extract_text_from_pdfs function to read PDFs from a
[p0317-l0017] [10.0pt] directory, extract their text, and save it. Next, we’ll chunk the extracted text using the
[p0317-l0018] [10.0pt] split_text_into_chunks function, which takes the path of the directory containing the
[p0317-l0019] [10.0pt] text files and a chunk size. It returns a dictionary mapping each original text filename
[p0317-l0020] [10.0pt] to its list of chunks.
[p0317-l0021] [10.0pt] Once the text chunks are available, we can query the model to identify entities and
[p0317-l0022] [10.0pt] relationships. We’ll assume the Mistral 7B model is deployed and available through our
[p0317-l0023] [10.0pt] local Ollama server. To send requests to the model, we’ll use the official ollama-python
[p0317-l0024] [10.0pt] client library (https://github.com/ollama/ollama-python).
[p0317-l0025] [10.0pt] We’ll also define a custom function, extract_entities_and_relationships, to make
[p0317-l0026] [10.0pt] these requests, but first we need to address an issue with the format of the generated
[p0317-l0027] [10.0pt] responses. I ran multiple experiments with the model using this final prompt:
[p0317-l0028] [8.0pt] prompt = f"""Extract entities and relationships from this
[p0317-l0029] [10.0pt] ➥ text:\n\n{chunk}\n\n
[p0317-l0030] [8.0pt] Relationships must follow the format 'Relationship, (Entity1, Entity2)'"""
[p0317-l0031] [10.0pt] I was prompting the model to extract entities and relationships from a text chunk and
[p0317-l0032] [10.0pt] return them in a fixed format, but even with the temperature set to 0, the responses
[p0317-l0033] [10.0pt] didn’t always match the expected format: a list of entities and a list of relationships.
[p0317-l0034] [10.0pt] This made parsing difficult before building the KG: about 6% of entity outputs and
[p0317-l0035] [10.0pt] 25% of relationship outputs had formatting errors.
[p0317-l0036] [10.0pt] To avoid this, we’ll use a feature in recent Ollama releases: structured outputs, which

[p0317-l0039] [8.0pt] from pydantic import BaseModel

[p0321-l0001] [9.0pt] 300
[p0321-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0321-l0003] [10.0pt] The generated graph can now be rendered. The visualize_graph_with_plotly func­
[p0321-l0004] [10.0pt] tion, which visualizes it using the Plotly API for Python, is available in the notebook.
[p0321-l0005] [10.0pt] The indexing isn’t finished yet. We still need to compute the communities in this
[p0321-l0006] [10.0pt] graph. NetworkX includes several community-detection algorithms, including the pop­
[p0321-l0007] [10.0pt] ular Louvain method. However, the GraphRAG paper reports better results with hier­
[p0321-l0008] [10.0pt] archical clustering using the Leiden algorithm (https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.08473),
[p0321-l0009] [10.0pt] which NetworkX doesn’t provide out of the box. The reference implementation is
[p0321-l0010] [10.0pt] a Python wrapper around the libleidenalg C++ library, so we’ll build a simple pure-­
[p0321-l0011] [10.0pt] Python version.
[p0321-l0012] [10.0pt] The Louvain algorithm starts from a singleton partition, with each node in its own
[p0321-l0013] [10.0pt] community. It then iteratively moves nodes between communities, builds an aggregated
[p0321-l0014] [10.0pt] network from the resulting partition, and iterates on the aggregated network until the
[p0321-l0015] [10.0pt] quality score no longer improves. According to the Leiden paper, one problem with the
[p0321-l0016] [10.0pt] Louvain algorithm is that it can identify communities that are internally disconnected.
[p0321-l0017] [10.0pt] The Leiden algorithm is partly based on its predecessor but addresses this issue. Like
[p0321-l0018] [10.0pt] Louvain, it starts from a singleton partition and moves nodes between communities to
[p0321-l0019] [10.0pt] improve the partition, but it refines the partition before aggregation. An aggregated
[p0321-l0020] [10.0pt] network is then created based on the refined partition. The algorithm then repeats the
[p0321-l0021] [10.0pt] move and aggregate steps until no further improvement is possible.
[p0321-l0022] [10.0pt] The Leiden algorithm optimizes modularity, a metric that measures how strongly a
[p0321-l0023] [10.0pt] network divides into clusters. Maximizing modularity helps ensure the communities
[p0321-l0024] [10.0pt] that are found are well defined and meaningful. The companion Colab notebook
[p0321-l0025] [10.0pt] includes a simple Python implementation, including a utility function that computes
[p0321-l0026] [10.0pt] the modularity gain from moving a node to a particular community in the graph:
[p0321-l0027] [8.0pt] def calculate_modularity_gain(graph, node, community,
[p0321-l0028] [10.0pt] ➥ communities, resolution):
[p0321-l0029] [8.0pt]   m = graph.number_of_edges()
[p0321-l0030] [8.0pt]   k_i = graph.degree(node)
[p0321-l0031] [8.0pt]   k_i_in = sum(1 for neighbor in graph.neighbors(node)
[p0321-l0032] [10.0pt]   ➥if communities[neighbor] == community)
[p0321-l0033] [8.0pt]   sigma_tot = sum(graph.degree(v) for v in graph.nodes
[p0321-l0034] [10.0pt]   ➥if communities[v] == community)
[p0321-l0035] [8.0pt]   return (k_i_in - k_i * sigma_tot / (2 * m)) * resolution
[p0321-l0036] [10.0pt] A higher modularity gain means that moving a node into a community would improve
[p0321-l0037] [10.0pt] the graph’s community structure. The resolution argument controls community size
[p0321-l0038] [10.0pt] (higher values produce smaller communities). The calculate_modularity_gain func­
[p0321-l0039] [10.0pt] tion computes the graph’s total edge count, the input node’s degree (number of con­
[p0321-l0040] [10.0pt] nections), the node’s number of connections to other nodes in the input community,
[p0321-l0041] [10.0pt] the target community’s total degree for all nodes in the input community, and the
[p0321-l0042] [10.0pt] change in modularity if the node is moved. This modularity gain formula compares
[p0321-l0043] [10.0pt] the actual number of edges within the community with the expected number if edges
[p0321-l0044] [10.0pt] were distributed randomly; the resolution parameter scales the gain.

[p0322-l0001] [9.0pt] 301
[p0322-l0002] [9.0pt] GraphRAG
[p0322-l0003] [10.0pt] A second utility function, aggregate_communities, aggregates (merges) communi­
[p0322-l0004] [10.0pt] ties in the graph based on their connectivity.
[p0322-l0005] [9.0pt] Listing 14.3  Custom function to aggregate communities within a graph
[p0322-l0006] [9.0pt] Iterates across the connected
[p0322-l0007] [9.0pt] component of the input graph
[p0322-l0008] [9.0pt] If the current node’s
[p0322-l0009] [9.0pt] community isn’t in the
[p0322-l0010] [9.0pt] community mapping, its
[p0322-l0011] [9.0pt] ID is assigned a new
[p0322-l0012] [9.0pt] aggregated community ID.
[p0322-l0013] [9.0pt] The current node’s community
[p0322-l0014] [9.0pt] assignment is updated to the
[p0322-l0015] [9.0pt] new aggregated community.
[p0322-l0016] [8.0pt] def aggregate_communities(graph, communities):
[p0322-l0017] [8.0pt]   community_mapping = {}
[p0322-l0018] [8.0pt]   next_community_id = 0
[p0322-l0019] [8.0pt]   for component in nx.connected_components(graph):
[p0322-l0020] [8.0pt]     for node in component:
[p0322-l0021] [8.0pt]       if communities[node]
[p0322-l0022] [10.0pt]       ➥not in community_mapping:
[p0322-l0023] [8.0pt]         community_mapping[communities[node]] = next_community_id
[p0322-l0024] [8.0pt]         next_community_id += 1
[p0322-l0025] [8.0pt]       communities[node]
[p0322-l0026] [10.0pt]      ➥ = community_mapping[communities[node]]
[p0322-l0027] [8.0pt]   num_communities = next_community_id
[p0322-l0028] [8.0pt]   return communities, num_communities
[p0322-l0029] [10.0pt] At this stage, each node has an assigned community ID. This function iterates over
[p0322-l0030] [10.0pt] each connected component (a subgraph in which every node is reachable from every
[p0322-l0031] [10.0pt] other) in the graph. For each node, it checks whether that community ID is already in
[p0322-l0032] [10.0pt] the community mapping; if not, it adds it and assigns it a new aggregated community
[p0322-l0033] [10.0pt] ID. It then updates the node’s community assignment to that aggregated ID. Finally,
[p0322-l0034] [10.0pt] it returns the updated mapping from nodes to aggregated community IDs, along with
[p0322-l0035] [10.0pt] the total number of aggregated communities.
[p0322-l0036] [10.0pt] The function containing our custom implementation of the Leiden algorithm,
[p0322-l0037] [10.0pt] leiden_algorithm, uses the two preceding utility functions.
[p0322-l0038] [9.0pt] Listing 14.4  The custom implementation of the Leiden algorithm
[p0322-l0039] [8.0pt] import random
[p0322-l0040] [8.0pt] def leiden_algorithm(graph, resolution=1.0, max_iterations=100):
[p0322-l0041] [8.0pt]   communities = {node: i for i, node in enumerate(graph.nodes)}
[p0322-l0042] [8.0pt]   num_communities = len(communities)
[p0322-l0043] [8.0pt]   for _ in range(max_iterations):
[p0322-l0044] [8.0pt]     improved = False
[p0322-l0045] [8.0pt]     for node in graph.nodes:
[p0322-l0046] [8.0pt]       best_community = communities[node]
[p0322-l0047] [8.0pt]       best_modularity_gain = 0
[p0322-l0048] [8.0pt]       for neighbor in graph.neighbors(node):

=== PDF page 323 / printed label 302 ===
[p0323-l0001] [9.0pt] 302
[p0323-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0323-l0003] [8.0pt]         neighbor_community = communities[neighbor]
[p0323-l0004] [8.0pt]         if neighbor_community != best_community:
[p0323-l0005] [8.0pt]           modularity_gain = calculate_modularity_gain(graph, node,
[p0323-l0006] [10.0pt]          ➥ neighbor_community, communities, resolution)
[p0323-l0007] [8.0pt]           if modularity_gain > best_modularity_gain:
[p0323-l0008] [8.0pt]             best_modularity_gain = modularity_gain
[p0323-l0009] [8.0pt]             best_community = neighbor_community
[p0323-l0010] [8.0pt]       if best_community != communities[node]:
[p0323-l0011] [8.0pt]         communities[node] = best_community
[p0323-l0012] [8.0pt]         improved = True
[p0323-l0013] [8.0pt]     for node in graph.nodes:
[p0323-l0014] [8.0pt]       if len([n for n in graph.nodes if communities[n]
[p0323-l0015] [10.0pt]       ➥ == communities[node]]) == 1:
[p0323-l0016] [8.0pt]         neighbors = list(graph.neighbors(node))
[p0323-l0017] [8.0pt]         if neighbors:
[p0323-l0018] [8.0pt]           communities[node] = communities[random.choice(neighbors)]
[p0323-l0019] [8.0pt]     if improved:
[p0323-l0020] [8.0pt]       communities, num_communities = aggregate_communities(graph,
[p0323-l0021] [10.0pt]       ➥ communities)
[p0323-l0022] [8.0pt]     else:
[p0323-l0023] [8.0pt]       break
[p0323-l0024] [8.0pt]   return [communities[node] for node in graph.nodes]
[p0323-l0025] [10.0pt] The goal is to identify groups of nodes (communities) that are more densely con­
[p0323-l0026] [10.0pt] nected to each other than to the rest of the input graph. Initially, each node is assigned
[p0323-l0027] [10.0pt] to its own community, so the number of communities equals the number of nodes. The
[p0323-l0028] [10.0pt] function then iterates for the number of steps specified by the max_iterations argu­
[p0323-l0029] [10.0pt] ment. For each node, it finds the community that would yield the largest modularity
[p0323-l0030] [10.0pt] gain if the node were moved. If it finds a better community, it moves the node and sets
[p0323-l0031] [10.0pt] the improved flag to True. It then runs a second pass across the nodes; any single-node
[p0323-l0032] [10.0pt] communities (singletons) are reassigned to a neighbor to keep them from being iso­
[p0323-l0033] [10.0pt] lated. The final step is community aggregation: if the community structure is improved
[p0323-l0034] [10.0pt] in the current iteration (that is, improved is True), the aggregate_­communities function
[p0323-l0035] [10.0pt] merges communities based on connectivity. If there is no improvement, the algorithm
[p0323-l0036] [10.0pt] terminates.
[p0323-l0037] [10.0pt] Finally, it returns a list of the final community assignment for each node in the
[p0323-l0038] [10.0pt] graph:
[p0323-l0039] [8.0pt] communities = leiden_algorithm(combined_graph)
[p0323-l0040] [10.0pt] As a final indexing step, we generate community summaries using a local Mistral 7B
[p0323-l0041] [10.0pt] model. First, we identify the unique communities in our list:
[p0323-l0042] [8.0pt] unique_communities = sorted(list(set(communities)))

=== PDF page 324 / printed label 303 ===
[p0324-l0001] [9.0pt] 303
[p0324-l0002] [9.0pt] GraphRAG
[p0324-l0003] [10.0pt] Next, we iterate through the communities to group the nodes by unique community:
[p0324-l0004] [8.0pt]  community_list = []
[p0324-l0005] [8.0pt] for community_id in unique_communities:
[p0324-l0006] [8.0pt]     community_nodes = [node for node, community in zip(graph.nodes,
[p0324-l0007] [10.0pt]     ➥community_assignments) if community == community_id]
[p0324-l0008] [8.0pt]     community_list.append(community_nodes)
[p0324-l0009] [10.0pt] community_list is a list of communities, each containing node IDs. In another for
[p0324-l0010] [10.0pt] loop, we iterate over community_list and extract the text chunks associated with each
[p0324-l0011] [10.0pt] node in a community:
[p0324-l0012] [8.0pt] community_summaries = {}
[p0324-l0013] [8.0pt]     for community_id, community_nodes in enumerate(community_list):
[p0324-l0014] [8.0pt]         community_text = ""
[p0324-l0015] [8.0pt]         for node in community_nodes:
[p0324-l0016] [8.0pt]           if node in chunks_dict:
[p0324-l0017] [8.0pt]               for chunk in chunks_dict[node]:
[p0324-l0018] [8.0pt]                   community_text += chunk + "\n"
[p0324-l0019] [10.0pt] The community text is used to build a prompt for the Mistral model, which then gen­
[p0324-l0020] [10.0pt] erates a summary:
[p0324-l0021] [8.0pt] prompt = f"""Summarize the following text which represents a community of
[p0324-l0022] [10.0pt]         ➥ related documents:
[p0324-l0023] [8.0pt] {community_text}
[p0324-l0024] [8.0pt] """
[p0324-l0025] [8.0pt] response: ChatResponse = chat(model=model_id, messages=[
[p0324-l0026] [8.0pt]     {
[p0324-l0027] [8.0pt]         'role': 'user',
[p0324-l0028] [8.0pt]         'content': prompt,
[p0324-l0029] [8.0pt]     },
[p0324-l0030] [8.0pt] ], options={"temperature": 0})
[p0324-l0031] [8.0pt] summary = response['message']['content']
[p0324-l0032] [10.0pt] Each generated summary is then added to the community_summaries list:
[p0324-l0033] [8.0pt] community_summaries[community_id] = summary
[p0324-l0034] [10.0pt] Generating community summaries is expensive because it requires many calls to the
[p0324-l0035] [10.0pt] model (depending on the number of communities and the size of the knowledge
[p0324-l0036] [10.0pt] base). If you are running locally, this mostly costs time; if you use a third-party API,
[p0324-l0037] [10.0pt] you’ll need to factor in charges for API calls and input or generated tokens.
[p0324-l0038] [10.0pt] The indexing process is now complete. Next, we’ll look at how we can search these
[p0324-l0039] [10.0pt] summaries. We’ll implement what the Microsoft paper calls global search. Microsoft’s
[p0324-l0040] [10.0pt] GraphRAG implementation also includes local search, which we’ll cover in section
[p0324-l0041] [10.0pt] 14.1.1.

=== PDF page 325 / printed label 304 ===
[p0325-l0001] [9.0pt] 304
[p0325-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0325-l0003] [10.0pt] Once we’ve completed the previous steps, users can start asking questions of our
[p0325-l0004] [10.0pt] knowledge base and receive answers generated by the SLM. Global search uses the fol­
[p0325-l0005] [10.0pt] lowing workflow:
[p0325-l0006] [10.0pt] 1	 Intermediate answers are generated for each community summary in relation to
[p0325-l0007] [10.0pt] the query.
[p0325-l0008] [10.0pt] 2	 The final answer is generated by combining the intermediate answers into a con­
[p0325-l0009] [10.0pt] cise response.
[p0325-l0010] [10.0pt] Let’s see what this implies in code. The notebook’s global search uses two functions:
[p0325-l0011] [10.0pt] generate_answers and generate_final_answer. The generate_answers function loops
[p0325-l0012] [10.0pt] through the community summaries and, for each one, queries the local model with the
[p0325-l0013] [10.0pt] following prompt:
[p0325-l0014] [8.0pt] prompt = f"""
[p0325-l0015] [8.0pt]         Query: {query}
[p0325-l0016] [8.0pt]         Use the following community summary to answer the query:
[p0325-l0017] [8.0pt]         {summary}
[p0325-l0018] [8.0pt]         Answer:
[p0325-l0019] [8.0pt]         """
[p0325-l0020] [10.0pt] It returns a list of generated answers for the user’s query and a summary for each commu­
[p0325-l0021] [10.0pt] nity (a dictionary whose keys are community IDs and whose values are the intermediate
[p0325-l0022] [10.0pt] answers). Downstream, the generate_final_answer function combines those intermedi­
[p0325-l0023] [10.0pt] ate answers to enrich the prompt for the local model and produce the final answer:
[p0325-l0024] [8.0pt] combined_answers_prompt = "Combine the following answers into a single,
[p0325-l0025] [10.0pt]                           ➥ concise response:\n\n"
[p0325-l0026] [8.0pt]     for community_id, answer in intermediate_answers.items():
[p0325-l0027] [8.0pt]         combined_answers_prompt += f"Community {community_id}: {answer}\n\n"
[p0325-l0028] [10.0pt] This is a naive implementation of the GraphRAG paper, and it’s a good way to under­
[p0325-l0029] [10.0pt] stand how GraphRAG works and why it can outperform vanilla RAG or other patterns
[p0325-l0030] [10.0pt] that rely mostly on embedding similarity. Our custom implementation still has plenty
[p0325-l0031] [10.0pt] of room for improvement, especially for local use. Here are some suggestions:
[p0325-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ Persist the generated graph elements (entities, entity summaries, communities,
[p0325-l0033] [10.0pt] and community summaries) in Parquet format to avoid rerunning the indexing
[p0325-l0034] [10.0pt] process for each new query.
[p0325-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Validate the generated entities.
[p0325-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ Export the graph as GraphML for visual analysis in a third-party tool.
[p0325-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ Rank the generated community summaries, and then filter them by relevance
[p0325-l0038] [10.0pt] to the user query before generating intermediate answers. This produces more
[p0325-l0039] [10.0pt] accurate answers and fewer calls to the generative model.

[p0326-l0002] [9.0pt] GraphRAG
[p0326-l0003] [10.5pt] 14.1.1	 Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG capabilities
[p0326-l0004] [10.0pt] As mentioned earlier in this chapter, Microsoft released an open source implemen­
[p0326-l0005] [10.0pt] tation based on the GraphRAG paper. In its implementation, it offers two options at
[p0326-l0006] [10.0pt] query time:
[p0326-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ Global search—Answers to user queries are based on community summaries gen­
[p0326-l0008] [10.0pt] erated at indexing time, which is the core idea of the GraphRAG paper. We used
[p0326-l0009] [10.0pt] the same strategy in our custom implementation.
[p0326-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Local search—Answers are generated by combining relevant data from an
[p0326-l0011] [10.0pt] AI-extracted KG (entities) with text chunks from the source documents
[p0326-l0012] [10.0pt] (embeddings). This option also converts the knowledge base to vectors and
[p0326-l0013] [10.0pt] stores them in a vector database. This approach is out of scope for this book.
[p0326-l0014] [10.0pt] Microsoft’s GraphRAG solution has been implemented in Python using only open
[p0326-l0015] [10.0pt] source packages, but it supports only OpenAI’s commercial generative and embedding
[p0326-l0016] [10.0pt] models via the OpenAI or Azure OpenAI APIs. It doesn’t support running open source
[p0326-l0017] [10.0pt] SLMs locally or using other providers’ APIs. Still, it’s worth considering as an end-to-
[p0326-l0018] [10.0pt] end solution: the code is open source, so you can fork the GitHub repository and adapt
[p0326-l0019] [10.0pt] it to use local models via the Hugging Face Transformers library, vLLM, or Ollama, or
[p0326-l0020] [10.0pt] use open source SLMs through Hugging Face endpoints.
[p0326-l0021] [10.0pt] Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG solution includes built-in logic to persist the
[p0326-l0022] [10.0pt] graph and related artifacts, such as communities and community summaries. It stores
[p0326-l0023] [10.0pt] everything in Parquet format on disk or in Azure Blob Storage or Cosmos DB.
[p0326-l0024] [10.0pt] NOTE  Apache Parquet (https://parquet.apache.org/) is an open source,
[p0326-l0025] [10.0pt] column-­oriented storage format designed for efficient analytics and large-scale
[p0326-l0026] [10.0pt] data processing. It uses compression and encoding to support complex data
[p0326-l0027] [10.0pt] structures and fast queries.
[p0326-l0028] [10.0pt] Microsoft’s local search option in GraphRAG stores document embeddings in a vector
[p0326-l0029] [10.0pt] database. This persistence works out of the box when you use a supported option: the
[p0326-l0030] [10.0pt] open source LanceDB (introduced in chapter 13) or the Azure services Cosmos DB and
[p0326-l0031] [10.0pt] Azure AI Search. Even if you plan to use only global search, indexing still requires a con­
[p0326-l0032] [10.0pt] nection to one of the supported vector databases. To use a different graph store or vector
[p0326-l0033] [10.0pt] database, you must fork the GraphRAG GitHub repository and implement it yourself.
[p0326-l0034] [10.0pt] Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG comes with a CLI, so we don’t need to write any
[p0326-l0035] [10.0pt] Python code (as long as we use only the supported models and storage systems). The
[p0326-l0036] [10.0pt] package can be installed as follows:
[p0326-l0037] [8.0pt] pip install graphrag
[p0326-l0038] [10.0pt] Once that’s done, we can initialize a GraphRAG space using the graphrag command,
[p0326-l0039] [10.0pt] providing the path to the workspace root directory:
[p0326-l0040] [8.0pt] graphrag init --root <graphrag_space_root_dir>

=== PDF page 327 / printed label 306 ===
[p0327-l0001] [9.0pt] 306
[p0327-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0327-l0003] [10.0pt] After the workspace is created, edit the two configuration files it generates: .env, where
[p0327-l0004] [10.0pt] you add your OpenAI or Azure OpenAI key, and settings.yaml, where you config­
[p0327-l0005] [10.0pt] ure everything else (vector database connection, graph storage, LLM and embedding
[p0327-l0006] [10.0pt] model settings, logging, and so on).
[p0327-l0007] [10.0pt] Then start indexing your knowledge base by running the same graphrag command
[p0327-l0008] [10.0pt] in a terminal and waiting for it to complete:
[p0327-l0009] [8.0pt] graphrag index --root <graphrag_space_root_dir>
[p0327-l0010] [10.0pt] Once the indexing process is completed, we can perform a query as follows:
[p0327-l0011] [8.0pt] graphrag query --root < graphrag_space_root_dir> --method <search_method>
[p0327-l0012] [10.0pt] ➥ --query "What are the main topic in this documents?"
[p0327-l0013] [10.0pt] In the simplest use case, we provide the workspace root path, the search method
[p0327-l0014] [10.0pt] (global or local), and a query. Although the CLI is straightforward, we can also use this
[p0327-l0015] [10.0pt] GraphRAG implementation programmatically via its Python API.
[p0327-l0016] [10.0pt] If you build a custom integration with other models, graph storage, or a vector store,
[p0327-l0017] [10.0pt] you can still use the CLI in your fork to initialize the workspace, index data, and run
[p0327-l0018] [10.0pt] queries.
[p0327-l0019] [10.0pt] Microsoft’s open source GraphRAG includes the building blocks, but it lacks capa­
[p0327-l0020] [10.0pt] bilities such as text extraction and document preprocessing, graph visualization, and
[p0327-l0021] [10.0pt] results evaluation. For these, you’ll need to integrate third-party open source or propri­
[p0327-l0022] [10.0pt] etary tools.
[p0327-l0023] [10.5pt] 14.1.2	 Evaluation metrics
[p0327-l0024] [10.0pt] RAG improves the accuracy of LLM responses. There are many techniques and frame­
[p0327-l0025] [10.0pt] works for evaluating LLM outputs (some covered in earlier chapters), but how can we
[p0327-l0026] [10.0pt] assess the language models used in a RAG system, including GraphRAG? Which met­
[p0327-l0027] [10.0pt] rics should we use?
[p0327-l0028] [10.0pt] Traditional metrics, such as BLEU and ROUGE, widely used in NLP, often fail to
[p0327-l0029] [10.0pt] capture what RAG applications require, such as factual accuracy and context relevance.
[p0327-l0030] [10.0pt] BLEU doesn’t account for the context or evidence in the retrieved documents, which
[p0327-l0031] [10.0pt] can leave gaps in evaluating factual accuracy, whereas ROUGE emphasizes recall and
[p0327-l0032] [10.0pt] largely ignores precision. RAG needs both precision (how much retrieved informa­
[p0327-l0033] [10.0pt] tion is relevant) and recall (how much relevant information is retrieved). We therefore
[p0327-l0034] [10.0pt] need specialized RAG metrics, including metrics tailored to each phase of the pipeline
[p0327-l0035] [10.0pt] (retrieval and generation).
[p0327-l0036] [10.0pt] NOTE  BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) is a precision-based met­
[p0327-l0037] [10.0pt] ric that evaluates the overlap of sequences of words between the generated
[p0327-l0038] [10.0pt] response and a reference response. ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for
[p0327-l0039] [10.0pt] Gisting Evaluation) measures the overlap of word sequences and word pairs
[p0327-l0040] [10.0pt] between the generated response and reference texts, with a focus on recall.

=== PDF page 328 / printed label 307 ===
[p0328-l0001] [9.0pt] 307
[p0328-l0002] [9.0pt] RAG + Agentic AI
[p0328-l0003] [10.0pt] For retrieval, these are meaningful dedicated evaluation metrics:
[p0328-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Context precision—This measures how precisely the retrieved documents provide
[p0328-l0005] [10.0pt] relevant information for a given query.
[p0328-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Context recall—This assesses how well the retrieved documents cover all relevant
[p0328-l0007] [10.0pt] aspects of a query.
[p0328-l0008] [10.0pt] For answer generation, these are meaningful dedicated evaluation metrics:
[p0328-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ Faithfulness—This measures the factual accuracy of a generated response against
[p0328-l0010] [10.0pt] the retrieved documents.
[p0328-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Answer relevancy—This assesses how relevant a generated response is to the orig­
[p0328-l0012] [10.0pt] inal query.
[p0328-l0013] [10.0pt] In theory, you can combine the preceding metrics into an average RAG score. In prac­
[p0328-l0014] [10.0pt] tice, you must assign a weight to each score based on its importance in your domain
[p0328-l0015] [10.0pt] (see table 14.1).
[p0328-l0016] [8.0pt] Table 14.1  RAG-specific metrics
[p0328-l0017] [8.0pt] Metric
[p0328-l0018] [8.0pt] RAG phase
[p0328-l0019] [8.0pt] Formula
[p0328-l0020] [8.0pt] Context precision
[p0328-l0021] [8.0pt] Retrieval
[p0328-l0022] [8.0pt] CP = Number of relevant sentences retrieved / Total number
[p0328-l0023] [8.0pt] of sentences retrieved
[p0328-l0024] [8.0pt] Context recall
[p0328-l0025] [8.0pt] Retrieval
[p0328-l0026] [8.0pt] CR = Number of relevant sentences retrieved / Total number
[p0328-l0027] [8.0pt] of relevant sentences available
[p0328-l0028] [8.0pt] Faithfulness
[p0328-l0029] [8.0pt] Generation
[p0328-l0030] [8.0pt] F = Number of correct facts in the response / Total number of
[p0328-l0031] [8.0pt] facts in the response
[p0328-l0032] [8.0pt] Answer relevancy
[p0328-l0033] [8.0pt] Generation
[p0328-l0034] [8.0pt] AR = Number of relevant concepts in the response / Total
[p0328-l0035] [8.0pt] number of concepts in the response
[p0328-l0036] [10.0pt] Table 14.1 summarizes these metrics for use in RAG systems. At the time of writing,
[p0328-l0037] [10.0pt] only one open source Python library, Ragas (https://github.com/explodinggradients/
[p0328-l0038] [10.0pt] ragas), implements these RAG-specific metrics, but it supports only commercial LLMs
[p0328-l0039] [10.0pt] via the OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, and Google Vertex AI APIs, or models deployed on
[p0328-l0040] [10.0pt] AWS Bedrock. You’ll need a custom implementation to support local SLMs and cus­
[p0328-l0041] [10.0pt] tom models.
[p0328-l0042] [12.5pt] 14.2	 RAG + Agentic AI
[p0328-l0043] [10.0pt] In chapter 13, we discussed RAG (and continued in the first part of this chapter) and
[p0328-l0044] [10.0pt] agentic AI. With those core concepts in mind, it’s natural to consider using them
[p0328-l0045] [10.0pt] together—a pattern commonly known as agentic RAG. In a traditional RAG system, a
[p0328-l0046] [10.0pt] retriever model pulls information relevant to a user query from one or more external
[p0328-l0047] [10.0pt] sources (databases, vector stores, the web, and so on) and passes it to a language model
[p0328-l0048] [10.0pt] that generates a response using the added context. When you add AI agents to a RAG
[p0328-l0049] [10.0pt] system, they can plan multi-step retrieval, adapt to what they find by updating queries,

=== PDF page 329 / printed label 308 ===
[p0329-l0001] [9.0pt] 308
[p0329-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0329-l0003] [10.0pt] and use multiple tools to improve response accuracy. By breaking complex tasks into
[p0329-l0004] [10.0pt] smaller, specialized ones (often using specialized tools and/or smaller agents), agentic
[p0329-l0005] [10.0pt] frameworks can make a RAG system more efficient, effective, and easier to understand
[p0329-l0006] [10.0pt] and maintain. This setup is well suited to customer support, research assistance, knowl­
[p0329-l0007] [10.0pt] edge management, and domain-specific problem solving. Figure 14.3 shows a logical
[p0329-l0008] [10.0pt] schema for a generic, basic agentic RAG system:
[p0329-l0009] [7.0pt] Query
[p0329-l0010] [7.0pt] User
[p0329-l0011] [7.0pt] Agentic AI
[p0329-l0012] [7.0pt] Vector
[p0329-l0013] [7.0pt] database
[p0329-l0014] [7.0pt] Has info been
[p0329-l0015] [7.0pt] Yes
[p0329-l0016] [7.0pt] Response
[p0329-l0017] [7.0pt] found in the
[p0329-l0018] [7.0pt] database?
[p0329-l0019] [7.0pt] No
[p0329-l0020] [7.0pt] Web search tool
[p0329-l0021] [7.0pt] Internet
[p0329-l0022] [8.0pt] Figure 14.3  The logical
[p0329-l0023] [8.0pt] schema of a basic
[p0329-l0024] [8.0pt] agentic RAG system
[p0329-l0025] [10.0pt] Given a user query, the agent searches the vector database. If the retrieved information
[p0329-l0026] [10.0pt] isn’t relevant to the question, it then searches the web for additional context before
[p0329-l0027] [10.0pt] generating the final answer.
[p0329-l0028] [10.0pt] Simple, flexible, and well integrated with the wider Python ecosystem for RAG—and
[p0329-l0029] [10.0pt] with broad support for SLMs—smolagents (introduced in chapter 13) is a great choice
[p0329-l0030] [10.0pt] for building an agentic RAG system. Let’s implement a basic example like the one in
[p0329-l0031] [10.0pt] figure 14.3.
[p0329-l0032] [10.0pt] A companion Colab notebook with the complete code is provided. We’ll use the fol­
[p0329-l0033] [10.0pt] lowing open source Python libraries:
[p0329-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ LangChain
[p0329-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ pypdf

=== PDF page 330 / printed label 309 ===
[p0330-l0001] [9.0pt] 309
[p0330-l0002] [9.0pt] RAG + Agentic AI
[p0330-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ LanceDB
[p0330-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ smolagents
[p0330-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ rank_bm25
[p0330-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ langchain-community
[p0330-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ langchain-huggingface
[p0330-l0008] [10.0pt] You’re already familiar with LanceDB, smolagents, and pypdf (from chapter 13).
[p0330-l0009] [10.0pt] LangChain (https://github.com/langchain-ai/langchain) is a framework for building
[p0330-l0010] [10.0pt] LLM-powered applications, with standard interfaces for models, embeddings, vector
[p0330-l0011] [10.0pt] stores, and more. I generally avoid frameworks that hide too much of the underlying
[p0330-l0012] [10.0pt] logic because they can be harder to debug or customize, but LangChain is handy for
[p0330-l0013] [10.0pt] implementing RAG systems. In this example, we’ll use it mainly for the RAG compo­
[p0330-l0014] [10.0pt] nents. We’ll also use LangChain Community, which provides third-party integrations
[p0330-l0015] [10.0pt] that implement the interfaces defined in the LangChain core framework. For a deeper
[p0330-l0016] [10.0pt] dive into the ecosystem, see AI Agents and Applications: With LangChain, LangGraph, and
[p0330-l0017] [10.0pt] MCP by Roberto Infante (Manning Publications, 2026).
[p0330-l0018] [10.0pt] For this example, we’ll use the same paper as before (https://arxiv.org/pdf/
[p0330-l0019] [10.0pt] 2502.12923) as our knowledge base. After downloading the PDF to the Colab VM, we’ll
[p0330-l0020] [10.0pt] use the LangChain utility classes PyPDFLoader and RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter to
[p0330-l0021] [10.0pt] load it, extract its text, and split it into chunks:
[p0330-l0022] [8.0pt] from langchain.document_loaders import PyPDFLoader
[p0330-l0023] [8.0pt] from langchain.text_splitter import RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter
[p0330-l0024] [8.0pt] loader = PyPDFLoader("/content/arxiv_250212923.pdf")
[p0330-l0025] [8.0pt] documents = loader.load()
[p0330-l0026] [8.0pt] text_splitter = RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=1000,
[p0330-l0027] [8.0pt]                                             chunk_overlap=100)
[p0330-l0028] [8.0pt] docs = text_splitter.split_documents(documents)
[p0330-l0029] [10.0pt] Here, docs is a list of LangChain langchain.docstore.document.Document objects—one
[p0330-l0030] [10.0pt] for each text chunk.
[p0330-l0031] [10.0pt] We can now implement the agent’s first tool. In chapter 13, we built smolagents tools
[p0330-l0032] [10.0pt] using the @tool decorator, and you also saw that you can achieve the same result by
[p0330-l0033] [10.0pt] extending the Tool class. Here we’ll use the latter approach because it makes it easier to
[p0330-l0034] [10.0pt] manage access to the knowledge base.
[p0330-l0035] [10.0pt] The first tool we’ll create performs traditional text search to retrieve the parts of the
[p0330-l0036] [10.0pt] source document most relevant to a user query. It uses BM25, a standard information-­
[p0330-l0037] [10.0pt] retrieval ranking algorithm that scores documents based on term frequency, inverse
[p0330-l0038] [10.0pt] document frequency, and document length. BM25 is widely used in search engines and
[p0330-l0039] [10.0pt] is the default ranking method in tools such as Elasticsearch and Apache Lucene. Lang­
[p0330-l0040] [10.0pt] Chain includes a built-in implementation.
[p0330-l0041] [10.0pt] This first tool class can be defined as follows:

=== PDF page 331 / printed label 310 ===
[p0331-l0001] [9.0pt] 310
[p0331-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0331-l0003] [8.0pt] from smolagents import Tool
[p0331-l0004] [8.0pt] class BM25SearchTool(Tool):
[p0331-l0005] [8.0pt]     name = "do_bm25_search_on_local_documents"
[p0331-l0006] [8.0pt]     description = "Uses text search to retrieve the parts of the
[p0331-l0007] [10.0pt] ➥ documentation that could be most relevant to answer a query."
[p0331-l0008] [8.0pt]     inputs = {
[p0331-l0009] [8.0pt]         "query": {
[p0331-l0010] [8.0pt]             "type": "string",
[p0331-l0011] [8.0pt]             "description": "The search query string."
[p0331-l0012] [8.0pt]         },
[p0331-l0013] [8.0pt]     }
[p0331-l0014] [8.0pt]     output_type = "string"
[p0331-l0015] [10.0pt] In addition to extending the smolagents Tool class, we have added the required attri­
[p0331-l0016] [10.0pt] butes: name, description, inputs, and output_type. The last two specify the tool’s input
[p0331-l0017] [10.0pt] and output types. BM25SearchTool implements the init function to initialize the class
[p0331-l0018] [10.0pt] with the knowledge base:
[p0331-l0019] [8.0pt] from typing import List
[p0331-l0020] [8.0pt] from langchain.docstore.document import Document
[p0331-l0021] [8.0pt] def __init__(self, docs: List[Document], **kwargs):
[p0331-l0022] [8.0pt]         super().__init__(**kwargs)
[p0331-l0023] [8.0pt]         self.docs = docs
[p0331-l0024] [10.0pt] The BM25SearchTool class also implements the forward method, which defines what the
[p0331-l0025] [10.0pt] agent does when it uses the BM25SearchTool :
[p0331-l0026] [8.0pt] from langchain_community.retrievers import BM25Retriever
[p0331-l0027] [8.0pt] def forward(self, query: str) -> str:
[p0331-l0028] [8.0pt]         retriever = BM25Retriever.from_documents(self.docs, k=3)
[p0331-l0029] [8.0pt]         docs = retriever.invoke(query)
[p0331-l0030] [8.0pt]         return "\nRetrieved documents:\n" + "".join(
[p0331-l0031] [8.0pt]             [f"\n\n===== Document {i} =====\n" + doc.page_content for i,
[p0331-l0032] [10.0pt]             ➥ doc in enumerate(docs)]
[p0331-l0033] [8.0pt]         )
[p0331-l0034] [10.0pt] It uses LangChain’s BM25Retriever to search the document chunks.
[p0331-l0035] [10.0pt] Now let’s download the SLMs for our agent (as we did in the example in chapter 13):

[p0331-l0040] [8.0pt]                           device_map="auto",

[p0331-l0042] [8.0pt]                           torch_dtype=torch.float16)

[p0334-l0006] [8.0pt] 3.1 Data and Pre-processing
[p0334-l0007] [8.0pt] To the best of our knowledge, there is no ex-
[p0334-l0008] [8.0pt] isting human-curated dataset specifically for the
[p0334-l0009] [8.0pt] Home Assistant software. Thus, we rely on syn-
[p0334-l0010] [8.0pt] thetic data. We use a publicly available synthetic
[p0334-l0011] [8.0pt] dataset (acon96, 2024), which consists of 35,840
[p0334-l0012] [8.0pt] synthetic examples designed to mimic Home As-
[p0334-l0013] [10.0pt] All three chunks are relevant to the query topic. The top result contains all three key­
[p0334-l0014] [10.0pt] words the agent passed to the tool, while the others contain only one keyword (or
[p0334-l0015] [10.0pt] closely related terms).
[p0334-l0016] [10.0pt] Let’s make the system more complex by adding a vector database to store our knowl­
[p0334-l0017] [10.0pt] edge base as embeddings and a new similarity-search tool. This will let us see whether
[p0334-l0018] [10.0pt] the agent chooses keyword search, vector search, or a hybrid of both. Hybrid search
[p0334-l0019] [10.0pt] combines keyword and vector search to further improve retrieval quality (and, in turn,
[p0334-l0020] [10.0pt] improve any downstream tasks that use the returned documents).
[p0334-l0021] [10.0pt] First, we need an embedding model:
[p0334-l0022] [8.0pt] from langchain_huggingface import HuggingFaceEmbeddings
[p0334-l0023] [8.0pt] embeddings = HuggingFaceEmbeddings(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
[p0334-l0024] [10.0pt] We use the langchain-huggingface package’s HuggingFaceEmbeddings class to down­
[p0334-l0025] [10.0pt] load the embedding model from the Hugging Face Hub. This time, we’ll use all
[p0334-l0026] [10.0pt] -MiniLM-L6-v2, also available via the sentence-transformers library; it’s fast and delivers
[p0334-l0027] [10.0pt] good quality.
[p0334-l0028] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll create and populate a vector database. We’ll use LanceDB, the same vec­
[p0334-l0029] [10.0pt] tor database we used for the RAG examples in chapter 13. We’ll create a local database

[p0341-l0012] [12.5pt] 14.3	 Long- and short-term memory management
[p0341-l0013] [10.0pt] You can further improve the performance of language-model applications—such as
[p0341-l0014] [10.0pt] RAG systems, chatbots, and AI agents—by enriching the model’s prompt with context
[p0341-l0015] [10.0pt] built from previous interactions with the same user (or session). Retrieving relevant con­
[p0341-l0016] [10.0pt] tent from past conversations and prompts, using short- or long-term memory, can nar­
[p0341-l0017] [10.0pt] row queries and searches and help models return more fine-grained, accurate answers.
[p0341-l0018] [10.0pt] NOTE  Short-term memory tracks the ongoing conversation by maintain­
[p0341-l0019] [10.0pt] ing message history within a session. Long-term memory stores user-specific
[p0341-l0020] [10.0pt] or application-level data across sessions and is shared across conversational
[p0341-l0021] [10.0pt] threads. It can be recalled at any time and in any thread.
[p0341-l0022] [10.0pt] This approach can also reduce costs by lowering the number of API calls and gen­
[p0341-l0023] [10.0pt] erated tokens. Even GraphRAG systems, which are more accurate than many other
[p0341-l0024] [10.0pt] LLM-based solutions by design, can benefit from a memory-management strategy.
[p0341-l0025] [10.0pt] Memoripy (https://github.com/caspianmoon/memoripy) is an open source Python

=== PDF page 342 / printed label 321 ===
[p0342-l0001] [9.0pt] 321
[p0342-l0002] [9.0pt] Long- and short-term memory management
[p0342-l0003] [10.0pt] package that addresses this need. It supports LLM-based applications that require
[p0342-l0004] [10.0pt] memory management, and it’s compatible with models behind the OpenAI and Azure
[p0342-l0005] [10.0pt] OpenAI APIs, models available through the OpenRouter commercial API, and local
[p0342-l0006] [10.0pt] open source SLMs available through the Ollama API.
[p0342-l0007] [10.0pt] Notable features that make Memoripy stand out include
[p0342-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Short- and long-term memory management—Based on relevance to the current user
[p0342-l0009] [10.0pt] conversation.
[p0342-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Contextual retrieval—Memory retrieval is based on embeddings, concepts, and
[p0342-l0011] [10.0pt] past interactions.
[p0342-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ Concept extraction and embeddings—It uses language models to extract concepts
[p0342-l0013] [10.0pt] and generate embeddings.
[p0342-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ Graph-based associations—It builds a concept graph and uses spreading activation
[p0342-l0015] [10.0pt] for relevance-based retrieval.
[p0342-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ Hierarchical clustering—Memoripy clusters similar memories into semantic groups
[p0342-l0017] [10.0pt] for more contextually relevant retrieval.
[p0342-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Decay and reinforcement—Older memories fade over time, while frequently
[p0342-l0019] [10.0pt] accessed memories are reinforced.
[p0342-l0020] [10.0pt] NOTE  Spreading activation is a method for searching associative networks,
[p0342-l0021] [10.0pt] artificial neural networks, or semantic networks. The search process is initiated
[p0342-l0022] [10.0pt] by labeling a set of source nodes (concepts) with weights (activation) and then
[p0342-l0023] [10.0pt] iteratively propagating (spreading) that activation out to other nodes linked to
[p0342-l0024] [10.0pt] the source nodes. It is often applied in information retrieval tasks.
[p0342-l0025] [10.0pt] Memoripy provides three built-in options for storing interaction data: in mem­
[p0342-l0026] [10.0pt] ory, in JSON files, or in Amazon DynamoDB (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/­
[p0342-l0027] [10.0pt] amazondynamodb­/latest/developerguide/Introduction.html). Memory storage is
[p0342-l0028] [10.0pt] suitable for development, debugging, and testing. JSON files can be a good option for
[p0342-l0029] [10.0pt] local deployments.  DynamoDB is more appropriate for large, distributed deployments.
[p0342-l0030] [10.0pt] You can also add other backends by implementing the BaseStorage abstract class.
[p0342-l0031] [10.0pt] As you saw in the previous Memoripy feature list, user–model interaction data
[p0342-l0032] [10.0pt] (prompts and responses in multi-turn conversations) is organized as a graph, like the
[p0342-l0033] [10.0pt] knowledge base in GraphRAG. The graph is built with the NetworkX library (used
[p0342-l0034] [10.0pt] earlier in this chapter). Indexes on the memory graph are created with Facebook AI
[p0342-l0035] [10.0pt] Similarity Search (FAISS, introduced in chapter 2). Graph creation and updates are
[p0342-l0036] [10.0pt] transparent to developers: Memoripy manages them internally, so you can focus on
[p0342-l0037] [10.0pt] application-specific requirements rather than low-level processes.
[p0342-l0038] [10.0pt] The Memoripy workflow is as follows:
[p0342-l0039] [10.0pt] 1	 Previous interactions are loaded from the chosen storage option, and memory is
[p0342-l0040] [10.0pt] initialized.
[p0342-l0041] [10.0pt] 2	 Once a new interaction has happened (the user’s prompt and the model’s
[p0342-l0042] [10.0pt] response), the system stores it with its embedding and concepts.

=== PDF page 343 / printed label 322 ===
[p0343-l0001] [9.0pt] 322
[p0343-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 14  Advanced components for LLM applications
[p0343-l0003] [10.0pt] 3	 Interactions relevant to the new one are retrieved by searching past interactions
[p0343-l0004] [10.0pt] using cosine similarity, decay factors, and spreading activation.
[p0343-l0005] [10.0pt] 4	 The final response combines the current prompt with the retrieved interactions
[p0343-l0006] [10.0pt] to keep it relevant to the context.
[p0343-l0007] [10.0pt] 5	 Unused memories decay faster, while frequently accessed ones are reinforced.
[p0343-l0008] [10.0pt] Again, this flow is transparent to developers, and it is fully managed by the underlying
[p0343-l0009] [10.0pt] library.
[p0343-l0010] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll implement memory management with Memoripy using only SLMs
[p0343-l0011] [10.0pt] served from a local Ollama instance. In this example, you’ll need an Ollama server
[p0343-l0012] [10.0pt] running with the mxbai-embed-large embedding model (https://huggingface.co/
[p0343-l0013] [10.0pt] mixedbread-ai/mxbai-embed-large-v1) and the Microsoft Phi-3 Mini 4K Instruct model
[p0343-l0014] [10.0pt] already pulled and available through the server’s REST API. You can install Memoripy
[p0343-l0015] [10.0pt] from PyPI, or clone the GitHub repository and install the requirements to get the latest
[p0343-l0016] [10.0pt] updates.
[p0343-l0017] [10.0pt] First, we’ll set up a storage option (a JSON file in this case):
[p0343-l0018] [8.0pt] from memoripy import JSONStorage
[p0343-l0019] [8.0pt] storage_option = JSONStorage("interaction_history.json")
[p0343-l0020] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll initialize the MemoryManager, specifying the generator and embedding mod­
[p0343-l0021] [10.0pt] els and the chosen storage option:
[p0343-l0022] [8.0pt] from memoripy import MemoryManager
[p0343-l0023] [8.0pt] from memoripy.implemented_models import OllamaChatModel,
[p0343-l0024] [10.0pt] ➥ OllamaEmbeddingModel
[p0343-l0025] [8.0pt] chat_model_name = "phi3.5"
[p0343-l0026] [8.0pt] embedding_model_name = "mxbai-embed-large"
[p0343-l0027] [8.0pt] memory_manager = MemoryManager(OllamaChatModel(chat_model_name),
[p0343-l0028] [8.0pt]                                OllamaEmbeddingModel(embedding_model_name),
[p0343-l0029] [8.0pt]                                storage=storage_option)
[p0343-l0030] [10.0pt] OllamaChatModel and OllamaEmbeddingModel are the classes for models hosted on an

[p0343-l0032] [10.0pt] OpenRouter models. During initialization, the MemoryManager loads any persisted
[p0343-l0033] [10.0pt] interactions.
[p0343-l0034] [10.0pt] Whenever a user submits a new prompt, we need to load the short-term interactions:
[p0343-l0035] [8.0pt] short_term, _ = memory_manager.load_history()
[p0343-l0036] [8.0pt] last_interactions = short_term[-short_term_threshold:]

[p0343-l0038] [10.0pt] We set a threshold, short_term_threshold, to define which interactions count as
[p0343-l0039] [10.0pt] short-term.
[p0343-l0040] [10.0pt] Also, the interactions most relevant to the current prompt need to be retrieved:
