[p0345-l0008] [8.0pt] }
[p0345-l0009] [10.0pt] There are two sections: one for short-term memory and one for long-term memory.
[p0345-l0010] [10.0pt] In the preceding example, the long-term memory section is empty because the file
[p0345-l0011] [10.0pt] reflects the model’s first user interaction. When populated, it follows the same schema
[p0345-l0012] [10.0pt] as the short-term section:
[p0345-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ id—The unique identifier of a memory entry
[p0345-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ prompt—The user input
[p0345-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ output—The generated response
[p0345-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ embedding—The vector corresponding to the response
[p0345-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ timestamp—The moment in time the response has been generated
[p0345-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ access_count—The number of times this entry has been retrieved for any fur­
[p0345-l0019] [10.0pt] ther interaction
[p0345-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ concepts—The list of concepts derived from this interaction
[p0345-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ decay_factor—A weight used to promote or demote an interaction in time
[p0345-l0022] [10.0pt] The library uses timestamp, access_count, and decay_factor for decay and reinforce­
[p0345-l0023] [10.0pt] ment, and embedding and concepts to retrieve relevant past interactions.
[p0345-l0024] [10.0pt] At the time of writing, Memoripy is a young but powerful Python project for memory
[p0345-l0025] [10.0pt] management in LLM-based applications. Keep an eye on the official GitHub repo for
[p0345-l0026] [10.0pt] updates.
[p0345-l0027] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0345-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ GraphRAG improves on traditional RAG by using knowledge graphs to
[p0345-l0029] [10.0pt] model entity relationships and support multihop reasoning across document
[p0345-l0030] [10.0pt] collections.
[p0345-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ Knowledge graphs (KGs) organize information, representing entities as nodes
[p0345-l0032] [10.0pt] and relationships as edges.
[p0345-l0033] [10.0pt] ¡ Microsoft’s GraphRAG approach builds entity KGs from source documents and
[p0345-l0034] [10.0pt] pregenerates community summaries for related entity groups.
[p0345-l0035] [10.0pt] ¡ Ollama structured outputs constrain responses to a specific JSON schema using
[p0345-l0036] [10.0pt] Pydantic classes for consistent data formatting.
[p0345-l0037] [10.0pt] ¡ The NetworkX library lets you create and manipulate graphs to build KGs from
[p0345-l0038] [10.0pt] extracted entities and relationships.
[p0345-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ The Leiden algorithm identifies graph communities by optimizing modularity
[p0345-l0040] [10.0pt] through iterative node movement and community aggregation.

=== PDF page 346 / printed label 325 ===
[p0346-l0001] [9.0pt] 325
[p0346-l0002] [9.0pt] Summary
[p0346-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Community detection groups densely connected entities into meaningful clus­
[p0346-l0004] [10.0pt] ters for downstream summarization.
[p0346-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ Community summaries are high-level overviews of entity groups that improve
[p0346-l0006] [10.0pt] global search quality in GraphRAG systems.
[p0346-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ Global search creates intermediate answers for each community summary and
[p0346-l0008] [10.0pt] then combines them into a final response.
[p0346-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ Local search combines KG entities with document embeddings for hybrid
[p0346-l0010] [10.0pt] retrieval.
[p0346-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Microsoft’s open-source GraphRAG supports only OpenAI models but includes
[p0346-l0012] [10.0pt] complete indexing and query workflows.
[p0346-l0013] [10.0pt] ¡ RAG evaluation calls for specialized metrics such as context precision, context
[p0346-l0014] [10.0pt] recall, faithfulness, and answer relevance rather than traditional NLP metrics.
[p0346-l0015] [10.0pt] ¡ Agentic RAG systems pair autonomous agents with retrieval to perform multistep
[p0346-l0016] [10.0pt] information gathering and reasoning.
[p0346-l0017] [10.0pt] ¡ smolagents’ CodeAgent can autonomously choose the right tools and search strat­
[p0346-l0018] [10.0pt] egy for a query.
[p0346-l0019] [10.0pt] ¡ The BM25 algorithm ranks documents for keyword-based retrieval using term
[p0346-l0020] [10.0pt] frequency, inverse document frequency, and document length.
[p0346-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ Hybrid search combines BM25 keyword retrieval with semantic similarity search
[p0346-l0022] [10.0pt] to improve retrieval.
[p0346-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ LangChain’s EnsembleRetriever combines results from multiple retrievers, using
[p0346-l0024] [10.0pt] configurable weights for different search methods.
[p0346-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Custom retriever classes extend LangChain’s BaseRetriever to implement
[p0346-l0026] [10.0pt] domain-specific search.
[p0346-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Memory management systems track short-term conversation history and long-
[p0346-l0028] [10.0pt] term interactions across sessions.
[p0346-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ Memoripy stores memory as a graph, extracting concepts, generating embed­
[p0346-l0030] [10.0pt] dings, and using spreading activation to retrieve relevant items.
[p0346-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ Decay and reinforcement mechanisms strengthen frequently accessed memories
[p0346-l0032] [10.0pt] while degrading unused interactions over time.

[p0347-l0001] [30.0pt] Test-time compute and
[p0347-l0002] [30.0pt] small language models
[p0347-l0003] [225.0pt] 15
[p0347-l0004] [12.0pt] This chapter covers
[p0347-l0005] [9.8pt] ¡ Defining test-time compute
[p0347-l0006] [9.8pt] ¡ Using the OptiLLM inference proxy for test-time
[p0347-l0007] [9.8pt] compute with large and small language models
[p0347-l0008] [9.8pt] ¡ Embedding test-time compute with open source
[p0347-l0009] [9.8pt] SLMs
[p0347-l0010] [9.8pt] ¡ Tuning an SLM to reason through GRPO for a
[p0347-l0011] [9.8pt] specific domain
[p0347-l0012] [10.0pt] This chapter introduces the concept of test-time compute, and it surveys state-of-
[p0347-l0013] [10.0pt] the-art SLMs and libraries. It also provides a complete commodity-hardware exam­
[p0347-l0014] [10.0pt] ple, showing how you can apply the Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO)
[p0347-l0015] [10.0pt] technique used to train the DeepSeek-R1 models to specialize an SLM for a given
[p0347-l0016] [10.0pt] domain.
[p0347-l0017] [12.5pt] 15.1	 Test-time compute
[p0347-l0018] [10.0pt] Test-time compute (TTC) is a new concept for LLMs—it emerged in 2024 and refers to
[p0347-l0019] [10.0pt] the computational resources a model uses at inference time to generate responses,
[p0347-l0020] [9.0pt] 326

=== PDF page 348 / printed label 327 ===
[p0348-l0001] [9.0pt] 327
[p0348-l0002] [9.0pt] Test-time compute
[p0348-l0003] [10.0pt] allowing it to “think” further and spend more time exploring alternatives before
[p0348-l0004] [10.0pt] answering. The idea is especially useful for difficult tasks where even large models can
[p0348-l0005] [10.0pt] struggle, such as math, logic, and coding. With TTC, a model can dynamically increase
[p0348-l0006] [10.0pt] its “reasoning” time during inference, using search methods such as beam search or
[p0348-l0007] [10.0pt] tree-based exploration (like Monte Carlo tree search) to explore multiple candidate
[p0348-l0008] [10.0pt] outputs within a compute budget. It can then score those candidates and pick the best
[p0348-l0009] [10.0pt] one or even execute generated code and check for errors. The tradeoff is simple: more
[p0348-l0010] [10.0pt] “thinking” time can improve accuracy, but it increases compute costs.
[p0348-l0011] [10.0pt] Recent commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic appear to use this
[p0348-l0012] [10.0pt] approach: on challenging queries, they pause longer before producing a final response,
[p0348-l0013] [10.0pt] likely because they generate multiple candidates and run evaluations to select the best
[p0348-l0014] [10.0pt] one. Vendors often market this as “reasoning,” but it is better understood as spending
[p0348-l0015] [10.0pt] more compute and time on additional statistical processing. While this will not lead us
[p0348-l0016] [10.0pt] to artificial general intelligence, it can improve performance on tasks where a single
[p0348-l0017] [10.0pt] static inference pass is not enough.
[p0348-l0018] [10.0pt] NOTE  Artificial general intelligence (AGI) is a hypothetical stage in the devel­
[p0348-l0019] [10.0pt] opment of machine learning in which a model can match or exceed the cogni­
[p0348-l0020] [10.0pt] tive abilities of human beings across any task.
[p0348-l0021] [10.0pt] This paradigm offers several potential benefits:
[p0348-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Enhanced accuracy and more reliable answers
[p0348-l0023] [10.0pt] ¡ Better adaptability to new data and contexts
[p0348-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ Reduced overfitting because we rely less on static pretrained knowledge that may
[p0348-l0025] [10.0pt] be outdated or biased
[p0348-l0026] [10.0pt] However, using this strategy on large commercial models comes with some risks:
[p0348-l0027] [10.0pt] ¡ Shifting more compute to inference could raise costs for subscribers—the big
[p0348-l0028] [10.0pt] companies that own the models and infrastructure can raise fees or change plans
[p0348-l0029] [10.0pt] to cover maintenance. We often assume the API is backed by coordinated hard­
[p0348-l0030] [10.0pt] ware that lets GPU or TPU capacity scale up and down with demand, but we don’t
[p0348-l0031] [10.0pt] actually know because we don’t own that infrastructure.
[p0348-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ In closed-source models, the “thinking” steps (or, more accurately, the “refining
[p0348-l0033] [10.0pt] process”) are hidden from end users. We cannot access logs showing the model’s
[p0348-l0034] [10.0pt] intermediate answers, which search algorithms it used, or what code it generated
[p0348-l0035] [10.0pt] for a task. For validation, especially in regulated industries, this poses a signifi­
[p0348-l0036] [10.0pt] cant problem.
[p0348-l0037] [10.0pt] This is the direction that large commercial models will continue to follow. But what
[p0348-l0038] [10.0pt] about SLMs? For domain-specific tasks, small models specialized on domain data or
[p0348-l0039] [10.0pt] prompted with up-to-date context (as in a RAG system) can outperform larger models
[p0348-l0040] [10.0pt] on the same tasks. Could we implement TTC for these SLMs and further boost perfor­
[p0348-l0041] [10.0pt] mance on tasks that require more reasoning? This chapter explores these questions.

=== PDF page 349 / printed label 328 ===
[p0349-l0001] [9.0pt] 328
[p0349-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
[p0349-l0003] [12.5pt] 15.2	 The OptiLLM inference proxy
[p0349-l0004] [10.0pt] OpenAI’s o1, its first reflective GPT model, was previewed in September 2024 and
[p0349-l0005] [10.0pt] released to ChatGPT users that December. By then, many commercial LLMs (from
[p0349-l0006] [10.0pt] OpenAI and other vendors) and many open source models, large and small, were
[p0349-l0007] [10.0pt] widely available, but they relied on static inference. This highlighted the need for a way
[p0349-l0008] [10.0pt] to bring TTC to open source models as well.
[p0349-l0009] [10.0pt] That need sparked Asankhaya Sharma, a seasoned cybersecurity expert and tech
[p0349-l0010] [10.0pt] lead, to create an open source project called OptiLLM (https://github.com/codelion/
[p0349-l0011] [10.0pt] optillm). OptiLLM is an OpenAI API–compatible inference-optimizing proxy that
[p0349-l0012] [10.0pt] implements several state-of-the-art techniques to improve LLM accuracy and perfor­
[p0349-l0013] [10.0pt] mance, especially for coding, logical, and mathematical queries.
[p0349-l0014] [10.0pt] NOTE  I’m a contributor to this open source project, but I also use it in real-
[p0349-l0015] [10.0pt] world projects, so I have been able to validate the pros and cons of this approach.
[p0349-l0016] [10.0pt] The OptiLLM proxy sits between clients and an OpenAI API–compatible service (such
[p0349-l0017] [10.0pt] as OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Cerebras, or LiteLLM). As shown in figure 15.1, the high-
[p0349-l0018] [10.0pt] level flow of requests and responses is as follows:
[p0349-l0019] [7.0pt] User request via
[p0349-l0020] [7.0pt] Multiple
[p0349-l0021] [7.0pt] OpenAI client
[p0349-l0022] [7.0pt] Final Response
[p0349-l0023] [7.0pt] Response
[p0349-l0024] [7.0pt] calls to
[p0349-l0025] [7.0pt] base model
[p0349-l0026] [7.0pt] Any OpenAI
[p0349-l0027] [7.0pt] API–compatible service
[p0349-l0028] [8.0pt] Figure 15.1  The flow of requests and responses through the OptiLLM proxy
[p0349-l0029] [10.0pt] ¡ A user submits a prompt through a client application, which sends a request to
[p0349-l0030] [10.0pt] the model’s API. You use the OpenAI SDK to implement the request logic, just

=== PDF page 350 / printed label 329 ===
[p0350-l0001] [9.0pt] 329
[p0350-l0002] [9.0pt] The OptiLLM inference proxy
[p0350-l0003] [10.0pt] as you would for direct calls to the third-party API. The only difference is that
[p0350-l0004] [10.0pt] the request can include an extra parameter specifying which algorithm to use to
[p0350-l0005] [10.0pt] refine the model’s answers.
[p0350-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ The request arrives at the OptiLLM proxy service (layer B in the figure), which
[p0350-l0007] [10.0pt] forwards it to the OpenAI API–compatible service (layer C), which performs
[p0350-l0008] [10.0pt] static inference.
[p0350-l0009] [10.0pt] ¡ The proxy iterates for a set number of times, making multiple calls to the service
[p0350-l0010] [10.0pt] API and applying the selected algorithm and conditions to the responses from
[p0350-l0011] [10.0pt] static inference. It sends the final response to the client application only after the
[p0350-l0012] [10.0pt] refinement cycle completes.
[p0350-l0013] [10.0pt] OptiLLM also supports local inference. You can load Hugging Face-hosted pretrained
[p0350-l0014] [10.0pt] models and LoRA weights directly or run the OptiLLM proxy against an external server
[p0350-l0015] [10.0pt] such as llama.cpp or Ollama. However, these servers currently can’t sample multiple
[p0350-l0016] [10.0pt] responses from a model, limiting the number of approaches available in OptiLLM out
[p0350-l0017] [10.0pt] of the box.

[p0352-l0011] [8.0pt]     messages, aggregate_paths=True,
[p0352-l0012] [8.0pt]     temperature=0.1, max_new_tokens=1024)
[p0352-l0013] [8.0pt] print(f"CoT Decoding:\n {result}")
[p0352-l0014] [10.0pt] and wait for the model to “think” and return the final answer. OptiLLM provides a ded­
[p0352-l0015] [10.0pt] icated function for each supported technique for local models. These functions take
[p0352-l0016] [10.0pt] the model, its tokenizer, a prompt, and a set of sampling parameters.
[p0352-l0017] [10.0pt] Let’s evaluate a local SLM on a challenging dataset using the AutoThink approach.
[p0352-l0018] [10.0pt] The complete code for this example is available in a companion Colab notebook. The
[p0352-l0019] [10.0pt] code and chosen model are small enough to run on a VM without hardware accelera­
[p0352-l0020] [10.0pt] tion, but using a GPU is recommended to speed up evaluation on the test samples.
[p0352-l0021] [10.0pt] AutoThink is a technique introduced in the “AutoThink: Efficient inference for rea­
[p0352-l0022] [10.0pt] soning LLMs” paper (https://dx.doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.5253327) and implemented in
[p0352-l0023] [10.0pt] the OptiLLM codebase. It addresses two aspects of efficient reasoning: choosing an
[p0352-l0024] [10.0pt] appropriate reasoning budget and steering the model toward more effective reason­
[p0352-l0025] [10.0pt] ing paths. To do this, it combines query-complexity classification (an adaptive classifier
[p0352-l0026] [10.0pt] decides whether a query needs high- or low-complexity reasoning) with steering-vector
[p0352-l0027] [10.0pt] guidance (activation-based steering vectors guide the model’s reasoning). AutoThink
[p0352-l0028] [10.0pt] runs in two phases, preprocessing and inference, as shown in figure 15.2 (from the orig­
[p0352-l0029] [10.0pt] inal paper).
[p0352-l0030] [10.0pt] In preprocessing, OptiLLM collects a dataset of query-response pairs, searches to iden­
[p0352-l0031] [10.0pt] tify pivotal tokens that affect reasoning quality, derives vectors from those tokens, and
[p0352-l0032] [10.0pt] trains a query-complexity classifier on the calibration dataset. As an OptiLLM user, you
[p0352-l0033] [10.0pt] don’t need to manage this step; at inference time, the library automatically downloads
[p0352-l0034] [10.0pt] a pretrained classifier from the Hugging Face Hub on the first run. During inference,
[p0352-l0035] [10.0pt] the classifier selects an appropriate token budget, control vectors steer decoding toward
[p0352-l0036] [10.0pt] effective reasoning paths, and, once the budget is reached, the model generates the final
[p0352-l0037] [10.0pt] response. All of these steps are transparent to the ML engineer implementing OptiLLM.
[p0352-l0038] [10.0pt] We’ll evaluate the Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct model (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/
[p0352-l0039] [10.0pt] Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct), available on the Hugging Face Hub. To measure its perfor­
[p0352-l0040] [10.0pt] mance with the AutoThink technique, we’ll use a subset of the OptiLLMBench test
[p0352-l0041] [10.0pt] split (https://huggingface.co/datasets/codelion/optillmbench). OptiLLMBench com­
[p0352-l0042] [10.0pt] bines samples from four datasets to test math and logic reasoning.

[p0358-l0003] [10.0pt] The only thing that kept this from being a good answer was misunderstanding the for­

[p0358-l0006] [10.0pt] OptiLLM is still a valid way to improve SLMs’ reasoning, but newer options do so
[p0358-l0007] [10.0pt] without adding extra components to an existing architecture. We’ll cover them in the

[p0358-l0009] [12.5pt] 15.3	 SLMs with embedded test-time compute
[p0358-l0010] [10.0pt] Reflective models are no longer limited to closed, commercial LLMs. The open source
[p0358-l0011] [10.0pt] community has helped bring reasoning capabilities to open models of all sizes. New
[p0358-l0012] [10.0pt] frameworks that combine reinforcement learning and process-reward models let
[p0358-l0013] [10.0pt] researchers and engineers fine-tune models transparently for domain-specific tasks.
[p0358-l0014] [10.0pt] These efforts have further democratized generative AI, enabling smaller organizations
[p0358-l0015] [10.0pt] and individuals to innovate without the cost and constraints of proprietary models and
[p0358-l0016] [10.0pt] APIs. They have also strengthened community collaboration, accelerating progress.
[p0358-l0017] [10.0pt] Here are the most popular and powerful open source SLMs with a thinking mode:
[p0358-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ Qwen3 (https://qwen.ai/blog?id=qwen3)—A Qwen-family model developed by
[p0358-l0019] [10.0pt] Alibaba Cloud’s Qwen team. It comes in small (0.6B to 32B) and large (235B)
[p0358-l0020] [10.0pt] sizes, all available on the Hugging Face Hub.
[p0358-l0021] [10.0pt] ¡ DeepSeek-R1 (https://github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-R1) and DeepSeek-R1-
[p0358-l0022] [10.0pt] Zero—The larger model has 671B parameters, and smaller distilled checkpoints
[p0358-l0023] [10.0pt] (1.5B to 70B) based on Qwen 2.5 or the Llama 3 series are available on the Hug­
[p0358-l0024] [10.0pt] ging Face Hub.
[p0358-l0025] [10.0pt] ¡ Phi-4 (https://huggingface.co/microsoft/phi-4)—This is the latest in Micro­
[p0358-l0026] [10.0pt] soft’s Phi family (at the time of writing). It comes in a single 14B-parameter size
[p0358-l0027] [10.0pt] and is trained with a particular focus on math problems.
[p0358-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ Open R1 (https://huggingface.co/open-r1)—A Hugging Face and community-­
[p0358-l0029] [10.0pt] driven, fully open reproduction of DeepSeek-R1 that lets anyone build the miss­
[p0358-l0030] [10.0pt] ing pieces of the R1 pipeline, reproduce it, and build on it.
[p0358-l0031] [10.0pt] ¡ Marco-o1 (https://github.com/aidc-ai/marco-o1)—Developed by the Marco­
[p0358-l0032] [10.0pt] Polo Team, AI Business, at Alibaba International Digital Commerce. It focuses on
[p0358-l0033] [10.0pt] domains with standard answers—such as math, physics, and coding (well suited
[p0358-l0034] [10.0pt] for reinforcement learning)—and also emphasizes open-ended problems. The
[p0358-l0035] [10.0pt] authors have tried to address the question, “Can the o1 model effectively gen­
[p0358-l0036] [10.0pt] eralize to broader domains where clear standards are absent and rewards are
[p0358-l0037] [10.0pt] challenging to quantify?” Checkpoints of pretrained models are available on the
[p0358-l0038] [10.0pt] Hugging Face Hub.
[p0358-l0039] [10.0pt] For local use, these open source options are available through Hugging Face’s Trans­
[p0358-l0040] [10.0pt] formers library, and most have been quantized and published in GGUF format in the
[p0358-l0041] [10.0pt] Ollama model catalog (chapter 12 covers serving GGUF models locally).

[p0359-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
[p0359-l0003] [10.0pt] What if these reasoning models can’t meet a task’s KPI because they’re too general-­
[p0359-l0004] [10.0pt] purpose? And if we need to tune a model on private, domain-specific data, how do we
[p0359-l0005] [10.0pt] preserve (or add) “thinking” capabilities in the baseline model? The next section walks
[p0359-l0006] [10.0pt] through an end-to-end process for tuning SLMs on custom data with reinforcement
[p0359-l0007] [10.0pt] learning, even with limited compute.
[p0359-l0008] [12.5pt] 15.4	 Building a reasoning domain-specific SLM
[p0359-l0009] [8.0pt] Before tuning
[p0359-l0010] [8.0pt] After tuning
[p0359-l0011] [7.0pt] Question
[p0359-l0012] [7.0pt] Question
[p0359-l0013] [7.0pt] SLM
[p0359-l0014] [7.0pt] "Reasoning" SLM
[p0359-l0015] [7.0pt] Thinking step 1
[p0359-l0016] [7.0pt] Answer
[p0359-l0017] [7.0pt] Thinking step 2
[p0359-l0018] [8.0pt] .
[p0359-l0019] [8.0pt] .
[p0359-l0020] [8.0pt] .
[p0359-l0021] [7.0pt] Thinking step N
[p0359-l0022] [7.0pt] Answer
[p0359-l0023] [8.0pt] Figure 15.3  Inference flow of an SLM before
[p0359-l0024] [8.0pt] GRPO (left) and after (right)
[p0359-l0025] [10.0pt] In the previous sections, we saw TTC
[p0359-l0026] [10.0pt] embedded in large and small language
[p0359-l0027] [10.0pt] models or provided through a third-
[p0359-l0028] [10.0pt] party proxy. In this section, you’ll learn
[p0359-l0029] [10.0pt] how to adapt an SLM to reason over a
[p0359-l0030] [10.0pt] custom domain and dataset. We’ll use
[p0359-l0031] [10.0pt] GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimi­
[p0359-l0032] [10.0pt] zation), a reinforcement learning (RL)
[p0359-l0033] [10.0pt] technique introduced in 2024 by the
[p0359-l0034] [10.0pt] DeepSeek team (https://www.deepseek
[p0359-l0035] [10.0pt] .com/en) in the “DeepSeekMath: Push­
[p0359-l0036] [10.0pt] ing the Limits of Mathematical Reason­
[p0359-l0037] [10.0pt] ing in Open Language Models” paper
[p0359-l0038] [10.0pt] (https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300).
[p0359-l0039] [10.0pt] GRPO is a variant of—and alternative
[p0359-l0040] [10.0pt] to—PPO (Proximal Policy Optimiza­
[p0359-l0041] [10.0pt] tion), which OpenAI uses to train its
[p0359-l0042] [10.0pt] reasoning models. By the end of tuning,
[p0359-l0043] [10.0pt] the model should show TTC capabili­
[p0359-l0044] [10.0pt] ties in the domain-specific subject it was
[p0359-l0045] [10.0pt] trained on (see figure 15.3).
[p0359-l0046] [10.0pt] Training a model with PPO is expen­
[p0359-l0047] [10.0pt] sive. It requires the LLM being trained (the policy model), a frozen copy of the original
[p0359-l0048] [10.0pt] (the reference model), and a value model that estimates long-term reward. Both the pol­
[p0359-l0049] [10.0pt] icy and value models have trainable parameters, so training requires backpropagation
[p0359-l0050] [10.0pt] through both, which consumes substantial memory.
[p0359-l0051] [10.0pt] Because GRPO doesn’t need a value model, it’s easier to optimize and uses much less
[p0359-l0052] [10.0pt] compute (especially GPU VRAM) without sacrificing quality; the model learns by com­
[p0359-l0053] [10.0pt] paring actions and making small, controlled updates. Combined with techniques such
[p0359-l0054] [10.0pt] as LoRA (introduced in chapter 2) and model quantization (introduced in chapter 5
[p0359-l0055] [10.0pt] and used elsewhere in this book), GRPO can even let you specialize an SLM on custom
[p0359-l0056] [10.0pt] data and reasoning tasks with a consumer GPU.
[p0359-l0057] [10.0pt] A companion Colab notebook with the full code for this example is provided; it
[p0359-l0058] [10.0pt] requires hardware acceleration. The baseline model we’ll tune is Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct
[p0359-l0059] [10.0pt] (https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct). In this example, we’ll specialize

=== PDF page 360 / printed label 339 ===
[p0360-l0001] [9.0pt] 339
[p0360-l0002] [9.0pt] Building a reasoning domain-specific SLM
[p0360-l0003] [10.0pt] it on additive manufacturing (3D printing) knowledge using a single GPU with 16 GB
[p0360-l0004] [10.0pt] of VRAM. The dataset focuses on domain-specific 3D printing knowledge, so the final
[p0360-l0005] [10.0pt] model can answer non-trivial questions about the topic using multi-step reasoning.
[p0360-l0006] [10.0pt] These are the main Python libraries we’ll use:
[p0360-l0007] [10.0pt] ¡ TRL—Hugging Face’s TRL (https://github.com/huggingface/trl) for training
[p0360-l0008] [10.0pt] transformer language models with reinforcement learning, including a solid
[p0360-l0009] [10.0pt] implementation of GRPO.
[p0360-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ vLLM—This library (introduced in chapter 11) reduces training time.
[p0360-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ Unsloth—Unsloth (https://github.com/unslothai/unsloth) is an open source
[p0360-l0012] [10.0pt] library that can fine-tune LLMs using up to 70% less memory with no loss in accu­
[p0360-l0013] [10.0pt] racy. Unsloth runs on multiple backends (including vLLM) and on any operating
[p0360-l0014] [10.0pt] system. At the time of writing, Unsloth supports only NVIDIA GPUs and provides
[p0360-l0015] [10.0pt] out-of-the-box support for a limited set of LLM families (Qwen, DeepSeek-R1,
[p0360-l0016] [10.0pt] Gemma, Llama, Phi, Mistral, TinyLlama, SmolLM); check the official GitHub
[p0360-l0017] [10.0pt] repo and documentation for the up-to-date list.
[p0360-l0018] [10.0pt] To complete training in a Colab VM (or any environment) with a single 16 GB GPU,
[p0360-l0019] [10.0pt] we’ll also use QLoRA (4-bit quantization plus LoRA, a PEFT technique introduced in
[p0360-l0020] [10.0pt] chapter 2).
[p0360-l0021] [10.0pt] After installing all dependencies in the training environment, we’ll patch it to enable
[p0360-l0022] [10.0pt] fast RL (GRPO in TRL):
[p0360-l0023] [8.0pt] from unsloth import PatchFastRL
[p0360-l0024] [8.0pt] PatchFastRL("GRPO", FastLanguageModel)
[p0360-l0025] [10.0pt] We can now use Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel class to download a pretrained model
[p0360-l0026] [10.0pt] from the Hugging Face Hub and initialize it:
[p0360-l0027] [8.0pt] from unsloth import FastLanguageModel
[p0360-l0028] [8.0pt] max_seq_length = 2048
[p0360-l0029] [8.0pt] lora_rank = 64
[p0360-l0030] [8.0pt] model_id = "Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct"
[p0360-l0031] [8.0pt] model, tokenizer = FastLanguageModel.from_pretrained(
[p0360-l0032] [8.0pt]     model_name = model_id,
[p0360-l0033] [8.0pt]     max_seq_length = max_seq_length,
[p0360-l0034] [8.0pt]     load_in_4bit = True,
[p0360-l0035] [8.0pt]     fast_inference = True,
[p0360-l0036] [8.0pt]     max_lora_rank = lora_rank,
[p0360-l0037] [8.0pt]     gpu_memory_utilization = 0.5,
[p0360-l0038] [8.0pt] )
[p0360-l0039] [10.0pt] In the preceding code
[p0360-l0040] [10.0pt] ¡ model_name is the ID of the base model on the Hugging Face Hub.
[p0360-l0041] [10.0pt] ¡ max_seq_length sets the maximum number of tokens to generate. Higher values
[p0360-l0042] [10.0pt] allow more thinking steps.

=== PDF page 361 / printed label 340 ===
[p0361-l0001] [9.0pt] 340
[p0361-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
[p0361-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ load_in_4bit, when set to True, specifies that the baseline model is quantized to
[p0361-l0004] [10.0pt] 4-bit.
[p0361-l0005] [10.0pt] ¡ fast_inference, when set to True, enables fast inference with the underlying
[p0361-l0006] [10.0pt] inference engine (vLLM in this case). This makes generation during the RL
[p0361-l0007] [10.0pt] phase about 50% faster.
[p0361-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ max_lora_rank sets the LoRA rank. Higher values can improve model quality but
[p0361-l0009] [10.0pt] slow inference. A rank of 64 is often a good tradeoff between performance and
[p0361-l0010] [10.0pt] memory, though the best setting will depend on your use case.
[p0361-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ gpu_memory_utilization specifies how much GPU memory to reserve for loading
[p0361-l0012] [10.0pt] model weights, leaving the rest for training and related operations. In our exam­
[p0361-l0013] [10.0pt] ple, it’s set to 50%, so QLoRA tuning can run on a large dataset.
[p0361-l0014] [10.0pt] After downloading the model, we can prepare it for PEFT as follows:
[p0361-l0015] [8.0pt] model = FastLanguageModel.get_peft_model(
[p0361-l0016] [8.0pt]     model,
[p0361-l0017] [8.0pt]     r = lora_rank,
[p0361-l0018] [8.0pt]     target_modules = [
[p0361-l0019] [8.0pt]         "q_proj", "k_proj", "v_proj", "o_proj",
[p0361-l0020] [8.0pt]         "gate_proj", "up_proj", "down_proj"
[p0361-l0021] [8.0pt]     ],
[p0361-l0022] [8.0pt]     lora_alpha = lora_rank,
[p0361-l0023] [8.0pt]     use_gradient_checkpointing = "unsloth",
[p0361-l0024] [8.0pt]     random_state = 3407,
[p0361-l0025] [8.0pt] )
[p0361-l0026] [10.0pt] We use FastLanguageModel’s get_peft_model function, specifying the base model, the
[p0361-l0027] [10.0pt] chosen LoRA and LoRA alpha ranks, and the model’s target modules. The target mod­
[p0361-l0028] [10.0pt] ules in the function call are specific to the Qwen 2.x and 3.x models; if you use a differ­
[p0361-l0029] [10.0pt] ent model family, replace them with modules that match that architecture.
[p0361-l0030] [10.0pt] Now we’ll pick a dataset. In this example, we’ll use the Additive Manufacturing Rea­
[p0361-l0031] [10.0pt] soning dataset, available on the Hugging Face Hub (http://huggingface.co/datasets/
[p0361-l0032] [10.0pt] g3lu/addictive_manufacturing_reasoning). It has three columns: question (additive-­
[p0361-l0033] [10.0pt] manufacturing–related questions), answer (answers to the questions), and reason (the
[p0361-l0034] [10.0pt] reasoning used to produce each answer). First, we’ll load the training split:
[p0361-l0035] [8.0pt] split='train'
[p0361-l0036] [8.0pt] data_qa = load_dataset("g3lu/addictive_manufacturing_reasoning",
[p0361-l0037] [10.0pt]         ➥ split=split)
[p0361-l0038] [10.0pt] Next, we’ll indicate the system content template:
[p0361-l0039] [8.0pt] SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
[p0361-l0040] [8.0pt] Respond in the following format:
[p0361-l0041] [8.0pt] <reasoning>
[p0361-l0042] [8.0pt] ...
[p0361-l0043] [8.0pt] </reasoning>

=== PDF page 362 / printed label 341 ===
[p0362-l0001] [9.0pt] 341
[p0362-l0002] [9.0pt] Building a reasoning domain-specific SLM
[p0362-l0003] [8.0pt] <answer>
[p0362-l0004] [8.0pt] ...
[p0362-l0005] [8.0pt] </answer>
[p0362-l0006] [8.0pt] """
[p0362-l0007] [10.0pt] Then we’ll prepare the raw data for training:
[p0362-l0008] [8.0pt] data_qa = data_qa.map(lambda x: {
[p0362-l0009] [8.0pt]         'prompt': [
[p0362-l0010] [8.0pt]             {'role': 'system', 'content': SYSTEM_PROMPT},
[p0362-l0011] [8.0pt]             {
[p0362-l0012] [8.0pt]                 "role": "user",
[p0362-l0013] [8.0pt]                 "content": "You are an expert in additive
[p0362-l0014] [10.0pt]                 ➥manufacturing.\n" +
[p0362-l0015] [8.0pt]                           "\n\nAnswer the following question:\n" +
[p0362-l0016] [8.0pt]                           x['question'] +
[p0362-l0017] [8.0pt]                           " You need to carefully review the
[p0362-l0018] [10.0pt]                           ➥question and reason before answering."
[p0362-l0019] [8.0pt]             },
[p0362-l0020] [8.0pt]         ],
[p0362-l0021] [8.0pt]         'answer': x['answer'],
[p0362-l0022] [8.0pt]         'db_set': 'addictive_manufacturing_reasoning'
[p0362-l0023] [8.0pt]     })
[p0362-l0024] [10.0pt] We use the question column to build the prompts and the answer column as ground
[p0362-l0025] [10.0pt] truth. We’ll drop columns that are unnecessary for training:
[p0362-l0026] [8.0pt] data_qa = data_qa.remove_columns(['question', 'reason'])
[p0362-l0027] [10.0pt] The dataset contains 10,000 samples, but we don’t need all of them for training and
[p0362-l0028] [10.0pt] testing in this example. With an instructed baseline model (more than 1.5 billion
[p0362-l0029] [10.0pt] parameters) and a well-curated training set, we can often get good performance with
[p0362-l0030] [10.0pt] only 200 to 300 samples. To limit the number of samples, we can set the split variable:
[p0362-l0031] [8.0pt] split = "train[0:200]"
[p0362-l0032] [10.0pt] We’ll split the data into training and test sets (10% for testing):
[p0362-l0033] [8.0pt] data_qa = data_qa.shuffle(seed=42)
[p0362-l0034] [8.0pt] train_test_split = data_qa.train_test_split(test_size=0.1)
[p0362-l0035] [8.0pt] train_dataset = train_test_split["train"]
[p0362-l0036] [8.0pt] test_dataset = train_test_split["test"]
[p0362-l0037] [10.0pt] Now that we have the training set, we can move on to the most important part of RL:
[p0362-l0038] [10.0pt] reward engineering. The goal in RL is to learn an optimal policy—a strategy for choos­
[p0362-l0039] [10.0pt] ing an action in a given state—that maximizes cumulative reward. A reward function in
[p0362-l0040] [10.0pt] RL assigns a numeric score to the actions the agent takes; this guides the agent toward
[p0362-l0041] [10.0pt] its goal by encouraging helpful behavior and discouraging unhelpful behavior. In our
[p0362-l0042] [10.0pt] example, we need to implement multiple reward functions that cover the following:

=== PDF page 363 / printed label 342 ===
[p0363-l0001] [9.0pt] 342
[p0363-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
[p0363-l0003] [10.0pt] ¡ Correctness—The answers must match the ground truth.
[p0363-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Formatting—Reasoning traces (records of the model’s reasoning steps) must fol­
[p0363-l0005] [10.0pt] low the specified XML-like format, as shown in the training-set preparation code.
[p0363-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Intermediate validation—The intermediate answers must also be valid.
[p0363-l0007] [10.0pt] We’re aiming not only for accuracy in the specific domain, additive manufacturing,
[p0363-l0008] [10.0pt] but also for clear intermediate steps and final answers. The Colab notebook imple­
[p0363-l0009] [10.0pt] ments several reward functions:
[p0363-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ correctness_reward_func—Assigns a reward based on final-answer correctness
[p0363-l0011] [10.0pt] ¡ xmlcount_reward_func—Assigns a reward for properly XML-formatted answers
[p0363-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ soft_format_reward_func—Assigns a reward based on how closely the response
[p0363-l0013] [10.0pt] formatting matches the expected format
[p0363-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ strict_format_reward_func—Assigns a reward based on strictly matching the
[p0363-l0015] [10.0pt] expected response format
[p0363-l0016] [10.0pt] We’re almost ready to start training, but first we need to set a training configuration.
[p0363-l0017] [10.0pt] We’ll use TRL’s GRPO-specific GRPOConfig to set vLLM as the backend, the maximum
[p0363-l0018] [10.0pt] prompt and completion lengths, the number of training steps, the checkpoint save
[p0363-l0019] [10.0pt] frequency, whether to keep results and checkpoints locally, and the output directory
[p0363-l0020] [10.0pt] for the experiment:
[p0363-l0021] [8.0pt] from trl import GRPOConfig
[p0363-l0022] [8.0pt] training_args = GRPOConfig(
[p0363-l0023] [8.0pt]     use_vllm = True,
[p0363-l0024] [8.0pt]     learning_rate = 5e-6,
[p0363-l0025] [8.0pt]     adam_beta1 = 0.9,
[p0363-l0026] [8.0pt]     adam_beta2 = 0.99,
[p0363-l0027] [8.0pt]     weight_decay = 0.1,
[p0363-l0028] [8.0pt]     warmup_ratio = 0.1,
[p0363-l0029] [8.0pt]     lr_scheduler_type = "cosine",
[p0363-l0030] [8.0pt]     optim = "adamw_8bit",
[p0363-l0031] [8.0pt]     logging_steps = 1,
[p0363-l0032] [8.0pt]     bf16 = is_bfloat16_supported(),
[p0363-l0033] [8.0pt]     fp16 = not is_bfloat16_supported(),
[p0363-l0034] [8.0pt]     per_device_train_batch_size = 1,
[p0363-l0035] [8.0pt]     gradient_accumulation_steps = 1,
[p0363-l0036] [8.0pt]     num_generations = 6,
[p0363-l0037] [8.0pt]     max_prompt_length = 1024,
[p0363-l0038] [8.0pt]     max_completion_length = 1024,
[p0363-l0039] [8.0pt]     max_steps = 200,
[p0363-l0040] [8.0pt]     save_steps = 10,
[p0363-l0041] [8.0pt]     max_grad_norm = 0.1,
[p0363-l0042] [8.0pt]     report_to = "none",
[p0363-l0043] [8.0pt]     output_dir = "outputs",
[p0363-l0044] [8.0pt] )

[p0364-l0001] [9.0pt] 343
[p0364-l0002] [9.0pt] Building a reasoning domain-specific SLM
[p0364-l0003] [10.0pt] The values of the model’s hyperparameters depend on the architecture and training
[p0364-l0004] [10.0pt] set. We’ll train the model with TRL’s GRPOTrainer, providing the model, tokenizer,
[p0364-l0005] [10.0pt] training and test datasets, the GRPO training configuration defined earlier, and our
[p0364-l0006] [10.0pt] custom reward functions:
[p0364-l0007] [8.0pt] from trl import GRPOTrainer
[p0364-l0008] [8.0pt] trainer = GRPOTrainer(
[p0364-l0009] [8.0pt]     model = model,
[p0364-l0010] [8.0pt]     processing_class = tokenizer,
[p0364-l0011] [8.0pt]     reward_funcs = [
[p0364-l0012] [8.0pt]         xmlcount_reward_func,
[p0364-l0013] [8.0pt]         soft_format_reward_func,
[p0364-l0014] [8.0pt]         strict_format_reward_func,
[p0364-l0015] [8.0pt]         correctness_reward_func,
[p0364-l0016] [8.0pt]     ],
[p0364-l0017] [8.0pt]     args = training_args,
[p0364-l0018] [8.0pt]     train_dataset = train_dataset,
[p0364-l0019] [8.0pt]     eval_dataset=test_dataset,
[p0364-l0020] [8.0pt] )
[p0364-l0021] [10.0pt] We can start the training by calling the trainer class’s train method:
[p0364-l0022] [8.0pt] trainer.train()
[p0364-l0023] [10.0pt] We can tell whether the training is on track by watching the stats printed to standard
[p0364-l0024] [10.0pt] output. If the combined reward increases after about a dozen steps, we’re headed in
[p0364-l0025] [10.0pt] the right direction.
[p0364-l0026] [10.0pt] Once the training is completed, we can save the LoRA weights to disk:
[p0364-l0027] [8.0pt] model.save_lora("grpo_saved_lora")
[p0364-l0028] [10.0pt] Then we can evaluate the model on unseen samples from the original dataset. Given
[p0364-l0029] [10.0pt] the following prompt (question), after tokenizing it
[p0364-l0030] [8.0pt] test_prompt = """
[p0364-l0031] [8.0pt] What strategies can be employed to balance the need for simplification
[p0364-l0032] [8.0pt] in simulation models with the preservation of critical geometric features,

[p0364-l0034] [8.0pt] of additive manufacturing designs and significantly impact
[p0364-l0035] [8.0pt] the product's performance, while also considering the limitations imposed
[p0364-l0036] [8.0pt] by computational resources and the potential for introducing significant
[p0364-l0037] [8.0pt]  errors in the results?
[p0364-l0038] [8.0pt] """

[p0364-l0042] [8.0pt]       ], tokenize = False, add_generation_prompt = True)

[p0365-l0017] [9.5pt] 	 <reasoning>
[p0365-l0018] [9.5pt] To balance the need for simplification in simulation models with the preservation
[p0365-l0019] [9.5pt] of critical geometric features, a multi-faceted approach is required. Here are some
[p0365-l0020] [9.5pt] strategies that can be employed:
[p0365-l0021] [9.5pt] 1	 Simplification Criteria: Establish clear criteria for simplification based on the simu­
[p0365-l0022] [9.5pt] lation’s goals and the importance of geometric features. For example, critical fea­
[p0365-l0023] [9.5pt] tures can be identified for preservation, while non-critical features can be simpli­
[p0365-l0024] [9.5pt] fied or omitted.
[p0365-l0025] [9.5pt] 2	 Feature Preserving Simplification: Use techniques like feature-preserving simplifi­
[p0365-l0026] [9.5pt] cation methods that maintain the integrity of critical features during simplification.
[p0365-l0027] [9.5pt] These methods involve identifying the most important features and simplifying the
[p0365-l0028] [9.5pt] rest while preserving the essential shape and properties.
[p0365-l0029] [9.5pt] 3	 Error Analysis: Perform a thorough error analysis to quantify the impact of sim­
[p0365-l0030] [9.5pt] plification on the simulation results. This will help in understanding the trade-off
[p0365-l0031] [9.5pt] between simplification and accuracy. If errors are significant, further simplification
[p0365-l0032] [9.5pt] or refinement may be necessary.
[p0365-l0033] [9.5pt] 4	 Adaptive Simplification: Implement an adaptive simplification approach that
[p0365-l0034] [9.5pt] dynamically adjusts the level of detail based on the simulation results. This
[p0365-l0035] [9.5pt] can help ensure that the most critical geometric features are preserved while
[p0365-l0036] [9.5pt] minimizing computational resources.
[p0365-l0037] [9.5pt] 5	 Incremental Simplification: Start with a detailed simulation and gradually simplify
[p0365-l0038] [9.5pt] it. This allows for a systematic approach to simplification and helps in identifying
[p0365-l0039] [9.5pt] which features are truly essential and which can be simplified without significant
[p0365-l0040] [9.5pt] impact on the results.
[p0365-l0041] [9.5pt] 6	 Use of Simplified Models for Early Stages: For early stages of simulation and de­
[p0365-l0042] [9.5pt] sign, simplified models can be used to quickly assess the feasibility and perfor­
[p0365-l0043] [9.5pt] mance of a design. Detailed models can then be used for more critical stages.
[p0365-l0044] [9.5pt] 7	 Validate Simplified Models: Validate the simplified models against detailed models
[p0365-l0045] [9.5pt] to ensure that the simplified version can accurately predict the performance of the
[p0365-l0046] [9.5pt] design. This can help in determining the appropriateness of the simplification.

[p0366-l0011] [9.5pt] gy based on new developments in additive manufacturing and computational mod­
[p0366-l0012] [9.5pt] eling techniques. This ensures that the approach remains effective and up-to-date.
[p0366-l0013] [9.5pt] ...
[p0366-l0014] [9.5pt] </reasoning>
[p0366-l0015] [9.5pt] <answer>
[p0366-l0016] [9.5pt] Strategies to balance the need for simplification in simulation models with the pres­

[p0366-l0018] [9.5pt] 1	 Establishing clear simplification criteria based on simulation goals and importance
[p0366-l0019] [9.5pt] of features.
[p0366-l0020] [9.5pt] 2	 Using feature-preserving simplification methods.
[p0366-l0021] [9.5pt] 3	 Performing error analysis to understand trade-offs between simplification and
[p0366-l0022] [9.5pt] accuracy.
[p0366-l0023] [9.5pt] 4	 Implementing adaptive simplification.
[p0366-l0024] [9.5pt] 5	 Employing incremental simplification techniques.
[p0366-l0025] [9.5pt] 6	 Using simplified models in early stages.
[p0366-l0026] [9.5pt] 7	 Validating simplified models against detailed models.
[p0366-l0027] [9.5pt] 8	 Leveraging advanced computational tools and hardware.
[p0366-l0028] [9.5pt] 9	 Collaborating with experts in additive manufacturing and simulation.
[p0366-l0029] [9.5pt] 10	 Regularly reviewing and updating the simplification strategy.
[p0366-l0030] [9.5pt] These strategies can help ensure that critical geometric features are preserved while
[p0366-l0031] [9.5pt] the model remains computationally feasible and accurately predicts the performance
[p0366-l0032] [9.5pt] of the design.

[p0367-l0001] [9.0pt] 346
[p0367-l0002] [9.0pt] Chapter 15  Test-time compute and small language models
[p0367-l0003] [12.5pt] Summary
[p0367-l0004] [10.0pt] ¡ Test-time compute refers to computational resources used during inference
[p0367-l0005] [10.0pt] when models are exploring multiple solutions before producing final answers.
[p0367-l0006] [10.0pt] ¡ Test-time compute lets models use search methods like beam search or tree-
[p0367-l0007] [10.0pt] based exploration to find optimal solutions within compute limits.
[p0367-l0008] [10.0pt] ¡ Commercial models from OpenAI and Anthropic use test-time compute to gen­
[p0367-l0009] [10.0pt] erate and score multiple candidate outputs before replying.
[p0367-l0010] [10.0pt] ¡ Test-time compute improves accuracy on complex tasks such as math, logic, and
[p0367-l0011] [10.0pt] coding, but it requires more computation.
[p0367-l0012] [10.0pt] ¡ OptiLLM provides an OpenAI API–compatible inference proxy that adds state-
[p0367-l0013] [10.0pt] of-the-art reasoning techniques to existing models.
[p0367-l0014] [10.0pt] ¡ OptiLLM supports commercial APIs and local inference using Hugging Face
[p0367-l0015] [10.0pt] models and LoRA weights.
[p0367-l0016] [10.0pt] ¡ OptiLLM uses techniques such as Chain-of-Thought reflection, PlanSearch,
[p0367-l0017] [10.0pt] Self-Consistency, and Monte Carlo Tree Search to improve reasoning.
[p0367-l0018] [10.0pt] ¡ AutoThink combines query-complexity classification with steering-vector guid­
[p0367-l0019] [10.0pt] ance to set an appropriate reasoning budget for each query.
[p0367-l0020] [10.0pt] ¡ AutoThink preprocesses data to identify pivotal tokens and train classifiers and
[p0367-l0021] [10.0pt] then applies control vectors during inference.
[p0367-l0022] [10.0pt] ¡ Qwen3, DeepSeek-R1, Phi-4, Open R1, and Marco-o1 are open source small lan­
[p0367-l0023] [10.0pt] guage models (SLMs) with test-time compute capabilities.
[p0367-l0024] [10.0pt] ¡ GRPO is a reinforcement learning (RL) technique that, unlike PPO, eliminates
[p0367-l0025] [10.0pt] the need for a value model, reducing compute requirements.
[p0367-l0026] [10.0pt] ¡ GRPO trains reasoning capabilities on domain-specific data using far less GPU
[p0367-l0027] [10.0pt] memory than traditional methods.
[p0367-l0028] [10.0pt] ¡ The Unsloth library cuts fine-tuning memory use by up to 70% while maintain­
[p0367-l0029] [10.0pt] ing accuracy and supporting multiple backends.
[p0367-l0030] [10.0pt] ¡ Unsloth’s FastLanguageModel enables 4-bit quantization with LoRA for efficient
[p0367-l0031] [10.0pt] training on consumer GPUs.
[p0367-l0032] [10.0pt] ¡ GRPO training requires multiple reward functions for correctness, formatting,
[p0367-l0033] [10.0pt] and intermediate output validation.
[p0367-l0034] [10.0pt] ¡ GRPOConfig and GRPOTrainer in the TRL library provide complete implementa­
[p0367-l0035] [10.0pt] tions of GRPO reinforcement learning.
[p0367-l0036] [10.0pt] ¡ Domain-specific reasoning models can be created by fine-tuning base models on
[p0367-l0037] [10.0pt] specialized datasets with GRPO and custom reward functions.
[p0367-l0038] [10.0pt] ¡ Integrating vLLM with GRPO training speeds up RL generation by about 50%.
[p0367-l0039] [10.0pt] ¡ Custom reward functions evaluate answer correctness, XML formatting compli­
[p0367-l0040] [10.0pt] ance, and adherence to the required response structure.
